Exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿He created man from a drop of fluid, and behold, he is an open adversary.﴾ ﴿And the cattle, He created them for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat.﴾ ﴿And in them is beauty for you when you bring them home at evening and when you drive them out to pasture.﴾ ﴿And they carry your loads to a land you could not reach except with great hardship to yourselves. Indeed your Lord is Kind and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And horses, mules and donkeys, for you to ride and as adornment. And He creates what you do not know.﴾ ﴿And upon God rests the direction of the path, and some paths deviate. Had He willed, He would have guided you all.﴾

Al-Hasan, ʿAta', ʿIkrimah and Jabir said: all of it is Makki. Ibn ʿAbbas said: except three verses of it, which were revealed in Medina after Hamzah, namely His saying: ﴿And do not sell the covenant of God for a small price…﴾ [al-Nahl: 95] up to His saying: ﴿…for the best of what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl: 97]. It was also said: except three verses: ﴿And if you punish, punish with the like…﴾ [al-Nahl: 126], which was revealed in Medina concerning the mutilation of Hamzah and the slain of Uhud; His saying: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is only by God﴾ [al-Nahl: 127]; and His saying: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated…﴾ [al-Nahl: 110]. It was also said: from its beginning up to His saying ﴿(what they associate)﴾ is Madani (revealed in Medina), and the rest is Makki. From Qatadah the opposite is reported.

As for its connection with what precedes it: when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 92], this was a reminder of their gathering on the Day of Resurrection and their being questioned about what they committed in the life of this world. So it was said: ﴿The command of God has come﴾, meaning, according to the majority, the Day of Resurrection. Ibn ʿAbbas reported that the "command" means the victory of the Messenger of God and his dominance over the disbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari said: they used to seek to hasten what they were promised of the coming of the Hour, or of the descent of punishment upon them on the day of Badr, mocking and denying the promise. Ibn Jurayj, who said this second view, said: the "command" here is what God promised His Prophet of victory, his triumph over his enemies, his vengeance upon them by killing, taking captives, plundering their wealth, and seizing their homes and dwellings. Al-Dahhak said: the "command" here is a verbal noun from amara, and what is meant is His obligations and rulings. It was said: this is far-fetched, since it is not reported that any of the Companions sought to hasten obligations before they were imposed upon them. Al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj also said: the "command" is God's punishment upon those who persist in polytheism and in denying the Messenger, and seeking to hasten punishment is reported of many of the disbelievers of Quraysh and others. Close to this view is that of al-Zajjaj: it is what He promised them of requital for their disbelief. It was also said: the "command" is some of the portents of the Hour.

As for ﴿has come﴾ (atā): it was said it remains in its past sense, and the meaning is: the command of God has come as a promise, so do not seek to hasten its occurrence. It was said: the command of God has come, meaning its beginnings and signs have come. It was also said: He used the past tense for the future because its occurrence is near and certain, and in this there is a warning to the disbelievers.

The majority read ﴿tastaʿjilūhu﴾ (do not seek to hasten it) with the tā' as a second-person address, which is either addressed to the believers or to the disbelievers, meaning: say to them, do not hasten it. God said: ﴿They seek to hasten it, those who do not believe in it﴾ [al-Shura: 18]. Ibn Jubayr read it with the yā' as a prohibition to the disbelievers. The apparent reference of the pronoun in ﴿fa-lā tastaʿjilūhu﴾ is to the command, since it is what is being spoken of. It was also said it refers to God, meaning: do not seek to hasten God with the punishment, or with the coming of the Day of Resurrection, as in His saying: ﴿And they seek from you to hasten the punishment﴾ [al-Hajj: 47].

Hamzah and al-Kisai read ﴿tushrikūna﴾ with the tā' of address. The rest of the seven, al-Aʿraj, his father Jaʿfar, Ibn Waddah, Abu Rajaʾ and al-Hasan read it with the yā'. ʿIsa read the first with tā' from above, and the second with both yā' and tā' from above; al-Aʿmash, Abu al-ʿAliyah, Talhah, Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman, Ibn Thabit, and al-Jahdari read it so. The word ﴿ma﴾ may be a relative pronoun (meaning "what") or a verbal (masdariyyah) particle. The best reading of "what they associate" is in view of their hastening, because their hastening is mockery and denial, and that is a form of associating partners.

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read ﴿yunzilu﴾ (He sends down) without the doubled letter, while the rest of the seven read it with the doubled letter. Zayd ibn ʿAli, al-Aʿmash and Abu Bakr read ﴿tunazzalu﴾ with the doubled letter in the passive voice, with ﴿al-malāʾikatu﴾ (the angels) in the nominative. Al-Jahdari did likewise, except that he did not double it. Al-Hasan, Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Aʿraj, al-Mufaddal from ʿAsim and Yaʿqub read it with a fatha on the tā' and doubled, in the active voice. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read ﴿mā nunazzilu﴾ with the nūn of majesty and doubling, and Qatadah with the nūn without doubling. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: in both of them there is much irregularity. Their irregularity is that what precedes and follows them is a third-person pronoun, and its justification is that it is an iltifat (a shift of grammatical person).

The angels here are Gabriel alone, as the majority said, or the angels referred to in His saying: ﴿And those who pull out violently﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 1]. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the Spirit is the revelation which the angels bring down upon the prophets, and its parallel is: ﴿He casts the Spirit by His command upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾ [Ghafir: 15]. Al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas said: it is the Qur'an, and from this is: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a Spirit of Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. Mujahid said: what is meant by the Spirit is the spirits of creation, and no angel descends except with a spirit with him. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the Spirit is mercy. Al-Zajjaj said, in substance: the Spirit is guidance, because hearts are given life by it, just as bodies are given life by spirits. It was said: the Spirit is Gabriel, and this is indicated by: ﴿The trustworthy Spirit brought it down﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 193]. The bāʾ (with) is then one of accompaniment, meaning: connected with the Spirit. It was said: it means maʿa (with). It was also said: the Spirit is guardians over the angels whom the angels do not see, just as the angels are guardians over us whom we do not see. Mujahid also said: the Spirit is the name of an angel, and from this is: ﴿On the day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows﴾ [al-Naba': 38]. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that the Spirit is a creation of God's creation, like the forms of the sons of Adam, and no angel descends from the heaven without one of them with him. Ibn Jurayj said similarly. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: this is a weak view, for no chain of transmission supports it.

Notes on the lexical discussion in this passage:

Al-nutfah: a drop of water; one says nataba his head with water, meaning it dripped.

Al-difʾ: a name for what one is warmed with, that is, what is heated. The Arabs say: dafiʾa yawmuna, so it is dafiʾ (warm), when there is heat in it which removes cold. Dafiʾa al-rajulu difāʾan and dafaʾan (the man became warm). The plural of difʾ is adfāʾ. A man is dafʾān and a woman is dafʾā. The daffiʾah is a herd of camels with abundant wool, because some of them warm others with their breath. It is also said with doubling. From al-Asmaʿi: the daffiʾah is one with abundant wool and fat. Al-Jawhari said: difʾ is the offspring of camels, their milk, and what benefit is derived from them.

Al-baghl: well known. ʿAmr ibn Bahr al-Jahiz has a book titled Kitab al-Bighal (The Book of Mules).

Al-himār: well known, its plural in the paucity form is ahmur, and in the abundance form is ḥumur, which is the regular form, and also ḥamīr.

Al-ṭariyy: a faʿīl form from ṭarra and yaṭurru, and ṭarāwah, like sarra and yasurru, sarāwah. Al-Farraʾ said: ṭaria yaṭri ṭirāʾan and ṭarāwah, like shaqiya yashqā shaqāʾan and shaqāwah.

Al-makhr: the splitting of water to the right and left; one says makhara al-māʾ al-arḍ (the water cut through the earth). Al-Farraʾ said: it is the sound of ships running with the winds. It was said: it is the sound made by the blowing of the wind when it grows strong, and it may also come from a ship and the like.

Māda: moved and turned.

Al-saqf: well known; its plural is sufuf, which is the regular form, and also sufuf and saqaf. The patterns fuʿul and faʿal are preserved for faʿl, and they are not regular in it.

* *

[p. 472]

Zamakhshari said: "*bil-ruh min amrihi*" means: by the Spirit of His command, through which dead hearts, dead through ignorance, are brought to life, namely His revelation, or that which takes the place in religion that the spirit takes in the body; end of quote. The *min* (مِن) is either partitive (*lil-tab'id*) or explanatory of the kind (*li-bayan al-jins*). "Whom He wills" refers to the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace. The *an* (أنْ) is a verbal (*masdariyyah*) particle, the kind that governs the imperfect verb (*mudari'*). It is joined to the imperative as in the expression "I wrote to him *bi-an qum*" ("that you rise"), and it is in apposition (*badal*) to "the Spirit." Alternatively, the preposition has been dropped and it reads "*bi-an andhiru*" ("that you warn"), and then the disagreement arises over whether it occupies a position of accusative (*nasb*) or genitive (*khafd*) in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis).

Zamakhshari said: "*(wa-an andhiru)* is in apposition to the Spirit, meaning: We send them down with *an andhiru*, and its estimate is: *andhiru*, i.e., *bi-anna al-sha'n aqulu lakum andhiru*" ("that the matter is: I say to you, warn"), "*annahu la ilaha illa ana*" ("that there is no god but I"); end of quote. Thus he made it the lightened form (*al-mukhaffafah*) of the heavy *inna*, its noun omitted as a pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*), and he estimated an omitted verb of saying, so that the predicate becomes a declarative clause, namely "I say." There is no need for this strain when it can easily be the second *an* (*al-thaniyyah*), the one that governs the imperfect verb. Ibn 'Atiyyah, Abu al-Baqa', and the author of al-Ghunyan permitted that it be the explanatory *an* (*mufassirah*), in which case it has no place in i'rab. This is because sending down with revelation contains the meaning of saying, i.e., "inform the people," from *nadhartu bi-kadhā* when I informed him of such. Zamakhshari said: "The meaning is that He says to them: Inform the people of My saying, *la ilaha illa ana, fa-ttaquni*" ("there is no god but I, so fear Me"); end of quote. When he made *an* the one from which the pronoun of the matter is omitted, he estimated this estimate, namely "He says to them: inform."

It was recited *li-yundhiru annahu* ("that He may warn that..."). Warning is appropriate here even though the wording contains nothing frightening, because the warners were disbelievers in His divinity, so within their command there is a place of fear, and within the report of His oneness is a prohibition against what they were upon, and a threat and warning against worshipping idols. The meaning of *fa-ttaquni* is: fear My punishment by your taking a god other than Me. The narration follows the sense in His saying *illa ana* ("but I"). Had it followed the wording, it would have been *la ilaha illa Allah* ("there is no god but God"). Both are permissible. Narration following the sense is more eloquent here, since in it the ruling is attributed to the speaking pronoun who sends down the angels. Then He indicated His oneness, and that there is no god but Him, by what He mentioned of creating the heavens and the earth, which no one else can do, and they acknowledge that He, exalted is He, is their Creator.

"*Bil-haqq*" means: by what is due and fitting, because these indicate attributes that entitle the one who possesses them to create and originate: life, knowledge, power, and will. This is unlike their partners, to whom none of that is due.

Al-A'mash recited *fa-ta'ala* with an added *fa'* (*fa-ta'ala*). This sentence serves to alert to the exaltation of God, Who originated this upper world and this lower world, above having a partner taken with Him in worship.

When He mentioned what indicates His oneness through the creation of the upper world and the earth, which is inference from the external, He mentioned inference from the human being himself, mentioning his creation from a drop of semen, and then he is a clear adversary. It was his duty and obligation to obey and submit to God's command.

*Khasim* (خَصِيمٌ, adversary) is among the intensive forms, from *khasama* in the sense of *ikhtasama* (to dispute), or in the sense of *mukhasim*, like *khalit* and *jalis*. *Mubin* means the one manifest in contention or the one who makes it manifest. The apparent point is that the context of these two descriptions is one of blame, for what preceded in His saying: "Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate" and His saying "that warn" and the verse. This is also due to the repetition of "and exalted is He above what they associate," and to His saying in Ya-Sin: "Does not man see" (Ya-Sin 36:77) and the verse, and He said: "Rather, they are a contentious people" (al-Zukhruf 43:58), meaning by it their disputing with the prophets of God and His friends with feeble proofs. The human being is mentioned most in the Qur'an in the context of blame, or followed by blame.

It was said: the intended meaning of the human being here is Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi. Others said: the context of the two descriptions is one of praise, because He, exalted is He, strengthened him to contend against adversaries, made him one who distinguishes truth from falsehood, and raised him from that inanimate state, which is being a drop of semen, to the lofty, noble state, which is the state of speech and clear expression. Here *idha* (إذْ) is for suddenness (*lil-mufaja'ah*), and after his creation from the drop, the sudden address did not occur except after states through which he developed; those states are omitted, and the suddenness occurs after them.

* *

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: Know that the noblest of bodies after the spheres and the stars is the human being. Then he mentioned the human being and that he is composed of a body and a soul, in a great discourse that is examined in his tafsir. We do not accept what he mentioned, that the spheres and stars are nobler than the human being.

When He mentioned the creation of the human being, He mentioned what He bestowed upon him as a favor for the sustenance of his livelihood. He first mentioned the most beneficial and most necessary of them for those to whom the Qur'an was revealed in their language, and that is the livestock (*al-an'am*), whose explanation has preceded in al-An'am. The more apparent view is that "*lakum fiha dif'un*" ("for you in them is warmth") is a resumptive statement (*istinaf*) to mention what benefit is derived from them in respect of themselves. *Dif'un* (دِفْءٌ) is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is "*lakum*" ("for you"), and "*fiha*" ("in them") is connected to the sense of settledness contained in "*lakum*." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "*fiha*" be a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) of *dif'un*, since if it were delayed it would be a qualifier (*sifah*). He also permitted that "*lakum*" be a circumstantial accusative of *dif'un*, with "*fiha*" as the predicate, but this is not permissible, because when the governing element of the circumstantial accusative is a meaning, it is not permissible to place it before the entire sentence; one may not say: "standing in the house is Zayd." If the circumstantial accusative is delayed after the whole sentence, it is permissible without disagreement; if it is placed in the middle, al-Akhfash permitted it, but the majority prohibited it. He also permitted that *dif'un* be raised by *lakum*, or that *lakum* qualify it with the definite article, and the whole sentence be a circumstantial accusative of the pronoun in the accusative position; end of quote. But it is not called a sentence, because the estimate is: "He created them for you, in them is warmth," or "He created them for you, being in them warmth," and this is of the category of the singular, not of the category of the sentence. They also permitted that "*lakum*" be connected to "*khalaqaha*" (He created them), and "*fiha dif'un*" be a resumptive statement mentioning the benefits of livestock.

What supports "*lakum fiha dif'un*" being a resumptive statement is that it is contrasted with His saying: "*wa-lakum fiha jamal*" ("and for you in them is beauty"). Thus He contrasted the necessary benefit with the non-necessary benefit.

(p-475) Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-dif'* is the offspring of every thing, and al-Umawi mentioned it from the dialect of some Arabs. The more apparent view is that "*wal-an'am*" ("and the livestock") is in the accusative by the construction of the verb being omitted (*al-ishtighal*), and what made the accusative preferable is that a verbal sentence preceded it. This is supported by the reading that has *al-an'am* in the nominative in an irregular recitation. Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is permissible that it be in apposition as an explanation (*'ataf 'ala al-bayan*), and in this case "*lakum*" would be a resumptive statement, or connected to "*khalaqaha*."

Al-Zuhri and Abu Ja'far recited *duff* with a *damma* on the *fa'*, its doubling, and its tanwin. The reasoning is that he transferred the vowel from the hamza to the *fa'* after deleting it, then doubled the *fa'*, treating the connected speech as if it were pausal, since it is permissible to double it in pause. Zayd ibn 'Ali recited *duf* with the transfer of the vowel and the deletion of the hamza without doubling the *fa'*. The owner of al-Lawami (*sahib al-lawami'*) said: al-Zuhri (recited) *duff* with a *damma* on the *fa'* without hamza, and the *fa'* is vocalized with the vowel of the deleted hamza. Some of them compensate for this hamza by doubling the *fa'*, and this is one of the two modes of Hamza ibn Habib in pause.

Mujahid said: the benefits of riding are carrying loads, milk, ghee, sprinkling upon them, and other things. He singled out the benefit of eating by mention, as He singled out the benefit of warmth, because these two are among the greatest benefits.

Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): the fronting of the adverbial phrase in His saying "*wa-minha ta'kulun*" ("and from them you eat") indicates exclusivity, while one may eat from other than them. (I answer): eating from them is the primary thing on which people rely for their livelihoods, while eating from other than them, such as chickens, ducks, and game of land and sea, is like what is not considered significant, and is like what is done for enjoyment. What he said about this, that the fronting of the adverbial phrase or the object indicates exclusivity, we have already refuted in His saying: "*iyyaka na'budu*" ("You alone we worship," al-Fatihah 1:5). The more apparent view is that "*min*" is partitive, as when you say: "when you eat of the loaf." Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that your sustenance is from them, because you plough with cattle, and the grain and fruits that you eat come from them, and you earn by hiring out camels, and you sell their offspring, their milk, and their hides; end of quote. In that case the partitive would be figurative, or *min* would be causal (*lil-sabab*).

*Al-jamal* (الجَمالُ) is the verbal noun of *jamula* with a *damma* on the *mim*. A man is *jamil*, a woman is *jamilah* and *jam'a'*, according to al-Kisa'i, who recited:

*She is a full-moon beauty, like a rising full moon,*
*She has surpassed all creation in beauty.*

Al-jamal is used to mean embellishment (*al-tajammul*), as if it were a verbal noun with the extra letters dropped. Beauty may be in form, through the goodness of composition that the eye perceives and that casts into hearts, so the soul clings to it without knowing why. In character, through its containing praiseworthy qualities such as knowledge, chastity, and forbearance; and in deeds, through their being suited to the interests of creatures, bringing benefit to them and averting harm from them. The beauty that we have in livestock is outside these three categories, and the meaning is that for us in them is beauty and grandeur in the eyes of people through owning them, and their indicating the happiness of the human being in this world, and his being among the people of abundance. So God, exalted is He, bestowed as a favor the embellishment with them, as He bestowed the favor of necessary benefit, because embellishment with them is among the aims of the owners of herds and the pride of their people, and the Arabs take pride in that. Do you not see the poet's saying:

*By my life, there are people among whom I have seen yesterday*
*Pens for the mares and the thick herd,*

*Dearer to us than people in a valley*
*Over whose flocks the leopard prowls.*

And the ʿakarah of camels is the herd between sixty and seventy, and its plural is ʿakar. And al-dathr means "the abundant." It is said: "He brought the livestock home" (arāḥa al-māshiyah), meaning he returned them in the evening from the pasture. And "sarahahā yasrahuhā sarḥan and surūḥan" means he drove them out in the morning to the pasture. And "sarahat" (they went out) can be transitive and intransitive. This mostly happens in the spring, when the rain falls, the grass grows tall, and they go out for the pasturing trip (al-nujʿah).

He placed the bringing home (al-ʾirāḥah) before the driving out (al-sarḥ) because the beauty of the camels is more evident in it, when they come back full-bellied with udders swollen, and then they take shelter in the pens (al-ḥaẓāʾir). This is unlike the time of their driving out, although in both times they adorn the courtyards, and the bellowing and bleating echo in them, so that their people feel at ease, their owners rejoice, and they make them honoured in the eyes of those who look at them. They bring them standing and esteem. This is in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾ [al-Kahf: 46], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Adorned for mankind is the love of desires﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 14]. Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿and the cattle and the tilth﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 14].

ʿIkrimah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Jaḥdarī read ḥīnan in both places with tanwīn (nunation) and with the idāfah (genitive construction) broken. They made the two clauses adjectives from which the returning pronoun (al-ʿāʾid) has been omitted, as in His saying: ﴿and fear a day when no soul will avail another﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48]. In this case the governing element (al-ʿāmil) in ḥīnan is either the subject (al-mubtadaʾ), because it carries the sense of adornment (al-tajammul), or its predicate (khabar) by virtue of the sense of settledness (al-istiqrār) in it. Al-athqāl are the goods (al-amtiʿah), whose singular is thiql. It is said they are the bodies, according to His saying: ﴿and the earth brings forth its burdens﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 2], meaning the bodies of the children of Adam.

His saying "to a land" (ilā baladin) does not intend a specific one; that is, to a distant land toward which you set out for your purposes. It is also said that what is intended is a specific one, which is Makkah, as said by Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas. It is also said it is the city of the Messenger (Madinah), and it is said Egypt (Miṣr). These sayings should be understood as examples and not as the intended meaning, since the favour is not restricted to carrying them to those places.

"Lam takūnū bālighīhi" (you would not have reached it) is an attribute of the land. It is possible that the implied sense is "with them" (the camels), and this indicates the remoteness of the land, and that even with the help of the camels in carrying the loads, you would not reach it except with hardship. Or the implied sense is: you would not reach it by yourselves without them, except with hardship, so that you would have to carry your loads on your backs.

Al-Jumhūr read bi-shiqq with the shīn kasrah (kasrah on the shīn). Mujāhid, al-Aʿraj, Abū Jaʿfar, ʿUmar ibn Maymūn and Ibn Arqam read it with fatḥah. It is also narrated from Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr. Both are verbal nouns (maṣdarān) whose meaning is hardship. It is said: al-shaqq with fatḥah is the verbal noun, and with kasrah is the noun, meaning hardship. The poet said with the kasrah:

*And a possessor of camels who travels and counts them for himself,*
*a brother of weariness and fatigue from their hardship.*

That is, from their hardship. The shiqq of a thing is its half, and al-Farrāʾ interpreted it here this way, meaning: they both carry away half of the souls, as if they had melted from fatigue and exhaustion, just as you say: "You cannot do such-and-such except by losing most of your soul, and a piece of your liver," and similar metaphor. One says: "I took the shiqq of the sheep," meaning its half. Al-shiqq also means the side, and al-akh al-shaqīq is the full brother, and Shaqq is the name of a soothsayer.

The mention of this favour of carrying the loads is fittingly concluded with the attribute of kindness (raʾfah) and mercy (raḥmah), because from His kindness is the facilitation of these benefits and the subjugation of the cattle for you. When He mentioned His favours through the cattle and their essential benefits, He then mentioned the favour of the benefits of animals that are not essential. Al-Jumhūr read "wa-l-khayl" (and the horses) and what is conjoined to it in the accusative, as a conjunction to "wa-l-anʿām" (and the cattle). Ibn Abī ʿAblah read it in the nominative.

Since riding is the greatest of their benefits, it was singled out for mention, and this does not indicate that it is not permitted for all horses, contrary to those who argued from it. And "wa-zīnatan" (and as an adornment) is in the accusative, and it was not with the lām (li-); the verb reached "riding" through the intermediary of the preposition. Both are objects of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi), because the sense is: He created them, and riding is an attribute of the created thing for them, so the condition for the accusative, which is the unity of the agent (ittiḥād al-fāʿil), is absent, and so it was transitively linked with the lām. And adornment is an attribute of the Creator, so the agent is unified, and the verb reached it directly.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "Wa-zīnatan" is in the accusative by an implied verb whose estimate is: "and We made them an adornment." Qatādah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās: "li-tarkabūhā zīnatan" without a waw. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ (a grammatical work) said: "Al-zīnah" is a verbal noun placed in the position of a noun, and its accusative is as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "khalaqahā," or from "li-tarkabūhā." Al-Zamakhsharī said: meaning "and He created them as an adornment so that you may ride them," or He makes zīnatan a circumstantial state from the hāʾ in "khalaqahā li-tarkabūhā," while they are an adornment and beauty. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: The accusative then is as a circumstantial state from the hāʾ in "tarkabūhā."

The apparent meaning is the negation of knowledge concerning the essences of what God creates. Al-Jumhūr said: the meaning is what you do not know of humans, animals and inanimate things, which He created all for your benefit. So He informs us that He has creations of which we have no knowledge, so that we may increase in proof of His power through the information, even though He has hidden its knowledge from us for a wisdom in its concealment. What God, exalted is He, created of animals and others is not encompassed in its knowledge by any human being.

Qatādah said: "What you do not know" is the origin of its occurrence, like the weevil in plants and the worm in fruits. Ibn Baḥr said: "You do not know how He creates it." Muqātil said: it is what God has prepared for His friends in Paradise, "what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human being." Al-Ṭabarī said: he added after this "in Paradise and in Hell for their people," and the rest is by meaning.

Interpretations have been narrated concerning "what you do not know" in a ḥadīth from Ibn ʿAbbās, Wahb ibn Munabbih and al-Shaʿbī; God knows best their soundness.

It is said: when He mentioned the animals from which one benefits in an essential way and in a non-essential way, He followed with mention of the animals from which one does not generally benefit, in a summary manner, since their details lie beyond enumeration and counting. And "al-qaṣd" is a verbal noun: it means the way which the traveller intends and does not deviate from. And "al-sabīl" (the way) here is singular in form. It is said: singular in what it signifies, and the alif-lām in it is for a specific reference (al-ʿahd), namely the way of the Sharīʿah (the sacred law), and it is not for the genus, since if it were for the genus, none of it would be deviant. The meaning: upon God is the clarifying of the path of guidance, and that is by setting up the proofs and sending the Messengers. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it is possible that the meaning is: whoever takes the straight path, then upon God is His mercy, His bounty and His path, and to that is his destination. And on the basis that the alif-lām is for specific reference, the pronoun in His saying "and of it is a deviant" returns to the way which the meaning of the verse includes, as if it were said: "and of the way is a deviant," so it returned to it although no mention of it had preceded, because its opposite indicates it. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it is possible that "of it" returns to the way of the Sharīʿah, and "min" (of) is partitive, and the intended meaning is: the sects of misguidance from the community of Muḥammad (ﷺ), as if He said: "and of the offshoots of paths within this way, and of its branches." It is said: the alif-lām in al-sabīl is for the genus, and it is divided into a verbal noun, which is the path of truth, and into a deviant, which is the path of falsehood. The deviant is one who swerves from uprightness and guidance, as he said:

*The sailor, at times, veers off course with it, and at times finds his way.*

And as another said:

*And of the path is a deviant, and guidance, the straight way, and of it is one with corruption.*

He divided the path into deviant, into guidance, and into corrupt, which is corruption. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the meaning of His saying "and upon God is the straightness of the way" is that guidance to the path which leads to the truth is obligatory upon Him, according to His saying: ﴿Indeed, upon Us is guidance﴾ [al-Layl: 12]. (If you say): why did He change the style of speech in His saying "and of it is a deviant"? (I say): so that it may be known which of the two ways may be attributed to Him and which may not. If it were as the Mujabbirah (Jabriyyah, the determinist sect) claim, it would have said: "and upon God is the straightness of the way, and upon Him is its deviant," or "and upon Him is the deviant." ʿAbdullāh read: "and of you is a deviant," meaning: and of you is one who deviates from the straight course through his bad choice, and God is free of him.

﴿And if He willed, He would have guided you all﴾, by compulsion and by force; end. This is an interpretation according to the method of the Muʿtazilah (rationalist school). It is said: the pronoun in "wa-minhā" (and of it) returns to the creatures, meaning: and of the creatures is one who deviates from the truth. This is supported by the reading of ʿIsā: "wa-minkum jāʾir," and likewise it is in the codex of ʿAbdullāh, and the reading of ʿAlī: "fa-minkum jāʾir," with the fāʾ. Ibn ʿAbbās said: they are the people of the divergent religions. It is said: the Jews, the Christians and the Magians. "Wa-la-hadākum": He would have created guidance within you, so that none of you would go astray, and this is the will of choice (mashīʾat al-ikhtiyār). Al-Zajjāj said: He would have imposed upon you a sign which compels you to guidance and faith. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this is a bad statement of the people of innovations who hold that God does not create the actions of the servants. Al-Zajjāj did not attain it, and he fell into it unintentionally, by God's mercy. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah did not know that al-Zajjāj was a Muʿtazilī, and therefore he interpreted that he had not attained it, and that he fell into it unintentionally. Abū ʿAlī said: "If He willed, He would have guided you" to the reward, or to Paradise without deserving it. Ibn Zayd said: "If He willed, He would have made the straight course pure, without the deviant." The object of "shāʾa" (He willed) is omitted, because "la-hadākum" indicates it, meaning: "If He willed your guidance."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 16, verses 1–9 (part 1 of 3):

Surat al-Nahl (The Bee) has one hundred and twenty-eight verses and is Makki (revealed in Mecca).

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The command of God has come, so do not seek to hasten it. Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command, upon whomever He wills of His servants, saying: Warn that there is no god but Me, so fear Me.﴾ ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿He created man from a drop of fluid, and behold, he is an open adversary.﴾ ﴿And the cattle, He created them for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat.﴾ ﴿And in them is beauty for you when you bring them home at evening and when you drive them out to pasture.﴾ ﴿And they carry your loads to a land you could not reach except with great hardship to yourselves. Indeed your Lord is Kind and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And horses, mules and donkeys, for you to ride and as adornment. And He creates what you do not know.﴾ ﴿And upon God rests the direction of the path, and some paths deviate. Had He willed, He would have guided you all.﴾

Al-Hasan, ʿAta', ʿIkrimah and Jabir said: all of it is Makki. Ibn ʿAbbas said: except three verses of it, which were revealed in Medina after Hamzah, namely His saying: ﴿And do not sell the covenant of God for a small price…﴾ [al-Nahl: 95] up to His saying: ﴿…for the best of what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl: 97]. It was also said: except three verses: ﴿And if you punish, punish with the like…﴾ [al-Nahl: 126], which was revealed in Medina concerning the mutilation of Hamzah and the slain of Uhud; His saying: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is only by God﴾ [al-Nahl: 127]; and His saying: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated…﴾ [al-Nahl: 110]. It was also said: from its beginning up to His saying ﴿(what they associate)﴾ is Madani (revealed in Medina), and the rest is Makki. From Qatadah the opposite is reported.

As for its connection with what precedes it: when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 92], this was a reminder of their gathering on the Day of Resurrection and their being questioned about what they committed in the life of this world. So it was said: ﴿The command of God has come﴾, meaning, according to the majority, the Day of Resurrection. Ibn ʿAbbas reported that the "command" means the victory of the Messenger of God and his dominance over the disbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari said: they used to seek to hasten what they were promised of the coming of the Hour, or of the descent of punishment upon them on the day of Badr, mocking and denying the promise. Ibn Jurayj, who said this second view, said: the "command" here is what God promised His Prophet of victory, his triumph over his enemies, his vengeance upon them by killing, taking captives, plundering their wealth, and seizing their homes and dwellings. Al-Dahhak said: the "command" here is a verbal noun from amara, and what is meant is His obligations and rulings. It was said: this is far-fetched, since it is not reported that any of the Companions sought to hasten obligations before they were imposed upon them. Al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj also said: the "command" is God's punishment upon those who persist in polytheism and in denying the Messenger, and seeking to hasten punishment is reported of many of the disbelievers of Quraysh and others. Close to this view is that of al-Zajjaj: it is what He promised them of requital for their disbelief. It was also said: the "command" is some of the portents of the Hour.

As for ﴿has come﴾ (atā): it was said it remains in its past sense, and the meaning is: the command of God has come as a promise, so do not seek to hasten its occurrence. It was said: the command of God has come, meaning its beginnings and signs have come. It was also said: He used the past tense for the future because its occurrence is near and certain, and in this there is a warning to the disbelievers.

The majority read ﴿tastaʿjilūhu﴾ (do not seek to hasten it) with the tā' as a second-person address, which is either addressed to the believers or to the disbelievers, meaning: say to them, do not hasten it. God said: ﴿They seek to hasten it, those who do not believe in it﴾ [al-Shura: 18]. Ibn Jubayr read it with the yā' as a prohibition to the disbelievers. The apparent reference of the pronoun in ﴿fa-lā tastaʿjilūhu﴾ is to the command, since it is what is being spoken of. It was also said it refers to God, meaning: do not seek to hasten God with the punishment, or with the coming of the Day of Resurrection, as in His saying: ﴿And they seek from you to hasten the punishment﴾ [al-Hajj: 47].

Hamzah and al-Kisai read ﴿tushrikūna﴾ with the tā' of address. The rest of the seven, al-Aʿraj, his father Jaʿfar, Ibn Waddah, Abu Rajaʾ and al-Hasan read it with the yā'. ʿIsa read the first with tā' from above, and the second with both yā' and tā' from above; al-Aʿmash, Abu al-ʿAliyah, Talhah, Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman, Ibn Thabit, and al-Jahdari read it so. The word ﴿ma﴾ may be a relative pronoun (meaning "what") or a verbal (masdariyyah) particle. The best reading of "what they associate" is in view of their hastening, because their hastening is mockery and denial, and that is a form of associating partners.

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read ﴿yunzilu﴾ (He sends down) without the doubled letter, while the rest of the seven read it with the doubled letter. Zayd ibn ʿAli, al-Aʿmash and Abu Bakr read ﴿tunazzalu﴾ with the doubled letter in the passive voice, with ﴿al-malāʾikatu﴾ (the angels) in the nominative. Al-Jahdari did likewise, except that he did not double it. Al-Hasan, Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Aʿraj, al-Mufaddal from ʿAsim and Yaʿqub read it with a fatha on the tā' and doubled, in the active voice. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read ﴿mā nunazzilu﴾ with the nūn of majesty and doubling, and Qatadah with the nūn without doubling. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: in both of them there is much irregularity. Their irregularity is that what precedes and follows them is a third-person pronoun, and its justification is that it is an iltifat (a shift of grammatical person).

The angels here are Gabriel alone, as the majority said, or the angels referred to in His saying: ﴿And those who pull out violently﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 1]. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the Spirit is the revelation which the angels bring down upon the prophets, and its parallel is: ﴿He casts the Spirit by His command upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾ [Ghafir: 15]. Al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas said: it is the Qur'an, and from this is: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a Spirit of Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. Mujahid said: what is meant by the Spirit is the spirits of creation, and no angel descends except with a spirit with him. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the Spirit is mercy. Al-Zajjaj said, in substance: the Spirit is guidance, because hearts are given life by it, just as bodies are given life by spirits. It was said: the Spirit is Gabriel, and this is indicated by: ﴿The trustworthy Spirit brought it down﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 193]. The bāʾ (with) is then one of accompaniment, meaning: connected with the Spirit. It was said: it means maʿa (with). It was also said: the Spirit is guardians over the angels whom the angels do not see, just as the angels are guardians over us whom we do not see. Mujahid also said: the Spirit is the name of an angel, and from this is: ﴿On the day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows﴾ [al-Naba': 38]. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that the Spirit is a creation of God's creation, like the forms of the sons of Adam, and no angel descends from the heaven without one of them with him. Ibn Jurayj said similarly. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: this is a weak view, for no chain of transmission supports it.

Notes on the lexical discussion in this passage:

Al-nutfah: a drop of water; one says nataba his head with water, meaning it dripped.

Al-difʾ: a name for what one is warmed with, that is, what is heated. The Arabs say: dafiʾa yawmuna, so it is dafiʾ (warm), when there is heat in it which removes cold. Dafiʾa al-rajulu difāʾan and dafaʾan (the man became warm). The plural of difʾ is adfāʾ. A man is dafʾān and a woman is dafʾā. The daffiʾah is a herd of camels with abundant wool, because some of them warm others with their breath. It is also said with doubling. From al-Asmaʿi: the daffiʾah is one with abundant wool and fat. Al-Jawhari said: difʾ is the offspring of camels, their milk, and what benefit is derived from them.

Al-baghl: well known. ʿAmr ibn Bahr al-Jahiz has a book titled Kitab al-Bighal (The Book of Mules).

Al-himār: well known, its plural in the paucity form is ahmur, and in the abundance form is ḥumur, which is the regular form, and also ḥamīr.

Al-ṭariyy: a faʿīl form from ṭarra and yaṭurru, and ṭarāwah, like sarra and yasurru, sarāwah. Al-Farraʾ said: ṭaria yaṭri ṭirāʾan and ṭarāwah, like shaqiya yashqā shaqāʾan and shaqāwah.

Al-makhr: the splitting of water to the right and left; one says makhara al-māʾ al-arḍ (the water cut through the earth). Al-Farraʾ said: it is the sound of ships running with the winds. It was said: it is the sound made by the blowing of the wind when it grows strong, and it may also come from a ship and the like.

Māda: moved and turned.

Al-saqf: well known; its plural is sufuf, which is the regular form, and also sufuf and saqaf. The patterns fuʿul and faʿal are preserved for faʿl, and they are not regular in it.

* *

[p. 472]

Zamakhshari said: "*bil-ruh min amrihi*" means: by the Spirit of His command, through which dead hearts, dead through ignorance, are brought to life, namely His revelation, or that which takes the place in religion that the spirit takes in the body; end of quote. The *min* (مِن) is either partitive (*lil-tab'id*) or explanatory of the kind (*li-bayan al-jins*). "Whom He wills" refers to the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace. The *an* (أنْ) is a verbal (*masdariyyah*) particle, the kind that governs the imperfect verb (*mudari'*). It is joined to the imperative as in the expression "I wrote to him *bi-an qum*" ("that you rise"), and it is in apposition (*badal*) to "the Spirit." Alternatively, the preposition has been dropped and it reads "*bi-an andhiru*" ("that you warn"), and then the disagreement arises over whether it occupies a position of accusative (*nasb*) or genitive (*khafd*) in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis).

Zamakhshari said: "*(wa-an andhiru)* is in apposition to the Spirit, meaning: We send them down with *an andhiru*, and its estimate is: *andhiru*, i.e., *bi-anna al-sha'n aqulu lakum andhiru*" ("that the matter is: I say to you, warn"), "*annahu la ilaha illa ana*" ("that there is no god but I"); end of quote. Thus he made it the lightened form (*al-mukhaffafah*) of the heavy *inna*, its noun omitted as a pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*), and he estimated an omitted verb of saying, so that the predicate becomes a declarative clause, namely "I say." There is no need for this strain when it can easily be the second *an* (*al-thaniyyah*), the one that governs the imperfect verb. Ibn 'Atiyyah, Abu al-Baqa', and the author of al-Ghunyan permitted that it be the explanatory *an* (*mufassirah*), in which case it has no place in i'rab. This is because sending down with revelation contains the meaning of saying, i.e., "inform the people," from *nadhartu bi-kadhā* when I informed him of such. Zamakhshari said: "The meaning is that He says to them: Inform the people of My saying, *la ilaha illa ana, fa-ttaquni*" ("there is no god but I, so fear Me"); end of quote. When he made *an* the one from which the pronoun of the matter is omitted, he estimated this estimate, namely "He says to them: inform."

It was recited *li-yundhiru annahu* ("that He may warn that..."). Warning is appropriate here even though the wording contains nothing frightening, because the warners were disbelievers in His divinity, so within their command there is a place of fear, and within the report of His oneness is a prohibition against what they were upon, and a threat and warning against worshipping idols. The meaning of *fa-ttaquni* is: fear My punishment by your taking a god other than Me. The narration follows the sense in His saying *illa ana* ("but I"). Had it followed the wording, it would have been *la ilaha illa Allah* ("there is no god but God"). Both are permissible. Narration following the sense is more eloquent here, since in it the ruling is attributed to the speaking pronoun who sends down the angels. Then He indicated His oneness, and that there is no god but Him, by what He mentioned of creating the heavens and the earth, which no one else can do, and they acknowledge that He, exalted is He, is their Creator.

"*Bil-haqq*" means: by what is due and fitting, because these indicate attributes that entitle the one who possesses them to create and originate: life, knowledge, power, and will. This is unlike their partners, to whom none of that is due.

Al-A'mash recited *fa-ta'ala* with an added *fa'* (*fa-ta'ala*). This sentence serves to alert to the exaltation of God, Who originated this upper world and this lower world, above having a partner taken with Him in worship.

When He mentioned what indicates His oneness through the creation of the upper world and the earth, which is inference from the external, He mentioned inference from the human being himself, mentioning his creation from a drop of semen, and then he is a clear adversary. It was his duty and obligation to obey and submit to God's command.

*Khasim* (خَصِيمٌ, adversary) is among the intensive forms, from *khasama* in the sense of *ikhtasama* (to dispute), or in the sense of *mukhasim*, like *khalit* and *jalis*. *Mubin* means the one manifest in contention or the one who makes it manifest. The apparent point is that the context of these two descriptions is one of blame, for what preceded in His saying: "Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate" and His saying "that warn" and the verse. This is also due to the repetition of "and exalted is He above what they associate," and to His saying in Ya-Sin: "Does not man see" (Ya-Sin 36:77) and the verse, and He said: "Rather, they are a contentious people" (al-Zukhruf 43:58), meaning by it their disputing with the prophets of God and His friends with feeble proofs. The human being is mentioned most in the Qur'an in the context of blame, or followed by blame.

It was said: the intended meaning of the human being here is Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi. Others said: the context of the two descriptions is one of praise, because He, exalted is He, strengthened him to contend against adversaries, made him one who distinguishes truth from falsehood, and raised him from that inanimate state, which is being a drop of semen, to the lofty, noble state, which is the state of speech and clear expression. Here *idha* (إذْ) is for suddenness (*lil-mufaja'ah*), and after his creation from the drop, the sudden address did not occur except after states through which he developed; those states are omitted, and the suddenness occurs after them.

* *

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: Know that the noblest of bodies after the spheres and the stars is the human being. Then he mentioned the human being and that he is composed of a body and a soul, in a great discourse that is examined in his tafsir. We do not accept what he mentioned, that the spheres and stars are nobler than the human being.

When He mentioned the creation of the human being, He mentioned what He bestowed upon him as a favor for the sustenance of his livelihood. He first mentioned the most beneficial and most necessary of them for those to whom the Qur'an was revealed in their language, and that is the livestock (*al-an'am*), whose explanation has preceded in al-An'am. The more apparent view is that "*lakum fiha dif'un*" ("for you in them is warmth") is a resumptive statement (*istinaf*) to mention what benefit is derived from them in respect of themselves. *Dif'un* (دِفْءٌ) is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is "*lakum*" ("for you"), and "*fiha*" ("in them") is connected to the sense of settledness contained in "*lakum*." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "*fiha*" be a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) of *dif'un*, since if it were delayed it would be a qualifier (*sifah*). He also permitted that "*lakum*" be a circumstantial accusative of *dif'un*, with "*fiha*" as the predicate, but this is not permissible, because when the governing element of the circumstantial accusative is a meaning, it is not permissible to place it before the entire sentence; one may not say: "standing in the house is Zayd." If the circumstantial accusative is delayed after the whole sentence, it is permissible without disagreement; if it is placed in the middle, al-Akhfash permitted it, but the majority prohibited it. He also permitted that *dif'un* be raised by *lakum*, or that *lakum* qualify it with the definite article, and the whole sentence be a circumstantial accusative of the pronoun in the accusative position; end of quote. But it is not called a sentence, because the estimate is: "He created them for you, in them is warmth," or "He created them for you, being in them warmth," and this is of the category of the singular, not of the category of the sentence. They also permitted that "*lakum*" be connected to "*khalaqaha*" (He created them), and "*fiha dif'un*" be a resumptive statement mentioning the benefits of livestock.

What supports "*lakum fiha dif'un*" being a resumptive statement is that it is contrasted with His saying: "*wa-lakum fiha jamal*" ("and for you in them is beauty"). Thus He contrasted the necessary benefit with the non-necessary benefit.

(p-475) Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-dif'* is the offspring of every thing, and al-Umawi mentioned it from the dialect of some Arabs. The more apparent view is that "*wal-an'am*" ("and the livestock") is in the accusative by the construction of the verb being omitted (*al-ishtighal*), and what made the accusative preferable is that a verbal sentence preceded it. This is supported by the reading that has *al-an'am* in the nominative in an irregular recitation. Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is permissible that it be in apposition as an explanation (*'ataf 'ala al-bayan*), and in this case "*lakum*" would be a resumptive statement, or connected to "*khalaqaha*."

Al-Zuhri and Abu Ja'far recited *duff* with a *damma* on the *fa'*, its doubling, and its tanwin. The reasoning is that he transferred the vowel from the hamza to the *fa'* after deleting it, then doubled the *fa'*, treating the connected speech as if it were pausal, since it is permissible to double it in pause. Zayd ibn 'Ali recited *duf* with the transfer of the vowel and the deletion of the hamza without doubling the *fa'*. The owner of al-Lawami (*sahib al-lawami'*) said: al-Zuhri (recited) *duff* with a *damma* on the *fa'* without hamza, and the *fa'* is vocalized with the vowel of the deleted hamza. Some of them compensate for this hamza by doubling the *fa'*, and this is one of the two modes of Hamza ibn Habib in pause.

Mujahid said: the benefits of riding are carrying loads, milk, ghee, sprinkling upon them, and other things. He singled out the benefit of eating by mention, as He singled out the benefit of warmth, because these two are among the greatest benefits.

Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): the fronting of the adverbial phrase in His saying "*wa-minha ta'kulun*" ("and from them you eat") indicates exclusivity, while one may eat from other than them. (I answer): eating from them is the primary thing on which people rely for their livelihoods, while eating from other than them, such as chickens, ducks, and game of land and sea, is like what is not considered significant, and is like what is done for enjoyment. What he said about this, that the fronting of the adverbial phrase or the object indicates exclusivity, we have already refuted in His saying: "*iyyaka na'budu*" ("You alone we worship," al-Fatihah 1:5). The more apparent view is that "*min*" is partitive, as when you say: "when you eat of the loaf." Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that your sustenance is from them, because you plough with cattle, and the grain and fruits that you eat come from them, and you earn by hiring out camels, and you sell their offspring, their milk, and their hides; end of quote. In that case the partitive would be figurative, or *min* would be causal (*lil-sabab*).

*Al-jamal* (الجَمالُ) is the verbal noun of *jamula* with a *damma* on the *mim*. A man is *jamil*, a woman is *jamilah* and *jam'a'*, according to al-Kisa'i, who recited:

*She is a full-moon beauty, like a rising full moon,*
*She has surpassed all creation in beauty.*

Al-jamal is used to mean embellishment (*al-tajammul*), as if it were a verbal noun with the extra letters dropped. Beauty may be in form, through the goodness of composition that the eye perceives and that casts into hearts, so the soul clings to it without knowing why. In character, through its containing praiseworthy qualities such as knowledge, chastity, and forbearance; and in deeds, through their being suited to the interests of creatures, bringing benefit to them and averting harm from them. The beauty that we have in livestock is outside these three categories, and the meaning is that for us in them is beauty and grandeur in the eyes of people through owning them, and their indicating the happiness of the human being in this world, and his being among the people of abundance. So God, exalted is He, bestowed as a favor the embellishment with them, as He bestowed the favor of necessary benefit, because embellishment with them is among the aims of the owners of herds and the pride of their people, and the Arabs take pride in that. Do you not see the poet's saying:

*By my life, there are people among whom I have seen yesterday*
*Pens for the mares and the thick herd,*

*Dearer to us than people in a valley*
*Over whose flocks the leopard prowls.*

And the ʿakarah of camels is the herd between sixty and seventy, and its plural is ʿakar. And al-dathr means "the abundant." It is said: "He brought the livestock home" (arāḥa al-māshiyah), meaning he returned them in the evening from the pasture. And "sarahahā yasrahuhā sarḥan and surūḥan" means he drove them out in the morning to the pasture. And "sarahat" (they went out) can be transitive and intransitive. This mostly happens in the spring, when the rain falls, the grass grows tall, and they go out for the pasturing trip (al-nujʿah).

He placed the bringing home (al-ʾirāḥah) before the driving out (al-sarḥ) because the beauty of the camels is more evident in it, when they come back full-bellied with udders swollen, and then they take shelter in the pens (al-ḥaẓāʾir). This is unlike the time of their driving out, although in both times they adorn the courtyards, and the bellowing and bleating echo in them, so that their people feel at ease, their owners rejoice, and they make them honoured in the eyes of those who look at them. They bring them standing and esteem. This is in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾ [al-Kahf: 46], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Adorned for mankind is the love of desires﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 14]. Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿and the cattle and the tilth﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 14].

ʿIkrimah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Jaḥdarī read ḥīnan in both places with tanwīn (nunation) and with the idāfah (genitive construction) broken. They made the two clauses adjectives from which the returning pronoun (al-ʿāʾid) has been omitted, as in His saying: ﴿and fear a day when no soul will avail another﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48]. In this case the governing element (al-ʿāmil) in ḥīnan is either the subject (al-mubtadaʾ), because it carries the sense of adornment (al-tajammul), or its predicate (khabar) by virtue of the sense of settledness (al-istiqrār) in it. Al-athqāl are the goods (al-amtiʿah), whose singular is thiql. It is said they are the bodies, according to His saying: ﴿and the earth brings forth its burdens﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 2], meaning the bodies of the children of Adam.

His saying "to a land" (ilā baladin) does not intend a specific one; that is, to a distant land toward which you set out for your purposes. It is also said that what is intended is a specific one, which is Makkah, as said by Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas. It is also said it is the city of the Messenger (Madinah), and it is said Egypt (Miṣr). These sayings should be understood as examples and not as the intended meaning, since the favour is not restricted to carrying them to those places.

"Lam takūnū bālighīhi" (you would not have reached it) is an attribute of the land. It is possible that the implied sense is "with them" (the camels), and this indicates the remoteness of the land, and that even with the help of the camels in carrying the loads, you would not reach it except with hardship. Or the implied sense is: you would not reach it by yourselves without them, except with hardship, so that you would have to carry your loads on your backs.

Al-Jumhūr read bi-shiqq with the shīn kasrah (kasrah on the shīn). Mujāhid, al-Aʿraj, Abū Jaʿfar, ʿUmar ibn Maymūn and Ibn Arqam read it with fatḥah. It is also narrated from Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr. Both are verbal nouns (maṣdarān) whose meaning is hardship. It is said: al-shaqq with fatḥah is the verbal noun, and with kasrah is the noun, meaning hardship. The poet said with the kasrah:

*And a possessor of camels who travels and counts them for himself,*
*a brother of weariness and fatigue from their hardship.*

That is, from their hardship. The shiqq of a thing is its half, and al-Farrāʾ interpreted it here this way, meaning: they both carry away half of the souls, as if they had melted from fatigue and exhaustion, just as you say: "You cannot do such-and-such except by losing most of your soul, and a piece of your liver," and similar metaphor. One says: "I took the shiqq of the sheep," meaning its half. Al-shiqq also means the side, and al-akh al-shaqīq is the full brother, and Shaqq is the name of a soothsayer.

The mention of this favour of carrying the loads is fittingly concluded with the attribute of kindness (raʾfah) and mercy (raḥmah), because from His kindness is the facilitation of these benefits and the subjugation of the cattle for you. When He mentioned His favours through the cattle and their essential benefits, He then mentioned the favour of the benefits of animals that are not essential. Al-Jumhūr read "wa-l-khayl" (and the horses) and what is conjoined to it in the accusative, as a conjunction to "wa-l-anʿām" (and the cattle). Ibn Abī ʿAblah read it in the nominative.

Since riding is the greatest of their benefits, it was singled out for mention, and this does not indicate that it is not permitted for all horses, contrary to those who argued from it. And "wa-zīnatan" (and as an adornment) is in the accusative, and it was not with the lām (li-); the verb reached "riding" through the intermediary of the preposition. Both are objects of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi), because the sense is: He created them, and riding is an attribute of the created thing for them, so the condition for the accusative, which is the unity of the agent (ittiḥād al-fāʿil), is absent, and so it was transitively linked with the lām. And adornment is an attribute of the Creator, so the agent is unified, and the verb reached it directly.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "Wa-zīnatan" is in the accusative by an implied verb whose estimate is: "and We made them an adornment." Qatādah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās: "li-tarkabūhā zīnatan" without a waw. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ (a grammatical work) said: "Al-zīnah" is a verbal noun placed in the position of a noun, and its accusative is as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "khalaqahā," or from "li-tarkabūhā." Al-Zamakhsharī said: meaning "and He created them as an adornment so that you may ride them," or He makes zīnatan a circumstantial state from the hāʾ in "khalaqahā li-tarkabūhā," while they are an adornment and beauty. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: The accusative then is as a circumstantial state from the hāʾ in "tarkabūhā."

The apparent meaning is the negation of knowledge concerning the essences of what God creates. Al-Jumhūr said: the meaning is what you do not know of humans, animals and inanimate things, which He created all for your benefit. So He informs us that He has creations of which we have no knowledge, so that we may increase in proof of His power through the information, even though He has hidden its knowledge from us for a wisdom in its concealment. What God, exalted is He, created of animals and others is not encompassed in its knowledge by any human being.

Qatādah said: "What you do not know" is the origin of its occurrence, like the weevil in plants and the worm in fruits. Ibn Baḥr said: "You do not know how He creates it." Muqātil said: it is what God has prepared for His friends in Paradise, "what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human being." Al-Ṭabarī said: he added after this "in Paradise and in Hell for their people," and the rest is by meaning.

Interpretations have been narrated concerning "what you do not know" in a ḥadīth from Ibn ʿAbbās, Wahb ibn Munabbih and al-Shaʿbī; God knows best their soundness.

It is said: when He mentioned the animals from which one benefits in an essential way and in a non-essential way, He followed with mention of the animals from which one does not generally benefit, in a summary manner, since their details lie beyond enumeration and counting. And "al-qaṣd" is a verbal noun: it means the way which the traveller intends and does not deviate from. And "al-sabīl" (the way) here is singular in form. It is said: singular in what it signifies, and the alif-lām in it is for a specific reference (al-ʿahd), namely the way of the Sharīʿah (the sacred law), and it is not for the genus, since if it were for the genus, none of it would be deviant. The meaning: upon God is the clarifying of the path of guidance, and that is by setting up the proofs and sending the Messengers. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it is possible that the meaning is: whoever takes the straight path, then upon God is His mercy, His bounty and His path, and to that is his destination. And on the basis that the alif-lām is for specific reference, the pronoun in His saying "and of it is a deviant" returns to the way which the meaning of the verse includes, as if it were said: "and of the way is a deviant," so it returned to it although no mention of it had preceded, because its opposite indicates it. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it is possible that "of it" returns to the way of the Sharīʿah, and "min" (of) is partitive, and the intended meaning is: the sects of misguidance from the community of Muḥammad (ﷺ), as if He said: "and of the offshoots of paths within this way, and of its branches." It is said: the alif-lām in al-sabīl is for the genus, and it is divided into a verbal noun, which is the path of truth, and into a deviant, which is the path of falsehood. The deviant is one who swerves from uprightness and guidance, as he said:

*The sailor, at times, veers off course with it, and at times finds his way.*

And as another said:

*And of the path is a deviant, and guidance, the straight way, and of it is one with corruption.*

He divided the path into deviant, into guidance, and into corrupt, which is corruption. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the meaning of His saying "and upon God is the straightness of the way" is that guidance to the path which leads to the truth is obligatory upon Him, according to His saying: ﴿Indeed, upon Us is guidance﴾ [al-Layl: 12]. (If you say): why did He change the style of speech in His saying "and of it is a deviant"? (I say): so that it may be known which of the two ways may be attributed to Him and which may not. If it were as the Mujabbirah (Jabriyyah, the determinist sect) claim, it would have said: "and upon God is the straightness of the way, and upon Him is its deviant," or "and upon Him is the deviant." ʿAbdullāh read: "and of you is a deviant," meaning: and of you is one who deviates from the straight course through his bad choice, and God is free of him.

﴿And if He willed, He would have guided you all﴾, by compulsion and by force; end. This is an interpretation according to the method of the Muʿtazilah (rationalist school). It is said: the pronoun in "wa-minhā" (and of it) returns to the creatures, meaning: and of the creatures is one who deviates from the truth. This is supported by the reading of ʿIsā: "wa-minkum jāʾir," and likewise it is in the codex of ʿAbdullāh, and the reading of ʿAlī: "fa-minkum jāʾir," with the fāʾ. Ibn ʿAbbās said: they are the people of the divergent religions. It is said: the Jews, the Christians and the Magians. "Wa-la-hadākum": He would have created guidance within you, so that none of you would go astray, and this is the will of choice (mashīʾat al-ikhtiyār). Al-Zajjāj said: He would have imposed upon you a sign which compels you to guidance and faith. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this is a bad statement of the people of innovations who hold that God does not create the actions of the servants. Al-Zajjāj did not attain it, and he fell into it unintentionally, by God's mercy. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah did not know that al-Zajjāj was a Muʿtazilī, and therefore he interpreted that he had not attained it, and that he fell into it unintentionally. Abū ʿAlī said: "If He willed, He would have guided you" to the reward, or to Paradise without deserving it. Ibn Zayd said: "If He willed, He would have made the straight course pure, without the deviant." The object of "shāʾa" (He willed) is omitted, because "la-hadākum" indicates it, meaning: "If He willed your guidance."

(p-478) ﴿It is He who sent down water from the sky; from it you have drink, and from it come trees on which you pasture your animals.﴾ ﴿With it He causes crops to grow for you, and olives, date palms, grapes, and all kinds of fruits. Surely in that is a sign for a people who reflect.﴾ ﴿He subjected for you the night and the day, the sun and the moon, and the stars are subjected by His command. Surely in that are signs for a people who use their reason.﴾ ﴿And what He has created for you on the earth in various colors. Surely in that is a sign for a people who take heed.﴾

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He bestowed favor by bringing them into being after non-existence, and by creating what benefits them among the livestock and other things for riding, He mentioned the favor of sending down water, which is the foundation of their life and the life of animals, and what comes forth from it of their sustenance and the sustenance of animals, namely crops. Then He joined to it what is linked with it. He mentioned the most common of these, then generalized with His words, ﴿and all kinds of fruits﴾. Then He followed this with the creation of the night, which is a repose for them, and the day, which is a means of livelihood. Then He mentioned the two luminaries that God Most High made to have effect by His will in setting right what they need. Then He mentioned what He has created on the earth.

It is apparent that (lakum) (for you) is in the position of a qualifier of "māʾan" (water), so it is attached to an omitted element, and "sharābun" (drink) is raised by it; that is, water existing for you, from it is drink. It may be attached to "anzala" (sent down), and it may be a resumptive new sentence, with "sharābun" as the subject (mubtadaʾ). Since He mentioned the sending down of water, He proceeded to divide it. "Al-sharāb" is the thing drunk. The partitive sense in (minhu) (from it) is apparent. As for (minhu shajarun) (from it, trees), it is figurative: since the growth of trees depends on being watered with water, He made the trees part of the water, as the poet said: "the humps of camels in its rain," meaning in the clouds of rain. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is by elision of an annexed noun (ḥadhf al-muḍāf), either before the pronoun, meaning "and from its direction," or "its watering is trees"; or before "shajar," meaning "trees were drunk," like His words, ﴿and they were made to drink the calf into their hearts﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 93), meaning their love for it. "Al-shajar" here means everything the earth produces; this was said by al-Zajjaj. He also said: "We feed them meat when grazing is scarce (shajar)," so pasture was called shajar. Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-shajar" here means pasture (kalaʾ), and in the saying of ʿIkrimah: "Do not eat the shajar, for it is unlawful gain (suḥt)," he meant pasture.

It is said: "asāma al-māshiyata" and "sawwamahā" meaning he made the livestock graze, and "sāmat bi-nafsihā" (it grazed on its own), so it is "sāʾimah" (grazing), and "siwām" (grazing freely) means it grazed wherever it wished. Al-Zajjaj said: it is from "al-sawmah," which is a mark, because they leave marks on the land. Zayd ibn ʿAli read "tusīmūna" with an open tāʾ (tasīmūna). If it is heard as transitive, then it and "asāma" have the same meaning; if it is intransitive, its interpretation is by elision of an annexed noun, "tusīmu" (you pasture), meaning you pasture your livestock, since He had mentioned "and from it are trees." He then proceeded to mention the most useful kinds of trees, if the meaning of "and from it are trees" is general. If the meaning is pasture, then it is a new statement about the benefits of water.

It is said: "nabata al-shayʾu" and "anbatahu Allāh," so it is "manbūt" (grown), and its regular form would be "manbat." It was also said: "anbata al-shajar" is used intransitively. Al-Farraʾ recited:

"I saw people in need around their tents, dwelling there, until the herbage grew (anbata)."

That is, it grew (nabata). Al-Asmaʿi refused to use "anbata" in the sense of "nabata." Abu Bakr read "nunbitu" (We cause to grow) with the royal "we." Al-Zuhri read "nunabbitu" with shadda (intensification), said to be for multiplication and repetition, but what appears is that it is intensification of transitivity. Ubayy read "yanbutu" (it grows) from "nabata," and raised "al-zarʿa" (crops) and what is joined to it. He singled out the four by mention because they are the most noble of what grows and the most comprehensive in benefits. He began with crops because they are the staple food of most of the world; then olives, because of the benefit of using their oil for lighting, which is essential, along with the benefit of eating them, using them as condiment, and anointing with their oil; then date palms, because their fruit is among the finest fruits and is a staple in some lands; then grapes, because they are purely fruit. Then He said, ﴿and all kinds of fruits﴾, using the word "min" (of/some), which indicates partiality, because all fruits would only be in Paradise, and only some of them are made to grow on the earth as a reminder. When He mentioned the animals that benefit them in detail, He followed it with His words, ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾ (An-Nahl: 8). Similarly here, He mentioned the kinds of plants that benefit them, (p-479) then said, ﴿and all kinds of fruits﴾, as an indication that detailing the discussion of their genera, types, qualities, and benefits is nearly beyond counting, just as the details of what He created of the rest of the animals are nearly beyond counting. God Most High concluded this with His words, ﴿Surely in that is a sign for a people who reflect﴾, because looking into that requires deep contemplation and the use of thought. Do you not see that a single seed, when placed in the earth and a certain period of time passes over it, receives moisture from the earth by which it swells, then its top splits, and from it rises a plant into the air, while its base penetrates into the depth of the earth as another plant, which is the roots; then the upper part grows and strengthens, and leaves, blossoms, sheaths, and fruits emerge, containing bodies of different natures, tastes, colors, scents, shapes, and benefits. This is by the decree of an Almighty, Choosing Creator, who is God Most High.

Qur'an readers read "wa-l-shamsa" and what follows it in the accusative case. "Musakhkharātin" (subjected) is in the accusative as an emphatic circumstantial clause (ḥāl muʾakkidah) if "musakhkharātin" is a passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl). This is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the majority. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is possible that the meaning is that He subjected them to various kinds of subjection, the plural of "musakhkhar," in the sense of "taskhīr" from your saying "sakhkharahu Allah musakhkharan," like your saying "sarrahahu musarrahan," as if it were said, "and He subjected them for you in subjections by His command." End of quote. Ibn ʿAmir read "wa-l-shamsu" and what follows it in the nominative, as subject and predicate (mubtadaʾ and khabar), and Hafs read "wa-l-nujūmu musakhkharātun" with both nominative. These two readings make Al-Zamakhshari's view that "musakhkharāt" means "taskhīrāt" unlikely. Ibn Masʿud, al-Aʿmash, and Ibn Musarrif read "wa-l-riyāḥu musakhkharātun" (and the winds are subjected) in place of "wa-l-nujūm," which contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf. In the reading where all are in the accusative, the apparent meaning is that "wa-l-nujūma" is conjoined to what precedes it. Al-Akhfash said: "wa-l-nujūma" is in the accusative by an implied verb whose estimated form is "and He made the stars subjected," so the verb was omitted. In this case, "musakhkharāt" is not an emphatic circumstantial but a second object of "jaʿala" (made) if the implied "jaʿala" means "ṣayyara" (rendered), and a clarifying circumstantial (ḥāl mubayyinah) if it means "khalaqa" (created). The explanation of the subjection of these luminaries was discussed in al-Aʿrāf. He used the plural for "signs" here, mentioned reason, and used the singular before, and mentioned reflection, because before there was an argument by the existence of water, which is one thing, though the kinds of plants are many; whereas the arguments here are multiple. Also, celestial phenomena are more evident in indicating the overwhelming power and clearer in testifying to majesty and greatness.

﴿And what He has created﴾ is conjoined to "the night and the day." It means: what He created in it of animals, trees, fruits, and other things, of various colors, white, black, and others. It was said: "mukhtalifan alwānuh" means its kinds, as you say: "these are colors (alwān) of fruit and food." It was also said: the intended meaning is minerals. ﴿Surely in that﴾, that is, in what He created in this state of varied colors; or ﴿surely in that﴾, that is, in the variety of colors. He concluded this with ﴿who take heed﴾, and its meaning is consideration and admonition. Their knowledge of that was previously present, but forgetfulness came upon it, so it was said "yadhdhakkarūn," meaning they remember what they forgot of the subjection of these created things on the earth.

﴿And He it is who subjected the sea that you may eat from it fresh flesh and extract from it ornaments that you wear, and you see the ships plowing through it, that you may seek of His bounty, and that perhaps you will be thankful.﴾ ﴿And He cast on the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you, and rivers and roads, that perhaps you will be guided.﴾ ﴿And landmarks; and by the star they are guided.﴾

When God Most High mentioned the argument by what He created on the earth, He mentioned the favor of subjecting the sea. The meaning of its subjection is that people are enabled to benefit from it, by riding for useful purposes, by diving to extract what is in it, and by fishing for what is in it. "Al-baḥr" (the sea) is a genus that includes both salt and fresh water. He began with the most important of its benefits, which is eating, and "minhu" (from it) is by elision of an annexed noun, meaning: that you may eat from its animals fresh flesh. Then He followed it with what is adorned with, which is ornament, of pearls and coral, and He indicated the purpose of ornament, which is wearing it. There are benefits other than wearing: fresh flesh is from both salt and fresh water, and ornament is from salt water. It was said: from fresh water comes a pearl that is rarely worn and is used only for medicine. It is said that there is a sea-green stone in emerald. As for ﴿that you may eat﴾, it is general for women and men. As for ﴿you wear them﴾, it is specific to women. The meaning is: your women wear them. The wearing is attributed to the males, because women adorn themselves with jewelry only for the sake of their men, so it is as if it is their adornment and their clothing. When God Most High mentioned the favor of eating from it and extracting ornaments, He mentioned the favor of ships moving upon it, "māxhirah" meaning plowing through it or making a sound as it splits the water, for carrying goods and provisions for trade and other purposes. He attributed the seeing to the singular addressee, saying ﴿and you see﴾, and made it a parenthetical clause between the two causal clauses: the cause of extracting and the cause of seeking. Therefore He turned away from addressing in the plural. The apparent conjunction is with "and that you may seek" to the causal clause before it, as we have indicated. Ibn al-Anbari allowed that it be conjoined to an omitted cause, meaning "that you may seek by that," and that it be by an implied verb, meaning "and He did that that you may seek." Here "al-fadl" (bounty) means gaining profits through trade and reaching distant lands. In this there is evidence for the permissibility of sailing the sea.

"...so that you may give thanks," for what He has bestowed upon you of these blessings. It is said: "God created the earth, and it began to sway, and the angels said: 'No one can settle upon its back.' So in the morning it had been anchored with mountains, and the angels did not know what it had been created from." And He coordinated (wa-anhaaran, "and rivers") with (rawasiya, "firm mountains").
