And 'alamat (landmarks): these are the markers of roads, and everything by which travelers are guided, such as a mountain, a plain, and other things; so said al-Zamakhshari, and this is the meaning of the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: I have seen a group of people recognizing roads by smelling the dust. Ibn 'Isa said: The 'alamah is a form by which is known what is intended, whether by writing, speech, sign, or shape. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "wa-'alamat" is in the accusative like a verbal noun, meaning: He did these things so that you may take heed by them, and "alamat" means a lesson and an indication in every path, for one may be guided by mountains, rivers, and roads. End of quote. Ibn al-Kalbi said: the 'alamat are the mountains. Al-Nakha'i and Mujahid said: the stars. The strangest explanation of 'alamat is that they are long, thin serpent-like fish in their colors and movements, called 'alamat, found in the Indian Ocean which is sailed from Yemen; when they appear, they are a sign of arrival at the land of India and an indication of safety. The majority (al-Jumhur) read: "wa-bi-l-najm" (and by the star), as a collective noun. The reading of Ibn Wathhab supports this: "wa-bi-l-nujum," with a damma on the nun and the jim, and the reading of al-Hasan: with a damma on the nun. In al-Lawami' (it is said): al-Hasan: "al-nujum" with two dammas, and Ibn Wathhab: with one damma; this has also come down thus from Ibn Hisham al-Rifa'i, and there is no doubt that he transmits it from the companions of 'Asim. End of quote. That is a plural like suqf and saqaf, and ruhn and rahan, and making it of the pattern fu'ul is better than taking it to mean "the stars" with the waw elided. However, Ibn 'Usfur mentioned that the saying "al-nujum" is a poetic necessity, and recited:
"Indeed He who decreed this is a judge who ruled / that the water be approached when the star has set."
He said: he means "al-nujum," like his saying:
"Until, when the throats of the throat became moistened..."
meaning: "al-hulq" (the throats). As for the sukun (quiescent form): it is said to be a lightening, and it is said to be a dialect. From al-Suddi: it is the Pleiades, the two Guardians (al-Farqadan), the Bier's Daughters (Banat Na'sh), and al-Jady. Al-Farra' said: the intended meaning is al-Jady and al-Farqadan; end of quote. It is said: al-Jady is the seventh of the Lesser Bear's daughters, and the two Farqadan are the first two of them, and it is not the al-Jady that is a lunar mansion; some of them diminutive it, saying "judayy." In a hadith: from Ibn 'Abbas that he asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about His saying "and by the star," and he said: "It is al-Jady." Had this been authentic, no one would deviate from it. Ibn 'Abbas said: upon it is your qibla, and by it you are guided in your land and sea. It is said: it is the pole star that does not move. It is said: it is the Pleiades. A poet said:
"When Orion is sought while the star is rising, every ford of the Euphrates becomes a crossing."
Another said:
"Until, when the star rose in the darkness and the herbage was left, withered and mown..."
i.e., and from it some are withered, and from it some are mown, and that only occurs at the rising of the Pleiades. Hum (they) is a third-person pronoun; it shifted from address to absence. The pronoun referred to Quraysh, since they had guidance by the stars on their journeys, and they had knowledge of it that others did not have, so gratitude was more binding on them and reflection more incumbent upon them. He placed the prepositional phrase before what it governs for emphasis and for the sake of the fasila (verse ending). Al-Zamakhshari, in his usual manner, as if it were said: "And by the star specifically, they are guided."

(p-478) ﴿It is He who sent down water from the sky; from it you have drink, and from it come trees on which you pasture your animals.﴾ ﴿With it He causes crops to grow for you, and olives, date palms, grapes, and all kinds of fruits. Surely in that is a sign for a people who reflect.﴾ ﴿He subjected for you the night and the day, the sun and the moon, and the stars are subjected by His command. Surely in that are signs for a people who use their reason.﴾ ﴿And what He has created for you on the earth in various colors. Surely in that is a sign for a people who take heed.﴾

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He bestowed favor by bringing them into being after non-existence, and by creating what benefits them among the livestock and other things for riding, He mentioned the favor of sending down water, which is the foundation of their life and the life of animals, and what comes forth from it of their sustenance and the sustenance of animals, namely crops. Then He joined to it what is linked with it. He mentioned the most common of these, then generalized with His words, ﴿and all kinds of fruits﴾. Then He followed this with the creation of the night, which is a repose for them, and the day, which is a means of livelihood. Then He mentioned the two luminaries that God Most High made to have effect by His will in setting right what they need. Then He mentioned what He has created on the earth.

It is apparent that (lakum) (for you) is in the position of a qualifier of "māʾan" (water), so it is attached to an omitted element, and "sharābun" (drink) is raised by it; that is, water existing for you, from it is drink. It may be attached to "anzala" (sent down), and it may be a resumptive new sentence, with "sharābun" as the subject (mubtadaʾ). Since He mentioned the sending down of water, He proceeded to divide it. "Al-sharāb" is the thing drunk. The partitive sense in (minhu) (from it) is apparent. As for (minhu shajarun) (from it, trees), it is figurative: since the growth of trees depends on being watered with water, He made the trees part of the water, as the poet said: "the humps of camels in its rain," meaning in the clouds of rain. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is by elision of an annexed noun (ḥadhf al-muḍāf), either before the pronoun, meaning "and from its direction," or "its watering is trees"; or before "shajar," meaning "trees were drunk," like His words, ﴿and they were made to drink the calf into their hearts﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 93), meaning their love for it. "Al-shajar" here means everything the earth produces; this was said by al-Zajjaj. He also said: "We feed them meat when grazing is scarce (shajar)," so pasture was called shajar. Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-shajar" here means pasture (kalaʾ), and in the saying of ʿIkrimah: "Do not eat the shajar, for it is unlawful gain (suḥt)," he meant pasture.

It is said: "asāma al-māshiyata" and "sawwamahā" meaning he made the livestock graze, and "sāmat bi-nafsihā" (it grazed on its own), so it is "sāʾimah" (grazing), and "siwām" (grazing freely) means it grazed wherever it wished. Al-Zajjaj said: it is from "al-sawmah," which is a mark, because they leave marks on the land. Zayd ibn ʿAli read "tusīmūna" with an open tāʾ (tasīmūna). If it is heard as transitive, then it and "asāma" have the same meaning; if it is intransitive, its interpretation is by elision of an annexed noun, "tusīmu" (you pasture), meaning you pasture your livestock, since He had mentioned "and from it are trees." He then proceeded to mention the most useful kinds of trees, if the meaning of "and from it are trees" is general. If the meaning is pasture, then it is a new statement about the benefits of water.

It is said: "nabata al-shayʾu" and "anbatahu Allāh," so it is "manbūt" (grown), and its regular form would be "manbat." It was also said: "anbata al-shajar" is used intransitively. Al-Farraʾ recited:

"I saw people in need around their tents, dwelling there, until the herbage grew (anbata)."

That is, it grew (nabata). Al-Asmaʿi refused to use "anbata" in the sense of "nabata." Abu Bakr read "nunbitu" (We cause to grow) with the royal "we." Al-Zuhri read "nunabbitu" with shadda (intensification), said to be for multiplication and repetition, but what appears is that it is intensification of transitivity. Ubayy read "yanbutu" (it grows) from "nabata," and raised "al-zarʿa" (crops) and what is joined to it. He singled out the four by mention because they are the most noble of what grows and the most comprehensive in benefits. He began with crops because they are the staple food of most of the world; then olives, because of the benefit of using their oil for lighting, which is essential, along with the benefit of eating them, using them as condiment, and anointing with their oil; then date palms, because their fruit is among the finest fruits and is a staple in some lands; then grapes, because they are purely fruit. Then He said, ﴿and all kinds of fruits﴾, using the word "min" (of/some), which indicates partiality, because all fruits would only be in Paradise, and only some of them are made to grow on the earth as a reminder. When He mentioned the animals that benefit them in detail, He followed it with His words, ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾ (An-Nahl: 8). Similarly here, He mentioned the kinds of plants that benefit them, (p-479) then said, ﴿and all kinds of fruits﴾, as an indication that detailing the discussion of their genera, types, qualities, and benefits is nearly beyond counting, just as the details of what He created of the rest of the animals are nearly beyond counting. God Most High concluded this with His words, ﴿Surely in that is a sign for a people who reflect﴾, because looking into that requires deep contemplation and the use of thought. Do you not see that a single seed, when placed in the earth and a certain period of time passes over it, receives moisture from the earth by which it swells, then its top splits, and from it rises a plant into the air, while its base penetrates into the depth of the earth as another plant, which is the roots; then the upper part grows and strengthens, and leaves, blossoms, sheaths, and fruits emerge, containing bodies of different natures, tastes, colors, scents, shapes, and benefits. This is by the decree of an Almighty, Choosing Creator, who is God Most High.

Qur'an readers read "wa-l-shamsa" and what follows it in the accusative case. "Musakhkharātin" (subjected) is in the accusative as an emphatic circumstantial clause (ḥāl muʾakkidah) if "musakhkharātin" is a passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl). This is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the majority. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is possible that the meaning is that He subjected them to various kinds of subjection, the plural of "musakhkhar," in the sense of "taskhīr" from your saying "sakhkharahu Allah musakhkharan," like your saying "sarrahahu musarrahan," as if it were said, "and He subjected them for you in subjections by His command." End of quote. Ibn ʿAmir read "wa-l-shamsu" and what follows it in the nominative, as subject and predicate (mubtadaʾ and khabar), and Hafs read "wa-l-nujūmu musakhkharātun" with both nominative. These two readings make Al-Zamakhshari's view that "musakhkharāt" means "taskhīrāt" unlikely. Ibn Masʿud, al-Aʿmash, and Ibn Musarrif read "wa-l-riyāḥu musakhkharātun" (and the winds are subjected) in place of "wa-l-nujūm," which contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf. In the reading where all are in the accusative, the apparent meaning is that "wa-l-nujūma" is conjoined to what precedes it. Al-Akhfash said: "wa-l-nujūma" is in the accusative by an implied verb whose estimated form is "and He made the stars subjected," so the verb was omitted. In this case, "musakhkharāt" is not an emphatic circumstantial but a second object of "jaʿala" (made) if the implied "jaʿala" means "ṣayyara" (rendered), and a clarifying circumstantial (ḥāl mubayyinah) if it means "khalaqa" (created). The explanation of the subjection of these luminaries was discussed in al-Aʿrāf. He used the plural for "signs" here, mentioned reason, and used the singular before, and mentioned reflection, because before there was an argument by the existence of water, which is one thing, though the kinds of plants are many; whereas the arguments here are multiple. Also, celestial phenomena are more evident in indicating the overwhelming power and clearer in testifying to majesty and greatness.

﴿And what He has created﴾ is conjoined to "the night and the day." It means: what He created in it of animals, trees, fruits, and other things, of various colors, white, black, and others. It was said: "mukhtalifan alwānuh" means its kinds, as you say: "these are colors (alwān) of fruit and food." It was also said: the intended meaning is minerals. ﴿Surely in that﴾, that is, in what He created in this state of varied colors; or ﴿surely in that﴾, that is, in the variety of colors. He concluded this with ﴿who take heed﴾, and its meaning is consideration and admonition. Their knowledge of that was previously present, but forgetfulness came upon it, so it was said "yadhdhakkarūn," meaning they remember what they forgot of the subjection of these created things on the earth.

﴿And He it is who subjected the sea that you may eat from it fresh flesh and extract from it ornaments that you wear, and you see the ships plowing through it, that you may seek of His bounty, and that perhaps you will be thankful.﴾ ﴿And He cast on the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you, and rivers and roads, that perhaps you will be guided.﴾ ﴿And landmarks; and by the star they are guided.﴾

When God Most High mentioned the argument by what He created on the earth, He mentioned the favor of subjecting the sea. The meaning of its subjection is that people are enabled to benefit from it, by riding for useful purposes, by diving to extract what is in it, and by fishing for what is in it. "Al-baḥr" (the sea) is a genus that includes both salt and fresh water. He began with the most important of its benefits, which is eating, and "minhu" (from it) is by elision of an annexed noun, meaning: that you may eat from its animals fresh flesh. Then He followed it with what is adorned with, which is ornament, of pearls and coral, and He indicated the purpose of ornament, which is wearing it. There are benefits other than wearing: fresh flesh is from both salt and fresh water, and ornament is from salt water. It was said: from fresh water comes a pearl that is rarely worn and is used only for medicine. It is said that there is a sea-green stone in emerald. As for ﴿that you may eat﴾, it is general for women and men. As for ﴿you wear them﴾, it is specific to women. The meaning is: your women wear them. The wearing is attributed to the males, because women adorn themselves with jewelry only for the sake of their men, so it is as if it is their adornment and their clothing. When God Most High mentioned the favor of eating from it and extracting ornaments, He mentioned the favor of ships moving upon it, "māxhirah" meaning plowing through it or making a sound as it splits the water, for carrying goods and provisions for trade and other purposes. He attributed the seeing to the singular addressee, saying ﴿and you see﴾, and made it a parenthetical clause between the two causal clauses: the cause of extracting and the cause of seeking. Therefore He turned away from addressing in the plural. The apparent conjunction is with "and that you may seek" to the causal clause before it, as we have indicated. Ibn al-Anbari allowed that it be conjoined to an omitted cause, meaning "that you may seek by that," and that it be by an implied verb, meaning "and He did that that you may seek." Here "al-fadl" (bounty) means gaining profits through trade and reaching distant lands. In this there is evidence for the permissibility of sailing the sea.

"...so that you may give thanks," for what He has bestowed upon you of these blessings. It is said: "God created the earth, and it began to sway, and the angels said: 'No one can settle upon its back.' So in the morning it had been anchored with mountains, and the angels did not know what it had been created from." And He coordinated (wa-anhaaran, "and rivers") with (rawasiya, "firm mountains"). The meaning of alqa is "made" or "placed." Do you not see His saying: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting place, and the mountains as pegs?﴾ [al-Naba: 6], and His saying: ﴿And He placed in it firm mountains above it﴾ [Fussilat: 10]. And He said: ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39], meaning: I made. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The commentators said: alqa is used in the sense of "created" and "made." In my view, however, it is more specific than khalaqa and ja'ala, because alqa implies that God brought the mountains into existence not from the earth but by His power and invention. This view is supported by what is narrated in the stories (al-qasas) from al-Hasan, from Qays ibn 'Abbad, that when God created the earth it began to sway... to the end of the preceding account, and this is also narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih. Ibn 'Atiyyah also said: His saying "and rivers" is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb whose estimate is: "and He made" or "He created rivers." The agreement of scholars on supplying this verb is evidence of the particularity of alqa; had alqa meant khalaqa, there would be no need for this supplying. End of quote. But what agreement is there in this, when it has been related from the commentators that alqa means khalaqa and ja'ala? Al-Zamakhshari said: "and rivers," and He made rivers therein, because alqa carries the meaning of ja'ala. Do you not see His saying: "Have We not made the earth a resting place and the mountains as pegs?" Abu al-Baqa' said: That is, "and He split rivers and landmarks," i.e., He placed landmarks; it is also permissible that it be conjoined to "rawasiya." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: It is established in the rational sciences that most rivers have their sources gushing forth from mountains, so for this reason He followed the mention of mountains with the making of rivers. And subulan (paths): roads to your destinations, ﴿so that you may be guided﴾ by the paths to your destinations. This is the apparent meaning, and what follows supports it. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He made for you therein paths, that you may be guided﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 10]. It is said: "tahtadun" means by reflecting on the indication of these created things of their Creator, so it is from guidance to the truth and the religion of God. And 'alamat (landmarks): these are the markers of roads, and everything by which travelers are guided, such as a mountain, a plain, and other things; so said al-Zamakhshari, and this is the meaning of the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: I have seen a group of people recognizing roads by smelling the dust. Ibn 'Isa said: The 'alamah is a form by which is known what is intended, whether by writing, speech, sign, or shape. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "wa-'alamat" is in the accusative like a verbal noun, meaning: He did these things so that you may take heed by them, and "alamat" means a lesson and an indication in every path, for one may be guided by mountains, rivers, and roads. End of quote. Ibn al-Kalbi said: the 'alamat are the mountains. Al-Nakha'i and Mujahid said: the stars. The strangest explanation of 'alamat is that they are long, thin serpent-like fish in their colors and movements, called 'alamat, found in the Indian Ocean which is sailed from Yemen; when they appear, they are a sign of arrival at the land of India and an indication of safety. The majority (al-Jumhur) read: "wa-bi-l-najm" (and by the star), as a collective noun. The reading of Ibn Wathhab supports this: "wa-bi-l-nujum," with a damma on the nun and the jim, and the reading of al-Hasan: with a damma on the nun. In al-Lawami' (it is said): al-Hasan: "al-nujum" with two dammas, and Ibn Wathhab: with one damma; this has also come down thus from Ibn Hisham al-Rifa'i, and there is no doubt that he transmits it from the companions of 'Asim. End of quote. That is a plural like suqf and saqaf, and ruhn and rahan, and making it of the pattern fu'ul is better than taking it to mean "the stars" with the waw elided. However, Ibn 'Usfur mentioned that the saying "al-nujum" is a poetic necessity, and recited:
"Indeed He who decreed this is a judge who ruled / that the water be approached when the star has set."
He said: he means "al-nujum," like his saying:
"Until, when the throats of the throat became moistened..."
meaning: "al-hulq" (the throats). As for the sukun (quiescent form): it is said to be a lightening, and it is said to be a dialect. From al-Suddi: it is the Pleiades, the two Guardians (al-Farqadan), the Bier's Daughters (Banat Na'sh), and al-Jady. Al-Farra' said: the intended meaning is al-Jady and al-Farqadan; end of quote. It is said: al-Jady is the seventh of the Lesser Bear's daughters, and the two Farqadan are the first two of them, and it is not the al-Jady that is a lunar mansion; some of them diminutive it, saying "judayy." In a hadith: from Ibn 'Abbas that he asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about His saying "and by the star," and he said: "It is al-Jady." Had this been authentic, no one would deviate from it. Ibn 'Abbas said: upon it is your qibla, and by it you are guided in your land and sea. It is said: it is the pole star that does not move. It is said: it is the Pleiades. A poet said:
"When Orion is sought while the star is rising, every ford of the Euphrates becomes a crossing."
Another said:
"Until, when the star rose in the darkness and the herbage was left, withered and mown..."
i.e., and from it some are withered, and from it some are mown, and that only occurs at the rising of the Pleiades. Hum (they) is a third-person pronoun; it shifted from address to absence. Al-Zamakhshari, in his usual manner, as if it were said: "And by the star specifically, they are guided."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 16, verses 17–23:**

﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not? Will you not then remember?﴾ ﴿And if you were to count the favours of Allah, you could not enumerate them. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you reveal.﴾ ﴿And those they invoke besides Allah create nothing, and they are themselves created.﴾ ﴿They are dead, not living, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.﴾ ﴿Your God is one God. As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying, and they are arrogant.﴾ ﴿Undoubtedly, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Indeed, He does not love the arrogant.﴾: He, exalted is He, mentioned the contrast between the One who creates, who is the Creator (al-Bari') exalted is He, and that which does not create, namely the idols, and whoever is worshipped among those who have no intellect. It is therefore fitting that worship be singled out for the One who has originated creation, and not for other than Him. The particle "man" (who) is used in the second part because the object of worship other than Allah includes those who have intellect and those who do not, or because the disbelievers believed that these had influence and actions, so they were treated as those possessing knowledge, or for the sake of parallelism (al-mushakalah) between it and the one who creates, or to restrict it to those who know. When the distinction between the Creator and that which does not create is established even among those who possess knowledge, how much more so for those who have no knowledge at all, as in His saying: ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 195]. That is: their gods are lower than the state of one who has feet, because the one who has these is alive, while those (the idols) are dead. So how could they be fit to be worshipped? It does not mean that whoever has a foot is fit to be worshipped. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: this is a rebuke to those who worshipped idols and called them gods, likening them to Allah, then they have made that which does not create equal to the Creator, so the proper rebuke would be to say to them: 'Is He who does not create like He who creates?'" (I say): When they made other than Allah equal to Allah in being named by His name and in being worshipped, and placed Him on a par with it, they made Allah of the same kind as the created things and similar to them. Therefore He rejected this from them by His saying: ﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not?﴾, then He reproached them by His saying: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾, that is: such a thing should not be a matter of heedlessness. The word "favour" (ni'mah) is intended in the plural (ni'am), not a single favour. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿And if you count﴾ and His saying: ﴿you could not enumerate them﴾, since counting and enumerating are impossible for a single favour. The meaning is: you cannot count their number, for because of their abundance they exceed your ability to enumerate them. The impossibility of enumerating them requires the impossibility of fulfilling their due by way of gratitude (shukr). When He mentioned previous favours, He informed that all of His favours cannot be counted by them. He followed that with His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, since He overlooks your shortcomings in rendering thanks for favours, does not cut them off from you because of your negligence, and does not hasten to punish you for denying them. Since man is not able to render thanks for favours in full, and since he has a state in which he falls short of gratitude, He said after the verse in Ibrahim: ﴿Indeed, mankind is a great wrongdoer, a great ingrate﴾ [Ibrahim: 34], that is, a wrongdoer by abandoning thanks, an ingrate toward the favour. In this verse, the mention of forgiveness and mercy is a kindness toward him and a declaration of overlooking his shortcomings. He, exalted is He, informed that He knows what they conceal, and included in this a threat for them and an announcement of His knowledge. It also contains an alert to the negation of this noble attribute from their gods.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read with the ta' from above in ﴿tusirrun﴾, ﴿tu'linun﴾ and ﴿tad'un﴾, and this is the reading of Mujahid, al-A'raj, Shayba, Abu Ja'far, and Hubayra from Asim, with the meaning: "Say to them." Asim, in his well-known reading, read ﴿yad'un﴾ with the ya' from below, and with the ta' in the two preceding words. Al-A'mash and the companions of Abd Allah read: ﴿ya'lamu alladhi yubduna wa ma yaktumun﴾ and ﴿tad'un﴾, with the ta' from above in all three. Talha read: ﴿ma yukhfun wa ma yu'linun﴾ and ﴿tad'un﴾ with the ta' from above. These two readings contradict the consonantal text of the Mushaf (the written Qur'an), and the well-known reading is what is transmitted from al-A'mash and others. Therefore it is obligatory to interpret them as explanation (tafsir), not as Qur'an.

When Allah made the contrast between the Creator and other than Him manifest, He stated explicitly that their gods do not create, and that they are themselves created. He informed that they are dead, and emphasized this by His saying: ﴿not living﴾. Then He negated from them the awareness that belongs to beasts, let alone the knowledge that characterises the intelligent. He expressed it with ﴿alladhina﴾ (those), which is for the rational, treating what is other than them as they are treated, because they were worshipped and divinity was ascribed to them. Muhammad al-Yamani read: ﴿yud'awna﴾, with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the 'ayn, in the passive voice. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and they are themselves created﴾ is: Allah brought them into existence and originated them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "There is another possibility, which is that the meaning is: people create them by carving and shaping, while they themselves cannot do that, so they are weaker than their worshippers." End of his words.

﴿Amwat﴾ (dead) is the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: they are dead. It may also be a second predicate after a predicate. The apparent meaning is that all of these statements are about the idols, and their resurrection would be their being restored after their annihilation. It is therefore fitting that worship be singled out for the One who has originated creation, and not for other than Him. The particle "man" (who) is used in the second part because the object of worship other than Allah includes those who have intellect and those who do not, or because the disbelievers believed that these had influence and actions, so they were treated as those possessing knowledge, or for the sake of parallelism (al-mushakalah) between it and the one who creates, or to restrict it to those who know. That is: their gods are lower than the state of one who has feet, because the one who has these is alive, while those (the idols) are dead. So how could they be fit to be worshipped? It does not mean that whoever has a foot is fit to be worshipped. Talha read: ﴿ma yukhfun wa ma yu'linun﴾ and ﴿tad'un﴾ with the ta' from above. He expressed it with ﴿alladhina﴾ (those), which is for the rational, treating what is other than them as they are treated, because they were worshipped and divinity was ascribed to them. Muhammad al-Yamani read: ﴿yud'awna﴾, with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the 'ayn, in the passive voice. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and they are themselves created﴾ is: Allah brought them into existence and originated them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "There is another possibility, which is that the meaning is: people create them by carving and shaping, while they themselves cannot do that, so they are weaker than their worshippers." End of his words.

﴿Amwat﴾ (dead) is the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: they are dead. It may also be a second predicate after a predicate. The apparent meaning is that all of these statements are about the idols, and their resurrection would be their being restored after their annihilation. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 98]? It has been said: the meaning of "resurrecting" them is stirring them up, as you say: "I awakened the sleeper from his sleep" when you rouse him. It is as though He described them with the utmost lifelessness: that is, even if you urged them with motion or moved them, they would not perceive that. He negated life from them because among the dead there are those whose death is followed by life, such as the sperm drops which Allah brings into being as living creatures, and the bodies of animals which are resurrected after their death. As for the idols of stone and wood, they are dead, and their death is not followed by life, and this is more deeply rooted in their death. It has also been said: "those you invoke" are the angels, and some of the disbelievers used to worship them. ﴿Amwat﴾ means: death is inevitable for them. ﴿Ghayr ahya'﴾ means: their life is not everlasting. ﴿Wa ma yash'urun﴾ means: they have no knowledge of the time of their resurrection.

Talha read: ﴿ma yukhfun wa ma yu'linun﴾ and ﴿tad'un﴾ with the ta' from above. These two readings contradict the consonantal text of the Mushaf (the written Qur'an), and the well-known reading is what is transmitted from al-A'mash and others. Therefore it is obligatory to interpret them as explanation (tafsir), not as Qur'an.

When Allah made the contrast between the Creator and other than Him manifest, He stated explicitly that their gods do not create, and that they are themselves created. He informed that they are dead, and emphasized this by His saying: ﴿not living﴾. Then He negated from them the awareness that belongs to beasts, let alone the knowledge that characterises the intelligent. He expressed it with ﴿alladhina﴾ (those), which is for the rational, treating what is other than them as they are treated, because they were worshipped and divinity was ascribed to them. Muhammad al-Yamani read: ﴿yud'awna﴾, with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the 'ayn, in the passive voice. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and they are themselves created﴾ is: Allah brought them into existence and originated them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "There is another possibility, which is that the meaning is: people create them by carving and shaping, while they themselves cannot do that, so they are weaker than their worshippers." End of his words.

﴿Amwat﴾ (dead) is the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: they are dead. It may also be a second predicate after a predicate. The apparent meaning is that all of these statements are about the idols, and their resurrection would be their being restored after their annihilation. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 98]? It has been said: the meaning of "resurrecting" them is stirring them up, as you say: "I awakened the sleeper from his sleep" when you rouse him. It is as though He described them with the utmost lifelessness: that is, even if you urged them with motion or moved them, they would not perceive that. He negated life from them because among the dead there are those whose death is followed by life, such as the sperm drops which Allah brings into being as living creatures, and the bodies of animals which are resurrected after their death. As for the idols of stone and wood, they are dead, and their death is not followed by life, and this is more deeply rooted in their death. It has also been said: "those you invoke" are the angels, and some of the disbelievers used to worship them. ﴿Amwat﴾ means: death is inevitable for them. ﴿Ghayr ahya'﴾ means: their life is not everlasting. ﴿Wa ma yash'urun﴾ means: they have no knowledge of the time of their resurrection.

In the reading ﴿wa alladhina yad'un﴾ with the ya' from below, they permitted that ﴿amwat﴾ refers to the disbelievers, whose pronoun is in ﴿yad'un﴾; He likened them to the dead who are not living, in that they are astray and not guided. What follows refers back to them, and "ba'th" (resurrection) means gathering from their graves. It has also been said that in this interpretation there is a threat, that is: when they will be resurrected to punishment. It has also been said: the pronoun in ﴿wa ma yash'urun﴾ is for the idols, and in ﴿yub'athun﴾ it is for their worshippers, meaning: the idols do not perceive when their worshippers will be resurrected. In this there is mockery of the polytheists, and that their gods do not know the time of the resurrection of their worshippers, so how could there be a time of reward for them for their worship?

What is summarised from these statements is: the reports of all these sentences may be about those invoked as gods, either the idols or the angels; or ﴿amwat﴾ to the end may be a report about those who are invoked, and ﴿yub'athun﴾ a report about those who invoke and worship. Abu Abd al-Rahman read ﴿iyyana﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, which is the dialect of his people, the Sulaym. The apparent meaning is that ﴿iyyana﴾ is the object of ﴿yub'athun﴾, and the clause is in a position of accusative object of ﴿yash'urun﴾, because it is suspended (mu'allaq), since its meaning is knowledge. The meaning is: He negated from them knowledge of what the Living, the Self-Subsisting (al-Qayyum) alone possesses, which is the time of resurrection, when "resurrection" means gathering to the Hereafter. It has also been said: the speech is complete at His saying ﴿wa ma yash'urun﴾, and ﴿iyyana yub'athun﴾ is an adverbial of time for His saying ﴿your God is one God﴾, informing about the Day of Resurrection that the God in it is one. End of his words. This view is not sound, because then ﴿iyyana﴾ would leave what it is established as, being an adverb of time, either an interrogative or a conditional. In this interpretation it would be an adverb meaning "time," governing the clause after it, and acting on His saying "one," like your saying: "the day when Zayd stands, he is standing."

In His saying ﴿iyyana yub'athun﴾ there is evidence that resurrection is inevitable, and that it is among the necessary consequences of moral responsibility (taklif). When He mentioned the attributes of their gods which contradict divinity, He informed that the God of the universe is one, not multiplied and not divisible. He also informed that those who do not believe in recompense, after the clarity of the falsehood of divinity belonging to other than Him—rather it belongs to Him alone—remain steadfast in their polytheism, deny His oneness, and are arrogant about affirming it, because they believe in the divinity of their idols and in their greatness in existence. Describing them as those who do not believe in the Hereafter is an exaggeration in attributing disbelief to them, since not affirming recompense in the Hereafter involves denying Allah, exalted is He, and the resurrection, for whoever believes in resurrection cannot possibly deny Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It has also been said: "arrogant" means arrogant toward believing in the Messenger of Allah and following him.

The scholars said: every sin can be concealed and hidden, except arrogance, for it is a grave transgression which necessarily entails public declaration. In the authentic hadith: "Indeed, the arrogant will come on the Day of Resurrection in the likeness of ants, trampled by people with their feet," or as he (ﷺ) said. The discussion of ﴿la jarama﴾ (undoubtedly) has preceded in Hud [Hud: 22]. Isa al-Thaqafi read ﴿inna﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, as a new sentence (isti'naf), cut off from what precedes it. Some of our companions said: "la jarama" may sometimes replace the word of oath; you say: "la jarama, I will surely come to you," and in this case ﴿inna Allah﴾ with a kasra on the hamza is governed by "la jarama," and is not a new sentence. Some Bedouin said to Mirdas the Kharijite: "La jarama, by Allah, I will surely part from you forever," thereby negating that its connection is to the oath.

In His saying ﴿He knows what they conceal and what they reveal﴾ there is a threat and an alert to recompense. Yahya ibn Salam and al-Naqqash said: what is meant here by "what they conceal" is their consultation in the Dar al-Nadwah (the council house of Quraysh) about killing the Prophet (ﷺ). End of his words. ﴿He does not love the arrogant﴾ is general, applying to both disbelievers and believers, each of whom receives his share of it.

Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you reveal.﴾ ﴿And those they invoke besides Allah create nothing, and they are themselves created.﴾ ﴿They are dead, not living, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.﴾ ﴿Your God is one God. As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying, and they are arrogant.﴾ ﴿Undoubtedly, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Indeed, He does not love the arrogant.﴾: He, exalted is He, mentioned the contrast between the One who creates, who is the Creator (al-Bari') exalted is He, and that which does not create, namely the idols, and whoever is worshipped among those who have no intellect. It is therefore fitting that worship be singled out for the One who has originated creation, and not for other than Him. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 16, verses 24–29 (part 1 of 2): ﴿When it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they say, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ ﴿So that they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Unquestionably evil is what they bear.﴾ ﴿Those before them had already schemed, so God came at their structure from its foundations, and the roof fell down on them from above, and punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive.﴾ ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them and say, "Where are My partners, about whom you used to dispute?" Those who were given knowledge will say, "Indeed, disgrace and misfortune today are upon the disbelievers,"﴾ ﴿those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves. Then they will offer submission, "We did not do any evil." "Yes, indeed God is Knowing of what you used to do."﴾ ﴿"So enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein. How wretched is the abode of the arrogant."﴾. It was said: The occasion of revelation of "When it is said to them" is that al-Nadr ibn al-Harith travelled from Mecca to al-Hira. He had acquired books of histories and parables, such as Kalila wa Dimna, and the accounts of Isfandiyar and Rustam. He came to Mecca and used to say, "Muhammad only relates the tales of the ancients, but my narration is more beautiful than his." (p-٤٨٤) "Madha" (what) is an interrogative word, and it is the object of anzala (sent down), or it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is dha, meaning alladhi (which), and its returning pronoun in anzala is elided, meaning: "What is it that He sent down?" Al-Zamakhshari permitted that madha be in the nominative by being a subject, and he said: the meaning is "What is it that your Lord has sent down?" This is not permissible according to the Basrans except in cases of poetic necessity. The pronoun in lahum (to them) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. Madha anzala is not an object of qila (it was said) according to the Basran school, because it is a clause, and a clause does not occupy the position of the object of a passive verb, just as it does not occupy the position of the subject. It was read anomalously as asatira (tales) in the accusative, meaning "you mentioned tales" or "He sent down tales," as a form of mockery and derision, because belief in the sending down contradicts "tales," and they believe that nothing was sent down, nor that there is any sender. The verb qila is in the passive, so it may be that the speaker is some of them to others, and it may be that the believers said it to them as a test. It was also said: the one who said this were those who stationed themselves at the entrances of Mecca to deter people from the Messenger (ﷺ) when the delegations of pilgrims asked them, "What has been sent down to the Messenger of God (ﷺ)?" They said, "The stories of the ancients." The majority of readers read asatiru with the nominative (raf'). It is possible that the implied expression is "They are tales," or "What was sent down is tales." They made it "sent down" in mockery, even though they did not believe in that. The lam in li-yahmilu (so that they may bear) is the lam of command in the sense of an obligation upon them and the humiliation that befits them, or it is the lam of causation without it being an aim, like your saying: "I left the town out of fear of harm." This is the one expressed as the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqiba), because they did not intend by their saying "tales of the ancients" that they should bear the burdens. When Ibn 'Atiyya said that it may be the lam of consequence, he said: "It may also be the explicit lam of kay (in order that), meaning 'this was decreed for that,' and it is the lam of causation, but he did not link it to his statement." They said: rather, he implied another verb, namely "He decreed this." Kamilatan (in full) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning that nothing of it is diminished. Min (some of) is partitive. The meaning is that He bears from the burden of each one who misled, that is, part of the burden of those who went astray by their misguidance, and this is the burden of misleading, because the misleader and the misled are partners: this one misleads, and that one obeys him in his misleading, so both share the burden. Al-Akhfash said: min is superfluous, meaning "and the burdens of those who mislead them," and the meaning is "like the burdens of those who mislead them," like His saying: "Upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection." The intended meaning is "like the burden of," and the meaning is that when a leader establishes a repugnant practice, his punishment becomes great, to the extent that this punishment is equal to the punishment of everyone who follows him in that. Al-Wahidi said: min is not partitive, because that would imply lightening the burdens of the followers, and that is not permissible, due to his saying, upon him be prayers and peace: "without any reduction in their burdens." Rather, it is for the genus, meaning: "that they may bear from the same kind as the burdens of the followers." He concluded. The min that indicates the genus (li-bayan al-jins) should not be estimated in the way Al-Wahidi estimated it. Rather, it should be estimated as: "the burdens which are the burdens of those who mislead them," so that in meaning it returns to the statement of al-Akhfash, although they differ in the estimation. "Without knowledge" (bi-ghayri 'ilm): Al-Zamakhshari said it is a circumstantial clause of the object, meaning they mislead those who do not know that they are misguided. Others said it is a circumstantial clause of the subject, and this is preferable, because he is the one spoken about, to whom misguidance is attributed in the sense of agency. The meaning is that they proceed to this misguidance out of ignorance of the severe punishment they deserve for that misguidance. Then He, exalted is He, informed about the evil of what they bear for the Hereafter. The discussion of the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of a phrase like sa'a ma yazirun (unquestionably evil is what they bear) has already been presented. Fa-ata Allah (God came): that is, His command and His punishment came. As for al-bunyan (the structure), it was said it is literal. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: "Those before them" refers to Nimrod, who built a tower to ascend to the sky according to his claim, and he exaggerated its height and length into the sky by two farsakhs, as al-Naqqash related, and Ka'b al-Ahbar said so. Ibn 'Abbas and Wahb said: its height into the sky was five thousand cubits and its width three thousand cubits. God sent a wind upon it that demolished it, and its roof fell upon him and upon his followers. It was also said that Jibril demolished it with his wing and threw its top into the sea, while its base was in the sand dune. Ibn al-Kalbi said: the intended are the "dividers" mentioned in Surah al-Hijr. It was said: "Those before them" refers to Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) and his companions. Al-Dahhak said: they were the cities of the people of Lut. A group said: the intended by "those before them" are those among the earlier nations who disbelieved and schemed, and punishment from God came upon them. "God came at their structure" through to the end is then an illustration. The meaning is that they built erected structures by which they schemed against God and His Messenger, so God made their destruction in those structures, like the situation of a people who built a building and supported it with pillars, and then the building was brought down from the pillars by its collapsing, so the roof fell upon them and they perished. Similar to this is the one who dug a pit for his brother and fell into it face down. "From the foundations" (min al-qawa'id) indicates the starting point of the end, meaning the command of God came to them from the direction of the foundations. A group said: the intended by His saying "the roof fell down on them from above" is that punishment came to them from the direction of the sky which is above them, and Ibn 'Abbas said this. It was also said: the meaning is that God nullified their deeds, so they were in the position of one whose building collapsed. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this leads to a riddle. The meaning of His saying "from above them" is to remove the possibility in His saying "the roof fell down on them," for you say: "His building collapsed upon so-and-so," and it was not beneath him, just as you say: "it became corrupt for him." His saying "from above him" necessitates that they were beneath it. He concluded. This is what Ibn al-A'rabi said. He said: it informs you that they were sitting beneath it. The Arabs say: "A roof fell down on us," "a roof fell upon us," and "a wall fell upon us" when it belonged to him. If it had not fallen upon him, He would have brought the phrase "from above them" to eliminate this ambiguity in the speech of the Arabs, so He said "from above them," meaning it fell upon them, and they were beneath it, so they perished, and punishment came to them. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means the gnat by which Nimrod was destroyed. It was said: "from where they did not perceive" means from where they thought they were in safety. Al-Jumhur read bunyanahum. A group read bunyatahum. Ja'far read baytahum (their house), and al-Dahhak read buyutahum (their houses). The Qur'anic reading of the majority is *al-saqf* in the singular. Al-A'raj read *al-suqf* with two dammas, and Zayd ibn Ali and Mujahid read it with only the *sin* damma. The justification for these two readings has already been given under *wa-bi-l-najm*. A group read *al-saqafu*, with a fatha on the *sin* and a damma on the *qaf*. This is a dialectal variant of *al-saqf*, and perhaps *al-saqf* is a lightened form of it, though its usage became more common, as they said of *rajul* and *rajl* (man). It is a Tamimi dialect form. Madha anzala is not an object of qila (it was said) according to the Basran school, because it is a clause, and a clause does not occupy the position of the object of a passive verb, just as it does not occupy the position of the subject. It was also said: the one who said this were those who stationed themselves at the entrances of Mecca to deter people from the Messenger (ﷺ) when the delegations of pilgrims asked them, "What has been sent down to the Messenger of God (ﷺ)?" They said: rather, he implied another verb, namely "He decreed this." Kamilatan (in full) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning that nothing of it is diminished. Min (some of) is partitive. The meaning is that He bears from the burden of each one who misled, that is, part of the burden of those who went astray by their misguidance, and this is the burden of misleading, because the misleader and the misled are partners: this one misleads, and that one obeys him in his misleading, so both share the burden. Al-Akhfash said: min is superfluous, meaning "and the burdens of those who mislead them," and the meaning is "like the burdens of those who mislead them," like His saying: "Upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection." The intended meaning is "like the burden of," and the meaning is that when a leader establishes a repugnant practice, his punishment becomes great, to the extent that this punishment is equal to the punishment of everyone who follows him in that. The meaning is that they proceed to this misguidance out of ignorance of the severe punishment they deserve for that misguidance. When Ibn 'Atiyya said that it may be the lam of consequence, he said: "It may also be the explicit lam of kay (in order that), meaning 'this was decreed for that,' and it is the lam of causation, but he did not link it to his statement." They said: rather, he implied another verb, namely "He decreed this." Kamilatan (in full) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning that nothing of it is diminished. Min (some of) is partitive. The meaning is that He bears from the burden of each one who misled, that is, part of the burden of those who went astray by their misguidance, and this is the burden of misleading, because the misleader and the misled are partners: this one misleads, and that one obeys him in his misleading, so both share the burden. Al-Akhfash said: min is superfluous, meaning "and the burdens of those who mislead them," and the meaning is "like the burdens of those who mislead them," like His saying: "Upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection." The intended meaning is "like the burden of," and the meaning is that when a leader establishes a repugnant practice, his punishment becomes great, to the extent that this punishment is equal to the punishment of everyone who follows him in that. Al-Wahidi said: min is not partitive, because that would imply lightening the burdens of the followers, and that is not permissible, due to his saying, upon him be prayers and peace: "without any reduction in their burdens." Rather, it is for the genus, meaning: "that they may bear from the same kind as the burdens of the followers." He concluded. The min that indicates the genus (li-bayan al-jins) should not be estimated in the way Al-Wahidi estimated it. Rather, it should be estimated as: "the burdens which are the burdens of those who mislead them," so that in meaning it returns to the statement of al-Akhfash, although they differ in the estimation. "Without knowledge" (bi-ghayri 'ilm): Al-Zamakhshari said it is a circumstantial clause of the object, meaning they mislead those who do not know that they are misguided. Others said it is a circumstantial clause of the subject, and this is preferable, because he is the one spoken about, to whom misguidance is attributed in the sense of agency. The meaning is that they proceed to this misguidance out of ignorance of the severe punishment they deserve for that misguidance. Then He, exalted is He, informed about the evil of what they bear for the Hereafter. The discussion of the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of a phrase like sa'a ma yazirun (unquestionably evil is what they bear) has already been presented. Fa-ata Allah (God came): that is, His command and His punishment came. As for al-bunyan (the structure), it was said it is literal. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: "Those before them" refers to Nimrod, who built a tower to ascend to the sky according to his claim, and he exaggerated its height and length into the sky by two farsakhs, as al-Naqqash related, and Ka'b al-Ahbar said so. Ibn 'Abbas and Wahb said: its height into the sky was five thousand cubits and its width three thousand cubits. God sent a wind upon it that demolished it, and its roof fell upon him and upon his followers. It was also said that Jibril demolished it with his wing and threw its top into the sea, while its base was in the sand dune. Al-Dahhak said: they were the cities of the people of Lut. A group said: the intended by "those before them" are those among the earlier nations who disbelieved and schemed, and punishment from God came upon them. "God came at their structure" through to the end is then an illustration. The meaning is that they built erected structures by which they schemed against God and His Messenger, so God made their destruction in those structures, like the situation of a people who built a building and supported it with pillars, and then the building was brought down from the pillars by its collapsing, so the roof fell upon them and they perished. Similar to this is the one who dug a pit for his brother and fell into it face down. "From the foundations" (min al-qawa'id) indicates the starting point of the end, meaning the command of God came to them from the direction of the foundations. A group said: the intended by His saying "the roof fell down on them from above" is that punishment came to them from the direction of the sky which is above them, and Ibn 'Abbas said this. It was also said: the meaning is that God nullified their deeds, so they were in the position of one whose building collapsed. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this leads to a riddle. The meaning of His saying "from above them" is to remove the possibility in His saying "the roof fell down on them," for you say: "His building collapsed upon so-and-so," and it was not beneath him, just as you say: "it became corrupt for him." A group also read it that way, but they pronounced the *ya'* with a sukun, so it drops in continuous speech because of the meeting of two sakins. The majority read *tushaqqunа* (you oppose) with a fatha on the *nun*, while Nafi' read it with a kasra. This reading is also narrated from al-Hasan, and Abu Hatim's weakening of it should not be heeded. A group read it with a shadda, where the *nun* of the nominative was assimilated into the *nun* of protection (*nun al-wiqaya*, the buffer nun). *Alladhina utu al-'ilm* (those who were given knowledge) is general, encompassing whoever was given knowledge among the prophets and the scholars of their nations, who used to call them to faith and admonish them, but they paid no heed and rejected them. Yahya ibn Sallam said: they are the believers. End of quote. The apparent meaning is that *alladhina* is an attribute of the disbelievers, so that this falls within the speech. If the speech is on the Day of Resurrection, then *tatawaffahum* is a narration of a past state. If the speech is in this world, then when He informed that He will disgrace them on the Day of Resurrection and will say to them what He will say, the people of knowledge said: when Allah informs of this, the disgrace is the day on which Allah said He will disgrace them, and *tatawaffahum* remains in its original sense. In meaning, it includes the one who *tawaffathu* and the one who *tatawaffahu*. It is permissible that *alladhina* is the predicate of an omitted subject, and that it is in the accusative as a term of censure. It may then be part of what the people of knowledge said, or it may not be spoken by them but be part of Allah's own report. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is possible that *alladhina* is nominative as a new subject, separate from what precedes it, with its predicate in His saying ﴿so they will cast forth submission﴾ (al-Nahl 16:28), with the *fa'* inserted into the predicate, and such a thing does occur. Or it means humbling oneself (*al-khudu'*), the statement of Muqatil; that is, they submitted when they saw death had come upon them. It is said that on the Day of Resurrection they submitted and responded with what they had opposed in the worldly life, namely enmity and arrogance. The apparent reading is that *fa-alqaw* (so they cast) is coordinated with *tatawaffahum*. Abu al-Baqa' permitted it to be coordinated with *alladhina*, or to be a fresh sentence. It is also said that the speech was complete at His saying ﴿wronging themselves﴾, and then the speech returned to narrating what the polytheists said on the Day of Resurrection. Or the meaning is "in our own estimation," that is: if disbelief were, in our own estimation, a matter of indifference, we would not have known it. The first interpretation is favoured by the rejoinder *bala* (Yes), since if that were in accordance with their belief, the answer would not be *bala*. Yet the second interpretation also permits a rejoinder with *bala*, and the meaning is: you lied in your belief that it is not evil; rather, you believed it to be evil, because you had clearly perceived the truth and recognized it, and you disbelieved, as in His saying ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:89), and His saying ﴿and they denied them while their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ (al-Naml 27:14). It is permissible that the refutation came from the angels, who are the ones commanding them to enter the Fire, driving them towards it. It is said that the custodians are meant, and the apparent meaning is that *al-abwab* (the gates) is literal. It is said that the levels are meant. It is said that the categories are meant, as one says, "So-and-so studies a gate of knowledge," meaning a category. Whoever said that what is meant by this is the punishment of the grave is farther from the truth, citing what has come: "The grave is a garden from the gardens of Paradise, or a pit from the pits of the Fire." When they refuted them in their claim, they were told that He is the Knower of their deeds, and so He is the one who recompenses them for them. Then they were commanded to enter, and the *lam* in *fa-la-bi'sa* (so evil is) is an emphatic *lam*, and it does not enter a past verb that is inflected, but it entered a rigid one because of its distance from verbs and its nearness to nouns. The one to whom the dispraise applies is omitted: that is, "so evil is the abode of the arrogant, it" (*hiya*), that is, Hell. The description of arrogance is evidence that its possessor deserves the Fire. And that is an allusion to His saying: ﴿Their hearts are deniers, and they are arrogant﴾ (al-Nahl 16:22).

In this case, His saying ﴿Those who said﴾ up to His saying *fa-alqaw* is a parenthetical sentence between the report of the disbelievers' states. ﴿We did no evil﴾ (al-Nahl 16:28) is with an implied *qawl* (saying): that is, their description is "bearing evil," and this is either an outright lie, as they said: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ (al-An'am 6:23), whereupon He said: ﴿Look how they lied against themselves﴾ (al-An'am 6:24). Or the meaning is "in our own estimation," that is: if disbelief were, in our own estimation, a matter of indifference, we would not have known it. The first interpretation is favoured by the rejoinder *bala* (Yes), since if that were in accordance with their belief, the answer would not be *bala*. Yet the second interpretation also permits a rejoinder with *bala*, and the meaning is: you lied in your belief that it is not evil; rather, you believed it to be evil, because you had clearly perceived the truth and recognized it, and you disbelieved, as in His saying ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:89), and His saying ﴿and they denied them while their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ (al-Naml 27:14). The apparent reading is that this whole context concerns the people of knowledge and the disbelievers, and that the people of knowledge are those who refuted their report denying that they did any evil. It is permissible that the refutation came from the angels, who are the ones commanding them to enter the Fire, driving them towards it. It is said that the custodians are meant, and the apparent meaning is that *al-abwab* (the gates) is literal. It is said that the levels are meant. It is said that the categories are meant, as one says, "So-and-so studies a gate of knowledge," meaning a category. Whoever said that what is meant by this is the punishment of the grave is farther from the truth, citing what has come: "The grave is a garden from the gardens of Paradise, or a pit from the pits of the Fire." When they refuted them in their claim, they were told that He is the Knower of their deeds, and so He is the one who recompenses them for them. Then they were commanded to enter, and the *lam* in *fa-la-bi'sa* (so evil is) is an emphatic *lam*, and it does not enter a past verb that is inflected, but it entered a rigid one because of its distance from verbs and its nearness to nouns. The one to whom the dispraise applies is omitted: that is, "so evil is the abode of the arrogant, it" (*hiya*), that is, Hell. The description of arrogance is evidence that its possessor deserves the Fire. And that is an allusion to His saying: ﴿Their hearts are deniers, and they are arrogant﴾ (al-Nahl 16:22).

He had acquired books of histories and parables, such as Kalila wa Dimna, and the accounts of Isfandiyar and Rustam. He came to Mecca and used to say, "Muhammad only relates the tales of the ancients, but my narration is more beautiful than his." This is not permissible according to the Basrans except in cases of poetic necessity. The pronoun in lahum (to them) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. Madha anzala is not an object of qila (it was said) according to the Basran school, because it is a clause, and a clause does not occupy the position of the object of a passive verb, just as it does not occupy the position of the subject. It was read anomalously as asatira (tales) in the accusative, meaning "you mentioned tales" or "He sent down tales," as a form of mockery and derision, because belief in the sending down contradicts "tales," and they believe that nothing was sent down, nor that there is any sender. The verb qila is in the passive, so it may be that the speaker is some of them to others, and it may be that the believers said it to them as a test. It was also said: the one who said this were those who stationed themselves at the entrances of Mecca to deter people from the Messenger (ﷺ) when the delegations of pilgrims asked them, "What has been sent down to the Messenger of God (ﷺ)?" They said, "The stories of the ancients." The majority of readers read asatiru with the nominative (raf'). It is possible that the implied expression is "They are tales," or "What was sent down is tales." They made it "sent down" in mockery, even though they did not believe in that. The lam in li-yahmilu (so that they may bear) is the lam of command in the sense of an obligation upon them and the humiliation that befits them, or it is the lam of causation without it being an aim, like your saying: "I left the town out of fear of harm." This is the one expressed as the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqiba), because they did not intend by their saying "tales of the ancients" that they should bear the burdens. When Ibn 'Atiyya said that it may be the lam of consequence, he said: "It may also be the explicit lam of kay (in order that), meaning 'this was decreed for that,' and it is the lam of causation, but he did not link it to his statement." They said: rather, he implied another verb, namely "He decreed this." Kamilatan (in full) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning that nothing of it is diminished. Min (some of) is partitive. The meaning is that He bears from the burden of each one who misled, that is, part of the burden of those who went astray by their misguidance, and this is the burden of misleading, because the misleader and the misled are partners: this one misleads, and that one obeys him in his misleading, so both share the burden. Al-Akhfash said: min is superfluous, meaning "and the burdens of those who mislead them," and the meaning is "like the burdens of those who mislead them," like His saying: "Upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection." The intended meaning is "like the burden of," and the meaning is that when a leader establishes a repugnant practice, his punishment becomes great, to the extent that this punishment is equal to the punishment of everyone who follows him in that. Al-Wahidi said: min is not partitive, because that would imply lightening the burdens of the followers, and that is not permissible, due to his saying, upon him be prayers and peace: "without any reduction in their burdens." Rather, it is for the genus, meaning: "that they may bear from the same kind as the burdens of the followers." He concluded. The min that indicates the genus (li-bayan al-jins) should not be estimated in the way Al-Wahidi estimated it. Rather, it should be estimated as: "the burdens which are the burdens of those who mislead them," so that in meaning it returns to the statement of al-Akhfash, although they differ in the estimation. "Without knowledge" (bi-ghayri 'ilm): Al-Zamakhshari said it is a circumstantial clause of the object, meaning they mislead those who do not know that they are misguided. Others said it is a circumstantial clause of the subject, and this is preferable, because he is the one spoken about, to whom misguidance is attributed in the sense of agency. The meaning is that they proceed to this misguidance out of ignorance of the severe punishment they deserve for that misguidance. Then He, exalted is He, informed about the evil of what they bear for the Hereafter. The discussion of the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of a phrase like sa'a ma yazirun (unquestionably evil is what they bear) has already been presented. Fa-ata Allah (God came): that is, His command and His punishment came. As for al-bunyan (the structure), it was said it is literal. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: "Those before them" refers to Nimrod, who built a tower to ascend to the sky according to his claim, and he exaggerated its height and length into the sky by two farsakhs, as al-Naqqash related, and Ka'b al-Ahbar said so. Ibn 'Abbas and Wahb said: its height into the sky was five thousand cubits and its width three thousand cubits. God sent a wind upon it that demolished it, and its roof fell upon him and upon his followers. It was also said that Jibril demolished it with his wing and threw its top into the sea, while its base was in the sand dune. Ibn al-Kalbi said: the intended are the "dividers" mentioned in Surah al-Hijr. It was said: "Those before them" refers to Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) and his companions. Al-Dahhak said: they were the cities of the people of Lut. A group said: the intended by "those before them" are those among the earlier nations who disbelieved and schemed, and punishment from God came upon them. "God came at their structure" through to the end is then an illustration. The meaning is that they built erected structures by which they schemed against God and His Messenger, so God made their destruction in those structures, like the situation of a people who built a building and supported it with pillars, and then the building was brought down from the pillars by its collapsing, so the roof fell upon them and they perished. Similar to this is the one who dug a pit for his brother and fell into it face down. "From the foundations" (min al-qawa'id) indicates the starting point of the end, meaning the command of God came to them from the direction of the foundations. A group said: the intended by His saying "the roof fell down on them from above" is that punishment came to them from the direction of the sky which is above them, and Ibn 'Abbas said this. It was also said: the meaning is that God nullified their deeds, so they were in the position of one whose building collapsed. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this leads to a riddle. The meaning of His saying "from above them" is to remove the possibility in His saying "the roof fell down on them," for you say: "His building collapsed upon so-and-so," and it was not beneath him, just as you say: "it became corrupt for him." His saying "from above him" necessitates that they were beneath it. He concluded. This is what Ibn al-A'rabi said. He said: it informs you that they were sitting beneath it. The Arabs say: "A roof fell down on us," "a roof fell upon us," and "a wall fell upon us" when it belonged to him. If it had not fallen upon him, He would have brought the phrase "from above them" to eliminate this ambiguity in the speech of the Arabs, so He said "from above them," meaning it fell upon them, and they were beneath it, so they perished, and punishment came to them. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means the gnat by which Nimrod was destroyed. It was said: "from where they did not perceive" means from where they thought they were in safety. Al-Jumhur read bunyanahum. A group read bunyatahum. Ja'far read baytahum (their house), and al-Dahhak read buyutahum (their houses). The Qur'anic reading of the majority is *al-saqf* in the singular. A group read *al-saqafu*, with a fatha on the *sin* and a damma on the *qaf*. This is a dialectal variant of *al-saqf*, and perhaps *al-saqf* is a lightened form of it, though its usage became more common, as they said of *rajul* and *rajl* (man). It is a Tamimi dialect form. When Allah mentioned what befell them in the worldly abode, He mentioned what will befall them in the Hereafter. *Yukhzihim* (He will disgrace them) encompasses all the hardships that will befall them, and this entails their being admitted to the Fire, as in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾ (Aal 'Imran 3:192); that is, You have humiliated him completely. He combined humiliation by action with humiliation by speech, through rebuke and reproach, in His saying: *yukhzihim wa-yaqulu ayna shuraka'i* (He will disgrace them and say, "Where are My partners?"). He attributed the partners to Himself, and attribution may be on the basis of the slightest connection; the meaning is "My partners according to your claim," as the attribution is made in mockery. The majority read *shuraka'iya*, with a long vowel, a hamza, and a fatha on the *ya'*. A group also read it that way, but they pronounced the *ya'* with a sukun, so it drops in continuous speech because of the meeting of two sakins. Al-Bazzi, on the authority of Ibn Kathir, with a variant from him, read it with a short vowel and a fatha on the *ya'* here only. It is also narrated from him that he dropped the hamza in *al-qasas* (the Stories), and that the practice follows the hamza there and shortens the long vowel. They mentioned that this is a poetic necessity, but it should not be so, since it is established in this reading, and it is permissible in ordinary speech only rarely. *Al-mushaqqa* means opposition and enmity towards the believers. The majority read *tushaqqunа* (you oppose) with a fatha on the *nun*, while Nafi' read it with a kasra. This reading is also narrated from al-Hasan, and Abu Hatim's weakening of it should not be heeded. A group read it with a shadda, where the *nun* of the nominative was assimilated into the *nun* of protection (*nun al-wiqaya*, the buffer nun). *Alladhina utu al-'ilm* (those who were given knowledge) is general, encompassing whoever was given knowledge among the prophets and the scholars of their nations, who used to call them to faith and admonish them, but they paid no heed and rejected them. It is said they are the angels, as Ibn 'Abbas said. It is said they are the guardian angels. It is said they are whoever attended the gathering, of angels and humans and others. Yahya ibn Sallam said: they are the believers. End of quote. The people of knowledge say, in mockery of the disbelievers and to make them hear: ﴿Those whose souls the angels take while they are wronging themselves﴾ (al-Nisa 4:97), whose tafsir was given in Surat al-Nisa. The apparent meaning is that *alladhina* is an attribute of the disbelievers, so that this falls within the speech. If the speech is on the Day of Resurrection, then *tatawaffahum* is a narration of a past state. If the speech is in this world, then when He informed that He will disgrace them on the Day of Resurrection and will say to them what He will say, the people of knowledge said: when Allah informs of this, the disgrace is the day on which Allah said He will disgrace them, and *tatawaffahum* remains in its original sense. In meaning, it includes the one who *tawaffathu* and the one who *tatawaffahu*. It is permissible that *alladhina* is the predicate of an omitted subject, and that it is in the accusative as a term of censure. If it had not fallen upon him, He would have brought the phrase "from above them" to eliminate this ambiguity in the speech of the Arabs, so He said "from above them," meaning it fell upon them, and they were beneath it, so they perished, and punishment came to them. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means the gnat by which Nimrod was destroyed. It was said: "from where they did not perceive" means from where they thought they were in safety. Al-Jumhur read bunyanahum. A group read bunyatahum. Ja'far read baytahum (their house), and al-Dahhak read buyutahum (their houses). The Qur'anic reading of the majority is *al-saqf* in the singular. Al-A'raj read *al-suqf* with two dammas, and Zayd ibn Ali and Mujahid read it with only the *sin* damma. The justification for these two readings has already been given under *wa-bi-l-najm*. A group read *al-saqafu*, with a fatha on the *sin* and a damma on the *qaf*. This is a dialectal variant of *al-saqf*, and perhaps *al-saqf* is a lightened form of it, though its usage became more common, as they said of *rajul* and *rajl* (man). It is a Tamimi dialect form. When Allah mentioned what befell them in the worldly abode, He mentioned what will befall them in the Hereafter. *Yukhzihim* (He will disgrace them) encompasses all the hardships that will befall them, and this entails their being admitted to the Fire, as in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾ (Aal 'Imran 3:192); that is, You have humiliated him completely. He combined humiliation by action with humiliation by speech, through rebuke and reproach, in His saying: *yukhzihim wa-yaqulu ayna shuraka'i* (He will disgrace them and say, "Where are My partners?"). He attributed the partners to Himself, and attribution may be on the basis of the slightest connection; the meaning is "My partners according to your claim," as the attribution is made in mockery. The majority read *shuraka'iya*, with a long vowel, a hamza, and a fatha on the *ya'*. A group also read it that way, but they pronounced the *ya'* with a sukun, so it drops in continuous speech because of the meeting of two sakins. Al-Bazzi, on the authority of Ibn Kathir, with a variant from him, read it with a short vowel and a fatha on the *ya'* here only. It is also narrated from him that he dropped the hamza in *al-qasas* (the Stories), and that the practice follows the hamza there and shortens the long vowel. They mentioned that this is a poetic necessity, but it should not be so, since it is established in this reading, and it is permissible in ordinary speech only rarely. *Al-mushaqqa* means opposition and enmity towards the believers. The majority read *tushaqqunа* (you oppose) with a fatha on the *nun*, while Nafi' read it with a kasra. This reading is also narrated from al-Hasan, and Abu Hatim's weakening of it should not be heeded. A group read it with a shadda, where the *nun* of the nominative was assimilated into the *nun* of protection (*nun al-wiqaya*, the buffer nun). *Alladhina utu al-'ilm* (those who were given knowledge) is general, encompassing whoever was given knowledge among the prophets and the scholars of their nations, who used to call them to faith and admonish them, but they paid no heed and rejected them. It is said they are the angels, as Ibn 'Abbas said. It is said they are the guardian angels. It is said they are whoever attended the gathering, of angels and humans and others. Yahya ibn Sallam said: they are the believers. End of quote. The people of knowledge say, in mockery of the disbelievers and to make them hear: ﴿Those whose souls the angels take while they are wronging themselves﴾ (al-Nisa 4:97), whose tafsir was given in Surat al-Nisa. The apparent meaning is that *alladhina* is an attribute of the disbelievers, so that this falls within the speech. If the speech is on the Day of Resurrection, then *tatawaffahum* is a narration of a past state. If the speech is in this world, then when He informed that He will disgrace them on the Day of Resurrection and will say to them what He will say, the people of knowledge said: when Allah informs of this, the disgrace is the day on which Allah said He will disgrace them, and *tatawaffahum* remains in its original sense. In meaning, it includes the one who *tawaffathu* and the one who *tatawaffahu*. It is permissible that *alladhina* is the predicate of an omitted subject, and that it is in the accusative as a term of censure. It may then be part of what the people of knowledge said, or it may not be spoken by them but be part of Allah's own report. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is possible that *alladhina* is nominative as a new subject, separate from what precedes it, with its predicate in His saying ﴿so they will cast forth submission﴾ (al-Nahl 16:28), with the *fa'* inserted into the predicate, and such a thing does occur. End of quote. This is not permissible except according to the view of al-Akhfash, who permits *Zayd fa-qama* meaning "Zayd, so he stood."
