It should not be thought that the *fa'* is the one that enters the predicate of a subject when the subject is a relative pronoun and has the sense of a condition, because it is not permissible for it to enter such a verb alongside an explicit conditional, so it is not permissible where the sense of a condition is merely implied. Hamza and al-A'mash read *yatawaffahum* with the *ya'* from below in both places. It was also read with the assimilation of the *ta'* of the present tense into the *ta'* after it. In the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), it is written with a single *ta'* in both places. *Al-salm* here means submission (*al-istislam*). This is the statement of al-Akhfash. Or it means humbling oneself (*al-khudu'*), the statement of Muqatil; that is, they submitted when they saw death had come upon them. It is said that on the Day of Resurrection they submitted and responded with what they had opposed in the worldly life, namely enmity and arrogance. The apparent reading is that *fa-alqaw* (so they cast) is coordinated with *tatawaffahum*. Abu al-Baqa' permitted it to be coordinated with *alladhina*, or to be a fresh sentence. It is also said that the speech was complete at His saying ﴿wronging themselves﴾, and then the speech returned to narrating what the polytheists said on the Day of Resurrection. In this case, His saying ﴿Those who said﴾ up to His saying *fa-alqaw* is a parenthetical sentence between the report of the disbelievers' states. ﴿We did no evil﴾ (al-Nahl 16:28) is with an implied *qawl* (saying): that is, their description is "bearing evil," and this is either an outright lie, as they said: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ (al-An'am 6:23), whereupon He said: ﴿Look how they lied against themselves﴾ (al-An'am 6:24). Or the meaning is "in our own estimation," that is: if disbelief were, in our own estimation, a matter of indifference, we would not have known it. The first interpretation is favoured by the rejoinder *bala* (Yes), since if that were in accordance with their belief, the answer would not be *bala*. Yet the second interpretation also permits a rejoinder with *bala*, and the meaning is: you lied in your belief that it is not evil; rather, you believed it to be evil, because you had clearly perceived the truth and recognized it, and you disbelieved, as in His saying ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:89), and His saying ﴿and they denied them while their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ (al-Naml 27:14). The apparent reading is that this whole context concerns the people of knowledge and the disbelievers, and that the people of knowledge are those who refuted their report denying that they did any evil. It is permissible that the refutation came from the angels, who are the ones commanding them to enter the Fire, driving them towards it. It is said that the custodians are meant, and the apparent meaning is that *al-abwab* (the gates) is literal. It is said that the levels are meant. It is said that the categories are meant, as one says, "So-and-so studies a gate of knowledge," meaning a category. Whoever said that what is meant by this is the punishment of the grave is farther from the truth, citing what has come: "The grave is a garden from the gardens of Paradise, or a pit from the pits of the Fire." When they refuted them in their claim, they were told that He is the Knower of their deeds, and so He is the one who recompenses them for them. Then they were commanded to enter, and the *lam* in *fa-la-bi'sa* (so evil is) is an emphatic *lam*, and it does not enter a past verb that is inflected, but it entered a rigid one because of its distance from verbs and its nearness to nouns. The one to whom the dispraise applies is omitted: that is, "so evil is the abode of the arrogant, it" (*hiya*), that is, Hell. The description of arrogance is evidence that its possessor deserves the Fire. And that is an allusion to His saying: ﴿Their hearts are deniers, and they are arrogant﴾ (al-Nahl 16:22).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 16, verses 30–42 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And it will be said to those who were mindful of God, "What has your Lord sent down?" They will say, "Good." For those who do good in this world there is good, and the abode of the Hereafter is better. How excellent is the abode of the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿Gardens of Eden which they will enter, with rivers flowing beneath them. For them therein is whatever they wish. Thus does God reward the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are good, saying, "Peace be upon you. Enter the Garden for what you used to do."﴾: The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of *mādhā* has already been discussed. However, if *dhā* is a relative pronoun (mawsūla), the answer does not correspond to the question, because *mādhā* is then a subject and predicate, or the answer is in the accusative case. This is permissible, but correspondence in i'rab is better. Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read *khayran* with a fatḥa, meaning: "He sent down good." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, why did he put this in the accusative and the first in the nominative?" I say: it is a distinction between the answer of the one who affirms and the answer of the one who denies. He means: when these people were asked, they did not hesitate, and they matched the answer to the question openly, making it the object of *al-inzāl* (the sending down). So they said: "Good." Those others evaded the answer to the question and said: "It is the fables of the ancients," which has nothing to do with sending down. End of quote. Zayd ibn ʿAli read *khayrun* with a ḍamma, meaning: "What was sent down is good," so this reading matches the interpretation of the one who makes *idhā* a relative pronoun, and does not match the one who makes *mādhā* accusative, because of the difference in i'rab. Although the difference is permissible, as we have mentioned. It is related that the tribes of the Arabs used to send, during the seasons of the markets, someone who would come to them with news of the Prophet (ﷺ). When the delegation came, the ones who divided the people would stop him and order him to turn back, and they would say: "If you do not meet him, it will be better for you." He would say: "I would be the worst delegate if I returned to my people without investigating the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and seeing him." So he would meet the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and they would inform him of his truthfulness and that he is a prophet sent. These are the ones who said "good." It is apparent that his saying "for those" falls under the statement, and it is an explanation of the good that God sent down in the revelation: that whoever does good in this world through obedience, for him is good in this world and bliss in the Hereafter by entering the Garden. Al-Zamakhshari said: *lillādhīna aḥsanū* and what follows it is a substitute (badal) for *khayran*, as a report of the saying of those who were mindful of God, meaning: they said this statement, so he placed before it the naming of it as good, then reported it. End of quote. A group said: it is the beginning of a speech from God, exalted, separate from what precedes it, and in meaning it is a promise connected with the mention of the good deeds of the God-fearing in their statement. The meaning of *ḥasana* ("good") is a reward in this world for their good deeds, and for them in the Hereafter is what is better than it. When he mentioned the state of the disbelievers in this world and the Hereafter, he mentioned the state of the believers in both abodes. It is apparent that the one specified for praise is the Gardens of Eden. Al-Zamakhshari said: *wa-la-niʿma dāru al-muttaqīn* means the abode of the Hereafter, so he omitted the one specified for praise because it was mentioned before. *Jannātu ʿadnin* is the predicate of an omitted subject. End of quote. Ibn ʿAtiyya said this, and before him al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari said it. They allowed that *jannātu ʿadnin* could be the subject, with the predicate being *yadkhulūnahā* (they will enter it). Zayd ibn Thabit and Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman read *jannāti ʿadnin* with a fatḥa, by al-ishtighāl (a construction in which the verb is elided and its object is pronominalized), meaning: they will enter the Gardens of Eden, they will enter them. This reading strengthens the i'rab of *jannātu ʿadnin* with a ḍamma, that it is the subject, and *yadkhulūnahā* is the predicate. Zayd ibn ʿAli read *wa-la-niʿmat dāri* with a tā' ḍamma, and *dār* in the genitive by idafa (construct), so *niʿmat* is the subject and *jannāt* is the predicate. Al-Sulami read *tadkhulūnahā* with a tā' of address. Isma'il ibn Ja'far, from Nafi', read *yadkhulūnahā* with a yā' of the third person, and the verb is in the passive voice. It is related from Abu Ja'far and Shayba: *tajrī*. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause). Al-Hawfi said: it is in the position of a na't (qualifying adjective) for *jannāt*. End of quote. So Ibn ʿAtiyya noticed that *jannātu ʿadnin* is definite, and al-Hawfi noticed that it is indefinite. This depends on the disagreement over whether *ʿadn* is a proper name or an indefinite noun meaning "residence." The *kāf* (in *kadhālika*) is in the position of accusative, as a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a reward like the reward of those who did good; He rewards. *Ṭayyibīn* is a ḥāl from the object of *tatawaffāhum* (take in death). The meaning: they are people of good condition, prepared for death and for the good that has no impurity in it. From this is: ﴿You are good, so enter it, abiding forever.﴾ Abu Muʿadh said: *ṭayyibīn* means pure from the ingratitude of the word of goodness. It is also said: *ṭayyibīn* means that their death is easy, with no hardship or pain in it, unlike what takes the soul of the disbeliever and the mixed (sinner). It is also said: their souls are good through their return to God, exalted. It is also said: their deeds and sayings are pure. It is also said: righteous. Al-Zamakhshari said: pure from wronging themselves through disbelief and sins, because it is in opposition to those who wronged themselves. *Yaqūlūna* is in the accusative as a ḥāl from the angels. The angels' greeting of peace upon them is a good news from God, exalted, and in this meaning there are sound hadiths. His saying ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqara: 2] refers to the time of taking their souls. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, and Mujahid. Most of them took the glad tidings of the Garden to be entry in a metaphorical sense. Muqatil and al-Hasan said: at the entry into the Garden, and it is the saying of the guardians of the Garden to them in the Hereafter: ﴿Peace be upon you, for what you patiently endured. How excellent is the final abode.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 24]. According to this view, *yaqūlūna* is a ḥāl muqaddara (a future-referring circumstantial clause), and the saying is not at the time of the taking in death. According to this, it is possible that *alladhīna* is a subject, and the predicate is *yaqūlūna*, meaning: they say to them, "Peace be upon you." What supports this view is their saying: "Enter the Garden," and at the time of death it is not said to them "Enter the Garden." So the taking in death here is the angels' taking of them at the time of the gathering. His saying ﴿for what you used to do﴾ apparently refers to entering the Garden by means of righteous deeds.

﴿They await nothing but that the angels come to them, or that the command of your Lord comes. Thus did those before them do, and God did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾ ﴿So the evils of what they did befell them, and what they used to mock surrounded them.﴾: The relation of this verse to what precedes it: when He mentioned the disbelievers' attack on the Qur'an by their saying "the fables of the ancients," then followed that with their threat and intimidation, then threatened those who described the Qur'an as good, He made clear that those disbelievers will not desist from their condition except that the angels come to them with the threat, or the command of God comes with the punishment of annihilation. Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read *yatiyahum* with a yā'. This is the reading of Ibn Thabat, Talha, and al-A'mash. The rest of the seven read it with a tā', in agreement with the feminine plural. The coming of the angels is to take souls, and they are those who wronged themselves. The command of your Lord is the punishment that annihilates, or the Resurrection. The *kāf* is in the accusative position, meaning: like their action in waiting for the angels and God's commands is the action of the disbelievers who precede them. It is also said: like their action in disbelief and persistence upon it, did those who went before them among the disbelievers do. It is also said: *fa'ala* here is a metonymy for their deception, as if it were said: like their deception in deferring the punishment, did those before them become deceived. The first view is more apparent, because of the indication of "Do they await," upon it. God did not wrong them by destroying them, but they wronged themselves by their disbelief and their denial, which required for them punishment in this world and the Hereafter. His saying *fa-aṣābahum* ("so befell them") is coordinated (ʿaṭf) on *faʿala*, and *mā ẓalamahumu* is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtirāḍ). *Sayyiʾāt* means the punishments of their disbelief. *Ḥāqa bihim* means surrounded them, the requital of their mockery. As for *Wa-qāla alladhīna ashrakū* ("And those who associated partners said"): the explanation of a verse like this has already been given at the end of al-Anʿām, so there is no need to discuss it again here. Al-Zamakhshari said: here, meaning that they associated partners with God and prohibited what God had made lawful, such as the *baḥīra* and the *sāʾiba* and others, then they attributed their action to God and said: "If God had willed, we would not have done it." This is exactly the doctrine of the Mujabbira (determinists). "Thus did those before them" means: they associated partners and prohibited what God made lawful. When they were alerted to the ugliness of their action and their associating partners with their Lord, the Messengers are only obligated to deliver the clear message. God does not will associating partners or sins, and by clear evidence and proof they make clear the falsity and ugliness of association, and God's freedom from the actions of servants; that they perform them by their own intention, will and choice, and God, exalted, prompts them to what is good, enables them to do it, restrains them from what is ugly, and threatens them for it. End of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila. This statement comes from one who affirms the existence of the Creator, exalted, and they are the majority, or from one who does not affirm His existence. On the assumption that the Lord whom Muhammad (ﷺ) worships and describes with knowledge and power knows our condition, this is a dispute from either of the two groups, and there is no mockery in it. Al-Zajjaj said: they said that as a form of mockery. Among the correspondences that deny the correspondence of the proofs to establish the argument from the opponent's position, mocking in that, is this.

[p. 490] ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying], "Worship Allah and avoid the Taghut (false deities and everything worshipped besides Allah)." Among them were those whom Allah guided, and among them were those upon whom error was justly decreed. So travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾ ﴿If you are eager for their guidance, indeed Allah does not guide those He leads astray, and they will have no helpers.﴾ ﴿And they swore by Allah their most emphatic oaths that Allah will not resurrect those who die. Yes, [He will], as a promise binding upon Him, true, but most people do not know.﴾ ﴿[He will resurrect them] so that He may make clear to them that about which they differ, and so that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars.﴾

Al-Zamakhshari said: He reinforced the refutation of the notion of evil fate and the course of wickedness by stating that there was no nation to which a messenger was not sent, commanding them with the good, which is faith and the worship of Allah, and with avoiding the evil, which is the Taghut. ﴿Among them were those whom Allah guided﴾, meaning He showed them kindness (lutf), because He knew them to be among the people of kindness. ﴿And among them were those upon whom error was justly decreed﴾, meaning that abandonment (khidhlan) and polytheism became firmly fixed upon them, [and this is] from [divine] kindness, because He knew them to be set upon disbelief, from whom no good would come.

﴿So travel through the earth and observe﴾ what I did to the deniers, so that no doubt remains for you. Indeed I do not decree evil nor will it, since I do what I do to the wicked; end of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school who held that Allah must act according to what is best and that humans create their own actions). When He said, ﴿Then upon the messengers is only the clear conveyance﴾, He explained this here: that He sent the messengers to worship Him and to avoid worshipping other than Him. Among them were those who took heed and Allah guided them, and among them were those who turned away and disbelieved. Then He referred them, for knowledge of this, to traveling through the earth, studying the nations, and standing at the punishment of the disbelieving deniers. Then He addressed His Prophet and informed him that the one whom error has been decreed upon, eagerness for his guidance will not benefit.

Al-Nakha'i recited "wa-in" (وإنْ) with an added waw, and so did al-Hasan. Abu Haywa recited "taḥraṣ" (تَحْرَصْ) with a fatḥa on the rā', the imperfect of "ḥaraṣa" (حَرِصَ) with a kasra, which is a dialectal form. The majority recited it with a kasra on the rā', the imperfect of "ḥaraṣa" (حَرَصَ) with a fatḥa, which is the dialect of the Ḥijāz. The two Ḥarams (Makki and Madani readers), the two ʿArabs, al-Hasan, al-Aʿraj, Mujahid, Shaybah, Shibl, Muzahim al-Khurasani, al-ʿUtaridi, and Ibn Sirin recited "lā yuhda" (لا يُهْدى) in the passive voice, with "man" (مَن) as the object whose subject was not named. The subject of "yuḍillu" (يُضِلُّ) is the pronoun of Allah, and the returning pronoun to "man" is omitted, its estimated form being: "whom Allah leads astray." The Kufans, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn al-Musayyab, and a group recited "yahdī" (يَهْدِي) in the active voice. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "yahdī" refers to Allah and "man" is the object. According to what al-Farra' reported, that "hadā" (هَدى) can mean "ihtadā" (اهْتَدى), being intransitive, in which case the subject is "man," meaning: whoever Allah leads astray will not be guided.

A group, including ʿAbd Allah [Ibn Mas'ud], recited "lā yahdi" (لا يَهِدِي) with a fatḥa on the yā' and a kasra on the hā' and dāl. Thus said Ibn ʿAṭiyya, meaning with the dāl doubled, and its origin is "yahtadī," which was assimilated, as in your saying "yakhtaṣimu" becoming "yakhṣimu." A group recited "yahdī" with a ḍamma on the yā' and a kasra on the dāl. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: this is weak. If it is established that "hadā" is intransitive with the meaning of "ihtadā," then it is not weak, since the transitivising hamza was added to the intransitive verb, and so the meaning is: He does not make guided one whom He has led astray. In the codex of Ubayy: "there is no guide for whom He has led astray." Al-Zamakhshari said: in the recitation of Ubayy: "indeed Allah has no guide for whom He leads astray and for whom He has led astray." It was also recited "yaḍilla" (يَضِلُّ) with a fatḥa on the yā'. He also said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was eager for the faith of Quraysh, and He informed him that they were among those upon whom error was decreed, and that He does not guide whom He leads astray, meaning: He does not show kindness to one whom He forsakes, because that would be vain, and Allah the Exalted is far above vanity, since it belongs to the category of ugly acts that are not permissible for Him; end of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah.

The pronoun in "lahum" (لَهم) refers to the meaning of "man," and the pronoun in "wa-aqsamū" (وأقْسَمُوا) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. It is reported from Abu al-ʿAliyah: it was revealed concerning a Muslim man who demanded a debt from a polytheist man. During what the Muslim said, which he had stored up for after death, the polytheist said, denying that you will be resurrected after death, "I swear by Allah that Allah will not resurrect whoever dies." So [Allah] answered: "Yes," rejecting what he had denied and emphasizing it with an oath. The estimated sense is: "Yes, He will resurrect him."

"Waʿdan" (وعْدًا) and "ḥaqqan" (حَقًّا) are in the accusative as two verbal nouns emphasizing what is indicated by "balā" (بَلى) of the omitted estimate, which is "yabʿathuhu" (He will resurrect him). Al-Ḥawfī said: "ḥaqqan" is an adjective of "waʿdan." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk recited "balā waʿdun ḥaqqun" (بَلى وعْدٌ حَقٌّ), with the estimate: "their resurrection is a promise upon Him that is true," and "ḥaqqun" is an adjective of "waʿdun."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "wa-aqsamū billāhi" (وأقْسَمُوا بِاللَّهِ) is conjoined to ﴿And those who associated said﴾, signifying that these two are great disbeliefs, described as true, deserving to be recorded and written down, exposing their sins to the will of Allah, and their denial of resurrection while swearing to it. He made clear that fulfilling this promise is a true and binding obligation upon Him. But most people do not know that they will be resurrected, or that it is a promise binding upon Allah, because they say: nothing is binding upon Allah, neither the reward of a doer nor anything else of the requirements of wisdom; end of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah. "Most people" are the disbelieving deniers of the resurrection.

As for the claim of the Shi'a (a sect who hold that Imam ʿAli and his descendants are the rightful successors to the Prophet) that the reference of this verse is only to ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, and that Allah will resurrect him in this world, it is a flimsy statement. The belief in the return (raj'ah, the return of certain dead people to this world before the Day of Resurrection) is false and a fabrication against Allah, in keeping with their habit. Ibn ʿAbbas and others refuted it.

The "lam" in "liyubayyina" (لِيُبَيِّنَ) is connected to the estimated verb after "balā," meaning: We will resurrect them so that He may make clear to them, as a man says: "I did not strike anyone," and the other says: "Yes, Zayd," meaning: I struck Zayd. The pronoun in the estimated "yabʿathuhum" (يَبْعَثُهم), and in "lahum," refers to the meaning of "man" in His saying "whoever dies," and it includes both believers and disbelievers. "That about which they differed" is the truth, and that they were liars in what they believed of setting up deities alongside Allah, denying the prophethoods, denying the resurrection, and other matters they were commanded to. He made clear to them that it is the religion of Allah, so they denied it and lied in attributing things to Allah the Exalted.

Al-Zamakhshari said: they lied in their saying: ﴿If Allah had willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him﴾, and in their saying: ﴿Allah will not resurrect whoever dies﴾; end of quote. In their saying there is the subtle influence of Mu'tazilite thought. It has been said: "liyubayyina" is connected to His saying: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger﴾, meaning: so that He may show them their disagreement, and that the disbelievers were in error before the coming of that messenger, lying in rejecting what the messengers brought.

﴿Indeed, Our word to a thing when We intend it is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ ﴿And those who emigrated for [the cause of] Allah after they had been wronged – We will surely settle them in this world in a good place. And the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew.﴾ ﴿Those who were patient and upon their Lord they rely.﴾

When their denial of resurrection was mentioned, and they emphasized it with an oath by Allah who brought them into being, and He answered them with His saying "Yes," and mentioned the truth of His promise in that regard, He clarified that whenever His will is connected to the existence of a thing, He brings it into existence. They acknowledged that He the Exalted is the creator of this world, its heavens and earth, and that His bringing that about was not dependent upon any prior material or tool. Just as He was able to originate creation at first, it must be that He is able to restore it. The explanation of His saying "Be, and it is" has already been given in al-Baqarah, so there is no need to repeat it.

The apparent reading is that the "lam" in "li-shayʾin" (لِشَيْءٍ) and in "lahu" (لَهُ) is for communication, like your saying: "I said to Zayd: stand up." Al-Zajjaj said: it is the "lam" of cause, meaning: for the sake of bringing a thing into existence, and likewise "lahu," meaning: for its sake. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: what the words of this verse contain of the sense of future and of beginning is only related to what is willed, not to the will itself, because the will and the command to it are eternal. Because of the willed things that come into existence and are future-oriented, He expressed it with "idhā" (إذا). As for His saying "li-shayʾin" (لِشَيْءٍ), it allows two interpretations: first, that since its existence is certain, it may be called a "thing" even while in a state of non-existence. Second, that His saying "li-shayʾin" is a notice of the examples He considers; whichever of them exists is willed, and it is told "Be," and it is; so it becomes an example of what comes later among matters by what came before. In this there is an escape from calling the non-existent a thing; end of quote. There is some abridgment in this. He also said: "idhā aradnāhu" (إذا أرَدْناهُ) is placed in the position of a willed thing, but He used these future-oriented expressions according to the fact that existing things come forth and appear one after another, as if He said: "when the willed [thing] appears." On this interpretation the following verses are explained: ﴿Allah will see your deeds﴾ [al-Tawbah: 105], and His saying: "that He may know those among you who believe," and similar wording, whose meaning is: what Allah the Exalted willed from eternity and knew occurs from you. His saying "an naqūla" (أنْ نَقُولَ) functions as a verbal noun, as if He said: "our saying," but "an" with the verb gives a sense of futurity not present in the verbal noun in most of its uses, and it may come in places where time is not intended, like this verse, and like His saying: ﴿And of His signs is that the heaven and earth stand by His command﴾ [al-Rum: 25], and other examples; end of quote. His saying "but 'an' with the verb" means the imperfect verb. His saying "in most of its uses" is not good; rather it indicates the future in all its uses. As for his saying "and it may come..." etc., this is not understood from the indication of "an" but from the attribution of the standing of heaven and earth to the command of Allah, because this is not restricted to the future rather than the past with respect to Him the Exalted. A parallel is ﴿Indeed Allah is ever, over all things, competent﴾ [al-Nisa': 33], where "kāna" (كانَ) indicates that the content of the sentence is connected to past time, and He is described by this attribute in past, present, and future. Restricting the verb to a time does not indicate its negation from other times.

"Those who emigrated": Qatadah said: it was revealed concerning the emigrants among the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ). Dawud ibn Abi Hind said: concerning Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl ibn ʿAmr. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: concerning Suhayb, Bilal, Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, and their likes, whom the polytheists tortured in Makkah, so Allah settled them in Madinah. Upon this difference in the occasion of revelation, the meaning of His saying "those who emigrated" is to be understood. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: when Allah mentioned the disbelievers of Makkah who swore that Allah will not resurrect whoever dies, and answered their claim, He mentioned the believers of Makkah contemporary with them, who are those who emigrated to the land of Abyssinia. This is the view of the majority and is the correct view regarding the occasion of the revelation, because the emigration to Madinah did not take place until after the time of the revelation of this verse; end of quote.

And those who emigrated (﴿والَّذِينَ هاجَرُوا﴾) is a general term covering the emigrants (al-muhajirun) in every case, so it includes the earliest and the latest of them. The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) recited ﴿لَنُبَوِّئِنَّهم﴾ (we will surely settle them). The apparent reading is that ﴿حَسَنَةٍ﴾ (good) is in the accusative as a qualifier (nat, adjective) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar, infinitive) indicated by the verb, meaning "a good settling." It has also been said that ﴿حَسَنَةٍ﴾ is in the accusative as a masdar not from the same root as the verb (ala ghayr al-sadr), because the meaning of ﴿لَنُبَوِّئِنَّهم فِي الدُّنْيا﴾ is "we will surely show them kindness in this world," so ﴿حَسَنَةٌ﴾ carries the meaning of "kindness" (ihsanan). Abu al-Baqa said: ﴿حَسَنَةً﴾ is a second object (maf'ul thani) of ﴿لَنُبَوِّئِنَّهم﴾, because its meaning is "we will surely give them," and it may also be a qualifier (sifa) of an omitted noun, meaning "a good abode." End of his words.

Al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, and Qatada said: "a good abode," which is Madinah. It has also been said that the implied phrase is "a good station" (manzilah hasanah), which is dominance over the people of Makkah who did wrong, over the Arabs as a whole, and over the people of the East and the West. Mujahid said: "good provision" (al-rizq al-hasan). Al-Dahhak said: "victory over their enemy." It has been said: "the conquests of lands that they took control of and the governorships they obtained in them." It has also been said: "the praise that remained for them in them, and the honor that came to their descendants in them." It has been said: "the good thing is everything praiseworthy that the emigrants attained."

Ali, Abdullah, Nu'aym ibn Maysara, and al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham recited ﴿لَنُثْوِيَنَّهم﴾ (we will surely settle them) with the letter tha' (ث) marked with three dots. This is the imperfect of athwa, which is derived with the causative hamza (hamzat al-ta'diyah) from thawa bil-makan, meaning "he stayed in the place." ﴿حَسَنَةً﴾ is in the accusative either by the assumption of "a good settling" (ithwatan hasanatan), or by the removal of the preposition (naz' al-khafid, dropping the particle), meaning "in a good [abode]," i.e., a good abode or a good station.

This emphatic announcement with an oath indicates the great status of emigration, because through it the strength of Islam became manifest, just as through the support of the Ansar its might was strengthened. The phrase ﴿فِي اللَّهِ﴾ (for the sake of Allah) is evidence that deeds must be sincere to Allah, and whoever emigrates for other than Allah, his emigration is toward what he emigrated for.

In the announcement about ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ with the omitted oath clause, which is indicated by the clause that is sworn to, there is evidence for the soundness of an oath clause occurring as the predicate of the subject (khabar lil-mubtada'), contrary to Tha'lab. Abu al-Baqa permitted ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ to be in the accusative by an omitted verb indicated by ﴿لَنُبَوِّئِنَّهم﴾, but this is not permissible, because one only interprets (by the verb) what it is permissible for it to govern. It is not permissible to say "Zaydan la-adribanna" (Zayd, I will surely strike), so it is not permissible to say "Zaydan la-adribannahu" (Zayd, I will surely strike him).

From Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: when he gave a man from among the emigrants his share, he would say: "Take it, may Allah bless it for you. This is what He promised you in this world, and what He has stored up for you in the Hereafter is greater." And the reward of the Hereafter (﴿ولَأجْرُ الآخِرَةِ﴾) is greater, meaning the reward of the abode of the Hereafter is greater, i.e., greater than anyone could know before witnessing it, as He said: ﴿وإذا رَأيْتَ ثَمَّ رَأيْتَ نَعِيمًا ومُلْكًا كَبِيرًا﴾ [Al-Insan: 20] (And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great dominion).

The pronoun in ﴿يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (they knew) refers to the disbelievers, meaning: if they knew that Allah gathers for these oppressed ones in their hands both this world and the Hereafter, they would have desired their religion. It has been said that it refers to the believers, meaning: if they knew that, they would have increased their striving and patience.

As for ﴿والَّذِينَ صَبَرُوا﴾ (those who were patient), it is in accordance with their estimate: "those who," or "I mean those who were patient" over punishment, and over separation from the homeland, especially the sacred precinct of Allah, which is beloved to every believing heart, so how much more so for one whose birthplace it was? And over giving up the soul for the sake of Allah, and enduring estrangement in a land where he did not grow up, and among people whom he did not know, strangers even in lineage.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 16, verses 30–42 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And it will be said to those who were mindful of God, "What has your Lord sent down?" They will say, "Good." For those who do good in this world there is good, and the abode of the Hereafter is better. How excellent is the abode of the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿Gardens of Eden which they will enter, with rivers flowing beneath them. For them therein is whatever they wish. Thus does God reward the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are good, saying, "Peace be upon you. Enter the Garden for what you used to do."﴾: The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of *mādhā* has already been discussed. However, if *dhā* is a relative pronoun (mawsūla), the answer does not correspond to the question, because *mādhā* is then a subject and predicate, or the answer is in the accusative case. This is permissible, but correspondence in i'rab is better. Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read *khayran* with a fatḥa, meaning: "He sent down good." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, why did he put this in the accusative and the first in the nominative?" I say: it is a distinction between the answer of the one who affirms and the answer of the one who denies. He means: when these people were asked, they did not hesitate, and they matched the answer to the question openly, making it the object of *al-inzāl* (the sending down). So they said: "Good." Those others evaded the answer to the question and said: "It is the fables of the ancients," which has nothing to do with sending down. End of quote. Zayd ibn ʿAli read *khayrun* with a ḍamma, meaning: "What was sent down is good," so this reading matches the interpretation of the one who makes *idhā* a relative pronoun, and does not match the one who makes *mādhā* accusative, because of the difference in i'rab. Although the difference is permissible, as we have mentioned. It is related that the tribes of the Arabs used to send, during the seasons of the markets, someone who would come to them with news of the Prophet (ﷺ). When the delegation came, the ones who divided the people would stop him and order him to turn back, and they would say: "If you do not meet him, it will be better for you." He would say: "I would be the worst delegate if I returned to my people without investigating the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and seeing him." So he would meet the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and they would inform him of his truthfulness and that he is a prophet sent. These are the ones who said "good." It is apparent that his saying "for those" falls under the statement, and it is an explanation of the good that God sent down in the revelation: that whoever does good in this world through obedience, for him is good in this world and bliss in the Hereafter by entering the Garden. Al-Zamakhshari said: *lillādhīna aḥsanū* and what follows it is a substitute (badal) for *khayran*, as a report of the saying of those who were mindful of God, meaning: they said this statement, so he placed before it the naming of it as good, then reported it. End of quote. A group said: it is the beginning of a speech from God, exalted, separate from what precedes it, and in meaning it is a promise connected with the mention of the good deeds of the God-fearing in their statement. The meaning of *ḥasana* ("good") is a reward in this world for their good deeds, and for them in the Hereafter is what is better than it. When he mentioned the state of the disbelievers in this world and the Hereafter, he mentioned the state of the believers in both abodes. It is apparent that the one specified for praise is the Gardens of Eden. Al-Zamakhshari said: *wa-la-niʿma dāru al-muttaqīn* means the abode of the Hereafter, so he omitted the one specified for praise because it was mentioned before. *Jannātu ʿadnin* is the predicate of an omitted subject. End of quote. Ibn ʿAtiyya said this, and before him al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari said it. They allowed that *jannātu ʿadnin* could be the subject, with the predicate being *yadkhulūnahā* (they will enter it). Zayd ibn Thabit and Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman read *jannāti ʿadnin* with a fatḥa, by al-ishtighāl (a construction in which the verb is elided and its object is pronominalized), meaning: they will enter the Gardens of Eden, they will enter them. This reading strengthens the i'rab of *jannātu ʿadnin* with a ḍamma, that it is the subject, and *yadkhulūnahā* is the predicate. Zayd ibn ʿAli read *wa-la-niʿmat dāri* with a tā' ḍamma, and *dār* in the genitive by idafa (construct), so *niʿmat* is the subject and *jannāt* is the predicate. Al-Sulami read *tadkhulūnahā* with a tā' of address. Isma'il ibn Ja'far, from Nafi', read *yadkhulūnahā* with a yā' of the third person, and the verb is in the passive voice. It is related from Abu Ja'far and Shayba: *tajrī*. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause). Al-Hawfi said: it is in the position of a na't (qualifying adjective) for *jannāt*. End of quote. So Ibn ʿAtiyya noticed that *jannātu ʿadnin* is definite, and al-Hawfi noticed that it is indefinite. This depends on the disagreement over whether *ʿadn* is a proper name or an indefinite noun meaning "residence." The *kāf* (in *kadhālika*) is in the position of accusative, as a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a reward like the reward of those who did good; He rewards. *Ṭayyibīn* is a ḥāl from the object of *tatawaffāhum* (take in death). The meaning: they are people of good condition, prepared for death and for the good that has no impurity in it. From this is: ﴿You are good, so enter it, abiding forever.﴾ Abu Muʿadh said: *ṭayyibīn* means pure from the ingratitude of the word of goodness. It is also said: *ṭayyibīn* means that their death is easy, with no hardship or pain in it, unlike what takes the soul of the disbeliever and the mixed (sinner). It is also said: their souls are good through their return to God, exalted. It is also said: their deeds and sayings are pure. It is also said: righteous. Al-Zamakhshari said: pure from wronging themselves through disbelief and sins, because it is in opposition to those who wronged themselves. *Yaqūlūna* is in the accusative as a ḥāl from the angels. The angels' greeting of peace upon them is a good news from God, exalted, and in this meaning there are sound hadiths. His saying ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqara: 2] refers to the time of taking their souls. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, and Mujahid. Most of them took the glad tidings of the Garden to be entry in a metaphorical sense. Muqatil and al-Hasan said: at the entry into the Garden, and it is the saying of the guardians of the Garden to them in the Hereafter: ﴿Peace be upon you, for what you patiently endured. How excellent is the final abode.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 24]. According to this view, *yaqūlūna* is a ḥāl muqaddara (a future-referring circumstantial clause), and the saying is not at the time of the taking in death. According to this, it is possible that *alladhīna* is a subject, and the predicate is *yaqūlūna*, meaning: they say to them, "Peace be upon you." What supports this view is their saying: "Enter the Garden," and at the time of death it is not said to them "Enter the Garden." So the taking in death here is the angels' taking of them at the time of the gathering. His saying ﴿for what you used to do﴾ apparently refers to entering the Garden by means of righteous deeds.

﴿They await nothing but that the angels come to them, or that the command of your Lord comes. Thus did those before them do, and God did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾ ﴿So the evils of what they did befell them, and what they used to mock surrounded them.﴾: The relation of this verse to what precedes it: when He mentioned the disbelievers' attack on the Qur'an by their saying "the fables of the ancients," then followed that with their threat and intimidation, then threatened those who described the Qur'an as good, He made clear that those disbelievers will not desist from their condition except that the angels come to them with the threat, or the command of God comes with the punishment of annihilation. Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read *yatiyahum* with a yā'. This is the reading of Ibn Thabat, Talha, and al-A'mash. The rest of the seven read it with a tā', in agreement with the feminine plural. The coming of the angels is to take souls, and they are those who wronged themselves. The command of your Lord is the punishment that annihilates, or the Resurrection. The *kāf* is in the accusative position, meaning: like their action in waiting for the angels and God's commands is the action of the disbelievers who precede them. It is also said: like their action in disbelief and persistence upon it, did those who went before them among the disbelievers do. It is also said: *fa'ala* here is a metonymy for their deception, as if it were said: like their deception in deferring the punishment, did those before them become deceived. The first view is more apparent, because of the indication of "Do they await," upon it. God did not wrong them by destroying them, but they wronged themselves by their disbelief and their denial, which required for them punishment in this world and the Hereafter. His saying *fa-aṣābahum* ("so befell them") is coordinated (ʿaṭf) on *faʿala*, and *mā ẓalamahumu* is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtirāḍ). *Sayyiʾāt* means the punishments of their disbelief. *Ḥāqa bihim* means surrounded them, the requital of their mockery. As for *Wa-qāla alladhīna ashrakū* ("And those who associated partners said"): the explanation of a verse like this has already been given at the end of al-Anʿām, so there is no need to discuss it again here. Al-Zamakhshari said: here, meaning that they associated partners with God and prohibited what God had made lawful, such as the *baḥīra* and the *sāʾiba* and others, then they attributed their action to God and said: "If God had willed, we would not have done it." This is exactly the doctrine of the Mujabbira (determinists). "Thus did those before them" means: they associated partners and prohibited what God made lawful. When they were alerted to the ugliness of their action and their associating partners with their Lord, the Messengers are only obligated to deliver the clear message. God does not will associating partners or sins, and by clear evidence and proof they make clear the falsity and ugliness of association, and God's freedom from the actions of servants; that they perform them by their own intention, will and choice, and God, exalted, prompts them to what is good, enables them to do it, restrains them from what is ugly, and threatens them for it. End of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila. This statement comes from one who affirms the existence of the Creator, exalted, and they are the majority, or from one who does not affirm His existence. On the assumption that the Lord whom Muhammad (ﷺ) worships and describes with knowledge and power knows our condition, this is a dispute from either of the two groups, and there is no mockery in it. Al-Zajjaj said: they said that as a form of mockery. Among the correspondences that deny the correspondence of the proofs to establish the argument from the opponent's position, mocking in that, is this.

[p. 490] ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying], "Worship Allah and avoid the Taghut (false deities and everything worshipped besides Allah)." Among them were those whom Allah guided, and among them were those upon whom error was justly decreed. So travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾ ﴿If you are eager for their guidance, indeed Allah does not guide those He leads astray, and they will have no helpers.﴾ ﴿And they swore by Allah their most emphatic oaths that Allah will not resurrect those who die. Yes, [He will], as a promise binding upon Him, true, but most people do not know.﴾ ﴿[He will resurrect them] so that He may make clear to them that about which they differ, and so that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars.﴾

Al-Zamakhshari said: He reinforced the refutation of the notion of evil fate and the course of wickedness by stating that there was no nation to which a messenger was not sent, commanding them with the good, which is faith and the worship of Allah, and with avoiding the evil, which is the Taghut. ﴿Among them were those whom Allah guided﴾, meaning He showed them kindness (lutf), because He knew them to be among the people of kindness. ﴿And among them were those upon whom error was justly decreed﴾, meaning that abandonment (khidhlan) and polytheism became firmly fixed upon them, [and this is] from [divine] kindness, because He knew them to be set upon disbelief, from whom no good would come.

﴿So travel through the earth and observe﴾ what I did to the deniers, so that no doubt remains for you. Indeed I do not decree evil nor will it, since I do what I do to the wicked; end of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school who held that Allah must act according to what is best and that humans create their own actions). When He said, ﴿Then upon the messengers is only the clear conveyance﴾, He explained this here: that He sent the messengers to worship Him and to avoid worshipping other than Him. Among them were those who took heed and Allah guided them, and among them were those who turned away and disbelieved. Then He referred them, for knowledge of this, to traveling through the earth, studying the nations, and standing at the punishment of the disbelieving deniers. Then He addressed His Prophet and informed him that the one whom error has been decreed upon, eagerness for his guidance will not benefit.

Al-Nakha'i recited "wa-in" (وإنْ) with an added waw, and so did al-Hasan. Abu Haywa recited "taḥraṣ" (تَحْرَصْ) with a fatḥa on the rā', the imperfect of "ḥaraṣa" (حَرِصَ) with a kasra, which is a dialectal form. The majority recited it with a kasra on the rā', the imperfect of "ḥaraṣa" (حَرَصَ) with a fatḥa, which is the dialect of the Ḥijāz. The two Ḥarams (Makki and Madani readers), the two ʿArabs, al-Hasan, al-Aʿraj, Mujahid, Shaybah, Shibl, Muzahim al-Khurasani, al-ʿUtaridi, and Ibn Sirin recited "lā yuhda" (لا يُهْدى) in the passive voice, with "man" (مَن) as the object whose subject was not named. The subject of "yuḍillu" (يُضِلُّ) is the pronoun of Allah, and the returning pronoun to "man" is omitted, its estimated form being: "whom Allah leads astray." The Kufans, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn al-Musayyab, and a group recited "yahdī" (يَهْدِي) in the active voice. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "yahdī" refers to Allah and "man" is the object. According to what al-Farra' reported, that "hadā" (هَدى) can mean "ihtadā" (اهْتَدى), being intransitive, in which case the subject is "man," meaning: whoever Allah leads astray will not be guided.

A group, including ʿAbd Allah [Ibn Mas'ud], recited "lā yahdi" (لا يَهِدِي) with a fatḥa on the yā' and a kasra on the hā' and dāl. Thus said Ibn ʿAṭiyya, meaning with the dāl doubled, and its origin is "yahtadī," which was assimilated, as in your saying "yakhtaṣimu" becoming "yakhṣimu." A group recited "yahdī" with a ḍamma on the yā' and a kasra on the dāl. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: this is weak. If it is established that "hadā" is intransitive with the meaning of "ihtadā," then it is not weak, since the transitivising hamza was added to the intransitive verb, and so the meaning is: He does not make guided one whom He has led astray. In the codex of Ubayy: "there is no guide for whom He has led astray." Al-Zamakhshari said: in the recitation of Ubayy: "indeed Allah has no guide for whom He leads astray and for whom He has led astray." It was also recited "yaḍilla" (يَضِلُّ) with a fatḥa on the yā'. He also said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was eager for the faith of Quraysh, and He informed him that they were among those upon whom error was decreed, and that He does not guide whom He leads astray, meaning: He does not show kindness to one whom He forsakes, because that would be vain, and Allah the Exalted is far above vanity, since it belongs to the category of ugly acts that are not permissible for Him; end of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah.

The pronoun in "lahum" (لَهم) refers to the meaning of "man," and the pronoun in "wa-aqsamū" (وأقْسَمُوا) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. It is reported from Abu al-ʿAliyah: it was revealed concerning a Muslim man who demanded a debt from a polytheist man. During what the Muslim said, which he had stored up for after death, the polytheist said, denying that you will be resurrected after death, "I swear by Allah that Allah will not resurrect whoever dies." So [Allah] answered: "Yes," rejecting what he had denied and emphasizing it with an oath. The estimated sense is: "Yes, He will resurrect him."

"Waʿdan" (وعْدًا) and "ḥaqqan" (حَقًّا) are in the accusative as two verbal nouns emphasizing what is indicated by "balā" (بَلى) of the omitted estimate, which is "yabʿathuhu" (He will resurrect him). Al-Ḥawfī said: "ḥaqqan" is an adjective of "waʿdan." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk recited "balā waʿdun ḥaqqun" (بَلى وعْدٌ حَقٌّ), with the estimate: "their resurrection is a promise upon Him that is true," and "ḥaqqun" is an adjective of "waʿdun."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "wa-aqsamū billāhi" (وأقْسَمُوا بِاللَّهِ) is conjoined to ﴿And those who associated said﴾, signifying that these two are great disbeliefs, described as true, deserving to be recorded and written down, exposing their sins to the will of Allah, and their denial of resurrection while swearing to it. He made clear that fulfilling this promise is a true and binding obligation upon Him. But most people do not know that they will be resurrected, or that it is a promise binding upon Allah, because they say: nothing is binding upon Allah, neither the reward of a doer nor anything else of the requirements of wisdom; end of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah. "Most people" are the disbelieving deniers of the resurrection.

As for the claim of the Shi'a (a sect who hold that Imam ʿAli and his descendants are the rightful successors to the Prophet) that the reference of this verse is only to ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, and that Allah will resurrect him in this world, it is a flimsy statement. The belief in the return (raj'ah, the return of certain dead people to this world before the Day of Resurrection) is false and a fabrication against Allah, in keeping with their habit. Ibn ʿAbbas and others refuted it.

The "lam" in "liyubayyina" (لِيُبَيِّنَ) is connected to the estimated verb after "balā," meaning: We will resurrect them so that He may make clear to them, as a man says: "I did not strike anyone," and the other says: "Yes, Zayd," meaning: I struck Zayd. The pronoun in the estimated "yabʿathuhum" (يَبْعَثُهم), and in "lahum," refers to the meaning of "man" in His saying "whoever dies," and it includes both believers and disbelievers. "That about which they differed" is the truth, and that they were liars in what they believed of setting up deities alongside Allah, denying the prophethoods, denying the resurrection, and other matters they were commanded to. He made clear to them that it is the religion of Allah, so they denied it and lied in attributing things to Allah the Exalted.

Al-Zamakhshari said: they lied in their saying: ﴿If Allah had willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him﴾, and in their saying: ﴿Allah will not resurrect whoever dies﴾; end of quote. In their saying there is the subtle influence of Mu'tazilite thought. It has been said: "liyubayyina" is connected to His saying: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger﴾, meaning: so that He may show them their disagreement, and that the disbelievers were in error before the coming of that messenger, lying in rejecting what the messengers brought.

﴿Indeed, Our word to a thing when We intend it is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ ﴿And those who emigrated for [the cause of] Allah after they had been wronged – We will surely settle them in this world in a good place. And the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew.﴾ ﴿Those who were patient and upon their Lord they rely.﴾

When their denial of resurrection was mentioned, and they emphasized it with an oath by Allah who brought them into being, and He answered them with His saying "Yes," and mentioned the truth of His promise in that regard, He clarified that whenever His will is connected to the existence of a thing, He brings it into existence. They acknowledged that He the Exalted is the creator of this world, its heavens and earth, and that His bringing that about was not dependent upon any prior material or tool. Just as He was able to originate creation at first, it must be that He is able to restore it. The explanation of His saying "Be, and it is" has already been given in al-Baqarah, so there is no need to repeat it.

The apparent reading is that the "lam" in "li-shayʾin" (لِشَيْءٍ) and in "lahu" (لَهُ) is for communication, like your saying: "I said to Zayd: stand up." Al-Zajjaj said: it is the "lam" of cause, meaning: for the sake of bringing a thing into existence, and likewise "lahu," meaning: for its sake. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: what the words of this verse contain of the sense of future and of beginning is only related to what is willed, not to the will itself, because the will and the command to it are eternal. Because of the willed things that come into existence and are future-oriented, He expressed it with "idhā" (إذا). As for His saying "li-shayʾin" (لِشَيْءٍ), it allows two interpretations: first, that since its existence is certain, it may be called a "thing" even while in a state of non-existence. Second, that His saying "li-shayʾin" is a notice of the examples He considers; whichever of them exists is willed, and it is told "Be," and it is; so it becomes an example of what comes later among matters by what came before. In this there is an escape from calling the non-existent a thing; end of quote. There is some abridgment in this. He also said: "idhā aradnāhu" (إذا أرَدْناهُ) is placed in the position of a willed thing, but He used these future-oriented expressions according to the fact that existing things come forth and appear one after another, as if He said: "when the willed [thing] appears." On this interpretation the following verses are explained: ﴿Allah will see your deeds﴾ [al-Tawbah: 105], and His saying: "that He may know those among you who believe," and similar wording, whose meaning is: what Allah the Exalted willed from eternity and knew occurs from you. His saying "an naqūla" (أنْ نَقُولَ) functions as a verbal noun, as if He said: "our saying," but "an" with the verb gives a sense of futurity not present in the verbal noun in most of its uses, and it may come in places where time is not intended, like this verse, and like His saying: ﴿And of His signs is that the heaven and earth stand by His command﴾ [al-Rum: 25], and other examples; end of quote. His saying "but 'an' with the verb" means the imperfect verb. His saying "in most of its uses" is not good; rather it indicates the future in all its uses. As for his saying "and it may come..." etc., this is not understood from the indication of "an" but from the attribution of the standing of heaven and earth to the command of Allah, because this is not restricted to the future rather than the past with respect to Him the Exalted. A parallel is ﴿Indeed Allah is ever, over all things, competent﴾ [al-Nisa': 33], where "kāna" (كانَ) indicates that the content of the sentence is connected to past time, and He is described by this attribute in past, present, and future. Restricting the verb to a time does not indicate its negation from other times.

"Those who emigrated": Qatadah said: it was revealed concerning the emigrants among the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ). Dawud ibn Abi Hind said: concerning Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl ibn ʿAmr. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: concerning Suhayb, Bilal, Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, and their likes, whom the polytheists tortured in Makkah, so Allah settled them in Madinah. Upon this difference in the occasion of revelation, the meaning of His saying "those who emigrated" is to be understood. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: when Allah mentioned the disbelievers of Makkah who swore that Allah will not resurrect whoever dies, and answered their claim, He mentioned the believers of Makkah contemporary with them, who are those who emigrated to the land of Abyssinia. This is the view of the majority and is the correct view regarding the occasion of the revelation, because the emigration to Madinah did not take place until after the time of the revelation of this verse; end of quote.

And those who emigrated (﴿والَّذِينَ هاجَرُوا﴾) is a general term covering the emigrants (al-muhajirun) in every case, so it includes the earliest and the latest of them. The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) recited ﴿لَنُبَوِّئِنَّهم﴾ (we will surely settle them). The apparent reading is that ﴿حَسَنَةٍ﴾ (good) is in the accusative as a qualifier (nat, adjective) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar, infinitive) indicated by the verb, meaning "a good settling." It has also been said that ﴿حَسَنَةٍ﴾ is in the accusative as a masdar not from the same root as the verb (ala ghayr al-sadr), because the meaning of ﴿لَنُبَوِّئِنَّهم فِي الدُّنْيا﴾ is "we will surely show them kindness in this world," so ﴿حَسَنَةٌ﴾ carries the meaning of "kindness" (ihsanan). Abu al-Baqa said: ﴿حَسَنَةً﴾ is a second object (maf'ul thani) of ﴿لَنُبَوِّئِنَّهم﴾, because its meaning is "we will surely give them," and it may also be a qualifier (sifa) of an omitted noun, meaning "a good abode." End of his words.

Al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, and Qatada said: "a good abode," which is Madinah. It has also been said that the implied phrase is "a good station" (manzilah hasanah), which is dominance over the people of Makkah who did wrong, over the Arabs as a whole, and over the people of the East and the West. Mujahid said: "good provision" (al-rizq al-hasan). Al-Dahhak said: "victory over their enemy." It has been said: "the conquests of lands that they took control of and the governorships they obtained in them." It has also been said: "the praise that remained for them in them, and the honor that came to their descendants in them." It has been said: "the good thing is everything praiseworthy that the emigrants attained."

Ali, Abdullah, Nu'aym ibn Maysara, and al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham recited ﴿لَنُثْوِيَنَّهم﴾ (we will surely settle them) with the letter tha' (ث) marked with three dots. This is the imperfect of athwa, which is derived with the causative hamza (hamzat al-ta'diyah) from thawa bil-makan, meaning "he stayed in the place." ﴿حَسَنَةً﴾ is in the accusative either by the assumption of "a good settling" (ithwatan hasanatan), or by the removal of the preposition (naz' al-khafid, dropping the particle), meaning "in a good [abode]," i.e., a good abode or a good station.

This emphatic announcement with an oath indicates the great status of emigration, because through it the strength of Islam became manifest, just as through the support of the Ansar its might was strengthened. The phrase ﴿فِي اللَّهِ﴾ (for the sake of Allah) is evidence that deeds must be sincere to Allah, and whoever emigrates for other than Allah, his emigration is toward what he emigrated for.

In the announcement about ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ with the omitted oath clause, which is indicated by the clause that is sworn to, there is evidence for the soundness of an oath clause occurring as the predicate of the subject (khabar lil-mubtada'), contrary to Tha'lab. Abu al-Baqa permitted ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ to be in the accusative by an omitted verb indicated by ﴿لَنُبَوِّئِنَّهم﴾, but this is not permissible, because one only interprets (by the verb) what it is permissible for it to govern. It is not permissible to say "Zaydan la-adribanna" (Zayd, I will surely strike), so it is not permissible to say "Zaydan la-adribannahu" (Zayd, I will surely strike him).

From Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: when he gave a man from among the emigrants his share, he would say: "Take it, may Allah bless it for you. This is what He promised you in this world, and what He has stored up for you in the Hereafter is greater." And the reward of the Hereafter (﴿ولَأجْرُ الآخِرَةِ﴾) is greater, meaning the reward of the abode of the Hereafter is greater, i.e., greater than anyone could know before witnessing it, as He said: ﴿وإذا رَأيْتَ ثَمَّ رَأيْتَ نَعِيمًا ومُلْكًا كَبِيرًا﴾ [Al-Insan: 20] (And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great dominion).

The pronoun in ﴿يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (they knew) refers to the disbelievers, meaning: if they knew that Allah gathers for these oppressed ones in their hands both this world and the Hereafter, they would have desired their religion. It has been said that it refers to the believers, meaning: if they knew that, they would have increased their striving and patience.

As for ﴿والَّذِينَ صَبَرُوا﴾ (those who were patient), it is in accordance with their estimate: "those who," or "I mean those who were patient" over punishment, and over separation from the homeland, especially the sacred precinct of Allah, which is beloved to every believing heart, so how much more so for one whose birthplace it was? And over giving up the soul for the sake of Allah, and enduring estrangement in a land where he did not grow up, and among people whom he did not know, strangers even in lineage.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 16, verses 30–42 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And it will be said to those who were mindful of God, "What has your Lord sent down?" They will say, "Good." For those who do good in this world there is good, and the abode of the Hereafter is better. How excellent is the abode of the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿Gardens of Eden which they will enter, with rivers flowing beneath them. For them therein is whatever they wish. Thus does God reward the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are good, saying, "Peace be upon you. Enter the Garden for what you used to do."﴾: The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of *mādhā* has already been discussed. However, if *dhā* is a relative pronoun (mawsūla), the answer does not correspond to the question, because *mādhā* is then a subject and predicate, or the answer is in the accusative case. This is permissible, but correspondence in i'rab is better. Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read *khayran* with a fatḥa, meaning: "He sent down good." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, why did he put this in the accusative and the first in the nominative?" I say: it is a distinction between the answer of the one who affirms and the answer of the one who denies. He means: when these people were asked, they did not hesitate, and they matched the answer to the question openly, making it the object of *al-inzāl* (the sending down). So they said: "Good." Those others evaded the answer to the question and said: "It is the fables of the ancients," which has nothing to do with sending down. End of quote. Zayd ibn ʿAli read *khayrun* with a ḍamma, meaning: "What was sent down is good," so this reading matches the interpretation of the one who makes *idhā* a relative pronoun, and does not match the one who makes *mādhā* accusative, because of the difference in i'rab. Although the difference is permissible, as we have mentioned. It is related that the tribes of the Arabs used to send, during the seasons of the markets, someone who would come to them with news of the Prophet (ﷺ). When the delegation came, the ones who divided the people would stop him and order him to turn back, and they would say: "If you do not meet him, it will be better for you." He would say: "I would be the worst delegate if I returned to my people without investigating the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and seeing him." So he would meet the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and they would inform him of his truthfulness and that he is a prophet sent. These are the ones who said "good." It is apparent that his saying "for those" falls under the statement, and it is an explanation of the good that God sent down in the revelation: that whoever does good in this world through obedience, for him is good in this world and bliss in the Hereafter by entering the Garden. Al-Zamakhshari said: *lillādhīna aḥsanū* and what follows it is a substitute (badal) for *khayran*, as a report of the saying of those who were mindful of God, meaning: they said this statement, so he placed before it the naming of it as good, then reported it. End of quote. A group said: it is the beginning of a speech from God, exalted, separate from what precedes it, and in meaning it is a promise connected with the mention of the good deeds of the God-fearing in their statement. The meaning of *ḥasana* ("good") is a reward in this world for their good deeds, and for them in the Hereafter is what is better than it. When he mentioned the state of the disbelievers in this world and the Hereafter, he mentioned the state of the believers in both abodes. It is apparent that the one specified for praise is the Gardens of Eden. Al-Zamakhshari said: *wa-la-niʿma dāru al-muttaqīn* means the abode of the Hereafter, so he omitted the one specified for praise because it was mentioned before. *Jannātu ʿadnin* is the predicate of an omitted subject. End of quote. Ibn ʿAtiyya said this, and before him al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari said it. They allowed that *jannātu ʿadnin* could be the subject, with the predicate being *yadkhulūnahā* (they will enter it). Zayd ibn Thabit and Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman read *jannāti ʿadnin* with a fatḥa, by al-ishtighāl (a construction in which the verb is elided and its object is pronominalized), meaning: they will enter the Gardens of Eden, they will enter them. This reading strengthens the i'rab of *jannātu ʿadnin* with a ḍamma, that it is the subject, and *yadkhulūnahā* is the predicate. Zayd ibn ʿAli read *wa-la-niʿmat dāri* with a tā' ḍamma, and *dār* in the genitive by idafa (construct), so *niʿmat* is the subject and *jannāt* is the predicate. Al-Sulami read *tadkhulūnahā* with a tā' of address. Isma'il ibn Ja'far, from Nafi', read *yadkhulūnahā* with a yā' of the third person, and the verb is in the passive voice. It is related from Abu Ja'far and Shayba: *tajrī*. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause). Al-Hawfi said: it is in the position of a na't (qualifying adjective) for *jannāt*. End of quote. So Ibn ʿAtiyya noticed that *jannātu ʿadnin* is definite, and al-Hawfi noticed that it is indefinite. This depends on the disagreement over whether *ʿadn* is a proper name or an indefinite noun meaning "residence." The *kāf* (in *kadhālika*) is in the position of accusative, as a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a reward like the reward of those who did good; He rewards. *Ṭayyibīn* is a ḥāl from the object of *tatawaffāhum* (take in death). The meaning: they are people of good condition, prepared for death and for the good that has no impurity in it. From this is: ﴿You are good, so enter it, abiding forever.﴾ Abu Muʿadh said: *ṭayyibīn* means pure from the ingratitude of the word of goodness. It is also said: *ṭayyibīn* means that their death is easy, with no hardship or pain in it, unlike what takes the soul of the disbeliever and the mixed (sinner). It is also said: their souls are good through their return to God, exalted. It is also said: their deeds and sayings are pure. It is also said: righteous. Al-Zamakhshari said: pure from wronging themselves through disbelief and sins, because it is in opposition to those who wronged themselves. *Yaqūlūna* is in the accusative as a ḥāl from the angels. The angels' greeting of peace upon them is a good news from God, exalted, and in this meaning there are sound hadiths. His saying ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqara: 2] refers to the time of taking their souls. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, and Mujahid. Most of them took the glad tidings of the Garden to be entry in a metaphorical sense. Muqatil and al-Hasan said: at the entry into the Garden, and it is the saying of the guardians of the Garden to them in the Hereafter: ﴿Peace be upon you, for what you patiently endured. How excellent is the final abode.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 24]. According to this view, *yaqūlūna* is a ḥāl muqaddara (a future-referring circumstantial clause), and the saying is not at the time of the taking in death. According to this, it is possible that *alladhīna* is a subject, and the predicate is *yaqūlūna*, meaning: they say to them, "Peace be upon you." What supports this view is their saying: "Enter the Garden," and at the time of death it is not said to them "Enter the Garden." So the taking in death here is the angels' taking of them at the time of the gathering. His saying ﴿for what you used to do﴾ apparently refers to entering the Garden by means of righteous deeds.

﴿They await nothing but that the angels come to them, or that the command of your Lord comes. Thus did those before them do, and God did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾ ﴿So the evils of what they did befell them, and what they used to mock surrounded them.﴾: The relation of this verse to what precedes it: when He mentioned the disbelievers' attack on the Qur'an by their saying "the fables of the ancients," then followed that with their threat and intimidation, then threatened those who described the Qur'an as good, He made clear that those disbelievers will not desist from their condition except that the angels come to them with the threat, or the command of God comes with the punishment of annihilation. Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read *yatiyahum* with a yā'. This is the reading of Ibn Thabat, Talha, and al-A'mash. The rest of the seven read it with a tā', in agreement with the feminine plural. The coming of the angels is to take souls, and they are those who wronged themselves. The command of your Lord is the punishment that annihilates, or the Resurrection. The *kāf* is in the accusative position, meaning: like their action in waiting for the angels and God's commands is the action of the disbelievers who precede them. It is also said: like their action in disbelief and persistence upon it, did those who went before them among the disbelievers do. It is also said: *fa'ala* here is a metonymy for their deception, as if it were said: like their deception in deferring the punishment, did those before them become deceived. The first view is more apparent, because of the indication of "Do they await," upon it. God did not wrong them by destroying them, but they wronged themselves by their disbelief and their denial, which required for them punishment in this world and the Hereafter. His saying *fa-aṣābahum* ("so befell them") is coordinated (ʿaṭf) on *faʿala*, and *mā ẓalamahumu* is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtirāḍ). *Sayyiʾāt* means the punishments of their disbelief. *Ḥāqa bihim* means surrounded them, the requital of their mockery. As for *Wa-qāla alladhīna ashrakū* ("And those who associated partners said"): the explanation of a verse like this has already been given at the end of al-Anʿām, so there is no need to discuss it again here. Al-Zamakhshari said: here, meaning that they associated partners with God and prohibited what God had made lawful, such as the *baḥīra* and the *sāʾiba* and others, then they attributed their action to God and said: "If God had willed, we would not have done it." This is exactly the doctrine of the Mujabbira (determinists). "Thus did those before them" means: they associated partners and prohibited what God made lawful. When they were alerted to the ugliness of their action and their associating partners with their Lord, the Messengers are only obligated to deliver the clear message. God does not will associating partners or sins, and by clear evidence and proof they make clear the falsity and ugliness of association, and God's freedom from the actions of servants; that they perform them by their own intention, will and choice, and God, exalted, prompts them to what is good, enables them to do it, restrains them from what is ugly, and threatens them for it. End of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila. This statement comes from one who affirms the existence of the Creator, exalted, and they are the majority, or from one who does not affirm His existence. On the assumption that the Lord whom Muhammad (ﷺ) worships and describes with knowledge and power knows our condition, this is a dispute from either of the two groups, and there is no mockery in it. Al-Zajjaj said: they said that as a form of mockery. Among the correspondences that deny the correspondence of the proofs to establish the argument from the opponent's position, mocking in that, is this.

[p. 490] ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying], "Worship Allah and avoid the Taghut (false deities and everything worshipped besides Allah)." Among them were those whom Allah guided, and among them were those upon whom error was justly decreed. So travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾ ﴿If you are eager for their guidance, indeed Allah does not guide those He leads astray, and they will have no helpers.﴾ ﴿And they swore by Allah their most emphatic oaths that Allah will not resurrect those who die. Yes, [He will], as a promise binding upon Him, true, but most people do not know.﴾ ﴿[He will resurrect them] so that He may make clear to them that about which they differ, and so that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars.﴾

Al-Zamakhshari said: He reinforced the refutation of the notion of evil fate and the course of wickedness by stating that there was no nation to which a messenger was not sent, commanding them with the good, which is faith and the worship of Allah, and with avoiding the evil, which is the Taghut. ﴿Among them were those whom Allah guided﴾, meaning He showed them kindness (lutf), because He knew them to be among the people of kindness. ﴿And among them were those upon whom error was justly decreed﴾, meaning that abandonment (khidhlan) and polytheism became firmly fixed upon them, [and this is] from [divine] kindness, because He knew them to be set upon disbelief, from whom no good would come.

﴿So travel through the earth and observe﴾ what I did to the deniers, so that no doubt remains for you. Indeed I do not decree evil nor will it, since I do what I do to the wicked; end of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school who held that Allah must act according to what is best and that humans create their own actions). When He said, ﴿Then upon the messengers is only the clear conveyance﴾, He explained this here: that He sent the messengers to worship Him and to avoid worshipping other than Him. Among them were those who took heed and Allah guided them, and among them were those who turned away and disbelieved. Then He referred them, for knowledge of this, to traveling through the earth, studying the nations, and standing at the punishment of the disbelieving deniers. Then He addressed His Prophet and informed him that the one whom error has been decreed upon, eagerness for his guidance will not benefit.

Al-Nakha'i recited "wa-in" (وإنْ) with an added waw, and so did al-Hasan. Abu Haywa recited "taḥraṣ" (تَحْرَصْ) with a fatḥa on the rā', the imperfect of "ḥaraṣa" (حَرِصَ) with a kasra, which is a dialectal form. The majority recited it with a kasra on the rā', the imperfect of "ḥaraṣa" (حَرَصَ) with a fatḥa, which is the dialect of the Ḥijāz. The two Ḥarams (Makki and Madani readers), the two ʿArabs, al-Hasan, al-Aʿraj, Mujahid, Shaybah, Shibl, Muzahim al-Khurasani, al-ʿUtaridi, and Ibn Sirin recited "lā yuhda" (لا يُهْدى) in the passive voice, with "man" (مَن) as the object whose subject was not named. The subject of "yuḍillu" (يُضِلُّ) is the pronoun of Allah, and the returning pronoun to "man" is omitted, its estimated form being: "whom Allah leads astray." The Kufans, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn al-Musayyab, and a group recited "yahdī" (يَهْدِي) in the active voice. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "yahdī" refers to Allah and "man" is the object. According to what al-Farra' reported, that "hadā" (هَدى) can mean "ihtadā" (اهْتَدى), being intransitive, in which case the subject is "man," meaning: whoever Allah leads astray will not be guided.

A group, including ʿAbd Allah [Ibn Mas'ud], recited "lā yahdi" (لا يَهِدِي) with a fatḥa on the yā' and a kasra on the hā' and dāl. Thus said Ibn ʿAṭiyya, meaning with the dāl doubled, and its origin is "yahtadī," which was assimilated, as in your saying "yakhtaṣimu" becoming "yakhṣimu." A group recited "yahdī" with a ḍamma on the yā' and a kasra on the dāl. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: this is weak. If it is established that "hadā" is intransitive with the meaning of "ihtadā," then it is not weak, since the transitivising hamza was added to the intransitive verb, and so the meaning is: He does not make guided one whom He has led astray. In the codex of Ubayy: "there is no guide for whom He has led astray." Al-Zamakhshari said: in the recitation of Ubayy: "indeed Allah has no guide for whom He leads astray and for whom He has led astray." It was also recited "yaḍilla" (يَضِلُّ) with a fatḥa on the yā'. He also said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was eager for the faith of Quraysh, and He informed him that they were among those upon whom error was decreed, and that He does not guide whom He leads astray, meaning: He does not show kindness to one whom He forsakes, because that would be vain, and Allah the Exalted is far above vanity, since it belongs to the category of ugly acts that are not permissible for Him; end of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah.

The pronoun in "lahum" (لَهم) refers to the meaning of "man," and the pronoun in "wa-aqsamū" (وأقْسَمُوا) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh.
