This takhawwuf means diminishing; it was said: from his deeds; it was said: he takes one after another, and both were narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Zajjaj said: He diminishes their fruits and wealth until He destroys them. It was said: ʿalā takhawwuf means: out of fear that He will punish them or pass them by; said by Qatadah. Al-Zamakhshari said: ʿalā takhawwuf: while they are fearing, and it is that He destroys a people before them so that they fear, and then He seizes them with punishment while they are in fear, expecting it; and this is contrary to His saying: "from where they do not perceive." End of quote. Al-Dahhak said it: He seizes one town so the other town is frightened. Ibn Bahr said: ʿalā takhawwuf is the opposite of suddenness, that is, upon the occurrence of states that are feared, such as winds, earthquakes and thunderbolts; and for this He concluded with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed your Lord is Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 7], because in that there is a respite and an extension of time, so repentance is possible in it. Al-Layth ibn Saʿd said: ʿalā takhawwuf means: hastily. It was also said: with a rebuke for what they have sent ahead; and this was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. Since He, Exalted is He, is able to do these things and did not hasten to them, it was fitting to describe Him with kindness and mercy.

﴿Have they not considered what things Allah has created, whose shadows incline to the right and the left, prostrating to Allah while they are humbled?﴾ ﴿To Allah prostrate whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures, and the angels, and they are not arrogant.﴾ ﴿They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded.﴾: When Exalted is He mentioned His power to punish the schemers and destroy them with kinds of seizing, He mentioned the obedience of what He created other than them and its submission, in contrast to the state of the schemers, to alert them that it is fitting, indeed obligatory, upon them to be obedient and submissive to His command. Al-Sulami, al-A'raj (p-496) and the two brothers read "awa lam tarawū" with the tā' of address, either as a general address to creation, begun as a statement, or, if it is a specific address, as meaning: "say to them." The rest of the seven read it with yā' as third person. It was also possible that the pronoun refers to those who schemed, and it was possible that it is a report about the responsible people; the first is more evident because of their prior mention. Abu ʿAmr, ʿIsa and Yaʿqub read "tatafayya'ū" with tā' as feminine; the rest of the seven with yā'. ʿIsa read "ẓilāluhu" as ẓulalahu, plural of ẓullah, like ḥullah and ḥulal. The seeing here is seeing of the heart by which contemplation occurs, but it is through the seeing of the eye. It was said: the interrogation here means rebuke. It was said: it may also mean wonder, and the sense is: "Be amazed at their taking partners with Allah, while they have seen these created things that display the wonders of His power and the strangeness of His craftsmanship, along with their knowledge that their gods which they took as partners cannot do anything at all." The clause "tatafayya'ū" is in the position of a qualifier; said by al-Hawfi, and this is the apparent view of Ibn ʿAtiyyah and al-Zamakhshari. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "min shay'" is a general term for everything that the qualifier in His saying "tatafayya'ū ẓilāluhu" requires, because that is a qualifier of what is presented for lesson among all the entities that have a shadow. Al-Zamakhshari said: "mā" is a relative pronoun linked to "khalq Allah," and it is vague, its clarification being "min shay' tatafayya'ū ẓilāluhu." Others said: the meaning is: from a thing that has a shadow, from a mountain, a tree, a building or an upright body; and His saying "tatafayya'ū ẓilāluhu" is a report about "min shay'," a description of it; and this report indicates that omitted description, which is that it has a shadow. "Tatafayya'ū" is "tatafa''alū" from al-fay', which is returning; it is said: "fā'a al-ẓill yafī'u," so it returns, and it returns after the sun has dispelled it. "Fā'a," when transitive, is with the hamzah as in His saying: ﴿what Allah restored to His Messenger﴾ [al-Hashr: 7], or with doubling as in: "fayyaʾa Allah al-ẓill, fa-tafayya'a"; and "tafayya'a" is of the category of intransitive reflexive, and it is intransitive, but Abu Tammam used it transitively, saying:
"I sought the spring of Rabi'ah, whose green pasture..., and I took shelter in a long shade for her."
That would need to be transmitted from Arabic usage as transitive. Al-Azhari said: the tafayyu' of shadows is their returning after midday; so tafayyu' occurs only in the evening, and what the sun has left, while the shadow is what occurs in the morning, which is what has not been reached by it.

The poet said:

؎Neither can you bear the shade of the forenoon's coolness, nor do you taste the afternoon shade of the evening's coolness.

Imru' al-Qays said:

؎Her eye turned toward the one near Darij, where the shade falls upon its gravel, overflowing.

From Ru'ba: "What the sun was upon and then left is *fay'* (afternoon shade), and what the sun was not upon is *zill* (shade). This is because the sun, from its rising until the time of zawal (the sun's decline after its zenith), abolishes the *zill*; when it declines, the shade returns and continues to grow until the sun sets." The well-known view is that *fay'* occurs only after zawal, while the consideration in this verse runs from the beginning of the day to its end. So the meaning of *tatafayya'u* (﴿يَتَفَيَّأُ﴾) is "moves about and inclines." He (the author) attributed *al-zilal* (shadows), which is plural, to a singular pronoun, because the pronoun refers to *ma* (what), which in meaning is plural, as in His saying: ﴿لِتَسْتَوُوا عَلى ظُهُورِهِ﴾ ("so that you may sit firmly upon its backs").

The author of *al-Lawami'* said: In the reading of ʿIsa, it is *ẓulalihi*. *Ẓill* (with a single *lam*, in the sense of shade) can mean a cloud, which is a body; with a *kasra* (*ẓill*), it means *fay'*, which is an accident. In the common reading, it is used metaphorically. ʿIsa therefore held that *tafayyu'* (returning), which concerns bodies, is more fitting. [Ended.] (p-٤٩٧) As for the common reading, it is by metaphor. End of quotation.

They discussed His saying ﴿عَنِ اليَمِينِ والشَّمائِلِ﴾ ("on the right and the left"), and there are two points. The first: what is meant by this? The second: what is the wisdom in using the singular *al-yamin* (right) and the plural *al-shama'il* (left)?

As for the first, they said: the right of the celestial sphere is the east, and its left is the west. These two names were assigned to these two sides because the stronger side of a person is his right, and from it the daily celestial motion appears, moving from the east to the west. Therefore the east is the right of the sphere and the west is its left. Accordingly, when the sun rises until it reaches the midpoint of the sphere, the shadows fall to the western side; if it descends from the midpoint of the sphere toward the western side, the shadows fall on the eastern side. This is the meaning of the shadows' shifting from right to left.

It was said: in a land whose latitude is less than the measure of a *mil* (a unit of distance), the sun in summer is to the right of the town, so the shadows fall on their right.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: "Have they not looked at what Allah has created of things which have shadows that shift from their right and their left, on each side and each of its two halves?" The use of "right and left" is a metaphor, drawn from the right and left of a person, for the two sides of a thing; that is, the shadows return from one side to another. End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: What is intended by the sign (*'ibra*) in this verse is every body that has a shadow, such as mountains, trees and other things. What has right and left in its arrangement is only a human being. But the mention of right and left here is by way of metaphorical usage without confusion; you assume: "possessing a right and a left," and you assume: "facing whichever direction you wish." Then you look at its shadow, and you see it inclining either toward the right or toward the left, and this occurs in every region of the world. This therefore covers the words of the verse, and there is in it figurative extension and breadth. As for the one who holds that the right is from the forenoon of zawal, and from zawal until sunset it is on the left, which is the view of Qatada and Ibn Jurayj, that applies only to someone who assumes facing the south. End of quotation.

As for the second point, al-Zamakhshari said: *al-yamin* is in the sense of *al-ayman* (the rights), so he made it, though singular, carry the sense of the plural, thereby matching *al-shama'il* in meaning, as in His saying: ﴿ويُوَلُّونَ الدُّبُرَ﴾ ("and they will turn their backs"), meaning "retreat."

Al-Farra' said: It is as if, when he uses the singular, he refers to one of the shadow-casting things; and when he uses the plural, he refers to all of them, because His saying ﴿ما خَلَقَ اللَّهِ مِن شَيْءٍ﴾ is a singular word whose meaning is plural. So he expressed one of them with a singular term, as in His saying: ﴿وجَعَلَ الظُّلُماتِ والنُّورَ﴾ ("and made the darknesses and the light") and His saying: ﴿خَتَمَ اللَّهُ عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ وعَلى سَمْعِهِمْ﴾ ("Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing").

It was said: if we interpret *al-yamin* as the east, then the point where the sun rises is one single point, so the right is one. As for *al-shama'il*, they are the deviations occurring in those shadows after they fall upon the earth, and these are many; therefore he expressed them with the plural form.

Al-Kirmani said: It is possible that by *al-shama'il* is meant the left, the front and the back, since the shadow shifts from all directions. It begins with the right, either because the shifting starts from it or out of seeking blessing by mentioning it. Then he put the rest into the form *al-shimal* (left), because of the opposition between right and left, and the front and back were given the status of the left because of their difference from the right. It was said: he used the singular for the right and the plural for the left, because the beginning is from the right, then it gradually contracts, state after state, so it has the sense of the plural. Thus the word *al-shimal* applies to every state, and it multiplies with the multiplication of states.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: What some people said, that the right is the first occurrence of shadow after zawal, and the last until sunset is from the left, and that therefore he used the singular for the right, is a confused statement and wrong in several respects.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: When you pray the dawn prayer, everything between the sun's rising and its setting is shadow. Then Allah sends the sun as a guide, and it draws the shadow toward itself. Accordingly, he interpreted the sun's circuit with the shadow on the right of one facing the south; then the deviation begins, and that is from the left, because it consists of many movements and disconnected shadows, so they are many lefts. Thus the shadow on the right was a single connected shadow, general to everything. End of quotation.

Our teacher, the professor Abu al-Hasan ʿAli ibn Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Kutami, known as Ibn al-Sa'igh, said: He used the singular and the plural with regard to the two extremes, because the shadow of the morning dwindles until only a little of it remains, so it appears to be in one direction. In the evening it is the reverse, (p-٤٩٨) since it spreads over all directions. Thus both extremes are taken into account in the verse. This is from the point of view of meaning. As for its wording, there is *muṭābaqa* (correspondence) in it: *sujjadan* is plural, and it corresponds to the plural *al-shama'il* because it is connected to it. Thus the verse contains a correspondence between wording and meaning, and the holding of both together is part of its inimitability. End of quotation.

The apparent reading is to take *al-zilal* (shadows) in their literal sense, and most commentators' discussions proceed on this basis. They said: When the sun rises while you face the qibla, the shadow is in front of you; when it rises higher, it is on your right; after that, it is behind you; and when you want sunset, it is on your left.

A group said: *al-zilal* here means the bodies themselves, which are the intended referents, and the Arabs sometimes refer to bodies by means of shadows. From this is the saying of ʿAbda ibn al-Tabib:

؎When we alight, we pitch the shade of tents, and the cooking-pots boil with meat for the people.

Tents are actually pitched, and from this is the saying of the poet:

؎Following the shadows' *afyā'* in the evening.

That is, the *afyā'* of the bodies. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: All of this is possible but not explicit, although Abu ʿAli established it. End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that prostration here is a figurative expression for submission: the shadows' inclining and turning in the way God wills is called "prostration" (sujud), just as one who gestures with his head toward the ground in humility is called "prostrating" (sajid). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Sujjadan (prostrating) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) of the shadows. Wahum dakhirun (while they are humbled) is a hal of the pronoun in zilaluhu (his shadows), because it has the sense of a plural, and it refers to whatever God created that has a shadow. It is pluralized with the wa-n ending because dukhur (humiliation) is an attribute of rational beings, or because among that whole group there are rational beings, so the masculine plural was given precedence. The meaning is: the shadows are submissive to God and not resistant to Him in what He has subjected them to, namely their shifting and their own movement. Dakhirah also means: humbled, submissive to God's acts upon them, not resisting; end of quotation."

Al-Zamakhshari thus differentiated between the two circumstantial clauses: he made sujjadan a hal of the shadows, and wahum dakhirun a hal of the pronoun in sujjadan. It could also be a second hal of the shadows, as when you say: "Zayd came riding, and he is laughing." Here wa-huwa dahik (and he is laughing) may be a hal of the pronoun in rakiban (riding), or it may be a hal of Zayd. The second possibility seems more apparent to me. The verb governing both circumstantial clauses is yatafayya'u (it turns, shifts), and 'an (from) is connected to it. This was also said by al-Hawfi. It has been said that it is in the position of a hal, as Abu al-Baqa said. It has also been said that 'an is a noun, meaning "the side of the right," in which case it is in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarf).

As for what al-Zamakhshari permitted, that wahum dakhirun is a hal of the pronoun in zilalihi (his shadows), according to the majority opinion (al-Jumhur) this is not permissible. It is the case of: "The servant of Hind came to me laughing (feminine)." Those who hold that when the mudaf (the noun in the construct) is a part or like a part, it is permissible, may say this here, since the shadows, although not a part of the bodies, are like a part, because their existence arises from the existence of the bodies.

A group held that prostration here is literal. Al-Dahhak said: "When the sun passes its zenith, everything prostrates before the qibla, from plants and trees; for this reason the righteous used to prefer praying at that time." Mujahid said: "Only the shadows prostrate, not the bodies." It is also reported from him: "When the sun passes its zenith, everything prostrates." Al-Hasan said: "As for your shadow, it prostrates to God; as for you, you do not prostrate to Him." It has been said: since the shadows are attached to the ground and fall upon it in the form of one prostrating, they are described as prostrating. But for prostration to be taken literally, meaning falling upon the ground as worship and intentionally, is far-fetched, since that requires life, knowledge, and the intention of worship.

Shadow is singled out for mention because it changes quickly, and change requires something other than itself that changes it and manages it. Since the prostration of shadows is most evident, it is mentioned first, and then the discussion moves to the prostration of what is in the heavens and the earth.

Min dabbah (of any creature that crawls): it may be an explanation of what is in the two places (heavens and earth), so that those in the heavens are creatures that crawl. It may also be an explanation of what is on the earth; for this reason Ibn 'Abbas said: "He means everything that crawls upon the earth."

He joined "and the angels" to "whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth," and they are included in the generality of "whatever" (ma), honoring and glorifying them. It may also be that by "those in the heavens" the intended meaning is their guardians (hafazah) who are on the earth, and by "what is in the heavens" their angels, in which case they are not included in the general term.

It has been said: in the verse of the shadows God showed that all inanimate things are submissive to God. He then showed that the most noble of existents, namely the angels, and the lowest of them, namely the creatures that crawl (al-dawabb), are all submissive to God Almighty, and this indicates that all of them are submissive to God Almighty.

It has been said: "dabbah" is a name for every physical animal that moves and crawls. When God Almighty distinguished the angels from the dabbah, we know that they are not among those that crawl; rather, they are spirits specially characterized by motion. End of quotation. This is a philosophical view.

Since there is a shared measure of prostration between the responsible (mukallafun) and others, namely submission to God's will, He joined them in it, even though they differ in the manner of prostration.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: why was ma used instead of man (who), to give precedence to the rational among the creatures that crawl over the others? I answer: if man had been used, there would have been no indication of precedence, and it would have applied only to rational beings. So what suits both rational beings and others was used, intending generality. End of quotation."

The apparent sense of the question is an acceptance that man may include rational beings and others by way of precedence, while the apparent sense of the answer restricts man to rational beings, and that what suits both rational beings and others is other than man. This is not an answer, because he raised the question on the premise of acceptance, then gave the answer on the basis of non-acceptance, so the sense becomes: man is given precedence by it, and the answer is not given precedence by it. This is in reality not an answer.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "yakhafun" (they fear) refers to those to whom prostration is attributed in "wa-lillahi yasjudu" (and to God prostrates). This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil said: "They fear" is an attribute of the angels specifically, so the pronoun refers to them.

Al-Kirmani said: "The angels are described as fearing, because they are able to disobey, even though they do not disobey."

The spatial sense of "above" (fawqiyyah) is impossible in relation to Him, Exalted. If you connect it to "yakhafun" (they fear), it requires the omission of a noun: that is, they fear His punishment coming from above them, since punishment only descends from above. If you connect it to "rabbihim" (their Lord), it is a hal of Him: that is, they fear their Lord being high over them, dominant, in accordance with His saying: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ [al-An'am 6:18], and ﴿And We are dominant over them﴾ [al-A'raf 7:127].

In attributing fear to those to whom prostration is attributed, or to the angels specifically, there is evidence that the angels are responsible like all other responsible beings, and that they are between fear and hope, governed by promise and threat, as God Almighty said: ﴿And they are fearful of Him﴾ [al-Anbiya 21:28]. And whoever among them says, "I am a god besides Him," that one We shall repay with Hell.

It has been said: the fear is the fear of majesty and awe.

The clause "yakhafun" may be a hal of the pronoun in "la yastakbirun" (they do not wax arrogant). It may also be an explanation of the negation of arrogance and an emphasis of it, because whoever fears God does not become arrogant toward His worship.

As for His saying: ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾, the believers do so according to the Law and obedience, while others among the animals do so by subjugation and by the decree that drives them toward what God Almighty has decreed.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 16, verse 43–50 (part 1 of 3):

﴿We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed. So ask the people of the reminder (ahl al-dhikr), if you do not know,﴾ ﴿with clear proofs and scriptures. And We have sent down to you the Reminder, so that you may make clear to mankind what has been sent down to them, and that they may reflect.﴾ ﴿Do those who devise evil deeds feel secure that Allah will cause the earth to swallow them, or that the punishment will come upon them from where they do not perceive?﴾ ﴿Or that He will seize them in their going back and forth, and they will not be able to escape?﴾ ﴿Or that He will seize them through gradual decrease? Indeed your Lord is Most Kind, Most Merciful.﴾: It was revealed concerning the polytheists of Makkah, who denied the prophethood of the Messenger (ﷺ), and said: "Allah is too great that His messenger should be a human being. Why did He not send an angel to us?" The explanation of this sentence has already been given at the end of Surah Yusuf. The meaning is: We reveal to them through the tongues of the angels. Al-Jumhur read yūḥā (with a yāʾ and a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ), a group read it with a yāʾ and a kasrah on the ḥāʾ; ʿAbd Allah, al-Sulami, Talhah and Hafs read it with a nūn and a kasrah. Ahl al-dhikr: the Jews and the Christians, said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and al-Hasan. Also from Mujahid: the Jews. The dhikr: the Torah, due to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We wrote in the Psalms after the Reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105]. And from ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and Salman. Al-Aʿmash and Ibn ʿUyaynah said: those among the Jews and Christians who embraced Islam. Al-Zajjaj said: it is general to whoever is ascribed knowledge. Abu Jaʿfar and Ibn Zayd said: the people of the Qur'an. This view is weakened, and so is the view of the one who says: those among the two groups who embraced Islam, because there is no proof against the disbelievers in the report of the believers, since they deny them. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: the most evident is that they are the Jews and Christians who did not embrace Islam, and they, in this noble verse, only report from the messengers about humans, and their report is a proof against these, for they have not ceased to confirm them, and they are not accused of testifying to them in our favour, because they are opponents at the dawn of the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is the breaking of their argument and their position, because we have been in need of the testimony of these people, whereas the truth is clear in itself. Quraysh had sent to the Jews of Yathrib asking them and seeking their guidance; end of quote. The better view is that His saying bi-l-bayyinat is connected to a implied element indicated by what precedes it, as if it was said: "Then were they sent?" He said: "We sent them with the clear proofs and the scriptures." Thus it is a two-sentence construction. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn ʿAtiyyah and others. It may also be connected to His saying: wa-mā arsalnā, and in this there are two possibilities: The first: that the intention is to place it before the exceptive particle, the sense being: "We did not send before you with the clear proofs and the scriptures except men," so that what follows "illa" is not two objects that are later both in wording and rank, included under the restriction of what precedes it; this was related by Ibn ʿAtiyyah from a group. The second possibility: that it is not intended to be placed earlier, but they both come after "illa" with the intention of restriction. This was said by al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari, and he began with it, saying: it is connected to arsalnā, included under the ruling of the exception together with rijālan, i.e., "We did not send except men with the clear proofs," like your saying: "I did not strike except Zayd with the whip," because its origin is "I struck Zayd with the whip." Abu al-Baqa' said: there is weakness in it, because what precedes "illa" does not govern what follows it when the sentence is complete with "illa" and what comes after it, except that it has come in poetry. The poet said:
"Would that they had punished their neighbour with fire, and none punishes with fire except Allah."
End of quote. What al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari permitted does not apply according to the school of the majority of the Basrans, because they do not permit that what comes after "illa" be anything other than an exception, or something excepted from, or a follower; and whatever is thought to be an object other than these three governed by what precedes "illa" is given a governing element. Al-Kisai permitted that it be an object governed by what precedes it: in the accusative, as in: "No one struck except Zayd ʿAmran"; in the genitive, as in: "No one passed except Zayd by ʿAmr"; and in the nominative, as in: "No one struck except Zayd ʿAmru." Ibn al-Anbari agreed with him regarding the nominative, and al-Akhfash regarding the adverbial phrase, the prepositional phrase and the circumstantial clause. So the view stated by al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari accords with the school of al-Kisai and al-Akhfash, and the proofs of these schools are mentioned in the science of grammar. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be a qualifier of rijālan, i.e., men associated with the clear proofs, so it is connected to an omitted element. This is a permissible view, because it is in the position of a qualifier for what follows "illa." So men are described as "to whom We reveal," and with that same governing element is "bi-l-bayyinat," just as you say: "I did not honour except a Muslim man associated with goodness." He also permitted that it be connected to yūḥā ilayhim, and that it be connected to lā yaʿlamūn. He said: on the basis that the conditional in the sense of rebuke and obligation is like the saying of a hired worker: "If I have worked for you, then give me my right." His saying: fa-s'alū ahl al-dhikr is a parenthetical insertion against the previous possibilities, meaning: among those he mentioned, other than the last possibility.

And: "We have sent down to you the Reminder" is the Qur'an, and it was called a reminder because it is an admonition and an alert for the heedless. It was also said: the Reminder is knowledge, what was sent down to them of the ambiguous and the allegorical, because the explicit text and the apparent meaning do not need clarification. Al-Zamakhshari said: of what they were commanded and forbidden, and promised and threatened. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "so that you may make clear" — by your recitation — through the explicit text of the Qur'an, what was sent down to them. It may be intended: "so that you may make clear" — by your detailed explanation and your exposition — what has become unclear; thus included in this is what the Sunnah makes clear of the matters of the Shariʿah, and this is the view of Mujahid; end of quote.

﴿And that they may reflect﴾: that is, with the intention that they may listen to its admonitions, so that they may take heed and ponder. As for "al-sayyiʿat": it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: the evil schemes, said by al-Zamakhshari; or it is an object of makarū, with makarū given the meaning of "did" and "worked," and "al-sayyiʿat" in this case means the sins of disbelief and other things; said by Qatadah. Or it is an object of amina, and it means the punishments that will afflict them; both were mentioned by Ibn ʿAtiyyah. According to this last view, "an yakhsifa" is a substitute for "al-sayyiʿat." In both views, the preceding word is an object of amina. The ones who devised (alladhina makarū) in the saying of most scholars are the people of Makkah, who schemed against the Messenger (ﷺ). Mujahid said: it is Nimrod. Al-khasf is the earth swallowing what is swallowed and its settling with it downward. Al-Naqqash mentioned that the sinking into the earth occurred among this nation as it did to Qarun, and it was reported to us that a mixed group of people from the lands of the Romans were swallowed by the earth; and when its people sensed that, most of them fled, and some merchants who used to come to it saw that from afar and turned back with their merchandise.

﴿From where they do not perceive﴾: from the direction from which they have no awareness of the punishment's coming, as was done to the people of Lut; "in their going back and forth" in their journeys, said by Qatadah; or in their sleep, this and what precedes it were narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Dahhak, Ibn Jurayj and Muqatil said: in their night and their day, that is, during their going and coming within them. It was said: in their going back and forth in their scheming and their stratagems, so He seizes them before they complete that. Al-Zajjaj said: all that they turn about in; so they are not outrunning Allah nor escaping Him. Here "al-akhdh" means destruction, as in His saying: ﴿So each We seized for his sin﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 40]. "ʿAla takhawwuf": on a gradual decrease, said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is said: "khawwafahu" and "takhawwafahu" when one diminishes him and takes from his wealth and body. Al-Haytham ibn ʿAdi said: it is the decrease, in the dialect of Azd Shanu'ah. In a hadith of ʿUmar, he asked about takhawwuf, and a shaykh answered him that it is the diminishing in the dialect of Hudhayl. And he recited the saying of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali:
"He feared the saddle from it, lean and bald, as the bow-wood of the nabʿah is worn by the file."
This takhawwuf means diminishing; it was said: from his deeds; it was said: he takes one after another, and both were narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Zajjaj said: He diminishes their fruits and wealth until He destroys them. It was said: ʿalā takhawwuf means: out of fear that He will punish them or pass them by; said by Qatadah. Al-Zamakhshari said: ʿalā takhawwuf: while they are fearing, and it is that He destroys a people before them so that they fear, and then He seizes them with punishment while they are in fear, expecting it; and this is contrary to His saying: "from where they do not perceive." End of quote. Al-Dahhak said it: He seizes one town so the other town is frightened. Ibn Bahr said: ʿalā takhawwuf is the opposite of suddenness, that is, upon the occurrence of states that are feared, such as winds, earthquakes and thunderbolts; and for this He concluded with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed your Lord is Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 7], because in that there is a respite and an extension of time, so repentance is possible in it. Al-Layth ibn Saʿd said: ʿalā takhawwuf means: hastily. It was also said: with a rebuke for what they have sent ahead; and this was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. Since He, Exalted is He, is able to do these things and did not hasten to them, it was fitting to describe Him with kindness and mercy.

﴿Have they not considered what things Allah has created, whose shadows incline to the right and the left, prostrating to Allah while they are humbled?﴾ ﴿To Allah prostrate whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures, and the angels, and they are not arrogant.﴾ ﴿They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded.﴾: When Exalted is He mentioned His power to punish the schemers and destroy them with kinds of seizing, He mentioned the obedience of what He created other than them and its submission, in contrast to the state of the schemers, to alert them that it is fitting, indeed obligatory, upon them to be obedient and submissive to His command. Al-Sulami, al-A'raj (p-496) and the two brothers read "awa lam tarawū" with the tā' of address, either as a general address to creation, begun as a statement, or, if it is a specific address, as meaning: "say to them." The rest of the seven read it with yā' as third person. It was also possible that the pronoun refers to those who schemed, and it was possible that it is a report about the responsible people; the first is more evident because of their prior mention. Abu ʿAmr, ʿIsa and Yaʿqub read "tatafayya'ū" with tā' as feminine; the rest of the seven with yā'. ʿIsa read "ẓilāluhu" as ẓulalahu, plural of ẓullah, like ḥullah and ḥulal. The seeing here is seeing of the heart by which contemplation occurs, but it is through the seeing of the eye. It was said: the interrogation here means rebuke. It was said: it may also mean wonder, and the sense is: "Be amazed at their taking partners with Allah, while they have seen these created things that display the wonders of His power and the strangeness of His craftsmanship, along with their knowledge that their gods which they took as partners cannot do anything at all." The clause "tatafayya'ū" is in the position of a qualifier; said by al-Hawfi, and this is the apparent view of Ibn ʿAtiyyah and al-Zamakhshari. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "min shay'" is a general term for everything that the qualifier in His saying "tatafayya'ū ẓilāluhu" requires, because that is a qualifier of what is presented for lesson among all the entities that have a shadow. Al-Zamakhshari said: "mā" is a relative pronoun linked to "khalq Allah," and it is vague, its clarification being "min shay' tatafayya'ū ẓilāluhu." Others said: the meaning is: from a thing that has a shadow, from a mountain, a tree, a building or an upright body; and His saying "tatafayya'ū ẓilāluhu" is a report about "min shay'," a description of it; and this report indicates that omitted description, which is that it has a shadow. "Tatafayya'ū" is "tatafa''alū" from al-fay', which is returning; it is said: "fā'a al-ẓill yafī'u," so it returns, and it returns after the sun has dispelled it. "Fā'a," when transitive, is with the hamzah as in His saying: ﴿what Allah restored to His Messenger﴾ [al-Hashr: 7], or with doubling as in: "fayyaʾa Allah al-ẓill, fa-tafayya'a"; and "tafayya'a" is of the category of intransitive reflexive, and it is intransitive, but Abu Tammam used it transitively, saying:
"I sought the spring of Rabi'ah, whose green pasture..., and I took shelter in a long shade for her."
That would need to be transmitted from Arabic usage as transitive. Al-Azhari said: the tafayyu' of shadows is their returning after midday; so tafayyu' occurs only in the evening, and what the sun has left, while the shadow is what occurs in the morning, which is what has not been reached by it.

The poet said:

؎Neither can you bear the shade of the forenoon's coolness, nor do you taste the afternoon shade of the evening's coolness.

Imru' al-Qays said:

؎Her eye turned toward the one near Darij, where the shade falls upon its gravel, overflowing.

From Ru'ba: "What the sun was upon and then left is *fay'* (afternoon shade), and what the sun was not upon is *zill* (shade). This is because the sun, from its rising until the time of zawal (the sun's decline after its zenith), abolishes the *zill*; when it declines, the shade returns and continues to grow until the sun sets." The well-known view is that *fay'* occurs only after zawal, while the consideration in this verse runs from the beginning of the day to its end. So the meaning of *tatafayya'u* (﴿يَتَفَيَّأُ﴾) is "moves about and inclines." He (the author) attributed *al-zilal* (shadows), which is plural, to a singular pronoun, because the pronoun refers to *ma* (what), which in meaning is plural, as in His saying: ﴿لِتَسْتَوُوا عَلى ظُهُورِهِ﴾ ("so that you may sit firmly upon its backs").

The author of *al-Lawami'* said: In the reading of ʿIsa, it is *ẓulalihi*. *Ẓill* (with a single *lam*, in the sense of shade) can mean a cloud, which is a body; with a *kasra* (*ẓill*), it means *fay'*, which is an accident. In the common reading, it is used metaphorically. ʿIsa therefore held that *tafayyu'* (returning), which concerns bodies, is more fitting. [Ended.] (p-٤٩٧) As for the common reading, it is by metaphor. End of quotation.

They discussed His saying ﴿عَنِ اليَمِينِ والشَّمائِلِ﴾ ("on the right and the left"), and there are two points. The first: what is meant by this? The second: what is the wisdom in using the singular *al-yamin* (right) and the plural *al-shama'il* (left)?

As for the first, they said: the right of the celestial sphere is the east, and its left is the west. These two names were assigned to these two sides because the stronger side of a person is his right, and from it the daily celestial motion appears, moving from the east to the west. Therefore the east is the right of the sphere and the west is its left. Accordingly, when the sun rises until it reaches the midpoint of the sphere, the shadows fall to the western side; if it descends from the midpoint of the sphere toward the western side, the shadows fall on the eastern side. This is the meaning of the shadows' shifting from right to left.

It was said: in a land whose latitude is less than the measure of a *mil* (a unit of distance), the sun in summer is to the right of the town, so the shadows fall on their right.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: "Have they not looked at what Allah has created of things which have shadows that shift from their right and their left, on each side and each of its two halves?" The use of "right and left" is a metaphor, drawn from the right and left of a person, for the two sides of a thing; that is, the shadows return from one side to another. End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: What is intended by the sign (*'ibra*) in this verse is every body that has a shadow, such as mountains, trees and other things. What has right and left in its arrangement is only a human being. But the mention of right and left here is by way of metaphorical usage without confusion; you assume: "possessing a right and a left," and you assume: "facing whichever direction you wish." Then you look at its shadow, and you see it inclining either toward the right or toward the left, and this occurs in every region of the world. This therefore covers the words of the verse, and there is in it figurative extension and breadth. As for the one who holds that the right is from the forenoon of zawal, and from zawal until sunset it is on the left, which is the view of Qatada and Ibn Jurayj, that applies only to someone who assumes facing the south. End of quotation.

As for the second point, al-Zamakhshari said: *al-yamin* is in the sense of *al-ayman* (the rights), so he made it, though singular, carry the sense of the plural, thereby matching *al-shama'il* in meaning, as in His saying: ﴿ويُوَلُّونَ الدُّبُرَ﴾ ("and they will turn their backs"), meaning "retreat."

Al-Farra' said: It is as if, when he uses the singular, he refers to one of the shadow-casting things; and when he uses the plural, he refers to all of them, because His saying ﴿ما خَلَقَ اللَّهِ مِن شَيْءٍ﴾ is a singular word whose meaning is plural. So he expressed one of them with a singular term, as in His saying: ﴿وجَعَلَ الظُّلُماتِ والنُّورَ﴾ ("and made the darknesses and the light") and His saying: ﴿خَتَمَ اللَّهُ عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ وعَلى سَمْعِهِمْ﴾ ("Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing").

It was said: if we interpret *al-yamin* as the east, then the point where the sun rises is one single point, so the right is one. As for *al-shama'il*, they are the deviations occurring in those shadows after they fall upon the earth, and these are many; therefore he expressed them with the plural form.

Al-Kirmani said: It is possible that by *al-shama'il* is meant the left, the front and the back, since the shadow shifts from all directions. It begins with the right, either because the shifting starts from it or out of seeking blessing by mentioning it. Then he put the rest into the form *al-shimal* (left), because of the opposition between right and left, and the front and back were given the status of the left because of their difference from the right. It was said: he used the singular for the right and the plural for the left, because the beginning is from the right, then it gradually contracts, state after state, so it has the sense of the plural. Thus the word *al-shimal* applies to every state, and it multiplies with the multiplication of states.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: What some people said, that the right is the first occurrence of shadow after zawal, and the last until sunset is from the left, and that therefore he used the singular for the right, is a confused statement and wrong in several respects.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: When you pray the dawn prayer, everything between the sun's rising and its setting is shadow. Then Allah sends the sun as a guide, and it draws the shadow toward itself. Accordingly, he interpreted the sun's circuit with the shadow on the right of one facing the south; then the deviation begins, and that is from the left, because it consists of many movements and disconnected shadows, so they are many lefts. Thus the shadow on the right was a single connected shadow, general to everything. End of quotation.

Our teacher, the professor Abu al-Hasan ʿAli ibn Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Kutami, known as Ibn al-Sa'igh, said: He used the singular and the plural with regard to the two extremes, because the shadow of the morning dwindles until only a little of it remains, so it appears to be in one direction. In the evening it is the reverse, (p-٤٩٨) since it spreads over all directions. Thus both extremes are taken into account in the verse. This is from the point of view of meaning. As for its wording, there is *muṭābaqa* (correspondence) in it: *sujjadan* is plural, and it corresponds to the plural *al-shama'il* because it is connected to it. Thus the verse contains a correspondence between wording and meaning, and the holding of both together is part of its inimitability. End of quotation.

The apparent reading is to take *al-zilal* (shadows) in their literal sense, and most commentators' discussions proceed on this basis. They said: When the sun rises while you face the qibla, the shadow is in front of you; when it rises higher, it is on your right; after that, it is behind you; and when you want sunset, it is on your left.

A group said: *al-zilal* here means the bodies themselves, which are the intended referents, and the Arabs sometimes refer to bodies by means of shadows. From this is the saying of ʿAbda ibn al-Tabib:

؎When we alight, we pitch the shade of tents, and the cooking-pots boil with meat for the people.

Tents are actually pitched, and from this is the saying of the poet:

؎Following the shadows' *afyā'* in the evening.

That is, the *afyā'* of the bodies. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: All of this is possible but not explicit, although Abu ʿAli established it. End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that prostration here is a figurative expression for submission: the shadows' inclining and turning in the way God wills is called "prostration" (sujud), just as one who gestures with his head toward the ground in humility is called "prostrating" (sajid). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Sujjadan (prostrating) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) of the shadows. Wahum dakhirun (while they are humbled) is a hal of the pronoun in zilaluhu (his shadows), because it has the sense of a plural, and it refers to whatever God created that has a shadow. It is pluralized with the wa-n ending because dukhur (humiliation) is an attribute of rational beings, or because among that whole group there are rational beings, so the masculine plural was given precedence. The meaning is: the shadows are submissive to God and not resistant to Him in what He has subjected them to, namely their shifting and their own movement. Dakhirah also means: humbled, submissive to God's acts upon them, not resisting; end of quotation."

Al-Zamakhshari thus differentiated between the two circumstantial clauses: he made sujjadan a hal of the shadows, and wahum dakhirun a hal of the pronoun in sujjadan. It could also be a second hal of the shadows, as when you say: "Zayd came riding, and he is laughing." Here wa-huwa dahik (and he is laughing) may be a hal of the pronoun in rakiban (riding), or it may be a hal of Zayd. The second possibility seems more apparent to me. The verb governing both circumstantial clauses is yatafayya'u (it turns, shifts), and 'an (from) is connected to it. This was also said by al-Hawfi. It has been said that it is in the position of a hal, as Abu al-Baqa said. It has also been said that 'an is a noun, meaning "the side of the right," in which case it is in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarf).

As for what al-Zamakhshari permitted, that wahum dakhirun is a hal of the pronoun in zilalihi (his shadows), according to the majority opinion (al-Jumhur) this is not permissible. It is the case of: "The servant of Hind came to me laughing (feminine)." Those who hold that when the mudaf (the noun in the construct) is a part or like a part, it is permissible, may say this here, since the shadows, although not a part of the bodies, are like a part, because their existence arises from the existence of the bodies.

A group held that prostration here is literal. Al-Dahhak said: "When the sun passes its zenith, everything prostrates before the qibla, from plants and trees; for this reason the righteous used to prefer praying at that time." Mujahid said: "Only the shadows prostrate, not the bodies." It is also reported from him: "When the sun passes its zenith, everything prostrates." Al-Hasan said: "As for your shadow, it prostrates to God; as for you, you do not prostrate to Him." It has been said: since the shadows are attached to the ground and fall upon it in the form of one prostrating, they are described as prostrating. But for prostration to be taken literally, meaning falling upon the ground as worship and intentionally, is far-fetched, since that requires life, knowledge, and the intention of worship.

Shadow is singled out for mention because it changes quickly, and change requires something other than itself that changes it and manages it. Since the prostration of shadows is most evident, it is mentioned first, and then the discussion moves to the prostration of what is in the heavens and the earth.

Min dabbah (of any creature that crawls): it may be an explanation of what is in the two places (heavens and earth), so that those in the heavens are creatures that crawl. It may also be an explanation of what is on the earth; for this reason Ibn 'Abbas said: "He means everything that crawls upon the earth."

He joined "and the angels" to "whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth," and they are included in the generality of "whatever" (ma), honoring and glorifying them. It may also be that by "those in the heavens" the intended meaning is their guardians (hafazah) who are on the earth, and by "what is in the heavens" their angels, in which case they are not included in the general term.

It has been said: in the verse of the shadows God showed that all inanimate things are submissive to God. He then showed that the most noble of existents, namely the angels, and the lowest of them, namely the creatures that crawl (al-dawabb), are all submissive to God Almighty, and this indicates that all of them are submissive to God Almighty.

It has been said: "dabbah" is a name for every physical animal that moves and crawls. When God Almighty distinguished the angels from the dabbah, we know that they are not among those that crawl; rather, they are spirits specially characterized by motion. End of quotation. This is a philosophical view.

Since there is a shared measure of prostration between the responsible (mukallafun) and others, namely submission to God's will, He joined them in it, even though they differ in the manner of prostration.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: why was ma used instead of man (who), to give precedence to the rational among the creatures that crawl over the others? I answer: if man had been used, there would have been no indication of precedence, and it would have applied only to rational beings. So what suits both rational beings and others was used, intending generality. End of quotation."

The apparent sense of the question is an acceptance that man may include rational beings and others by way of precedence, while the apparent sense of the answer restricts man to rational beings, and that what suits both rational beings and others is other than man. This is not an answer, because he raised the question on the premise of acceptance, then gave the answer on the basis of non-acceptance, so the sense becomes: man is given precedence by it, and the answer is not given precedence by it. This is in reality not an answer.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "yakhafun" (they fear) refers to those to whom prostration is attributed in "wa-lillahi yasjudu" (and to God prostrates). This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil said: "They fear" is an attribute of the angels specifically, so the pronoun refers to them.

Al-Kirmani said: "The angels are described as fearing, because they are able to disobey, even though they do not disobey."

The spatial sense of "above" (fawqiyyah) is impossible in relation to Him, Exalted. If you connect it to "yakhafun" (they fear), it requires the omission of a noun: that is, they fear His punishment coming from above them, since punishment only descends from above. If you connect it to "rabbihim" (their Lord), it is a hal of Him: that is, they fear their Lord being high over them, dominant, in accordance with His saying: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ [al-An'am 6:18], and ﴿And We are dominant over them﴾ [al-A'raf 7:127].

In attributing fear to those to whom prostration is attributed, or to the angels specifically, there is evidence that the angels are responsible like all other responsible beings, and that they are between fear and hope, governed by promise and threat, as God Almighty said: ﴿And they are fearful of Him﴾ [al-Anbiya 21:28]. And whoever among them says, "I am a god besides Him," that one We shall repay with Hell.

It has been said: the fear is the fear of majesty and awe.

The clause "yakhafun" may be a hal of the pronoun in "la yastakbirun" (they do not wax arrogant). It may also be an explanation of the negation of arrogance and an emphasis of it, because whoever fears God does not become arrogant toward His worship.

As for His saying: ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾, the believers do so according to the Law and obedience, while others among the animals do so by subjugation and by the decree that drives them toward what God Almighty has decreed.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 16, verse 43–50 (part 1 of 3):

﴿We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed. So ask the people of the reminder (ahl al-dhikr), if you do not know,﴾ ﴿with clear proofs and scriptures. And We have sent down to you the Reminder, so that you may make clear to mankind what has been sent down to them, and that they may reflect.﴾ ﴿Do those who devise evil deeds feel secure that Allah will cause the earth to swallow them, or that the punishment will come upon them from where they do not perceive?﴾ ﴿Or that He will seize them in their going back and forth, and they will not be able to escape?﴾ ﴿Or that He will seize them through gradual decrease? Indeed your Lord is Most Kind, Most Merciful.﴾: It was revealed concerning the polytheists of Makkah, who denied the prophethood of the Messenger (ﷺ), and said: "Allah is too great that His messenger should be a human being. Why did He not send an angel to us?" The explanation of this sentence has already been given at the end of Surah Yusuf. The meaning is: We reveal to them through the tongues of the angels. Al-Jumhur read yūḥā (with a yāʾ and a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ), a group read it with a yāʾ and a kasrah on the ḥāʾ; ʿAbd Allah, al-Sulami, Talhah and Hafs read it with a nūn and a kasrah. Ahl al-dhikr: the Jews and the Christians, said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and al-Hasan. Also from Mujahid: the Jews. The dhikr: the Torah, due to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We wrote in the Psalms after the Reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105]. And from ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and Salman. Al-Aʿmash and Ibn ʿUyaynah said: those among the Jews and Christians who embraced Islam. Al-Zajjaj said: it is general to whoever is ascribed knowledge. Abu Jaʿfar and Ibn Zayd said: the people of the Qur'an. This view is weakened, and so is the view of the one who says: those among the two groups who embraced Islam, because there is no proof against the disbelievers in the report of the believers, since they deny them. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: the most evident is that they are the Jews and Christians who did not embrace Islam, and they, in this noble verse, only report from the messengers about humans, and their report is a proof against these, for they have not ceased to confirm them, and they are not accused of testifying to them in our favour, because they are opponents at the dawn of the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is the breaking of their argument and their position, because we have been in need of the testimony of these people, whereas the truth is clear in itself. Quraysh had sent to the Jews of Yathrib asking them and seeking their guidance; end of quote. The better view is that His saying bi-l-bayyinat is connected to a implied element indicated by what precedes it, as if it was said: "Then were they sent?" He said: "We sent them with the clear proofs and the scriptures." Thus it is a two-sentence construction. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn ʿAtiyyah and others. It may also be connected to His saying: wa-mā arsalnā, and in this there are two possibilities: The first: that the intention is to place it before the exceptive particle, the sense being: "We did not send before you with the clear proofs and the scriptures except men," so that what follows "illa" is not two objects that are later both in wording and rank, included under the restriction of what precedes it; this was related by Ibn ʿAtiyyah from a group. The second possibility: that it is not intended to be placed earlier, but they both come after "illa" with the intention of restriction. This was said by al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari, and he began with it, saying: it is connected to arsalnā, included under the ruling of the exception together with rijālan, i.e., "We did not send except men with the clear proofs," like your saying: "I did not strike except Zayd with the whip," because its origin is "I struck Zayd with the whip." Abu al-Baqa' said: there is weakness in it, because what precedes "illa" does not govern what follows it when the sentence is complete with "illa" and what comes after it, except that it has come in poetry. The poet said:
"Would that they had punished their neighbour with fire, and none punishes with fire except Allah."
End of quote. What al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari permitted does not apply according to the school of the majority of the Basrans, because they do not permit that what comes after "illa" be anything other than an exception, or something excepted from, or a follower; and whatever is thought to be an object other than these three governed by what precedes "illa" is given a governing element. Al-Kisai permitted that it be an object governed by what precedes it: in the accusative, as in: "No one struck except Zayd ʿAmran"; in the genitive, as in: "No one passed except Zayd by ʿAmr"; and in the nominative, as in: "No one struck except Zayd ʿAmru." Ibn al-Anbari agreed with him regarding the nominative, and al-Akhfash regarding the adverbial phrase, the prepositional phrase and the circumstantial clause. So the view stated by al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari accords with the school of al-Kisai and al-Akhfash, and the proofs of these schools are mentioned in the science of grammar. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be a qualifier of rijālan, i.e., men associated with the clear proofs, so it is connected to an omitted element. This is a permissible view, because it is in the position of a qualifier for what follows "illa." So men are described as "to whom We reveal," and with that same governing element is "bi-l-bayyinat," just as you say: "I did not honour except a Muslim man associated with goodness." He also permitted that it be connected to yūḥā ilayhim, and that it be connected to lā yaʿlamūn. He said: on the basis that the conditional in the sense of rebuke and obligation is like the saying of a hired worker: "If I have worked for you, then give me my right." His saying: fa-s'alū ahl al-dhikr is a parenthetical insertion against the previous possibilities, meaning: among those he mentioned, other than the last possibility.

And: "We have sent down to you the Reminder" is the Qur'an, and it was called a reminder because it is an admonition and an alert for the heedless. It was also said: the Reminder is knowledge, what was sent down to them of the ambiguous and the allegorical, because the explicit text and the apparent meaning do not need clarification. Al-Zamakhshari said: of what they were commanded and forbidden, and promised and threatened. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "so that you may make clear" — by your recitation — through the explicit text of the Qur'an, what was sent down to them. It may be intended: "so that you may make clear" — by your detailed explanation and your exposition — what has become unclear; thus included in this is what the Sunnah makes clear of the matters of the Shariʿah, and this is the view of Mujahid; end of quote.

﴿And that they may reflect﴾: that is, with the intention that they may listen to its admonitions, so that they may take heed and ponder. As for "al-sayyiʿat": it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: the evil schemes, said by al-Zamakhshari; or it is an object of makarū, with makarū given the meaning of "did" and "worked," and "al-sayyiʿat" in this case means the sins of disbelief and other things; said by Qatadah. Or it is an object of amina, and it means the punishments that will afflict them; both were mentioned by Ibn ʿAtiyyah. According to this last view, "an yakhsifa" is a substitute for "al-sayyiʿat." In both views, the preceding word is an object of amina. The ones who devised (alladhina makarū) in the saying of most scholars are the people of Makkah, who schemed against the Messenger (ﷺ). Mujahid said: it is Nimrod. Al-khasf is the earth swallowing what is swallowed and its settling with it downward. Al-Naqqash mentioned that the sinking into the earth occurred among this nation as it did to Qarun, and it was reported to us that a mixed group of people from the lands of the Romans were swallowed by the earth; and when its people sensed that, most of them fled, and some merchants who used to come to it saw that from afar and turned back with their merchandise.

﴿From where they do not perceive﴾: from the direction from which they have no awareness of the punishment's coming, as was done to the people of Lut; "in their going back and forth" in their journeys, said by Qatadah; or in their sleep, this and what precedes it were narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Dahhak, Ibn Jurayj and Muqatil said: in their night and their day, that is, during their going and coming within them. It was said: in their going back and forth in their scheming and their stratagems, so He seizes them before they complete that. Al-Zajjaj said: all that they turn about in; so they are not outrunning Allah nor escaping Him. Here "al-akhdh" means destruction, as in His saying: ﴿So each We seized for his sin﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 40]. "ʿAla takhawwuf": on a gradual decrease, said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is said: "khawwafahu" and "takhawwafahu" when one diminishes him and takes from his wealth and body. Al-Haytham ibn ʿAdi said: it is the decrease, in the dialect of Azd Shanu'ah. In a hadith of ʿUmar, he asked about takhawwuf, and a shaykh answered him that it is the diminishing in the dialect of Hudhayl. And he recited the saying of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali:
"He feared the saddle from it, lean and bald, as the bow-wood of the nabʿah is worn by the file."
This takhawwuf means diminishing; it was said: from his deeds; it was said: he takes one after another, and both were narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Zajjaj said: He diminishes their fruits and wealth until He destroys them. It was said: ʿalā takhawwuf means: out of fear that He will punish them or pass them by; said by Qatadah. Al-Zamakhshari said: ʿalā takhawwuf: while they are fearing, and it is that He destroys a people before them so that they fear, and then He seizes them with punishment while they are in fear, expecting it; and this is contrary to His saying: "from where they do not perceive." End of quote. Al-Dahhak said it: He seizes one town so the other town is frightened. Ibn Bahr said: ʿalā takhawwuf is the opposite of suddenness, that is, upon the occurrence of states that are feared, such as winds, earthquakes and thunderbolts; and for this He concluded with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed your Lord is Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 7], because in that there is a respite and an extension of time, so repentance is possible in it. Al-Layth ibn Saʿd said: ʿalā takhawwuf means: hastily. It was also said: with a rebuke for what they have sent ahead; and this was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. Since He, Exalted is He, is able to do these things and did not hasten to them, it was fitting to describe Him with kindness and mercy.

﴿Have they not considered what things Allah has created, whose shadows incline to the right and the left, prostrating to Allah while they are humbled?﴾ ﴿To Allah prostrate whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures, and the angels, and they are not arrogant.﴾ ﴿They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded.﴾: When Exalted is He mentioned His power to punish the schemers and destroy them with kinds of seizing, He mentioned the obedience of what He created other than them and its submission, in contrast to the state of the schemers, to alert them that it is fitting, indeed obligatory, upon them to be obedient and submissive to His command. Al-Sulami, al-A'raj (p-496) and the two brothers read "awa lam tarawū" with the tā' of address, either as a general address to creation, begun as a statement, or, if it is a specific address, as meaning: "say to them." The rest of the seven read it with yā' as third person. It was also possible that the pronoun refers to those who schemed, and it was possible that it is a report about the responsible people; the first is more evident because of their prior mention. Abu ʿAmr, ʿIsa and Yaʿqub read "tatafayya'ū" with tā' as feminine; the rest of the seven with yā'. ʿIsa read "ẓilāluhu" as ẓulalahu, plural of ẓullah, like ḥullah and ḥulal. The seeing here is seeing of the heart by which contemplation occurs, but it is through the seeing of the eye. It was said: the interrogation here means rebuke. It was said: it may also mean wonder, and the sense is: "Be amazed at their taking partners with Allah, while they have seen these created things that display the wonders of His power and the strangeness of His craftsmanship, along with their knowledge that their gods which they took as partners cannot do anything at all." The clause "tatafayya'ū" is in the position of a qualifier; said by al-Hawfi, and this is the apparent view of Ibn ʿAtiyyah and al-Zamakhshari. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "min shay'" is a general term for everything that the qualifier in His saying "tatafayya'ū ẓilāluhu" requires, because that is a qualifier of what is presented for lesson among all the entities that have a shadow. Al-Zamakhshari said: "mā" is a relative pronoun linked to "khalq Allah," and it is vague, its clarification being "min shay' tatafayya'ū ẓilāluhu." Others said: the meaning is: from a thing that has a shadow, from a mountain, a tree, a building or an upright body; and His saying "tatafayya'ū ẓilāluhu" is a report about "min shay'," a description of it; and this report indicates that omitted description, which is that it has a shadow. "Tatafayya'ū" is "tatafa''alū" from al-fay', which is returning; it is said: "fā'a al-ẓill yafī'u," so it returns, and it returns after the sun has dispelled it. "Fā'a," when transitive, is with the hamzah as in His saying: ﴿what Allah restored to His Messenger﴾ [al-Hashr: 7], or with doubling as in: "fayyaʾa Allah al-ẓill, fa-tafayya'a"; and "tafayya'a" is of the category of intransitive reflexive, and it is intransitive, but Abu Tammam used it transitively, saying:
"I sought the spring of Rabi'ah, whose green pasture..., and I took shelter in a long shade for her."
That would need to be transmitted from Arabic usage as transitive. Al-Azhari said: the tafayyu' of shadows is their returning after midday; so tafayyu' occurs only in the evening, and what the sun has left, while the shadow is what occurs in the morning, which is what has not been reached by it.

The poet said:

؎Neither can you bear the shade of the forenoon's coolness, nor do you taste the afternoon shade of the evening's coolness.

Imru' al-Qays said:

؎Her eye turned toward the one near Darij, where the shade falls upon its gravel, overflowing.

From Ru'ba: "What the sun was upon and then left is *fay'* (afternoon shade), and what the sun was not upon is *zill* (shade). This is because the sun, from its rising until the time of zawal (the sun's decline after its zenith), abolishes the *zill*; when it declines, the shade returns and continues to grow until the sun sets." The well-known view is that *fay'* occurs only after zawal, while the consideration in this verse runs from the beginning of the day to its end. So the meaning of *tatafayya'u* (﴿يَتَفَيَّأُ﴾) is "moves about and inclines." He (the author) attributed *al-zilal* (shadows), which is plural, to a singular pronoun, because the pronoun refers to *ma* (what), which in meaning is plural, as in His saying: ﴿لِتَسْتَوُوا عَلى ظُهُورِهِ﴾ ("so that you may sit firmly upon its backs").

The author of *al-Lawami'* said: In the reading of ʿIsa, it is *ẓulalihi*. *Ẓill* (with a single *lam*, in the sense of shade) can mean a cloud, which is a body; with a *kasra* (*ẓill*), it means *fay'*, which is an accident. In the common reading, it is used metaphorically. ʿIsa therefore held that *tafayyu'* (returning), which concerns bodies, is more fitting. [Ended.] (p-٤٩٧) As for the common reading, it is by metaphor. End of quotation.

They discussed His saying ﴿عَنِ اليَمِينِ والشَّمائِلِ﴾ ("on the right and the left"), and there are two points. The first: what is meant by this? The second: what is the wisdom in using the singular *al-yamin* (right) and the plural *al-shama'il* (left)?

As for the first, they said: the right of the celestial sphere is the east, and its left is the west. These two names were assigned to these two sides because the stronger side of a person is his right, and from it the daily celestial motion appears, moving from the east to the west. Therefore the east is the right of the sphere and the west is its left. Accordingly, when the sun rises until it reaches the midpoint of the sphere, the shadows fall to the western side; if it descends from the midpoint of the sphere toward the western side, the shadows fall on the eastern side. This is the meaning of the shadows' shifting from right to left.

It was said: in a land whose latitude is less than the measure of a *mil* (a unit of distance), the sun in summer is to the right of the town, so the shadows fall on their right.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: "Have they not looked at what Allah has created of things which have shadows that shift from their right and their left, on each side and each of its two halves?" The use of "right and left" is a metaphor, drawn from the right and left of a person, for the two sides of a thing; that is, the shadows return from one side to another. End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: What is intended by the sign (*'ibra*) in this verse is every body that has a shadow, such as mountains, trees and other things. What has right and left in its arrangement is only a human being. But the mention of right and left here is by way of metaphorical usage without confusion; you assume: "possessing a right and a left," and you assume: "facing whichever direction you wish." Then you look at its shadow, and you see it inclining either toward the right or toward the left, and this occurs in every region of the world. This therefore covers the words of the verse, and there is in it figurative extension and breadth. As for the one who holds that the right is from the forenoon of zawal, and from zawal until sunset it is on the left, which is the view of Qatada and Ibn Jurayj, that applies only to someone who assumes facing the south. End of quotation.

As for the second point, al-Zamakhshari said: *al-yamin* is in the sense of *al-ayman* (the rights), so he made it, though singular, carry the sense of the plural, thereby matching *al-shama'il* in meaning, as in His saying: ﴿ويُوَلُّونَ الدُّبُرَ﴾ ("and they will turn their backs"), meaning "retreat."

Al-Farra' said: It is as if, when he uses the singular, he refers to one of the shadow-casting things; and when he uses the plural, he refers to all of them, because His saying ﴿ما خَلَقَ اللَّهِ مِن شَيْءٍ﴾ is a singular word whose meaning is plural. So he expressed one of them with a singular term, as in His saying: ﴿وجَعَلَ الظُّلُماتِ والنُّورَ﴾ ("and made the darknesses and the light") and His saying: ﴿خَتَمَ اللَّهُ عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ وعَلى سَمْعِهِمْ﴾ ("Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing").

It was said: if we interpret *al-yamin* as the east, then the point where the sun rises is one single point, so the right is one. As for *al-shama'il*, they are the deviations occurring in those shadows after they fall upon the earth, and these are many; therefore he expressed them with the plural form.

Al-Kirmani said: It is possible that by *al-shama'il* is meant the left, the front and the back, since the shadow shifts from all directions. It begins with the right, either because the shifting starts from it or out of seeking blessing by mentioning it. Then he put the rest into the form *al-shimal* (left), because of the opposition between right and left, and the front and back were given the status of the left because of their difference from the right. It was said: he used the singular for the right and the plural for the left, because the beginning is from the right, then it gradually contracts, state after state, so it has the sense of the plural. Thus the word *al-shimal* applies to every state, and it multiplies with the multiplication of states.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: What some people said, that the right is the first occurrence of shadow after zawal, and the last until sunset is from the left, and that therefore he used the singular for the right, is a confused statement and wrong in several respects.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: When you pray the dawn prayer, everything between the sun's rising and its setting is shadow. Then Allah sends the sun as a guide, and it draws the shadow toward itself. Accordingly, he interpreted the sun's circuit with the shadow on the right of one facing the south; then the deviation begins, and that is from the left, because it consists of many movements and disconnected shadows, so they are many lefts. Thus the shadow on the right was a single connected shadow, general to everything. End of quotation.

Our teacher, the professor Abu al-Hasan ʿAli ibn Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Kutami, known as Ibn al-Sa'igh, said: He used the singular and the plural with regard to the two extremes, because the shadow of the morning dwindles until only a little of it remains, so it appears to be in one direction. In the evening it is the reverse, (p-٤٩٨) since it spreads over all directions. Thus both extremes are taken into account in the verse. This is from the point of view of meaning. As for its wording, there is *muṭābaqa* (correspondence) in it: *sujjadan* is plural, and it corresponds to the plural *al-shama'il* because it is connected to it. Thus the verse contains a correspondence between wording and meaning, and the holding of both together is part of its inimitability. End of quotation.

The apparent reading is to take *al-zilal* (shadows) in their literal sense, and most commentators' discussions proceed on this basis. They said: When the sun rises while you face the qibla, the shadow is in front of you; when it rises higher, it is on your right; after that, it is behind you; and when you want sunset, it is on your left.

A group said: *al-zilal* here means the bodies themselves, which are the intended referents, and the Arabs sometimes refer to bodies by means of shadows. From this is the saying of ʿAbda ibn al-Tabib:

؎When we alight, we pitch the shade of tents, and the cooking-pots boil with meat for the people.

Tents are actually pitched, and from this is the saying of the poet:

؎Following the shadows' *afyā'* in the evening.

That is, the *afyā'* of the bodies. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: All of this is possible but not explicit, although Abu ʿAli established it. End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that prostration here is a figurative expression for submission: the shadows' inclining and turning in the way God wills is called "prostration" (sujud), just as one who gestures with his head toward the ground in humility is called "prostrating" (sajid). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Sujjadan (prostrating) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) of the shadows. Wahum dakhirun (while they are humbled) is a hal of the pronoun in zilaluhu (his shadows), because it has the sense of a plural, and it refers to whatever God created that has a shadow. It is pluralized with the wa-n ending because dukhur (humiliation) is an attribute of rational beings, or because among that whole group there are rational beings, so the masculine plural was given precedence. The meaning is: the shadows are submissive to God and not resistant to Him in what He has subjected them to, namely their shifting and their own movement. Dakhirah also means: humbled, submissive to God's acts upon them, not resisting; end of quotation."

Al-Zamakhshari thus differentiated between the two circumstantial clauses: he made sujjadan a hal of the shadows, and wahum dakhirun a hal of the pronoun in sujjadan. It could also be a second hal of the shadows, as when you say: "Zayd came riding, and he is laughing." Here wa-huwa dahik (and he is laughing) may be a hal of the pronoun in rakiban (riding), or it may be a hal of Zayd. The second possibility seems more apparent to me. The verb governing both circumstantial clauses is yatafayya'u (it turns, shifts), and 'an (from) is connected to it. This was also said by al-Hawfi. It has been said that it is in the position of a hal, as Abu al-Baqa said. It has also been said that 'an is a noun, meaning "the side of the right," in which case it is in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarf).

As for what al-Zamakhshari permitted, that wahum dakhirun is a hal of the pronoun in zilalihi (his shadows), according to the majority opinion (al-Jumhur) this is not permissible. It is the case of: "The servant of Hind came to me laughing (feminine)." Those who hold that when the mudaf (the noun in the construct) is a part or like a part, it is permissible, may say this here, since the shadows, although not a part of the bodies, are like a part, because their existence arises from the existence of the bodies.

A group held that prostration here is literal. Al-Dahhak said: "When the sun passes its zenith, everything prostrates before the qibla, from plants and trees; for this reason the righteous used to prefer praying at that time." Mujahid said: "Only the shadows prostrate, not the bodies." It is also reported from him: "When the sun passes its zenith, everything prostrates." Al-Hasan said: "As for your shadow, it prostrates to God; as for you, you do not prostrate to Him." It has been said: since the shadows are attached to the ground and fall upon it in the form of one prostrating, they are described as prostrating. But for prostration to be taken literally, meaning falling upon the ground as worship and intentionally, is far-fetched, since that requires life, knowledge, and the intention of worship.

Shadow is singled out for mention because it changes quickly, and change requires something other than itself that changes it and manages it. Since the prostration of shadows is most evident, it is mentioned first, and then the discussion moves to the prostration of what is in the heavens and the earth.

Min dabbah (of any creature that crawls): it may be an explanation of what is in the two places (heavens and earth), so that those in the heavens are creatures that crawl. It may also be an explanation of what is on the earth; for this reason Ibn 'Abbas said: "He means everything that crawls upon the earth."

He joined "and the angels" to "whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth," and they are included in the generality of "whatever" (ma), honoring and glorifying them. It may also be that by "those in the heavens" the intended meaning is their guardians (hafazah) who are on the earth, and by "what is in the heavens" their angels, in which case they are not included in the general term.

It has been said: in the verse of the shadows God showed that all inanimate things are submissive to God. He then showed that the most noble of existents, namely the angels, and the lowest of them, namely the creatures that crawl (al-dawabb), are all submissive to God Almighty, and this indicates that all of them are submissive to God Almighty.

It has been said: "dabbah" is a name for every physical animal that moves and crawls. When God Almighty distinguished the angels from the dabbah, we know that they are not among those that crawl; rather, they are spirits specially characterized by motion. End of quotation. This is a philosophical view.

Since there is a shared measure of prostration between the responsible (mukallafun) and others, namely submission to God's will, He joined them in it, even though they differ in the manner of prostration.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: why was ma used instead of man (who), to give precedence to the rational among the creatures that crawl over the others? I answer: if man had been used, there would have been no indication of precedence, and it would have applied only to rational beings. So what suits both rational beings and others was used, intending generality. End of quotation."

The apparent sense of the question is an acceptance that man may include rational beings and others by way of precedence, while the apparent sense of the answer restricts man to rational beings, and that what suits both rational beings and others is other than man.
