"The maidservants hastened, turning around them, and the reins of the camels were relinquished by their hands."

Al-A'sha said:
"She burdened her utmost effort upon Yemeni she-camels, when the drivers hastened upon their saddles."

It is transitive, so one says: ḥafadanī, so he is my ḥāfid (one who serves me). The poet said:
"They serve the guest in their tents, out of generosity, that is from them without humiliation."

Abu 'Ubaydah said: there is another dialect for it: aḥfada iḥfādan. He said: al-ḥafad is labor and service. Al-Khalil said: al-ḥafadah among the Arabs are servants. Al-Azhari said: al-ḥafadah are the children of children, and it is said: in-laws. He recited:
"If my soul had obeyed me, it would have had for her a ḥafad (grandchildren) of considerable number."
"But it is a soul proud against me, averse to the company of the base, exceedingly repelled."

﴿And Allah said: Do not take two gods. He is only one God, so fear Me alone.﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and to Him belongs religion, perpetually. Will you then fear other than Allah?﴾ ﴿Whatever blessing you have is from Allah, then when harm touches you, to Him you cry for help.﴾ (p-501) ﴿Then when He removes the harm from you, behold, a group of you associate others with their Lord.﴾ ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them. Enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know.﴾

When He mentioned the submission of what is in the heavens and what is on the earth to what He wills of them, and He alone was singular in that, He prohibited associating anything with Him. The prohibition against taking two gods indicates the prohibition against taking gods in general. Since the noun designed for singular and dual may be used figuratively to mean the category, as in "the man Zayd is excellent" (ni'ma al-rajul Zayd) and "the two men, Zayd and 'Amr, are excellent" (ni'ma al-rajulān al-Zaydān), and the poet's saying:
"Indeed, fire is kindled by two sticks, and indeed war begins with words,"
He emphasized the subject for both by the qualifier, so it is said: "two gods, two" (ilahayni ithnayni), and it is said: "one God" (ilah wahid). Al-Zamakhshari said: the noun carrying the meaning of singular or dual indicates two things: the category, and the specific number. When you want to indicate that the meaning is vague, and what the discourse is directed at is the number, you follow it with something that emphasizes it, indicating intent and care for it. Do you not see that if you say "indeed it is a god" and do not emphasize it with "one," it is not good, and it implies that you affirm divinity but not oneness. End of quote.

Apparently, "do not take" (la tattakhidhu) is transitive to one object, and then to two, as emphasized earlier. It is also said that it is transitive to two objects. It is said that the second was placed before the first, which is permissible; the estimate being: "do not take two gods." It is also said the second object was omitted for indication, estimated as "worshipped," and "two" in this view is emphasis. The explanation of the incompatibility of duality with divinity is given in several ways mentioned in the science of the foundations of religion (usul al-din).

When He prohibited taking two gods, and this implied the prohibition against taking gods, Allah informed that He is one God, as He said: "And your God is one God" (al-Baqarah: 163), with the particle of restriction and emphasis by oneness. Then He commanded them to fear Him. He turned from the third person to the second person, as this is more forceful in inspiring awe. "Wa-iyyaya" is governed by a verb omitted, of which the position is delayed, indicated by "fa-rhabun" (so fear), and its estimate is: "and fear Me." Ibn 'Atiyyah's statement that "fa-iyyaya" is governed by a hidden verb whose estimate is "fa-rhabū iyyāya fa-rhabūn," is a lapse from the grammatical rule: when the object is a detached pronoun and the verb is transitive to one object which is that pronoun, the verb must come after it, as in "You alone we worship" (Iyyāka na'budu, al-Fatihah: 5). It is not permitted to precede it except in poetic necessity, as in the poet's saying:
"To you, when you reached, iyyāka."

Then he turned from the first person to the third person pronoun, informing that to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, because since He is the one God who is necessarily existent in Himself, everything else exists by His origination and creation. He informed that to Him belongs religion, perpetually.

Mujahid said: religion means sincerity. Ibn Jubayr said: worship. Ikrimah said: the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and the establishment of the limits and obligations. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah said: obedience; Ibn 'Atiyyah added: and dominion. He recited:
"In the religion of 'Amr, and Fadak came between us."
That is, in His obedience and His dominion. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Awwaluh al-Haddad" (its first is the smith), meaning always, established, eternal, not ceasing, meaning reward and punishment. Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrimah, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, and al-Thawri said: "wāṣiban" means perpetual. Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-wāṣib" is the obligatory and established, because every blessing from Him is obligatory to obedience for Him upon every recipient of blessing. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned that it is from "al-waṣab," which is fatigue, and it is in the sense of a relative noun, meaning "possessor of waṣab," as in "my heart became besotted with him," meaning possessor of infatuation. Al-Zamakhshari said: or "and to Him belongs religion, with hardship and difficulty," and for this it is called "taklif" (obligation); end of quote. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning may be: "to Him belongs religion and obedience," whether the servant is content with what he is commanded and it is easy for him, or it is not easy; still, religion is His, even if there is waṣab in it. Waṣab is intensity of fatigue. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "wāṣiban" means sincere. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the waw in "wa-lahu mā fi al-samāwāti wa-al-arḍ" is conjunctive, referring to "one God," and it may be a waw of initiation. End of quote. It is not said "waw of initiation" except for the waw of circumstance (waw al-ḥāl), and it does not appear here that it is circumstantial. It is rather conjunctive: either upon the predicate, as he mentioned earlier, so the clause (p-502) is equivalent to a single noun, being conjoined to the predicate; or upon the entire clause "indeed He is only one God," so it would be conjunction of clauses. "Wāṣiban" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and the governing element is what the prepositional phrase is attached to.

"Afa-ghayra Allāh" is an interrogative that includes rebuke and wonder, meaning: after you have known His oneness, and that everything other than Him belongs to Him and is in need of Him, how do you fear and dread other than Him, when neither benefit nor harm is in the power of that other? Then Allah informed that all the blessings acquired from us are only from His origination and invention. This contains an indication of the obligation of gratitude for the blessings He has bestowed, religious and worldly. His blessings cannot be counted, as Allah said: "And if you count the blessing of Allah, you cannot enumerate it" (al-Nahl: 18). Ma is a relative pronoun, and its clause is "bikum" (with you), and the governing verb is the verb of establishment, meaning: what is established with you. "Min ni'mah" is an explanation of "ma," and the predicate is "fa-min Allāh," meaning: it is from the side of Allah. Estimating the governing verb for "bikum" as specifically "ḥalla" or "nazala" (came down/dwelt) is not good. Al-Farra' and al-Hawfi permitted that ma be conditional, with the verb of the condition omitted. Al-Farra' said: the estimate is: "And whatever may be with you of blessing," and this is very weak, because it is not permitted to omit it except after the verb has been made the subject of the topic of al-ishtighal (object-verb ellipsis), or if it is followed by the negative "ma," indicated by what precedes it, as in the poet's saying:
"So divorce her, for you are not a match for her, and otherwise the sword will reach your forehead."
That is, "and otherwise you divorce her," omitting "tuṭalliqhā" because "ṭalliqhā" indicates it. Its omission after "an" followed by "lā" is restricted to poetic necessity, as in the poet's saying:
"The cousins said: O Salma, and if he was poor and destitute, she said: and if."

i.e. even if he is poor and destitute. As for particles of condition other than (إن, in), it is not permitted to omit them except when the omitted item is indicated by context in the construction of *ishtighal* (verbal preoccupation, where a noun is governed by a verb that is elided and must be implied), and that is restricted to poetic necessity, as in his saying: *أينما الريح تميلها تمل* ("Wherever the wind inclines it, it inclines"). The implied sense is: *أينما تميلها الريح تملها تمل* ("Wherever the wind inclines it, it inclines").

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that all blessings come from Him, He mentioned the state in which the servant is in need of Him alone, such that he calls upon no one else and humbles himself to no one else. This is the state of *ḍurr* (hardship), and *ḍurr* covers everything by which one is harmed: sickness, poverty, imprisonment, the plundering of wealth, and other things.

Al-Zuhri read *تَجْرُونَ* (tajrūna), with the hamza removed and its vowel transferred to the *jīm*. Qatada read *كاشَفَ* (kāshafa), and the *fā'il* (agent form) here has the meaning of *fa'ala* (the basic form). The second *إذا* (idhā) is for *al-fujā'a* (sudden surprise). In this there is evidence that the conditional *idhā* is not governed by its answer (*jawāb*), because what follows the sudden-surprise *idhā* does not govern what comes before it.

*ومنكم* (minkum, "from you"): this is an address to those who were addressed in His saying *وما بكم من نعمة* ("and whatever blessing you have is from Allah"), since *بكم* (bikum, "with you") is a general address. *Al-farīq* (the group) here refers to the polytheists who believe, at the time of hope, that their gods benefit, harm and cause misery. From Ibn ʿAbbas it is reported: the hypocrites. From Ibn al-Sa'ib it is reported: the disbelievers. *مِنكم* (minkum) is in the position of a qualifier (ṣifa), and *مِن* (min) is partitive (*li-l-tab'īḍ*). Al-Zamakhshari permitted that *مِن* be explanatory (*li-l-bayān*) and not partitive. He said: "It is as if he said: then a group who are disbelievers, namely you." He said: "It is also possible that among them are those who take heed, as in His saying: *فلما نجاهم إلى البر فمنهم مقتصد* ("Then when He brought them safely to land, some of them remained moderate") [Luqman: 32]." End of quotation.

The *lām* in *ليكفروا* (liyakfurū, "so that they may disbelieve"): if it is the *lām* of purpose (*li-l-ta'līl*), the meaning is that their associating others with Allah is caused by their disbelief in Him, that is, their denial, or their ingratitude for His blessing, and for what We have given them of blessings, or of the removal of harm, or of the Qur'an revealed to them. If it is the *lām* of outcome (*li-l-ṣayrūra*), the meaning is: their affair ended up in disbelief, though they did not intend by those actions to disbelieve; rather, that supplication and eagerness resulted in disbelief in the blessings He bestowed upon them, or in the disbelief that is their denial of Him and their association of others with Him. If it is the *lām* of command (*li-l-amr*), its meaning is threat and warning. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Liyakfurū*: then enjoy yourselves. It is possible that it is from the imperative that carries the sense of abandonment and leaving to oneself, and the *lām* is the *lām* of command." End of quotation. His words were not free of the terminology of the Mu'tazila (a theological school), namely his phrase "in the sense of abandonment and leaving to oneself."

Abu al-ʿĀliya read *فَيُمَتَّعُوا* (fa-yumatta'ū) with a *yā'* at the beginning, with a *ḍamma* on the *yā'*, in the passive form, with the *mīm* sukūn, and it is the imperfect of *matta'a* in its light form. It is coordinated with *ليكفروا* (liyakfurū). The *nūn* is dropped, either for the accusative by coordination if *يكفروا* is accusative, or for the jussive if it is jussive by coordination, or *an* (the particle "that") for the accusative if it is the answer to the imperative. From him also: *فسوف يعلمون* (fa-sawfa ya'lamūn) with the *yā'* indicating the third person. Makhul al-Shami narrated both readings from Abu Rafi', a freedman of the Prophet, from the Prophet ﷺ. The enjoyment here is with the life of this world, and its outcome is towards cessation.

﴿And they assign to what they do not know a share of what We have provided for them. By Allah, you will surely be questioned about what you used to fabricate.﴾ ﴿And they assign to Allah daughters—glory be to Him—while they have for themselves what they desire.﴾ ﴿And when one of them is given good news of a female, his face becomes dark, and he is filled with suppressed grief.﴾ ﴿He hides himself from the people because of the evil of what he has been given news of. Shall he keep it despite disgrace, or bury it in the dust? Evil is what they judge.﴾ ﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the evil description, and for Allah is the highest description, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

The pronoun in *ويجعلون* (wa-yaj'alūn, "and they assign") refers to the disbelievers. Apparently the pronoun in *يعلمون* (ya'lamūn, "they know") also refers to them. *Ma* (in *لما لا يعلمون*, "what they do not know") refers to the idols, that is, to the idols that the disbelievers do not know to harm or benefit, or they have no knowledge, in taking them as gods, of any proof or evidence. In reality they are inanimate objects that neither harm, benefit, nor intercede, so they are ignorant of them. It has been said: the pronoun in *لا يعلمون* (lā ya'lamūn) refers to the idols, that is, to the idols that know nothing and perceive nothing, since they are inanimate and have never had any of that at all.

*Al-naṣīb* (the share) is what they assigned to them of the tillage and livestock. Allah, exalted is He, censured their action, which was to set aside a share of what Allah, exalted is He, had bestowed upon them for inanimate objects that neither harm nor benefit, and those objects do not benefit from the setting aside of that share for them. Then Allah, exalted is He, swore an oath that He will question them about their fabrication and invention in associating gods with Allah, and that these are worthy of being drawn near to by assigning a share to them, and about the questioning in the Hereafter, or at the punishment of the grave, or at the approach of death—there are various opinions.

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that He will question them about their fabrication, He mentioned that, along with taking gods, they attributed to Allah, exalted is He, procreation, which is impossible, and they attributed that to Him in what they themselves did not approve of, and their faces grow dark when it is attributed to them, and they hate it most intensely. The tribes of Khuzaʿa and Kinana used to say: "The angels are the daughters of Allah, glory be to Him," declaring Him far above being attributed offspring. *ولهم ما يشتهون* (wa-lahum mā yashtahūn, "and they have what they desire"): that is, males. This sentence is a subject and predicate. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is permissible for *ما يشتهون* to be in the nominative as a new subject, and in the accusative as coordinated with *البنات* (the daughters), that is: they assigned to themselves what they desire of males." End of quotation. This permitted accusative reading was followed by al-Farra' and al-Hawfi. Abu al-Baqa' said, having related it: "There is something to consider in this." These scholars overlooked a grammatical rule: that a verb which takes as its agent a pronoun attached to a noun does not transitively govern its own attached pronoun in the accusative. So it is not permitted to say *zayd darabahu zayd* (Zayd struck him, Zayd) meaning "he struck himself," except in the construction of *ẓanna* (to think) and its sisters among the mental verbs, or verbs of loss and absence, so it is permitted to say *zayd ẓannahu qā'iman* (Zayd thought him standing), *zayd faqadahu* (Zayd lost him) and *zayd 'adimahu* (Zayd lacked him). The attached pronoun governed by an accusative preposition is also not permitted: one may not say *zayd ghaḍiba 'alayhi* (Zayd became angry at him), meaning "angry at himself." On the basis of what has been established, the accusative is not permitted, since the meaning would be: *wa-yaj'alūna lahum mā yashtahūn* (and they assign to themselves what they desire). They said: the pronoun is nominative, and *lahum* (for them) is genitive with the *lām*, so it is like: *zayd ghaḍiba 'alayhi* (Zayd became angry at him).

*Wa-idhā bushshira* (and when one is given good news): the well-known meaning is that *bishāra* (good news) is the first report that gladdens. Here it may mean the general sense of reporting, or the change of the complexion, which is the common element between a joyful report and the bearers of it. In this there is a censure of their attributing to Allah, who is far above having offspring, daughters, whom each of them most hates to have, and whose nature most recoils from them. *Ẓalla* (became, remained) is used to mean *ṣāra* (became), and also to mean "to remain during the day in the state described by its predicate," and the wording allows both meanings. The more apparent is that it means *ṣāra* (became), because the giving of news may happen by night or by day, and the predominant state is considered. Most births happen at night, and news of the birth reaches the father later, in the daytime, especially if it is a girl, so his remaining in that state is for the whole day. The darkening of the face is a metaphor for frowning, sorrow, aversion and the repulsion that befalls him at the birth of a female. It has been said: when joy is strong, the spirit of the heart expands from within and reaches the extremities, especially the face, because of the strong connection between the heart and the brain, so you see the face bright and radiant. When grief is strong, the spirit retreats into the inner heart and leaves no strong trace on the outer face, so the face turns pale, yellow and dark, and the trace of earthiness appears in it. Thus it is a necessary consequence of joy that the face is illuminated and shines, and a necessary consequence of sorrow and grief that it turns pale and dark. For this reason joy is described with illumination and grief with darkening.

*Wa-huwa kaẓīm* (and he is suppressed): that is, his heart is full of grief and sorrow. It reports what appears on his face and what he conceals in his heart. *Kaẓīm* may be intensive (*lil-mubālagha*), and it may be in the sense of a passive participle corresponding to His saying *wa-huwa makẓūm* ("and he is suppressed") [al-Qalam: 48]. It is said: a *siqā'* (waterskin) is *makẓūm*, that is, filled and tied at the mouth.

Al-Asmaʿi related that a woman gave birth to a girl whom she named al-Dhalfa. Her husband deserted her, so she said:

*Mā li-abī al-Dhalfā lā ya'tīnā*
*yaẓallu fī al-bayti alladhī yalīnā*
*ghaḍbāna an lā nalidu al-banīnā*
*wa-innamā na'khudhu mā yu'ṭīnā*

(What is wrong with Abu al-Dhalfa that he does not come to us, / he remains in the house that is nearest to us? / Angry that we do not bear sons, / for we only take what he gives us.)

*Yatawārā* (he hides himself): he conceals himself from the people. *Min sū'* (because of the evil) is causal (*li-l-ta'līl*): that is, what drives him to hide is the evil of what he was given news of. Some of them in the pre-Islamic era used to hide during labour: if he was given news of a male, he rejoiced, and if a female, he grieved. He would remain hidden for days, planning what he would do.

*Ayumsikuhu* (shall he keep it): before it there is an omitted state (*ḥāl*), indicated by the meaning, and the implied sense is: "pondering or deliberating: shall he keep it?" The pronoun is masculine, taking account of the wording *mā* in His saying *min sū' mā bushshira bihi* ("because of the evil of what he was given news of"). Al-Jahdari read *ayumsikuhā ʿalā hawān, am yadussuhā* with the feminine pronoun, referring either to *bil-unthā* (with the female) or to the sense of *mā bushshira bihi*. ʿĪsā agreed with him in the reading *hawān* on the pattern *fiʿāl*. One group read *ayumsikuhu* with the masculine pronoun, and *am yadussuhā* with the feminine pronoun. Another group read *ʿalā hawn* with an open *hā'* (*hawn*). Al-Aʿmash read *ʿalā sū'* (in evil), and this, in my view, is an explanation rather than a reading, because it contradicts the consensus of the standard text.

The meaning of *al-imsāk* (keeping) is keeping him and raising him. *Al-hawn* (the *hā'* with a *ḍamma*) is disgrace, as in His saying *ʿadhāb al-hūn* ("the punishment of disgrace") [al-An'am: 93]. *Al-haun* (with a *fatḥa*) is gentleness and softness, as in *yamshūna ʿalā al-arḍi haunan* ("they walk upon the earth in humility") [al-Furqan: 63]. Regarding His saying *ʿalā hūn* there are two opinions. The first is that it is a state of the agent (*ḥāl min al-fā'il*), and this is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is a description of the father, and the meaning is: "shall he keep her while being pleased with the disgrace of his own self, and in spite of his nose?" It has been said: it is a state of the object (*ḥāl min al-maf'ūl*), that is: shall he keep her as one humiliated and abased? The apparent sense of His saying *am yadussuhu fī al-turāb* ("or bury it in the dust") is that he buries her: that is, burying her alive until she dies. It has been said: *dassuhā* (burying her) is concealing her from the people so that she is not known, like something hidden in the dust.

The apparent sense of His saying *alā sā'a mā yaḥkumūn* ("Evil is what they judge") is that it refers back to His saying *wa-yaj'alūna lillāhi al-banāt* ("and they assign to Allah daughters") and so on, that is: evil is what they judge in attributing to Allah what they themselves find abhorrent, whose nature recoils from them, such that they cannot bear to attribute females to themselves, and they bury them out of disdain for them, while attributing males to Allah. As He said: *alakumu al-dhakaru wa-lahu al-unthā* ("Is the male for you and the female for Him?") [al-Najm: 21]. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the meaning of the verse, "he deliberates: shall he keep this female in disgrace which he bears with fortitude, or bury her alive, which is the 'burying in the dust'?" Then Allah censured the evil of their action and their judgement in this matter concerning their daughters, while the provision of all is upon Allah. End of quotation. So He linked *alā sā'a mā yaḥkumūn* ("Evil is what they judge") to their conduct towards their daughters. It has been said: *mathal* (description) here means a quality, that is: the quality of evil, namely the need for male children, the dislike of females, their burying out of fear of poverty, and their confession against themselves of extreme stinginess.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 16, verses 51–65 (part 3 of 3):

﴿To God belongs the highest description﴾, i.e., the highest attribute, which is independence from the worlds and freedom from the marks of created things. It was also said: ﴿the evil description﴾ is their description of God as having daughters. He called it "the evil description" because they attributed offspring to God, especially in the female form, which they themselves disdained. Ibn Abbas said: ﴿the evil description﴾ is the Fire. Ibn Atiyyah said: a group said that *mathal* (description) here means "attribute," i.e., these people have the attribute of evil, and God has the highest attribute. We do not need this interpretation, because it departs from the wording. Rather, the word *mathal* remains in its normal sense. When they said that daughters belong to God, they made a *mathal* (likeness) for God, since daughters are human, and having many daughters is hateful and blameworthy to them. So this is "the evil *mathal*." What God says, that they have it (the sons), is not limited to daughters only. Rather, when they attributed daughters to Him, He attributed to them, without restriction, every evil, and there is no greater end than the punishment of the Fire. His saying ﴿To God belongs the highest description﴾ is unrestricted, meaning the perfection that is free of need. Qatadah said: "the highest description" is "there is no god but God," end of quote. Qatadah's statement is also transmitted from Ibn Abbas. Since His saying ﴿and they attribute to God daughters﴾ (the verse) came earlier, what they attributed to God came first. Then He mentioned what was attributed to themselves, and began here with ﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the evil description﴾. After that He mentioned what corresponds to His saying ﴿Glorified is He and exalted﴾ [al-Nahl: 1] of transcendence, namely ﴿To God belongs the highest description﴾, which is the attribute free of the marks of createdness and procreation. It is the highest attribute, which no other shares. This fits the closing with *al-Aziz* (the Mighty), the One whose like is not found. *Al-Hakim* (the Wise) is the One who places things in their proper places.

﴿If God were to take people to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it (the earth) a single creature. But He defers them to a specified term. When their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they advance it.﴾ ﴿And they assign to God what they dislike, and their tongues describe a lie, that for them is the best. Undoubtedly, for them is the Fire, and they will be neglected.﴾ ﴿By God, We sent (messengers) to nations before you, but Satan made their deeds seem good to them. So he is their guardian today, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿We have not sent down to you the Book except that you may make clear to them that about which they differ, and as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾ ﴿And God sends down water from the sky, and by it gives life to the earth after its death. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who listen.﴾

When God related the great sins the disbelievers committed, including the attribution of offspring to Him, He explained that He gives them respite and does not hasten punishment upon them (p-506), to show His grace and mercy. *Yu'akhidhu* (He takes to task) is the imperfect of *akhadha*, and the apparent meaning is that it has the sense of the basic form *akhadha* (to seize). Ibn Atiyyah said: it is as if each of the two parties taking to task takes from the other, either by disobedience, as in the case of God's right, or by harm in relation to created beings, and the other takes from the first by punishment and retribution, end of quote. The apparent meaning is the generality of people. It was also said that it refers to the people of Mecca. The *ba'* in *bi-zulmihim* (for their wrongdoing) indicates cause. Their wrongdoing is their disbelief and sins. The pronoun in *'alayha* (upon it) refers to something not mentioned, and what indicates that it is the earth is His saying *min dabbah* (a creature), because crawling among people happens only on the earth. This is like His saying ﴿and raise dust thereby﴾ [al-Adiyat: 4], meaning "by the place," because it is known that ﴿those that run﴾ [al-Adiyat: 1] run only in a place, and likewise the stirring up and the dust. The apparent meaning of *min dabbah* is general, so He would destroy the righteous along with the wicked. He would destroy everything that crawls on the earth, even dung beetles in their holes. This was said by Ibn Masud. Qatadah said: God did this in the time of Noah, peace be upon him. Al-Suddi and Muqatil said: when rain is withheld, no creature remains except that it perishes. Abu Hurayrah heard a man say: "A wrongdoer harms only himself." He said: "No, by God, even the bustard dies in its nest because of the wrongdoing of the wrongdoer." This is similar to His saying ﴿And beware of a trial﴾ [al-Anfal: 25], and the hadith: "Shall we be destroyed while there are righteous people among us?" Ibn al-Sa'ib, and al-Zajjaj chose this: *min dabbah* means "from among humans and jinn." Ibn Jurayj said: from among people only. A group, including Ibn Abbas, said: *min dabbah* means: from a polytheist who crawls upon it. ﴿But He defers them to a specified term﴾ (the verse). The explanation of similar wording has already been discussed in al-A'raf.

The *ma* in *ma yakrahun* (what they dislike) is used for the one who understands, and the intended sense is the type, like His saying ﴿marry what is good for you﴾ [al-Nisa: 3]. The meaning of *wa-yaj'alun* (and they assign) is that they describe God with it and judge by it. Al-Zamakhshari said: what they dislike for themselves includes daughters, and partners in their leadership, and mocking their messengers and neglecting their messages. They assign to Him their worst wealth, and to their idols their most honored. ﴿And their tongues describe﴾, along with this, ﴿that for them is the best﴾ with God, like His saying ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, indeed I shall have with Him the best [reward]﴾ [Fussilat: 50], end of quote.

Mujahid said: "the best" is the saying of Quraysh: "For us are the sons," meaning they said: "Daughters belong to God, and sons belong to us." It was also said: "the best" is Paradise. This is supported by ﴿Undoubtedly, for them is the Fire﴾. The meaning according to this view is: they assign to God what is hateful, and yet claim that they will enter Paradise, as when you say: "You disobey God, and yet you claim that you will be saved." That is, this is far from that. This view is only possible from someone who believes in resurrection, and some of them did believe in it. Or, on the assumption that what he says about resurrection is true, then *anna lahumu al-husna* (that for them is the best) is an apposition to *al-kadhib* (the lie), or the preposition has been dropped, meaning "that for them." Al-Hasan and Mujahid read *bi-ikhtilafi alsinatihim* (their tongues) with the *ta'* (tongue) pronounced with sukun, which is the dialect of Tamim. The plural of *lisan*, masculine, is like *himar* and *ahmirah* (donkey, donkeys), and for the feminine: *alsun*, like *dhira'* and *adhru'* (forearm, forearms). Mu'adh ibn Jabal and some people of Syria read *al-kudhub* (the lies), with a *damma* on the *kaf* and the *dhal*, and the *ba'* as an adjective of the tongues, the plural of *kadhub* like *sabur* and *subur*, which is regular, or the plural of *kadhib* like *sharif* and *shurf*, which is not regular. In this reading, *anna lahum* is the object of *tasif* (describe). The discussion of *la jarama anna* has already passed.

Al-Hasan and Isa ibn Imran read *innahum* (with *inna*) with a *kasra* on the hamza, and *inna* is the answer to an oath that *la jarama* has replaced. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Raja', Shaybah, Nafi', and most of the people of Medina read *mufrituna* (neglected) with a *kasra* on the *ra'*, from *afrata* in its literal sense, meaning: those who exceed the limit in disobedience to God. The rest of the seven readers, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, the companions of Ibn Abbas, and Nafi' in one narration, read it with a *fatha* on the *ra'*, from *afrattuhu ila kadhā* (I sent him ahead to such-and-such), meaning "I made him precede," transitive by the hamza from *faraṭa ila kadhā* (he went ahead to such-and-such). Al-Qatami said:

*They hurried us, though they were of our companions,*
*As the forerunners hurry for the ones who come to water.*

From this is the hadith: "I will be your *faraṭ* (forerunner) at the Basin," meaning: I will precede you. Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and Ibn Abi Hind said: *mufratuna* means "left behind and abandoned in the Fire," from *afrattu fulanan khalfi* (I left someone behind me) when I left him and forgot him. Abu al-Baqa' said: the Arabs say *afrattu minhum nasan* (I left people behind), meaning: I left them and forgot them. Abu Ja'far read *mufarritun* with shaddah, from *farrata*, meaning "negligent, wasteful." Also from him: *fatha* on the *ra'* with shaddah, meaning "those who are sent ahead," from *farrattuhu*, the causative form of *farrata* in the sense of *taqaddama* (went ahead). Then (p-507) God informed of the sending of messengers to nations before your nation, swearing an oath to that effect and emphasizing it with the oath and with *qad*, which requires confirmation of the matter, as consolation for the Messenger ﷺ, for what he endured because of the ignorance of his people and their attributing to God what is not permissible. ﴿So Satan made their deeds seem good to them﴾, in their persistence in disbelief. ﴿So he is their guardian today﴾: this is a narration of a past situation, meaning that they had no helper during their lives except him. Or the word "today" refers to the time of sending and the messengers' dialogue with them. Or it is a narration of a future situation, namely the Day of Resurrection. The *al-* in *al-yawm* (today) is for a known referent, the day that is witnessed, so he is their guardian on that day, meaning their companion, and what an evil companion. The apparent reference of the pronoun in *waliyyuhum* (their guardian) is to the nations. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is possible that the pronoun refers to the polytheists of Quraysh, and that Satan made their deeds seem good to the disbelievers before them, so he is the guardian of these people, because they are of them. It is also possible that there is an omitted *mudaf* (the first noun of an idafa construction), meaning: he is the guardian of their like today, end of quote. This has some distance, because of the change of pronouns without any necessity requiring it, and without any need to omit the *mudaf*.

The *lam* in *li-tubayyina* (that you may make clear) is the *lam al-ta'lil* (the lam of purpose). *Al-Kitab* (the Book) is the Qur'an. *Alladhi ikhtalafu fihi* (that about which they differ) refers to shirk and monotheism, determinism and free will, the affirmation and denial of the Return, and other matters they believe about rulings, such as the prohibition of the *bahirah* (a she-camel left unridden and unmilked) and the permissibility of carrion and blood, and other rulings.

﴿And as guidance and mercy﴾: this is in the accusative position as an object of purpose (*maf'ul min ajlihi*). Both are in the accusative because the subject of the verb and of these two is the same, since the one who sends down is God, and He is the Guide and the Merciful. The *lam* is present in *li-tubayyina* because the subject differs, since the one who sends down is God, while the making clear is attributed to the addressee, who is the Messenger ﷺ. Al-Zamakhshari's statement that it is coordinated with the position of *li-tubayyina* is not correct, because its position is not accusative, so that an accusative noun could be coordinated with it. Do you not see that if he had put it in the accusative, it would not be permissible because of the difference of subject?

﴿And God sends down water from the sky﴾: Abu Abd Allah al-Razi said: the purpose of the Qur'an is four things: theology, prophethood, the Return, and the greatest part of these is theology. So He began mentioning its proofs with celestial bodies, then with humans, then with animals, then with plants, then with the conditions of the sea and land, then returned to theology and began with mention of celestial matters, end of summary. Ibn Atiyyah said: when He commanded him to make clear what had been disputed, He related the lessons leading to clarifying the matter of lordship. He began with the blessing of rain, which is the clearest lesson, the foundation of life, which is most evident, and about which no reasonable person disagrees, end of quote. We say: when He mentioned the sending down of the Book for clarification, the Qur'an is the life of souls and a cure for what is in the chests from the diseases of beliefs. For this reason He concluded with His saying ﴿for a people who believe﴾, meaning: who affirm. Affirmation has its place in the heart. Likewise the sending down of rain, which is the life of bodies and the cause of their survival. Then by the revival of the earth after its death He pointed to the revival of hearts through the Qur'an, as God said ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life﴾ [al-An'am: 122]. Just as the earth becomes green with plants, fresh after its stillness, so the heart lives by the Qur'an after it was dead through ignorance. Likewise He concluded with His saying ﴿who listen﴾, pointing to this comparison, and the meaning is the hearing of fairness and reflection. Because of this consideration, God knows best, He did not conclude with ﴿for a people who see﴾, even though the sending down of rain is something seen and witnessed. Ibn Atiyyah said: His saying "who listen" indicates the manifestness of this consideration and its clarity, because it needs no observation or reflection, but only needs to hear the statement alone.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 16, verse 51–65 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And Allah said: Do not take two gods. He is only one God, so fear Me alone.﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and to Him belongs religion, perpetually. Will you then fear other than Allah?﴾ ﴿Whatever blessing you have is from Allah. Then when harm touches you, to Him you cry for help.﴾ ﴿Then when He removes the harm from you, behold, a group of you associate others with their Lord.﴾ ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them. Enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know.﴾ ﴿And they assign to what they do not know a portion of what We have provided for them. By Allah, you will surely be questioned about what you used to fabricate.﴾ ﴿And they assign to Allah daughters, glory be to Him, while for themselves is what they desire.﴾ ﴿When one of them is given the good news of a female, his face darkens, and he is filled with suppressed grief.﴾ ﴿He hides from the people because of the evil of what he has been given good news of. Shall he keep it despite humiliation, or bury it in the dust? Evil is what they judge.﴾ ﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the evil description, and to Allah belongs the highest description. He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿If Allah were to seize mankind for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it a single creature, but He defers them to a specified term. When their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they advance it.﴾ ﴿And they assign to Allah what they dislike, and their tongues describe a lie that for them is the best. Undoubtedly, for them is the Fire, and they will be abandoned.﴾ ﴿By Allah, We certainly sent [messengers] to nations before you, but Satan made their deeds appear fair to them. So he is their ally today, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And We did not send down to you the Book except that you may make clear to them that about which they differ, and as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾ ﴿And Allah sends down water from the sky and with it gives life to the earth after its death. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who listen.﴾ ﴿And indeed, in livestock there is a lesson for you. We give you to drink from what is in their bellies, from between digestive content and blood, pure milk, palatable to the drinkers.﴾ [An-Nahl: 66] ﴿And from the fruits of palm trees and grapes, you take from them intoxicant and good provision. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reason.﴾ [An-Nahl: 67] ﴿And your Lord inspired the bee: "Take for yourself dwellings in the mountains, and in the trees, and in what they construct.﴾ [An-Nahl: 68] ﴿Then eat from all the fruits and follow the ways of your Lord, made easy." From their bellies emerges a drink of varying colors, in which is healing for mankind. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who give thought.﴾ [An-Nahl: 69] ﴿And Allah created you, then He causes you to die, and among you is one who is returned to the most decrepit age, so that he knows nothing after having knowledge. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Competent.﴾ [An-Nahl: 70] ﴿And Allah has favored some of you over others in provision. Yet those who were favored do not give their provision to those whom their right hands possess, so that they are equal therein. Then do they deny the favor of Allah?﴾ [An-Nahl: 71] ﴿And Allah made for you spouses from yourselves, and made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren, and provided you with good things. Then do they believe in falsehood and deny the favor of Allah?﴾ [An-Nahl: 72]

(p-500) Wa-ṣaba al-shay' means it persisted (dāma). Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali said:
He said: "I do not seek a little praise whose duration is brief, but rather, all-encompassing blame of time, perpetual."

Hassan said:
"The wind changed it, sweeping over it, and the thunder of its roar is persistent."

And "al-'alil" (the sick person) is "waṣib," but the illness is constant for him. It is said: al-waṣab means fatigue. Ṣaba al-shay' means it was difficult. A "mafāzah wāṣibah" is a vast desert with no end. Al-jiwār means raising the voice in supplication. Al-A'sha, describing a monk, said:
"He persists in prayers to Malik, at times prostrating, and at times crying out."
It is also narrated as: "yurāwiḥu" (alternates).

Dassa al-shay' fi al-shay' means he hid it within it. Al-farth is the thick residue of what remains of food in the rumen or the intestine. Al-naḥl is a well-known animal (the bee). Al-ḥafadah are helpers and servants, and those who hasten in obedience. Ḥafada yaḥfidu ḥafdan, ḥufūdan, ḥafadānan. From this comes: "And to You we strive and hasten" (wa-ilayka nas'ā wa-naḥfidu), meaning we hasten in obedience. The poet said:
"The maidservants hastened, turning around them, and the reins of the camels were relinquished by their hands."

Al-A'sha said:
"She burdened her utmost effort upon Yemeni she-camels, when the drivers hastened upon their saddles."

It is transitive, so one says: ḥafadanī, so he is my ḥāfid (one who serves me). The poet said:
"They serve the guest in their tents, out of generosity, that is from them without humiliation."

Abu 'Ubaydah said: there is another dialect for it: aḥfada iḥfādan. He said: al-ḥafad is labor and service. Al-Khalil said: al-ḥafadah among the Arabs are servants. Al-Azhari said: al-ḥafadah are the children of children, and it is said: in-laws. He recited:
"If my soul had obeyed me, it would have had for her a ḥafad (grandchildren) of considerable number."
"But it is a soul proud against me, averse to the company of the base, exceedingly repelled."

﴿And Allah said: Do not take two gods. He is only one God, so fear Me alone.﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and to Him belongs religion, perpetually. Will you then fear other than Allah?﴾ ﴿Whatever blessing you have is from Allah, then when harm touches you, to Him you cry for help.﴾ (p-501) ﴿Then when He removes the harm from you, behold, a group of you associate others with their Lord.﴾ ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them. Enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know.﴾

When He mentioned the submission of what is in the heavens and what is on the earth to what He wills of them, and He alone was singular in that, He prohibited associating anything with Him. The prohibition against taking two gods indicates the prohibition against taking gods in general. Since the noun designed for singular and dual may be used figuratively to mean the category, as in "the man Zayd is excellent" (ni'ma al-rajul Zayd) and "the two men, Zayd and 'Amr, are excellent" (ni'ma al-rajulān al-Zaydān), and the poet's saying:
"Indeed, fire is kindled by two sticks, and indeed war begins with words,"
He emphasized the subject for both by the qualifier, so it is said: "two gods, two" (ilahayni ithnayni), and it is said: "one God" (ilah wahid). Al-Zamakhshari said: the noun carrying the meaning of singular or dual indicates two things: the category, and the specific number. When you want to indicate that the meaning is vague, and what the discourse is directed at is the number, you follow it with something that emphasizes it, indicating intent and care for it. Do you not see that if you say "indeed it is a god" and do not emphasize it with "one," it is not good, and it implies that you affirm divinity but not oneness. End of quote.

Apparently, "do not take" (la tattakhidhu) is transitive to one object, and then to two, as emphasized earlier. It is also said that it is transitive to two objects. It is said that the second was placed before the first, which is permissible; the estimate being: "do not take two gods." It is also said the second object was omitted for indication, estimated as "worshipped," and "two" in this view is emphasis. The explanation of the incompatibility of duality with divinity is given in several ways mentioned in the science of the foundations of religion (usul al-din).

When He prohibited taking two gods, and this implied the prohibition against taking gods, Allah informed that He is one God, as He said: "And your God is one God" (al-Baqarah: 163), with the particle of restriction and emphasis by oneness. Then He commanded them to fear Him. He turned from the third person to the second person, as this is more forceful in inspiring awe. "Wa-iyyaya" is governed by a verb omitted, of which the position is delayed, indicated by "fa-rhabun" (so fear), and its estimate is: "and fear Me." Ibn 'Atiyyah's statement that "fa-iyyaya" is governed by a hidden verb whose estimate is "fa-rhabū iyyāya fa-rhabūn," is a lapse from the grammatical rule: when the object is a detached pronoun and the verb is transitive to one object which is that pronoun, the verb must come after it, as in "You alone we worship" (Iyyāka na'budu, al-Fatihah: 5). It is not permitted to precede it except in poetic necessity, as in the poet's saying:
"To you, when you reached, iyyāka."

Then he turned from the first person to the third person pronoun, informing that to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, because since He is the one God who is necessarily existent in Himself, everything else exists by His origination and creation. He informed that to Him belongs religion, perpetually.

Mujahid said: religion means sincerity. Ibn Jubayr said: worship. Ikrimah said: the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and the establishment of the limits and obligations. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah said: obedience; Ibn 'Atiyyah added: and dominion. He recited:
"In the religion of 'Amr, and Fadak came between us."
That is, in His obedience and His dominion. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Awwaluh al-Haddad" (its first is the smith), meaning always, established, eternal, not ceasing, meaning reward and punishment. Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrimah, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, and al-Thawri said: "wāṣiban" means perpetual. Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-wāṣib" is the obligatory and established, because every blessing from Him is obligatory to obedience for Him upon every recipient of blessing. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned that it is from "al-waṣab," which is fatigue, and it is in the sense of a relative noun, meaning "possessor of waṣab," as in "my heart became besotted with him," meaning possessor of infatuation. Al-Zamakhshari said: or "and to Him belongs religion, with hardship and difficulty," and for this it is called "taklif" (obligation); end of quote. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning may be: "to Him belongs religion and obedience," whether the servant is content with what he is commanded and it is easy for him, or it is not easy; still, religion is His, even if there is waṣab in it. Waṣab is intensity of fatigue. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "wāṣiban" means sincere. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the waw in "wa-lahu mā fi al-samāwāti wa-al-arḍ" is conjunctive, referring to "one God," and it may be a waw of initiation. End of quote. It is not said "waw of initiation" except for the waw of circumstance (waw al-ḥāl), and it does not appear here that it is circumstantial. It is rather conjunctive: either upon the predicate, as he mentioned earlier, so the clause (p-502) is equivalent to a single noun, being conjoined to the predicate; or upon the entire clause "indeed He is only one God," so it would be conjunction of clauses. "Wāṣiban" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and the governing element is what the prepositional phrase is attached to.

"Afa-ghayra Allāh" is an interrogative that includes rebuke and wonder, meaning: after you have known His oneness, and that everything other than Him belongs to Him and is in need of Him, how do you fear and dread other than Him, when neither benefit nor harm is in the power of that other? Then Allah informed that all the blessings acquired from us are only from His origination and invention. This contains an indication of the obligation of gratitude for the blessings He has bestowed, religious and worldly. His blessings cannot be counted, as Allah said: "And if you count the blessing of Allah, you cannot enumerate it" (al-Nahl: 18). Ma is a relative pronoun, and its clause is "bikum" (with you), and the governing verb is the verb of establishment, meaning: what is established with you. "Min ni'mah" is an explanation of "ma," and the predicate is "fa-min Allāh," meaning: it is from the side of Allah. Estimating the governing verb for "bikum" as specifically "ḥalla" or "nazala" (came down/dwelt) is not good. Al-Farra' and al-Hawfi permitted that ma be conditional, with the verb of the condition omitted. Al-Farra' said: the estimate is: "And whatever may be with you of blessing," and this is very weak, because it is not permitted to omit it except after the verb has been made the subject of the topic of al-ishtighal (object-verb ellipsis), or if it is followed by the negative "ma," indicated by what precedes it, as in the poet's saying:
"So divorce her, for you are not a match for her, and otherwise the sword will reach your forehead."
That is, "and otherwise you divorce her," omitting "tuṭalliqhā" because "ṭalliqhā" indicates it. Its omission after "an" followed by "lā" is restricted to poetic necessity, as in the poet's saying:
"The cousins said: O Salma, and if he was poor and destitute, she said: and if."

i.e. even if he is poor and destitute. As for particles of condition other than (إن, in), it is not permitted to omit them except when the omitted item is indicated by context in the construction of *ishtighal* (verbal preoccupation, where a noun is governed by a verb that is elided and must be implied), and that is restricted to poetic necessity, as in his saying: *أينما الريح تميلها تمل* ("Wherever the wind inclines it, it inclines"). The implied sense is: *أينما تميلها الريح تملها تمل* ("Wherever the wind inclines it, it inclines").

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that all blessings come from Him, He mentioned the state in which the servant is in need of Him alone, such that he calls upon no one else and humbles himself to no one else. This is the state of *ḍurr* (hardship), and *ḍurr* covers everything by which one is harmed: sickness, poverty, imprisonment, the plundering of wealth, and other things.

Al-Zuhri read *تَجْرُونَ* (tajrūna), with the hamza removed and its vowel transferred to the *jīm*. Qatada read *كاشَفَ* (kāshafa), and the *fā'il* (agent form) here has the meaning of *fa'ala* (the basic form). The second *إذا* (idhā) is for *al-fujā'a* (sudden surprise). In this there is evidence that the conditional *idhā* is not governed by its answer (*jawāb*), because what follows the sudden-surprise *idhā* does not govern what comes before it.

*ومنكم* (minkum, "from you"): this is an address to those who were addressed in His saying *وما بكم من نعمة* ("and whatever blessing you have is from Allah"), since *بكم* (bikum, "with you") is a general address. *Al-farīq* (the group) here refers to the polytheists who believe, at the time of hope, that their gods benefit, harm and cause misery. From Ibn ʿAbbas it is reported: the hypocrites. From Ibn al-Sa'ib it is reported: the disbelievers. *مِنكم* (minkum) is in the position of a qualifier (ṣifa), and *مِن* (min) is partitive (*li-l-tab'īḍ*). Al-Zamakhshari permitted that *مِن* be explanatory (*li-l-bayān*) and not partitive. He said: "It is as if he said: then a group who are disbelievers, namely you." He said: "It is also possible that among them are those who take heed, as in His saying: *فلما نجاهم إلى البر فمنهم مقتصد* ("Then when He brought them safely to land, some of them remained moderate") [Luqman: 32]." End of quotation.

The *lām* in *ليكفروا* (liyakfurū, "so that they may disbelieve"): if it is the *lām* of purpose (*li-l-ta'līl*), the meaning is that their associating others with Allah is caused by their disbelief in Him, that is, their denial, or their ingratitude for His blessing, and for what We have given them of blessings, or of the removal of harm, or of the Qur'an revealed to them. If it is the *lām* of outcome (*li-l-ṣayrūra*), the meaning is: their affair ended up in disbelief, though they did not intend by those actions to disbelieve; rather, that supplication and eagerness resulted in disbelief in the blessings He bestowed upon them, or in the disbelief that is their denial of Him and their association of others with Him. If it is the *lām* of command (*li-l-amr*), its meaning is threat and warning. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Liyakfurū*: then enjoy yourselves. It is possible that it is from the imperative that carries the sense of abandonment and leaving to oneself, and the *lām* is the *lām* of command." End of quotation. His words were not free of the terminology of the Mu'tazila (a theological school), namely his phrase "in the sense of abandonment and leaving to oneself."

Abu al-ʿĀliya read *فَيُمَتَّعُوا* (fa-yumatta'ū) with a *yā'* at the beginning, with a *ḍamma* on the *yā'*, in the passive form, with the *mīm* sukūn, and it is the imperfect of *matta'a* in its light form. It is coordinated with *ليكفروا* (liyakfurū). The *nūn* is dropped, either for the accusative by coordination if *يكفروا* is accusative, or for the jussive if it is jussive by coordination, or *an* (the particle "that") for the accusative if it is the answer to the imperative. From him also: *فسوف يعلمون* (fa-sawfa ya'lamūn) with the *yā'* indicating the third person. Makhul al-Shami narrated both readings from Abu Rafi', a freedman of the Prophet, from the Prophet ﷺ. The enjoyment here is with the life of this world, and its outcome is towards cessation.

﴿And they assign to what they do not know a share of what We have provided for them. By Allah, you will surely be questioned about what you used to fabricate.﴾ ﴿And they assign to Allah daughters—glory be to Him—while they have for themselves what they desire.﴾ ﴿And when one of them is given good news of a female, his face becomes dark, and he is filled with suppressed grief.﴾ ﴿He hides himself from the people because of the evil of what he has been given news of. Shall he keep it despite disgrace, or bury it in the dust? Evil is what they judge.﴾ ﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the evil description, and for Allah is the highest description, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

The pronoun in *ويجعلون* (wa-yaj'alūn, "and they assign") refers to the disbelievers. Apparently the pronoun in *يعلمون* (ya'lamūn, "they know") also refers to them. *Ma* (in *لما لا يعلمون*, "what they do not know") refers to the idols, that is, to the idols that the disbelievers do not know to harm or benefit, or they have no knowledge, in taking them as gods, of any proof or evidence. In reality they are inanimate objects that neither harm, benefit, nor intercede, so they are ignorant of them. It has been said: the pronoun in *لا يعلمون* (lā ya'lamūn) refers to the idols, that is, to the idols that know nothing and perceive nothing, since they are inanimate and have never had any of that at all.

*Al-naṣīb* (the share) is what they assigned to them of the tillage and livestock. Allah, exalted is He, censured their action, which was to set aside a share of what Allah, exalted is He, had bestowed upon them for inanimate objects that neither harm nor benefit, and those objects do not benefit from the setting aside of that share for them. Then Allah, exalted is He, swore an oath that He will question them about their fabrication and invention in associating gods with Allah, and that these are worthy of being drawn near to by assigning a share to them, and about the questioning in the Hereafter, or at the punishment of the grave, or at the approach of death—there are various opinions.

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that He will question them about their fabrication, He mentioned that, along with taking gods, they attributed to Allah, exalted is He, procreation, which is impossible, and they attributed that to Him in what they themselves did not approve of, and their faces grow dark when it is attributed to them, and they hate it most intensely. The tribes of Khuzaʿa and Kinana used to say: "The angels are the daughters of Allah, glory be to Him," declaring Him far above being attributed offspring. *ولهم ما يشتهون* (wa-lahum mā yashtahūn, "and they have what they desire"): that is, males. This sentence is a subject and predicate. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is permissible for *ما يشتهون* to be in the nominative as a new subject, and in the accusative as coordinated with *البنات* (the daughters), that is: they assigned to themselves what they desire of males." End of quotation. This permitted accusative reading was followed by al-Farra' and al-Hawfi. Abu al-Baqa' said, having related it: "There is something to consider in this." These scholars overlooked a grammatical rule: that a verb which takes as its agent a pronoun attached to a noun does not transitively govern its own attached pronoun in the accusative. So it is not permitted to say *zayd darabahu zayd* (Zayd struck him, Zayd) meaning "he struck himself," except in the construction of *ẓanna* (to think) and its sisters among the mental verbs, or verbs of loss and absence, so it is permitted to say *zayd ẓannahu qā'iman* (Zayd thought him standing), *zayd faqadahu* (Zayd lost him) and *zayd 'adimahu* (Zayd lacked him). The attached pronoun governed by an accusative preposition is also not permitted: one may not say *zayd ghaḍiba 'alayhi* (Zayd became angry at him), meaning "angry at himself." On the basis of what has been established, the accusative is not permitted, since the meaning would be: *wa-yaj'alūna lahum mā yashtahūn* (and they assign to themselves what they desire). They said: the pronoun is nominative, and *lahum* (for them) is genitive with the *lām*, so it is like: *zayd ghaḍiba 'alayhi* (Zayd became angry at him).

*Wa-idhā bushshira* (and when one is given good news): the well-known meaning is that *bishāra* (good news) is the first report that gladdens. Here it may mean the general sense of reporting, or the change of the complexion, which is the common element between a joyful report and the bearers of it. In this there is a censure of their attributing to Allah, who is far above having offspring, daughters, whom each of them most hates to have, and whose nature most recoils from them. *Ẓalla* (became, remained) is used to mean *ṣāra* (became), and also to mean "to remain during the day in the state described by its predicate," and the wording allows both meanings. The more apparent is that it means *ṣāra* (became), because the giving of news may happen by night or by day, and the predominant state is considered. Most births happen at night, and news of the birth reaches the father later, in the daytime, especially if it is a girl, so his remaining in that state is for the whole day. The darkening of the face is a metaphor for frowning, sorrow, aversion and the repulsion that befalls him at the birth of a female. It has been said: when joy is strong, the spirit of the heart expands from within and reaches the extremities, especially the face, because of the strong connection between the heart and the brain, so you see the face bright and radiant. When grief is strong, the spirit retreats into the inner heart and leaves no strong trace on the outer face, so the face turns pale, yellow and dark, and the trace of earthiness appears in it. Thus it is a necessary consequence of joy that the face is illuminated and shines, and a necessary consequence of sorrow and grief that it turns pale and dark. For this reason joy is described with illumination and grief with darkening.

*Wa-huwa kaẓīm* (and he is suppressed): that is, his heart is full of grief and sorrow. It reports what appears on his face and what he conceals in his heart. *Kaẓīm* may be intensive (*lil-mubālagha*), and it may be in the sense of a passive participle corresponding to His saying *wa-huwa makẓūm* ("and he is suppressed") [al-Qalam: 48]. It is said: a *siqā'* (waterskin) is *makẓūm*, that is, filled and tied at the mouth.

Al-Asmaʿi related that a woman gave birth to a girl whom she named al-Dhalfa. Her husband deserted her, so she said:

*Mā li-abī al-Dhalfā lā ya'tīnā*
*yaẓallu fī al-bayti alladhī yalīnā*
*ghaḍbāna an lā nalidu al-banīnā*
*wa-innamā na'khudhu mā yu'ṭīnā*

(What is wrong with Abu al-Dhalfa that he does not come to us, / he remains in the house that is nearest to us? / Angry that we do not bear sons, / for we only take what he gives us.)

*Yatawārā* (he hides himself): he conceals himself from the people. *Min sū'* (because of the evil) is causal (*li-l-ta'līl*): that is, what drives him to hide is the evil of what he was given news of. Some of them in the pre-Islamic era used to hide during labour: if he was given news of a male, he rejoiced, and if a female, he grieved. He would remain hidden for days, planning what he would do.

*Ayumsikuhu* (shall he keep it): before it there is an omitted state (*ḥāl*), indicated by the meaning, and the implied sense is: "pondering or deliberating: shall he keep it?" The pronoun is masculine, taking account of the wording *mā* in His saying *min sū' mā bushshira bihi* ("because of the evil of what he was given news of"). Al-Jahdari read *ayumsikuhā ʿalā hawān, am yadussuhā* with the feminine pronoun, referring either to *bil-unthā* (with the female) or to the sense of *mā bushshira bihi*. ʿĪsā agreed with him in the reading *hawān* on the pattern *fiʿāl*. One group read *ayumsikuhu* with the masculine pronoun, and *am yadussuhā* with the feminine pronoun. Another group read *ʿalā hawn* with an open *hā'* (*hawn*). Al-Aʿmash read *ʿalā sū'* (in evil), and this, in my view, is an explanation rather than a reading, because it contradicts the consensus of the standard text.

The meaning of *al-imsāk* (keeping) is keeping him and raising him. *Al-hawn* (the *hā'* with a *ḍamma*) is disgrace, as in His saying *ʿadhāb al-hūn* ("the punishment of disgrace") [al-An'am: 93]. *Al-haun* (with a *fatḥa*) is gentleness and softness, as in *yamshūna ʿalā al-arḍi haunan* ("they walk upon the earth in humility") [al-Furqan: 63]. Regarding His saying *ʿalā hūn* there are two opinions. The first is that it is a state of the agent (*ḥāl min al-fā'il*), and this is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is a description of the father, and the meaning is: "shall he keep her while being pleased with the disgrace of his own self, and in spite of his nose?" It has been said: it is a state of the object (*ḥāl min al-maf'ūl*), that is: shall he keep her as one humiliated and abased? The apparent sense of His saying *am yadussuhu fī al-turāb* ("or bury it in the dust") is that he buries her: that is, burying her alive until she dies. It has been said: *dassuhā* (burying her) is concealing her from the people so that she is not known, like something hidden in the dust.

The apparent sense of His saying *alā sā'a mā yaḥkumūn* ("Evil is what they judge") is that it refers back to His saying *wa-yaj'alūna lillāhi al-banāt* ("and they assign to Allah daughters") and so on, that is: evil is what they judge in attributing to Allah what they themselves find abhorrent, whose nature recoils from them, such that they cannot bear to attribute females to themselves, and they bury them out of disdain for them, while attributing males to Allah. As He said: *alakumu al-dhakaru wa-lahu al-unthā* ("Is the male for you and the female for Him?") [al-Najm: 21]. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the meaning of the verse, "he deliberates: shall he keep this female in disgrace which he bears with fortitude, or bury her alive, which is the 'burying in the dust'?" Then Allah censured the evil of their action and their judgement in this matter concerning their daughters, while the provision of all is upon Allah. End of quotation. So He linked *alā sā'a mā yaḥkumūn* ("Evil is what they judge") to their conduct towards their daughters. It has been said: *mathal* (description) here means a quality, that is: the quality of evil, namely the need for male children, the dislike of females, their burying out of fear of poverty, and their confession against themselves of extreme stinginess.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 16, verses 51–65 (part 3 of 3):

﴿To God belongs the highest description﴾, i.e., the highest attribute, which is independence from the worlds and freedom from the marks of created things. It was also said: ﴿the evil description﴾ is their description of God as having daughters. He called it "the evil description" because they attributed offspring to God, especially in the female form, which they themselves disdained. Ibn Abbas said: ﴿the evil description﴾ is the Fire. Ibn Atiyyah said: a group said that *mathal* (description) here means "attribute," i.e., these people have the attribute of evil, and God has the highest attribute. We do not need this interpretation, because it departs from the wording. Rather, the word *mathal* remains in its normal sense. When they said that daughters belong to God, they made a *mathal* (likeness) for God, since daughters are human, and having many daughters is hateful and blameworthy to them. So this is "the evil *mathal*." What God says, that they have it (the sons), is not limited to daughters only. Rather, when they attributed daughters to Him, He attributed to them, without restriction, every evil, and there is no greater end than the punishment of the Fire. His saying ﴿To God belongs the highest description﴾ is unrestricted, meaning the perfection that is free of need. Qatadah said: "the highest description" is "there is no god but God," end of quote. Qatadah's statement is also transmitted from Ibn Abbas. Since His saying ﴿and they attribute to God daughters﴾ (the verse) came earlier, what they attributed to God came first. Then He mentioned what was attributed to themselves, and began here with ﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the evil description﴾. After that He mentioned what corresponds to His saying ﴿Glorified is He and exalted﴾ [al-Nahl: 1] of transcendence, namely ﴿To God belongs the highest description﴾, which is the attribute free of the marks of createdness and procreation. It is the highest attribute, which no other shares. This fits the closing with *al-Aziz* (the Mighty), the One whose like is not found. *Al-Hakim* (the Wise) is the One who places things in their proper places.

﴿If God were to take people to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it (the earth) a single creature. But He defers them to a specified term. When their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they advance it.﴾ ﴿And they assign to God what they dislike, and their tongues describe a lie, that for them is the best. Undoubtedly, for them is the Fire, and they will be neglected.﴾ ﴿By God, We sent (messengers) to nations before you, but Satan made their deeds seem good to them. So he is their guardian today, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿We have not sent down to you the Book except that you may make clear to them that about which they differ, and as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾ ﴿And God sends down water from the sky, and by it gives life to the earth after its death. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who listen.﴾

When God related the great sins the disbelievers committed, including the attribution of offspring to Him, He explained that He gives them respite and does not hasten punishment upon them (p-506), to show His grace and mercy. *Yu'akhidhu* (He takes to task) is the imperfect of *akhadha*, and the apparent meaning is that it has the sense of the basic form *akhadha* (to seize). Ibn Atiyyah said: it is as if each of the two parties taking to task takes from the other, either by disobedience, as in the case of God's right, or by harm in relation to created beings, and the other takes from the first by punishment and retribution, end of quote. The apparent meaning is the generality of people. It was also said that it refers to the people of Mecca. The *ba'* in *bi-zulmihim* (for their wrongdoing) indicates cause. Their wrongdoing is their disbelief and sins. The pronoun in *'alayha* (upon it) refers to something not mentioned, and what indicates that it is the earth is His saying *min dabbah* (a creature), because crawling among people happens only on the earth. This is like His saying ﴿and raise dust thereby﴾ [al-Adiyat: 4], meaning "by the place," because it is known that ﴿those that run﴾ [al-Adiyat: 1] run only in a place, and likewise the stirring up and the dust. The apparent meaning of *min dabbah* is general, so He would destroy the righteous along with the wicked. He would destroy everything that crawls on the earth, even dung beetles in their holes. This was said by Ibn Masud. Qatadah said: God did this in the time of Noah, peace be upon him. Al-Suddi and Muqatil said: when rain is withheld, no creature remains except that it perishes. Abu Hurayrah heard a man say: "A wrongdoer harms only himself." He said: "No, by God, even the bustard dies in its nest because of the wrongdoing of the wrongdoer." This is similar to His saying ﴿And beware of a trial﴾ [al-Anfal: 25], and the hadith: "Shall we be destroyed while there are righteous people among us?" Ibn al-Sa'ib, and al-Zajjaj chose this: *min dabbah* means "from among humans and jinn." Ibn Jurayj said: from among people only. A group, including Ibn Abbas, said: *min dabbah* means: from a polytheist who crawls upon it. ﴿But He defers them to a specified term﴾ (the verse). The explanation of similar wording has already been discussed in al-A'raf.

The *ma* in *ma yakrahun* (what they dislike) is used for the one who understands, and the intended sense is the type, like His saying ﴿marry what is good for you﴾ [al-Nisa: 3]. The meaning of *wa-yaj'alun* (and they assign) is that they describe God with it and judge by it. Al-Zamakhshari said: what they dislike for themselves includes daughters, and partners in their leadership, and mocking their messengers and neglecting their messages. They assign to Him their worst wealth, and to their idols their most honored. ﴿And their tongues describe﴾, along with this, ﴿that for them is the best﴾ with God, like His saying ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, indeed I shall have with Him the best [reward]﴾ [Fussilat: 50], end of quote.

Mujahid said: "the best" is the saying of Quraysh: "For us are the sons," meaning they said: "Daughters belong to God, and sons belong to us." It was also said: "the best" is Paradise. This is supported by ﴿Undoubtedly, for them is the Fire﴾. The meaning according to this view is: they assign to God what is hateful, and yet claim that they will enter Paradise, as when you say: "You disobey God, and yet you claim that you will be saved." That is, this is far from that. This view is only possible from someone who believes in resurrection, and some of them did believe in it. Or, on the assumption that what he says about resurrection is true, then *anna lahumu al-husna* (that for them is the best) is an apposition to *al-kadhib* (the lie), or the preposition has been dropped, meaning "that for them." Al-Hasan and Mujahid read *bi-ikhtilafi alsinatihim* (their tongues) with the *ta'* (tongue) pronounced with sukun, which is the dialect of Tamim. The plural of *lisan*, masculine, is like *himar* and *ahmirah* (donkey, donkeys), and for the feminine: *alsun*, like *dhira'* and *adhru'* (forearm, forearms). Mu'adh ibn Jabal and some people of Syria read *al-kudhub* (the lies), with a *damma* on the *kaf* and the *dhal*, and the *ba'* as an adjective of the tongues, the plural of *kadhub* like *sabur* and *subur*, which is regular, or the plural of *kadhib* like *sharif* and *shurf*, which is not regular. In this reading, *anna lahum* is the object of *tasif* (describe). The discussion of *la jarama anna* has already passed.

Al-Hasan and Isa ibn Imran read *innahum* (with *inna*) with a *kasra* on the hamza, and *inna* is the answer to an oath that *la jarama* has replaced. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Raja', Shaybah, Nafi', and most of the people of Medina read *mufrituna* (neglected) with a *kasra* on the *ra'*, from *afrata* in its literal sense, meaning: those who exceed the limit in disobedience to God. The rest of the seven readers, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, the companions of Ibn Abbas, and Nafi' in one narration, read it with a *fatha* on the *ra'*, from *afrattuhu ila kadhā* (I sent him ahead to such-and-such), meaning "I made him precede," transitive by the hamza from *faraṭa ila kadhā* (he went ahead to such-and-such). Al-Qatami said:

*They hurried us, though they were of our companions,*
*As the forerunners hurry for the ones who come to water.*

From this is the hadith: "I will be your *faraṭ* (forerunner) at the Basin," meaning: I will precede you. Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and Ibn Abi Hind said: *mufratuna* means "left behind and abandoned in the Fire," from *afrattu fulanan khalfi* (I left someone behind me) when I left him and forgot him. Abu al-Baqa' said: the Arabs say *afrattu minhum nasan* (I left people behind), meaning: I left them and forgot them. Abu Ja'far read *mufarritun* with shaddah, from *farrata*, meaning "negligent, wasteful." Also from him: *fatha* on the *ra'* with shaddah, meaning "those who are sent ahead," from *farrattuhu*, the causative form of *farrata* in the sense of *taqaddama* (went ahead). Then (p-507) God informed of the sending of messengers to nations before your nation, swearing an oath to that effect and emphasizing it with the oath and with *qad*, which requires confirmation of the matter, as consolation for the Messenger ﷺ, for what he endured because of the ignorance of his people and their attributing to God what is not permissible. ﴿So Satan made their deeds seem good to them﴾, in their persistence in disbelief. ﴿So he is their guardian today﴾: this is a narration of a past situation, meaning that they had no helper during their lives except him. Or the word "today" refers to the time of sending and the messengers' dialogue with them. Or it is a narration of a future situation, namely the Day of Resurrection. The *al-* in *al-yawm* (today) is for a known referent, the day that is witnessed, so he is their guardian on that day, meaning their companion, and what an evil companion. The apparent reference of the pronoun in *waliyyuhum* (their guardian) is to the nations. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is possible that the pronoun refers to the polytheists of Quraysh, and that Satan made their deeds seem good to the disbelievers before them, so he is the guardian of these people, because they are of them. It is also possible that there is an omitted *mudaf* (the first noun of an idafa construction), meaning: he is the guardian of their like today, end of quote. This has some distance, because of the change of pronouns without any necessity requiring it, and without any need to omit the *mudaf*.

The *lam* in *li-tubayyina* (that you may make clear) is the *lam al-ta'lil* (the lam of purpose). *Al-Kitab* (the Book) is the Qur'an. *Alladhi ikhtalafu fihi* (that about which they differ) refers to shirk and monotheism, determinism and free will, the affirmation and denial of the Return, and other matters they believe about rulings, such as the prohibition of the *bahirah* (a she-camel left unridden and unmilked) and the permissibility of carrion and blood, and other rulings.

﴿And as guidance and mercy﴾: this is in the accusative position as an object of purpose (*maf'ul min ajlihi*). Both are in the accusative because the subject of the verb and of these two is the same, since the one who sends down is God, and He is the Guide and the Merciful. The *lam* is present in *li-tubayyina* because the subject differs, since the one who sends down is God, while the making clear is attributed to the addressee, who is the Messenger ﷺ. Al-Zamakhshari's statement that it is coordinated with the position of *li-tubayyina* is not correct, because its position is not accusative, so that an accusative noun could be coordinated with it. Do you not see that if he had put it in the accusative, it would not be permissible because of the difference of subject?

﴿And God sends down water from the sky﴾: Abu Abd Allah al-Razi said: the purpose of the Qur'an is four things: theology, prophethood, the Return, and the greatest part of these is theology. So He began mentioning its proofs with celestial bodies, then with humans, then with animals, then with plants, then with the conditions of the sea and land, then returned to theology and began with mention of celestial matters, end of summary. Ibn Atiyyah said: when He commanded him to make clear what had been disputed, He related the lessons leading to clarifying the matter of lordship. He began with the blessing of rain, which is the clearest lesson, the foundation of life, which is most evident, and about which no reasonable person disagrees, end of quote. We say: when He mentioned the sending down of the Book for clarification, the Qur'an is the life of souls and a cure for what is in the chests from the diseases of beliefs. For this reason He concluded with His saying ﴿for a people who believe﴾, meaning: who affirm. Affirmation has its place in the heart. Likewise the sending down of rain, which is the life of bodies and the cause of their survival. Then by the revival of the earth after its death He pointed to the revival of hearts through the Qur'an, as God said ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life﴾ [al-An'am: 122]. Just as the earth becomes green with plants, fresh after its stillness, so the heart lives by the Qur'an after it was dead through ignorance. Likewise He concluded with His saying ﴿who listen﴾, pointing to this comparison, and the meaning is the hearing of fairness and reflection. Because of this consideration, God knows best, He did not conclude with ﴿for a people who see﴾, even though the sending down of rain is something seen and witnessed. Ibn Atiyyah said: His saying "who listen" indicates the manifestness of this consideration and its clarity, because it needs no observation or reflection, but only needs to hear the statement alone.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 16, verse 51–65 (part 1 of 3):
