The yellow bile goes to the gall bladder, the black bile to the spleen, the water to the kidney, and the pure blood goes to the *awrid* (the vessels arising from the liver). Then the third digestion takes place. Between the liver and the udder there are many vessels through which blood pours into the udder, which is a soft white flesh, and it is transformed from the form of blood into the form of milk. This is the correct account of how milk is generated. End of quotation, summarized.

He also said: As for us, we say: The meaning of the verse is that milk is only generated from some parts of the blood, and blood is only generated from the subtle parts found in the digestive contents, which are the edible things present in the rumen. So the milk is generated from what was present between the digestive contents first, then from what was present between the blood second. End of quotation, also summarized.

What appears from the wording of the verse is that the milk is a middle between the digestive contents and the blood. The "between" may be taken literally in terms of place, as the commentators said, though al-Razi claimed this is contrary to sense and observation. It may also be taken figuratively, in terms of its generation from what arises in the digestive contents first and from the blood that results from the subtle part of what was in the digestive contents second, as al-Razi established.

The first *min* is partitive, related to *nusqikum*. The second *min* denotes the beginning of the limit, related to *nusqikum*. Both may be related to one governing verb because their meanings differ. It is also permissible that *min bayni* be in the position of a circumstantial clause, and so it is related to an omitted element, because if it were postponed it would be a qualifier, meaning: existing from between digestive contents and blood. It is also permissible that *min bayni farthin* be a substitute for *mā fī buṭunihi*.

A group read *sayyighan* with a shadda on the ya'. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read *saygh*, unshadda, from *sayyigh*, like *hayn* from *hayyin*, and it is not an intransitive verb that would be *sawgh*. *Al-sa'igh* is what is easy to swallow and delicious. It is narrated in a hadith that "no one has ever choked on milk."

When Allah mentioned what He bestowed of the benefits of livestock, He mentioned what He bestowed of some benefits of plants.

The apparent meaning is that *wa min thamarāt* is related to *tattakhidhūna*. *Min* is repeated for emphasis, and the pronoun is singular, taking account of an omitted element, meaning: and from the juice of fruits, or in view of the meaning of *al-thamarat*, which is fruit, or by an omitted element from what was mentioned. It has been said: it is related to *nusqikum*, so it is coordinated with *mimma fi buṭunihi*. Or it is related to an omitted *nusqikum* indicated by the earlier *nusqikum*, so it is coordination of clauses, whereas the preceding is coordination of single words when they share a governing element. It has been said: it is coordinated with *al-an'am*, meaning: and from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines there is a lesson, and then He explained the lesson by His words *tattakhidhūna*. Al-Tabari said: The estimate is: "and from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines what you take," so he omitted *mā*, which is not permissible according to the Basrans. Al-Zamakhshari said: It may be a qualifier of an omitted noun, as in the verse: *bikaffī kāna man armī al-bashar* (with my hand was he who shot the most among men). Its estimate: "and from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines, a fruit from which you take." End of quotation. What he permitted was said by al-Hawfi, who said: That is, "and from the fruits," and if you wish "a thing," with a raised *shay'un* as an inchoative, and *min thamarat* is its predicate. End of quotation.

*Al-sakar* in the language means wine. The poet said:

*Evil are the sober, and evil is their drinking, when the intoxicant and the sakar flow among them*

Al-Zamakhshari said: It was named by the verbal noun of *sakira*, *sukran* and *sakaran*, like *rashida rushdan* and *rashadan*. The poet said:

*They came to us with sakar against us, so the sober is now dispelled, and the drunkard is sober*

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, Abu Razin, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Kalbi, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Thawr and the majority (al-Jumhur) said this. This verse is Meccan. It was revealed before the prohibition of wine (khamr), and wine was prohibited later in Medina, so the verse is abrogated (mansukh). Al-Hasan said: "God mentioned His favour regarding intoxicant (sakar) before the prohibition of wine." Ibn 'Abbas said: it is vinegar (khall) in the language of the Abyssinians (Habasha). It was also said: it is sweet unfermented juice that is lawful, and it was called sakar because of what it becomes if left. Abu 'Ubayda said: sakar means food. It is said, "This is sakar for you," meaning food. Al-Tabari chose this view and said: in the speech of the Arabs, sakar is what is eaten. Abu 'Ubayda recited:

"She made the honour of the noble into sakar"

meaning she passed around (tanaqqalat) their honour. It was also said: it is from khamr, and that when a person plunges into people's honour, it is as if he has become intoxicated (takhammara) by it. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, and al-Zajjaj followed him, saying: it describes that one is intoxicated by people's faults. According to these views, there is no abrogation. Al-Zajjaj said: Abu 'Ubayda's view is not sound, and the people of tafsir are against it. It was also said: sakar is what is non-intoxicating of the nabidh (date and grape beverages). It was also said: sakar is nabidh, which is the juice of grapes, raisins and dates when it is boiled until two-thirds of it is gone, then left until it becomes strong. This is lawful according to Abu Hanifa up to the point of intoxication. End of quote. If sakar is taken to mean khamr, then it has already been stated that this is abrogated. If we do not say abrogation, then it is said: it combines reproach (itab) and favour (minna). By reproach is meant the taking of what is prohibited, and by favour the taking of what is lawful, which is vinegar, syrup (rubb), raisins and dates. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also possible that sakar is made a good provision (rizq hasan), as if it were said: "You take from it what is sakar and a good provision." End of quote. In this case it is a conjunction of attributes, and the apparent sense of the conjunction is difference.

Since the opening of the discourse is: ﴿And indeed in the livestock there is a lesson for you﴾, it suits that the verse end with His saying: "they reflect (ya'qilun)", because only those with intellects take heed, as He said: ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for those of understanding﴾ [Al 'Imran: 13].

Observe the report of the favour of milk, the favour of sakar and good provision. Since milk does not need processing by people, God reported about Himself with His saying: "We give you to drink (nusqikum)." Since sakar and good provision need processing, He said: "you take (tattakhidhun)," reporting about them that they take sakar and provision from it. For this reason the pure Arabs (al-'Arab al-'Ariba) were unable to match it. When God mentioned the favour of drink, milk and others, He completed the favour by mentioning honey of the bee (al-nahl). Since drinks from milk and others were more common among people than honey, He placed milk and others before it, and placed milk before what follows it, because it is what people need most and it is evidence of the natural disposition (fitra). For this reason the Messenger (ﷺ) chose it when he was taken on the Night Journey (isra'), when milk, wine and honey were presented to him. Their order in Paradise also corresponds to this verse. God says: ﴿And rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers, and rivers of honey, purified﴾ [Muhammad: 15]. So in the bringing out of milk from the livestock, and sakar and good provision from the fruits of palms and grapes, and honey from the bee, there are dazzling signs of divinity, power and choice.

Revelation (al-iyha') here means inspiration (al-ilham) and casting into its heart, and teaching it in a manner that He, exalted is He, knows best, and no path leads to comprehending it. The bee (al-nahl) is a genus, its singular is nahla, and it is feminine in the dialect of the Hijaz, which is why He said: ﴿Take (ittakhidhi)﴾. Ibn Wathhab read: "al-nahal" with a fatha on the ha. The "an" here is explanatory (tafsiriyya), since the meaning of speech (qawl) precedes it, which is "wa-awha" (and He inspired). Or it is verbal-source (masdariyya), meaning "by taking." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "an" is the one explaining what is in the revelation of the meaning of speech. This is the view of the majority of the commentators, but there is an objection to it, because the revelation here is by consensus of them the inspiration, and there is no meaning of speech in inspiration. He said: God established in the bees amazing works that are beyond rational humans, among them building hexagonal houses from equal sides by their nature alone. Such a thing is not achieved by rational beings except with tools like the ruler and the compass. They do not build with other shapes, lest those houses become too narrow for them, leaving gaps they cannot fill. They have a leader larger in body than them, whose command is executed, and they serve him. When they swarm away from their hive to another place and want to return to it, they strike drums and musical instruments, and by the mediation of those tunes they return to their hive. Since they are distinguished by these amazing properties, and this is only by way of inspiration, which is a state resembling revelation, for this reason He said: "Your Lord inspired the bee." End of summary. The "min" (from) is partitive, because they do not build in every mountain, every tree, and everything that is trellised, nor in every place within them. The apparent meaning is that the houses here refer to the cavities found in mountains and in the hollows of trees. As for "from what the son of Adam trellises," it refers to the hives that the son of Adam makes for the bees, and the openings found in walls. Since the bee has two types: one that dwells in mountains and thickets and no one cares for it, and one that lives in people's houses and is cared for in hives and the like, the command to take houses includes both types. Al-Zamakhshari said, indicating that the houses are not the openings, but rather what they themselves build: "The meaning of partitiveness is intended by min, and that their houses are not built in every mountain, every tree and everything that is trellised." Ibn Zayd said: "And of what they trellis": the vineyards. Al-Tabari said: of what they build of roofs. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this from both of them is an unsound interpretation. End of quote.

Al-Sulami, 'Ubayd ibn Nadla, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read the word "yarish" (trellis) with a damma on the ra'. The rest of the seven read it with a kasra. "Thumma" (then) indicates a delay and interval between the taking and the eating from which the honey is stored. For this reason the conjunction is with "thumma", and it is coordinated with "ittakhidhi" (take). It is a command conjoined to a command. The discussion of a command addressed to a non-accountable creature will come later in His saying: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾ [al-Naml: 18], God willing. "All the fruits" is a general term that is specified, meaning the customary ones, not all of them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "meaning: build the houses, then eat from every fruit you desire." End of quote. His saying "meaning: build the houses" shows that by "houses" He does not mean the openings in mountains and hollows of trees, nor the hives, but rather the hexagonal houses that they build themselves. The apparent meaning of "min" in His saying ﴿from all the fruits﴾ is partitive, so they eat from the good trees and fragrant leaves things from which God produces honey in their bodies. Ibn 'Atiyya said: they only eat the blossoms of trees.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said, in summary: God causes in the air much shade, from which gather perceptible particles, such as manna (al-narjabin), which is perceptible, and a small amount of very fine, tiny particles. It is this that God inspired the bees to collect from flowers and leaves of trees, and they feed on it. When they are sated, they pick up with their mouths some of those particles and place them in their hives, as if trying to store their food for themselves. So what gathers from that is honey. According to this view, "min" is for the beginning of the end (ibtida' al-ghaya), not partitive. End of quote.

The apparent meaning of the conjunction with "fa" in ﴿then travel﴾ (fa-uslukī) is that it follows immediately after eating: "When you have eaten, then travel the ways of your Lord," that is, the paths of your Lord back to your houses. The "subul" (paths) at that time are their routes in flight. Perhaps they settle in place and then seek a distant place, and then return to their first place. It was also said: "the ways of your Lord" means the paths that He inspired and taught you in making honey. Or, "travel what you have eaten", that is, in the paths of your Lord, meaning in His pathways in which, by His power, He transforms bitter flowers into honey from your bellies and the outlets of your mouths. According to this view, "subul" in "the ways of your Lord" is in the accusative as an adverb of place. According to what preceded it, it is in the accusative as an object. It was also said: what is meant by His saying ﴿then eat﴾ is: then intend to eat from the fruits, and then travel in seeking them the ways of your Lord. This view and the first view are closer in metaphor regarding "ways of your Lord" than the two views between them, except that "eat" in the sense of "intend to eat" is a metaphor. He attributed the paths to the Lord of the bee because He, exalted is He, is their creator, owner, and the one who provides for their welfare and sustenance.

Mujahid said: "dhululan" means not rugged; there is no difficult path for them to travel. On this view "dhululan" is a state (hal) of "subula Rabbiki", like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He is the One who made the earth docile for you﴾ [al-Mulk: 15]. Qatada said: that is, obedient and submissive. Ibn Zayd said: they go out with the bees, seeking pasture, and they follow them. On this view "dhululan" is a state of the bees, like His saying: ﴿And We made them subservient to them﴾ [Ya-Sin: 72].

Then God, by way of enumerating the favour and alerting to the kindness, mentioned the outcome of this taking, eating and travelling, which is His saying: ﴿There comes out from their bellies a drink﴾, and this is honey. He called it "drink" because it is something drunk, just as He mentioned the outcome of livestock, which is giving milk to drink, and the outcome of palms and grapes, which is the making of sakar and good provision. He mentioned the place from which the drink comes out, which is their bellies, and this is the beginning of the first end. The majority hold that it comes out from their mouths, and this is the beginning of the final end. For this reason al-Hariri said:

"You say: this is the regurgitation of the bee, you praise it,
and if you blame it, you say: the vomit of wasps."

The honey and the vomit can only come from the mouth. It is reported from ʿAlī, may Allah honour his face, that in belittling this world he said: "The finest clothing of the son of Adam in it is the saliva of a worm, and the finest of his drinks is the excrement of a bee." And also from him: "As for honey, it is the vomit of a fly." The apparent meaning of this is that honey comes out from somewhere other than the mouth, and it is unclear from which of the two outlets it comes: the mouth, or below?

It is related that Solomon, peace be upon him, Alexander, and Aristotle made houses of glass for the bees so that they could observe how they make them and whether honey comes out from their mouths or from beneath them. But the bees did not release any honey until they smeared the inside of the glass with mud, so that it prevented observation.

Al-Ḥasan said: "The pure part of the wheat, mixed with the saliva of the bee and pure ghee, which no Muslim has disliked, [God] made it a saliva like the constant spittle that comes out of the mouth of the son of Adam."

It was said: ﴿from their bellies﴾ means from their mouths. He called the mouth a "belly" because it is in the position of the belly, and because it is something that is hidden inside and does not appear.

The variation in its colours, white, yellow, red and black, is due to the differing natures of the bees and the differing pastures. Its taste may also vary according to the pasture, as in the ḥadīth: "His bees grazed on the ʿarfaṭ [a bitter shrub]." It was said: the white is what the young bees produce, the yellow what their elderly produce, and the red what their adolescents produce.

The apparent reference of the pronoun in ﴿fīhi﴾ is to the drink, which is honey, because it is a cure among the well-known and beneficial remedies and medicines. Hardly any compound medicine has been listed by physicians without honey in it, and honey is found in abundance in most lands.

As for sugar (al-sukkar), it is specific to some lands and is a recent development; in earlier times, in most lands, nothing but honey was put into drinks and medicines.

The word "people" (al-nās) here does not mean all people in general, because honey does not enter the treatment of many illnesses; rather the meaning is "for those people whose illnesses honey benefits."

The word "shifāʾ" (cure) is indefinite, either for the sake of magnification, so that the meaning is "a cure, a great cure," or to indicate the general notion of cure, so that the meaning is "in it there is some cure."

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Farrāʾ and Ibn Kaysān that the pronoun in (fīhi) refers to the Qur'an, meaning: "In the Qur'an there is a cure for people." Al-Naḥḥās said: "This is a good opinion," meaning: "In what We have related to you of the signs and proofs there is a cure for people."

Al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "I consider that this opinion cannot be validly transmitted from these men, and even if it were validly transmitted, it would not be sound on reason. For the whole context of the speech is about honey, and there is no mention of the Qur'an in it. And since the matter of the bees is wondrous in their building of those hexagonal houses, in their eating of all kinds of flowers, leaves, sour, bitter and harmful things, and in their obedience to their leader and to whoever owns them when they migrate with him, the consideration of this seems to need reflection and further contemplation." He concluded with His words, exalted is He: ﴿Surely in that is a sign for a people who reflect﴾.

﴿And Allah created you, then He causes you to die, and among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after having known. Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Powerful.﴾ ﴿And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision. Yet those who have been favoured do not give up their provision to those whom their right hands possess, so that they are equal in it. Do they then deny the blessing of Allah?﴾ ﴿And Allah made for you spouses from among yourselves, and made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren, and provided you with good things. Do they then believe in falsehood and deny the blessing of Allah?﴾ ﴿And they worship, besides Allah, what possesses no provision for them from the heavens and the earth at all, and they are not able.﴾ ﴿So do not strike similitudes for Allah. Surely Allah knows, and you do not know.﴾

When He, exalted is He, mentioned those signs that are in the cattle, the fruits and the bees, He mentioned what alerts us to His complete power in bringing us into being from nothing and in causing us to die, and in our transition, during life, from the state of ignorance to the state of knowledge. All of this is evidence of complete power and vast knowledge, and for this reason He concluded with His words: ﴿All-Knowing, All-Powerful﴾.

﴿The most abject age﴾ is its last part, in which the senses decline and speech and thought deteriorate. He singled it out with the word "abjectness" because it is a state after which there is no hope of repairing what has decayed, unlike the state of childhood, in which one progresses towards strength and the comprehension of things. The "most abject age" is not restricted to a specific age, as is reported from ʿAlī: that it is seventy-five years, and from Qatāda: that it is ninety. Rather it depends on each individual: for many a person of fifty has reached the abject age, and many a person of a hundred has not been returned to it.

The apparent meaning is that the one who is returned to the most abject age is general, applying to whoever is afflicted by senility (al-kharaf) and decrepitude (al-haram). It was also said that this refers to the disbeliever, because the Muslim does not increase in his long life except in honour before Allah. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tīn: 5] ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Tīn: 6], meaning: they were not returned to the lowest of the low.

Qatāda said: "Whoever recites the Qur'an will not be returned to the most abject age."

As for the lām in (li-kay), al-Ḥawfī said: it is the lām of kay, a lām that entered upon (kay) for emphasis, and it is connected to (yuradd). Those who have investigated the grammarians' views regarding such a case as (li-kay) hold that kay is a verbal particle (ḥarf maṣdarī) when the lām enters upon it, and it functions like an, while the lām is a preposition (jārra). So from kay and the present tense verb after it there forms a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the genitive governed by the lām, in its implied sense. Accordingly, the lām here did not enter on (kay) for emphasis, because their meanings and their functions differ: the lām indicates causation, while kay is a verbal particle and the lām is a preposition, and kay is a particle that governs the subjunctive.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It seems that it is the lām of ṣayrūrah (lām of becoming), and the meaning is: so that his state after knowing things becomes one in which he knows nothing. This is an expression of the paucity of his knowledge, not that he knows absolutely nothing."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "So that he comes to a state resembling his state of forgetfulness, and he learns something, then quickly forgets it, so that if he is asked about it he does not know it." It was also said: "So that he does not understand anything after his first understanding." It was said: "So that he does not know any increase in knowledge beyond his knowledge." End of quote.

The word (shayʾan) is in the accusative either by the verbal noun, according to the Basran school's preference for the closer governing element, or by (yaʿlama), according to the Kufan school's preference for the element that precedes.

When He mentioned the decline of strength and power and the absence of knowledge that occur in old age, He mentioned His knowledge and power, which do not change, do not alter, and to which contingent events do not reach. The attribute of knowledge follows what is adjacent to it, namely the absence of knowledge. It was also previously mentioned that there is a reason for concluding with these two attributes.

When He, exalted is He, mentioned our creation, then our causing to die, and the variation in our ages, He mentioned our variation in provision, and that our provision is superior to the provision of the slaves, though they are human beings like us. It may be that the slave is better than the master in intellect, religion and conduct. And the one who is favoured in provision does not share with his slave what he has been given, so that they are equal. It would have been fitting for him to give back the surplus of what he has been given to them and to make them equal in food and clothing. Thus it is related of Abū Dharr that his slave was dressed, and his waist-wrap and his cloak were like his own cloak, without any difference, acting on the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "They are your brothers, so clothe them with what you wear, and feed them with what you eat."

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda that the statement ﴿So those who have been favoured do not give up their provision to them﴾ is by way of parable, meaning: those who are favoured in provision are not right to share with their slaves in what they have been given until their conditions are equal. If this is the case among human beings, how then do you, O disbelievers, attribute to Allah, exalted is He, that He associates with His divinity idols and images, and those among the angels and others who are worshipped, when they are all His slaves and His creation?

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that the verse alludes to ʿĪsā, son of Maryam, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet, the best of blessings and peace.

The exegetes said: "This verse is like His words: ﴿He has struck for you a parable from yourselves﴾ [al-Rūm: 28]" ... (p-515) "the verse."

It was also said: the meaning is that the masters and the slaves, I provide for all of them, so they are equal in My provision. Therefore let the masters not suppose that they give anything of provision to their slaves from themselves; rather that is delivered to them through their hands.

According to this opinion, (fahum fīhi sawāʾ) is a nominal sentence stating that all are equal in that Allah, exalted is He, is their provider. According to the other two opinions, the sentence is in the place of the answer to a negation, as if it were said: "So they would be equal."

It was also said: it is an interrogative sentence from which the hamza has been deleted. The estimate is: "Are they equal in it?" meaning: they are not equal in provision, rather favouring is inevitable. Then He asked about their denial of His blessing, as an interrogative of denial, and He used the word "blessing" which includes provision and other countless blessings. That is: the One who has favoured you with origination first, and then with what sustains your life, is worthy that His blessings be thanked and not denied.

Abū Bakr, from ʿĀṣim, Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and al-Aʿraj, in one of the reports from him, read (tajḥadūna) with the letter tāʾ, addressing the subject of (faḍḍala): as a rebuke for them for denying the blessing of Allah.

When He, exalted is He, mentioned His favour in bringing into being, then in the provision with which some are favoured over others, He mentioned His favour in what establishes human welfare, that with which one is comforted, which one relies on for help, and which serves him. The phrase ﴿from yourselves﴾ may mean from your own kind and species, and it may also mean by way of the creation of Ḥawwāʾ from a rib of the ribs of Ādam, so that this is attributed to the sons of Ādam. Both possibilities are figurative.

The apparent meaning is that the conjunction of (ḥafadatan) with (banīn) indicates that all of them are from the spouses, and that the grandchildren are other than the sons. Al-Ḥasan said: "They are the sons of your son." Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Azharī said: "The ḥafada are the children of children," and Ibn al-ʿArabī preferred this. Ibn ʿAbbās also said: "The banūn are the young children, and the ḥafada are their elders." Muqātil said the opposite. It was also said: "They are the daughters, because they serve in the houses in the most complete service." In this view, (banīn) was restricted to males because it is the masculine plural, as He said: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾ [al-Kahf: 46], while adornment lies in maleness.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās: "They are the children of the wife, from a husband other than the one who has her in his keeping." It was also said: (wa-ḥafadatan) is in the accusative governed by an implied (jaʿala), and they are not included in being among the spouses. Ibn Masʿūd, ʿAlqama, Abū al-Ḍuḥā and Ibrāhīm ibn Jubayr said: "The ṣihr (in-laws) are the relatives of the wife, such as her father and her brother." Mujāhid said: "They are the helpers, the assistants and the servants." A group said: "The ḥafada are the banūn," meaning: they combine sonship with service, so it is a conjunction of attributes for a single described subject.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said, in substance: "These opinions are based on the assumption that each person has been given sons and grandchildren from his spouse, and this is generally true of most people. In my view it is possible that His words ﴿from your spouses﴾ are general and collective: that is, from the spouses of mankind Allah has made sons, and from them He has made service, and in this way the verse arranges the blessing that encompasses the world. The word ḥafada remains correct in its linguistic sense, since no human being in his entirety can dispense with ḥafada." End of quote.

In His words ﴿spouses from yourselves﴾ there is an indication of the falsehood of the Arabs' belief that a human may marry a jinn and have intercourse with her, to the point that they related this about ʿAmr ibn Hind, that he married a siʿlāt (a female ghoul).

(مِن) in (الطَّيِّباتِ) is partitive (lit-tab'id, "some of"), because all the good things belong to Paradise, and what is in this world is only a sample (unmudhaj) of them. The apparent meaning of (الطَّيِّباتِ) here is "the pleasant things" (al-mustaladdhat), not "the lawful" (al-halal), because those addressed are disbelievers who are not bound by the Law (shar').

When the Exalted mentioned His favour in creating spouses and the two ways in which they benefit people, He then mentioned His favour in provision (rizq). "The good things" (al-tayyibat) is general, covering plants, fruits, grains, drinks, and animals. It has also been said: "The good things" are the spoils of war (al-ghana'im). It has also been said: they are what comes without toil (nasab). Muqatil said: "The falsehood" (al-batil) is Satan, and "the blessing of Allah" (ni'mat Allah) is Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Kalbi said: it is obedience to Satan in what is lawful and unlawful. It has also been said: it is the hoped-for intercession (shafa'a) and blessing (barakah) of the idols.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Do they then believe in falsehood?" refers to what they believe about the benefit, blessing, and intercession of the idols, which is nothing but an empty illusion, to which they have reached no proof or sign, so they have no faith except in it, as though it were a known and certain thing. "The blessing of Allah" refers to what is witnessed and seen directly, which is beyond doubt for anyone of intellect and discernment, yet they disbelieve in it and deny it, as one denies an impossibility that minds cannot conceive. It has also been said: "the falsehood" is what Satan embellishes for them of forbidding the baheerah, the sa'ibah, and others, and "the blessing of Allah" is what He has made lawful for them. End of quotation.

The majority (al-jumhur) read "yu'minun" with the letter ya', which is a rebuke addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ) concerning their belief in falsehood, and what is conjoined after it falls under this rebuke. As-Sulami read it with ta' (tu'minun), and it is also narrated from 'Asim. It is then a direct address of denunciation and reproach to them, and the sentence after that is merely a report about them. The apparent meaning is that it does not fall under the reproach.

"Ya'budun" (they worship) is an interrogative of report about their condition in worshipping idols. This clarifies His words "Do they then believe in falsehood?", condemning the corruption of their judgment in worshipping what cannot possibly produce for its worshipper what he seeks to obtain from it, namely provision, nor is it within its capacity. He first negated that any part of the provision is in their possession, and then negated secondly the ability of these idols to attempt that. "What they do not possess" is general, covering all who are worshipped besides Allah, whether angel, human, or otherwise.

They permitted the accusative (nasb) of "shay'an" (anything) to depend on "rizqan" (provision). Abu 'Ali and others permitted this. Ibn at-Tarawah refuted this, saying that "rizq" (with a kasra) is the thing provided, like "ar-ra'y" (grazing) and "at-tahn" (grinding), whereas the verbal noun (masdar) is "ar-rizq" (with a fatha on the ra'), like "ar-ra'y" and "at-tahn." It was objected against Ibn at-Tarawah that "ar-rizq" with a kasra is also a verbal noun, and this usage has been heard for it, so it is valid for it to govern the direct object. The meaning is: "what does not possess the ability to provide anything from the heavens and the earth." In this case, "min as-samawat" (from the heavens) is connected to the verbal noun.

Ibn 'Atiyya said, after mentioning the governing of a verbal noun when it is nunated: "The verbal noun governs when it is in the construct (idafa) by consensus, because it is in the sense of separation (taqdir al-infisal), and it does not govern when the definite article (al-) enters it, because it has become strongly nominal and far from the verbal nature." He said: "The sense of separation in the construct made its governing good, and it has come governing with the definite article in the poet's words:"

*"Weak in harming his enemies"* (the line in full)

and his words:

*"I reached them and did not hold back from striking the ear"* (the line in full);

end of quotation.

As for his words, "governs when in construct by consensus," if he meant among the Basrans, then it is correct; if he meant among the grammarians in general, then it is not correct, because some grammarians held that a verbal noun in the construct does not govern even if it puts into the accusative or nominative what follows it; rather that is by an implied verb indicated by the verbal noun. As for his words, "because it is in the sense of separation," this is not so, because if it were in the sense of separation, the construct would not be a pure (mahda) construct. Abu al-Qasim ibn Burhan and Abu al-Husayn ibn at-Tarawah said this, and their view is corrupt, because of the adjective of this construct verbal noun and its emphasis (tawkid) by a definite noun. As for his words, "and it does not govern" to the end, he contradicted himself in his final statement: "it has come governing with the definite article." As for its not governing with the definite article, this is a view transmitted from the Kufans, while Sibawayh's view is that its governing is permissible. Sibawayh said: "You say 'I was amazed at the striking Zayd,' just as you say 'I was amazed at the striker Zayd,' the definite article being in the position of the nunation (tanwin)."

When "rizqan" is meant as "the thing provided," they said: "shay'an" is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "rizqan," as if it were said: "what does not possess for them anything from the heavens and the earth." This substitute would be "by way of explanation" (bayan), because it is more general than "rizq," and not "by way of emphasis" (tawkid), because being general, it is not synonymous; so it should not be permitted, since a substitute must be of one of these two kinds: either explanation or emphasis. They also permitted that it be a verbal noun, meaning "anything of ownership," as in His words: "and they will not harm Him at all" (Hud 57), meaning "any harm." On these two parsings, "min as-samawat" connects to "la yamliku" (does not possess), or it is in the position of an adjective for "rizq," so it is connected to an implied element ("and from the heavens a provision"), meaning by it: rain, and it is called "provision" because provision arises from it. "The earth" means: trees, fruits, and crops.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "yastati'un" (they are able) returns to what is in the sense of "ma," because by it their gods are meant, after it had returned to the wording in His words "what does not possess." It was singular, and it is permitted for it to be included in the relative clause of "ma," and it is permitted that it not be included, but rather a report about them of the negation of ability at all, because they are dead.

As for al-Zamakhshari's statement that by combining the negation of ownership and of ability, emphasis is intended, it is not as he mentioned, because the negation of ownership is different from the negation of ability. Ibn 'Abbas said: "and they are not able to provide for themselves." Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that the pronoun return to what it returned to in His words "and they worship," and they are the disbelievers; i.e., these people, despite being living, active, and endowed with minds, are not able to do any of that, so how about the inanimate that has no sense? This is what al-Zamakhshari said. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "They are not able to do that by any proof they show or argument they establish"; end of quotation.

The Exalted forbade "striking examples for Allah" (darb al-amthal li-Allah). "Striking examples" means depicting them. The meaning here is: a depiction of associating partners with Allah and likening Him to them, because whoever strikes examples likens one state to another. "And a story with a story" comes from their saying: "This is a striking (darb) of this," i.e., an example (mathal), and "darb" means a kind. You say: "Animals are of many kinds (durub)," i.e., types, and "this is of one kind," i.e., of one type. Ibn 'Abbas said: its meaning is "do not liken Him to His creation"; end of quotation.

He said: "Indeed Allah knows": He affirmed knowledge for Himself. The meaning is that He knows what you do of worshipping others and associating partners with Him. He expressed the requital by knowledge: "and you do not know" the reality of what you have undertaken, nor the evil consequence of its outcome. So your lack of knowledge of that has led you on and emboldened you, and this is like a reason (ta'lil) for the prohibition against associating partners.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permitted that the meaning be that Allah knows how We strike examples, while you do not know. End of quotation. Ibn as-Sa'ib said this, saying: "He knows by the striking of an example, and you do not know that." Muqatil said: "He knows that He has no partner, and you do not know that." It has been said: "He knows the error of the examples you strike, and you do not know the correctness of that from its error."

[p. 508]

﴿And indeed, in livestock there is a lesson for you: We give you to drink of what is in their bellies, from between digestive contents and blood, pure milk, palatable to the drinkers.﴾ ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines you derive intoxicant and good provision. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who reason.﴾ ﴿And your Lord inspired the bee: "Take for yourself dwellings in the mountains, and in the trees, and in what they erect.﴾ ﴿Then eat from all the fruits and follow the ways of your Lord, submissively." There emerges from their bellies a drink of varying colors, in which is healing for mankind. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who give thought.﴾

Al-Zamakhshari... (no) — Abu Hayyan said: When Allah mentioned the revival of the earth after its death, He mentioned what arises from the rain, namely the life of livestock, which are what the Arabs are accustomed to, through what they consume of the plants that arise from the rain. He drew attention to the great lesson, which is the emergence of milk from between digestive contents and blood.

Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, Zayd ibn Ali, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr, Nafi', and the people of Madina recited, with a variant reported for Ibn Mas'ud: *nasqikum* here and in *Qad aflaha al-mu'minun* [al-Mu'minun: 1], with a fatha on the nun, as the imperfect of *saqa*. The rest of the seven readers read it with a damma, as the imperfect of *asqa*. The discussion of *saqa* and *asqa* has already occurred in His words: *fa-asqaynakumuhu* [al-Hijr: 22].

Abu Raja' recited *yusqikum*, with a damma on the ya', and the pronoun refers to Allah, meaning: Allah gives you to drink.

The author of *al-Lawaqih* said: It is also permissible that it be attributed to *al-ni'am* (the livestock/bounties), and it is masculine because *al-ni'am* may be treated as masculine or feminine. Its meaning: "And indeed, in the livestock there are bounties for you that give you drink," i.e., He makes for you a drinking. End of quotation.

A group recited *tusqikum* with a fatha on the ta'. Among them was Abu Ja'far. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is weak. End of quotation. Its weakness in his view, and Allah knows best, is from the fact that it is feminine in *tusqikum* and masculine in His words *mimma fi buṭunihi*. There is no weakness in that respect, because feminine and masculine are considered from two aspects. He returned the pronoun in the masculine out of regard for the collective noun, because when the singular noun that denotes a genus can stand in place of its plural, it may be referred back to in the masculine, as in their saying: *huwa ahsan al-fityan wa anbaluhu* (he is the best of the youths and the most noble of them), because it is valid to say *huwa ahsanu fata*. Although this is not analogically productive according to Sibawayh, it is restricted to what the Arabs have said.

It has been said: a broken plural for what lacks intellect is treated as a group and as a plural, so the pronoun returns to it in the singular, as in his saying:

*Like young birds whose crops have been swollen*

It has been said: He used the singular with consideration of the mentioned item, just as the demonstrative is used in the singular after a plural, as he said:

*In them are lines of black and white, as if on the skin it is the streak of leprosy (al-bahaq)*

So he said *ka'annahu* (as if it), taking into account *dhalika al-mudhkur* (the mentioned thing).

Al-Kisa'i said: i.e., in the bellies of what we have mentioned. Al-Mubarrad said: This is permissible in the Qur'an. Allah the Exalted said: *Indeed, this is a reminder* [al-Muzzammil: 19] and *so whoever wills, let him take heed of it* [al-Muddaththir: 55], i.e., let him take heed of this thing. And He said: *So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my Lord"* [al-An'am: 78], i.e., this rising thing. This is only in metaphorical feminine, and one may not say: *jariyatuka dhahaba* (your slave-girl went).

A group said: The pronoun refers to a part, since males have no milk, so the lesson is really in some of the livestock.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Sibawayh mentioned *al-an'am* in the chapter of what is not declined among single nouns of the pattern *af'al*, as in their saying *thawb akyash* (a garment of akyash). For this reason the pronoun returned to it in the singular. As for *fi buṭunihā* [al-Mu'minun: 21] in *Surat al-Mu'minun*, it is because its meaning is plural. It is permissible to say about *al-an'am* two things: one of them is that it is a broken plural of *na'am*, like *ajbal* (mountains) from *jabal*; and that it is a singular noun implying the meaning of plurality, like *na'am*. When it is masculine, then just as *na'am* is treated as masculine in His words:

*Every year there is a na'am that you keep, which some breed and some bring forth*

And when it is feminine, there are two aspects: that it is a broken plural of *na'am*, and that it has the meaning of a plural. End of quotation.

As for what he attributed to Sibawayh, in his book, in this matter, in the chapter on what has the pattern *mufā'il* and *mafā'il*, the text is: "As for *ajmal* (camels) and *fulus* (copper coins), they are declined and similar things, because they resemble the singular. Do you not see that you say: *aqwal* and *aqawil* (sayings), *a'rab* and *a'arib* (Arabs), *ayd* and *ayad* (hands)? These letters go out to the pattern *mufā'il* and *mafā'il*, just as the singular goes out to it when broken for the plural. As for *mafā'il* and *mafā'il*, they are not broken, so the plural goes out to another form, because this form is the ultimate. When they resembled the singular, they were declined." Then he said: "Likewise *fu'ul*, if it were broken like *fulus*, so as to be pluralized, it would take the form *fa'a'il*, as you say: *judud* and *jada'id* (ancestors/grandfathers?), *rukub* and *raka'ib* (riding-animals). If you did that with *mufa'il* and *mafa'il*, it would not go beyond this form. This is reinforced by the fact that some Arabs say *atā* for the singular, pronouncing the alif with a damma. As for *af'al*, it may be used for the singular. Among the Arabs there is one who says *huwa al-an'am* (it is the livestock)." Allah, majestic and mighty, said: *nusqikum mimma fi buṭunihi* [al-Mu'minun: 21]. Abu al-Khattab said: I heard the Arabs say: "This is a garment of akyash." End of quotation.

What Sibawayh mentioned is the distinction between *mufā'il* and *mafā'il*, and between *af'al* and *fu'ul*. Although all of them are patterns of the plural, in that *mufā'il* and *mafā'il* are not themselves pluralized, whereas *af'al* and *fu'ul* may go out to a pattern resembling *mufā'il* or *mafā'il*, owing to their resemblance to the singular in that they may be pluralized, while those two are not pluralized. Then the resemblance of the two to the singular was strengthened by the fact that some Arabs said *utā* for *atā*, with a damma on the hamza. He means that *fu'ul* from other than the verbal noun has rarely come for the singular. And that some Arabs use *af'al* for the singular, when they make the pronoun singular, so they say *huwa al-an'am*. He only means that this is by way of metaphor, because *al-an'am* has the meaning of *al-ni'am*, as the poet said:

*We left the horses and the precious camels, and said to the women, "Stay here with them."*

For this reason Sibawayh said: "As for *af'al*, it may be used for the singular," which is evidence that this is not by original imposition. So al-Zamakhshari's saying that he mentioned it among single nouns of the pattern *af'al* is a distortion of the wording and a misunderstanding of what Sibawayh did not intend. What proves our view is that when Sibawayh mentioned the patterns of single nouns, he explicitly stated that *af'al* is not among their patterns. Sibawayh said in the chapter on triliteral words that have received added letters and which are not in the language: *af'il*, *uf'ul*, *af'āl*, *if'il* and *if'āl*, except that you break a noun for a collective to it. End of quotation. This is an explicit statement from him that *af'āl* does not occur among the patterns of single nouns.

*Nusqikum mimma fi buṭunihi* is an explanation of the lesson.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is a resumptive clause, as if it were said: "What is the lesson?" So it was said: "We give you to drink from between digestive contents and blood." That is, Allah creates milk as a middle between the digestive contents and the blood, which surround it, and between it and them is a barrier from the power of Allah, so that neither of them oppresses it with color, taste, or smell; rather it is pure from all of them. End of quotation.

Ibn 'Abbas said: When the fodder settles in the rumen, its lowest part becomes digestive contents which remain in it, its highest part becomes blood which flows through the veins, and its middle becomes milk which flows into the udder.

Ibn Jubayr said: The digestive contents are in the middle of the intestines, the blood is in their upper part, and the milk is between them. The liver divides the digestive contents toward the rumen, the blood toward the veins, and the milk toward the udders.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: The commentators said: What is meant by His words *min bayni farthin wa dam* is that these three are generated in one place: the digestive contents are at the bottom of the rumen, the blood at its top, and the milk in the middle. We have shown that this view is contrary to sensation and experience. Al-Razi had previously stated that when an animal is slaughtered, no blood or milk is seen in its rumen. The truth is that when the animal consumes food, it reaches the rumen and is cooked there, and the first digestion takes place in it. What is thick descends into the intestines, and what is clear descends to the liver, where it is cooked and becomes blood, which is the second digestion, mixed with yellow bile, black bile, and an increase of watery matter. The yellow bile goes to the gall bladder, the black bile to the spleen, the water to the kidney, and the pure blood goes to the *awrid* (the vessels arising from the liver). Then the third digestion takes place. Between the liver and the udder there are many vessels through which blood pours into the udder, which is a soft white flesh, and it is transformed from the form of blood into the form of milk. This is the correct account of how milk is generated. End of quotation, summarized.

He also said: As for us, we say: The meaning of the verse is that milk is only generated from some parts of the blood, and blood is only generated from the subtle parts found in the digestive contents, which are the edible things present in the rumen. So the milk is generated from what was present between the digestive contents first, then from what was present between the blood second. End of quotation, also summarized.

What appears from the wording of the verse is that the milk is a middle between the digestive contents and the blood. The "between" may be taken literally in terms of place, as the commentators said, though al-Razi claimed this is contrary to sense and observation. It may also be taken figuratively, in terms of its generation from what arises in the digestive contents first and from the blood that results from the subtle part of what was in the digestive contents second, as al-Razi established.

The first *min* is partitive, related to *nusqikum*. The second *min* denotes the beginning of the limit, related to *nusqikum*. Both may be related to one governing verb because their meanings differ. It is also permissible that *min bayni* be in the position of a circumstantial clause, and so it is related to an omitted element, because if it were postponed it would be a qualifier, meaning: existing from between digestive contents and blood. It is also permissible that *min bayni farthin* be a substitute for *mā fī buṭunihi*.

A group read *sayyighan* with a shadda on the ya'. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read *saygh*, unshadda, from *sayyigh*, like *hayn* from *hayyin*, and it is not an intransitive verb that would be *sawgh*. *Al-sa'igh* is what is easy to swallow and delicious. It is narrated in a hadith that "no one has ever choked on milk."

When Allah mentioned what He bestowed of the benefits of livestock, He mentioned what He bestowed of some benefits of plants.

The apparent meaning is that *wa min thamarāt* is related to *tattakhidhūna*. *Min* is repeated for emphasis, and the pronoun is singular, taking account of an omitted element, meaning: and from the juice of fruits, or in view of the meaning of *al-thamarat*, which is fruit, or by an omitted element from what was mentioned. It has been said: it is related to *nusqikum*, so it is coordinated with *mimma fi buṭunihi*. Or it is related to an omitted *nusqikum* indicated by the earlier *nusqikum*, so it is coordination of clauses, whereas the preceding is coordination of single words when they share a governing element. It has been said: it is coordinated with *al-an'am*, meaning: and from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines there is a lesson, and then He explained the lesson by His words *tattakhidhūna*. Al-Tabari said: The estimate is: "and from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines what you take," so he omitted *mā*, which is not permissible according to the Basrans. Al-Zamakhshari said: It may be a qualifier of an omitted noun, as in the verse: *bikaffī kāna man armī al-bashar* (with my hand was he who shot the most among men). Its estimate: "and from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines, a fruit from which you take." End of quotation. What he permitted was said by al-Hawfi, who said: That is, "and from the fruits," and if you wish "a thing," with a raised *shay'un* as an inchoative, and *min thamarat* is its predicate. End of quotation.

*Al-sakar* in the language means wine. The poet said:

*Evil are the sober, and evil is their drinking, when the intoxicant and the sakar flow among them*

Al-Zamakhshari said: It was named by the verbal noun of *sakira*, *sukran* and *sakaran*, like *rashida rushdan* and *rashadan*. The poet said:

*They came to us with sakar against us, so the sober is now dispelled, and the drunkard is sober*

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, Abu Razin, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Kalbi, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Thawr and the majority (al-Jumhur) said this. This verse is Meccan. It was revealed before the prohibition of wine (khamr), and wine was prohibited later in Medina, so the verse is abrogated (mansukh). Al-Hasan said: "God mentioned His favour regarding intoxicant (sakar) before the prohibition of wine." Ibn 'Abbas said: it is vinegar (khall) in the language of the Abyssinians (Habasha). It was also said: it is sweet unfermented juice that is lawful, and it was called sakar because of what it becomes if left. Abu 'Ubayda said: sakar means food. It is said, "This is sakar for you," meaning food. Al-Tabari chose this view and said: in the speech of the Arabs, sakar is what is eaten. Abu 'Ubayda recited:

"She made the honour of the noble into sakar"

meaning she passed around (tanaqqalat) their honour. It was also said: it is from khamr, and that when a person plunges into people's honour, it is as if he has become intoxicated (takhammara) by it. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, and al-Zajjaj followed him, saying: it describes that one is intoxicated by people's faults. According to these views, there is no abrogation. Al-Zajjaj said: Abu 'Ubayda's view is not sound, and the people of tafsir are against it. It was also said: sakar is what is non-intoxicating of the nabidh (date and grape beverages). It was also said: sakar is nabidh, which is the juice of grapes, raisins and dates when it is boiled until two-thirds of it is gone, then left until it becomes strong. This is lawful according to Abu Hanifa up to the point of intoxication. End of quote. If sakar is taken to mean khamr, then it has already been stated that this is abrogated. If we do not say abrogation, then it is said: it combines reproach (itab) and favour (minna). By reproach is meant the taking of what is prohibited, and by favour the taking of what is lawful, which is vinegar, syrup (rubb), raisins and dates. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also possible that sakar is made a good provision (rizq hasan), as if it were said: "You take from it what is sakar and a good provision." End of quote. In this case it is a conjunction of attributes, and the apparent sense of the conjunction is difference.

Since the opening of the discourse is: ﴿And indeed in the livestock there is a lesson for you﴾, it suits that the verse end with His saying: "they reflect (ya'qilun)", because only those with intellects take heed, as He said: ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for those of understanding﴾ [Al 'Imran: 13].

Observe the report of the favour of milk, the favour of sakar and good provision. Since milk does not need processing by people, God reported about Himself with His saying: "We give you to drink (nusqikum)." Since sakar and good provision need processing, He said: "you take (tattakhidhun)," reporting about them that they take sakar and provision from it. For this reason the pure Arabs (al-'Arab al-'Ariba) were unable to match it. When God mentioned the favour of drink, milk and others, He completed the favour by mentioning honey of the bee (al-nahl). Since drinks from milk and others were more common among people than honey, He placed milk and others before it, and placed milk before what follows it, because it is what people need most and it is evidence of the natural disposition (fitra). For this reason the Messenger (ﷺ) chose it when he was taken on the Night Journey (isra'), when milk, wine and honey were presented to him. Their order in Paradise also corresponds to this verse. God says: ﴿And rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers, and rivers of honey, purified﴾ [Muhammad: 15]. So in the bringing out of milk from the livestock, and sakar and good provision from the fruits of palms and grapes, and honey from the bee, there are dazzling signs of divinity, power and choice.

Revelation (al-iyha') here means inspiration (al-ilham) and casting into its heart, and teaching it in a manner that He, exalted is He, knows best, and no path leads to comprehending it. The bee (al-nahl) is a genus, its singular is nahla, and it is feminine in the dialect of the Hijaz, which is why He said: ﴿Take (ittakhidhi)﴾. Ibn Wathhab read: "al-nahal" with a fatha on the ha. The "an" here is explanatory (tafsiriyya), since the meaning of speech (qawl) precedes it, which is "wa-awha" (and He inspired). Or it is verbal-source (masdariyya), meaning "by taking." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "an" is the one explaining what is in the revelation of the meaning of speech. This is the view of the majority of the commentators, but there is an objection to it, because the revelation here is by consensus of them the inspiration, and there is no meaning of speech in inspiration. He said: God established in the bees amazing works that are beyond rational humans, among them building hexagonal houses from equal sides by their nature alone. Such a thing is not achieved by rational beings except with tools like the ruler and the compass. They do not build with other shapes, lest those houses become too narrow for them, leaving gaps they cannot fill. They have a leader larger in body than them, whose command is executed, and they serve him. When they swarm away from their hive to another place and want to return to it, they strike drums and musical instruments, and by the mediation of those tunes they return to their hive. Since they are distinguished by these amazing properties, and this is only by way of inspiration, which is a state resembling revelation, for this reason He said: "Your Lord inspired the bee." End of summary. The "min" (from) is partitive, because they do not build in every mountain, every tree, and everything that is trellised, nor in every place within them. The apparent meaning is that the houses here refer to the cavities found in mountains and in the hollows of trees. As for "from what the son of Adam trellises," it refers to the hives that the son of Adam makes for the bees, and the openings found in walls. Since the bee has two types: one that dwells in mountains and thickets and no one cares for it, and one that lives in people's houses and is cared for in hives and the like, the command to take houses includes both types. Al-Zamakhshari said, indicating that the houses are not the openings, but rather what they themselves build: "The meaning of partitiveness is intended by min, and that their houses are not built in every mountain, every tree and everything that is trellised." Ibn Zayd said: "And of what they trellis": the vineyards. Al-Tabari said: of what they build of roofs. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this from both of them is an unsound interpretation. End of quote.

Al-Sulami, 'Ubayd ibn Nadla, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read the word "yarish" (trellis) with a damma on the ra'. The rest of the seven read it with a kasra. "Thumma" (then) indicates a delay and interval between the taking and the eating from which the honey is stored. For this reason the conjunction is with "thumma", and it is coordinated with "ittakhidhi" (take). It is a command conjoined to a command. The discussion of a command addressed to a non-accountable creature will come later in His saying: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾ [al-Naml: 18], God willing. "All the fruits" is a general term that is specified, meaning the customary ones, not all of them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "meaning: build the houses, then eat from every fruit you desire." End of quote. His saying "meaning: build the houses" shows that by "houses" He does not mean the openings in mountains and hollows of trees, nor the hives, but rather the hexagonal houses that they build themselves. The apparent meaning of "min" in His saying ﴿from all the fruits﴾ is partitive, so they eat from the good trees and fragrant leaves things from which God produces honey in their bodies. Ibn 'Atiyya said: they only eat the blossoms of trees.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said, in summary: God causes in the air much shade, from which gather perceptible particles, such as manna (al-narjabin), which is perceptible, and a small amount of very fine, tiny particles. It is this that God inspired the bees to collect from flowers and leaves of trees, and they feed on it. When they are sated, they pick up with their mouths some of those particles and place them in their hives, as if trying to store their food for themselves. So what gathers from that is honey. According to this view, "min" is for the beginning of the end (ibtida' al-ghaya), not partitive. End of quote.

The apparent meaning of the conjunction with "fa" in ﴿then travel﴾ (fa-uslukī) is that it follows immediately after eating: "When you have eaten, then travel the ways of your Lord," that is, the paths of your Lord back to your houses. The "subul" (paths) at that time are their routes in flight. Perhaps they settle in place and then seek a distant place, and then return to their first place. It was also said: "the ways of your Lord" means the paths that He inspired and taught you in making honey. Or, "travel what you have eaten", that is, in the paths of your Lord, meaning in His pathways in which, by His power, He transforms bitter flowers into honey from your bellies and the outlets of your mouths. According to this view, "subul" in "the ways of your Lord" is in the accusative as an adverb of place. According to what preceded it, it is in the accusative as an object. It was also said: what is meant by His saying ﴿then eat﴾ is: then intend to eat from the fruits, and then travel in seeking them the ways of your Lord. This view and the first view are closer in metaphor regarding "ways of your Lord" than the two views between them, except that "eat" in the sense of "intend to eat" is a metaphor. He attributed the paths to the Lord of the bee because He, exalted is He, is their creator, owner, and the one who provides for their welfare and sustenance.

Mujahid said: "dhululan" means not rugged; there is no difficult path for them to travel. On this view "dhululan" is a state (hal) of "subula Rabbiki", like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He is the One who made the earth docile for you﴾ [al-Mulk: 15]. Qatada said: that is, obedient and submissive. Ibn Zayd said: they go out with the bees, seeking pasture, and they follow them. On this view "dhululan" is a state of the bees, like His saying: ﴿And We made them subservient to them﴾ [Ya-Sin: 72].

Then God, by way of enumerating the favour and alerting to the kindness, mentioned the outcome of this taking, eating and travelling, which is His saying: ﴿There comes out from their bellies a drink﴾, and this is honey. He called it "drink" because it is something drunk, just as He mentioned the outcome of livestock, which is giving milk to drink, and the outcome of palms and grapes, which is the making of sakar and good provision. He mentioned the place from which the drink comes out, which is their bellies, and this is the beginning of the first end. The majority hold that it comes out from their mouths, and this is the beginning of the final end. For this reason al-Hariri said:

"You say: this is the regurgitation of the bee, you praise it,
and if you blame it, you say: the vomit of wasps."

The honey and the vomit can only come from the mouth. It is reported from ʿAlī, may Allah honour his face, that in belittling this world he said: "The finest clothing of the son of Adam in it is the saliva of a worm, and the finest of his drinks is the excrement of a bee." And also from him: "As for honey, it is the vomit of a fly." The apparent meaning of this is that honey comes out from somewhere other than the mouth, and it is unclear from which of the two outlets it comes: the mouth, or below?

It is related that Solomon, peace be upon him, Alexander, and Aristotle made houses of glass for the bees so that they could observe how they make them and whether honey comes out from their mouths or from beneath them. But the bees did not release any honey until they smeared the inside of the glass with mud, so that it prevented observation.

Al-Ḥasan said: "The pure part of the wheat, mixed with the saliva of the bee and pure ghee, which no Muslim has disliked, [God] made it a saliva like the constant spittle that comes out of the mouth of the son of Adam."

It was said: ﴿from their bellies﴾ means from their mouths. He called the mouth a "belly" because it is in the position of the belly, and because it is something that is hidden inside and does not appear.

The variation in its colours, white, yellow, red and black, is due to the differing natures of the bees and the differing pastures. Its taste may also vary according to the pasture, as in the ḥadīth: "His bees grazed on the ʿarfaṭ [a bitter shrub]." It was said: the white is what the young bees produce, the yellow what their elderly produce, and the red what their adolescents produce.

The apparent reference of the pronoun in ﴿fīhi﴾ is to the drink, which is honey, because it is a cure among the well-known and beneficial remedies and medicines. Hardly any compound medicine has been listed by physicians without honey in it, and honey is found in abundance in most lands.

As for sugar (al-sukkar), it is specific to some lands and is a recent development; in earlier times, in most lands, nothing but honey was put into drinks and medicines.

The word "people" (al-nās) here does not mean all people in general, because honey does not enter the treatment of many illnesses; rather the meaning is "for those people whose illnesses honey benefits."

The word "shifāʾ" (cure) is indefinite, either for the sake of magnification, so that the meaning is "a cure, a great cure," or to indicate the general notion of cure, so that the meaning is "in it there is some cure."

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Farrāʾ and Ibn Kaysān that the pronoun in (fīhi) refers to the Qur'an, meaning: "In the Qur'an there is a cure for people." Al-Naḥḥās said: "This is a good opinion," meaning: "In what We have related to you of the signs and proofs there is a cure for people."

Al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "I consider that this opinion cannot be validly transmitted from these men, and even if it were validly transmitted, it would not be sound on reason. For the whole context of the speech is about honey, and there is no mention of the Qur'an in it. And since the matter of the bees is wondrous in their building of those hexagonal houses, in their eating of all kinds of flowers, leaves, sour, bitter and harmful things, and in their obedience to their leader and to whoever owns them when they migrate with him, the consideration of this seems to need reflection and further contemplation." He concluded with His words, exalted is He: ﴿Surely in that is a sign for a people who reflect﴾.

﴿And Allah created you, then He causes you to die, and among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after having known. Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Powerful.﴾ ﴿And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision. Yet those who have been favoured do not give up their provision to those whom their right hands possess, so that they are equal in it. Do they then deny the blessing of Allah?﴾ ﴿And Allah made for you spouses from among yourselves, and made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren, and provided you with good things. Do they then believe in falsehood and deny the blessing of Allah?﴾ ﴿And they worship, besides Allah, what possesses no provision for them from the heavens and the earth at all, and they are not able.﴾ ﴿So do not strike similitudes for Allah. Surely Allah knows, and you do not know.﴾

When He, exalted is He, mentioned those signs that are in the cattle, the fruits and the bees, He mentioned what alerts us to His complete power in bringing us into being from nothing and in causing us to die, and in our transition, during life, from the state of ignorance to the state of knowledge. All of this is evidence of complete power and vast knowledge, and for this reason He concluded with His words: ﴿All-Knowing, All-Powerful﴾.

﴿The most abject age﴾ is its last part, in which the senses decline and speech and thought deteriorate. He singled it out with the word "abjectness" because it is a state after which there is no hope of repairing what has decayed, unlike the state of childhood, in which one progresses towards strength and the comprehension of things. The "most abject age" is not restricted to a specific age, as is reported from ʿAlī: that it is seventy-five years, and from Qatāda: that it is ninety. Rather it depends on each individual: for many a person of fifty has reached the abject age, and many a person of a hundred has not been returned to it.

The apparent meaning is that the one who is returned to the most abject age is general, applying to whoever is afflicted by senility (al-kharaf) and decrepitude (al-haram). It was also said that this refers to the disbeliever, because the Muslim does not increase in his long life except in honour before Allah. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tīn: 5] ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Tīn: 6], meaning: they were not returned to the lowest of the low.

Qatāda said: "Whoever recites the Qur'an will not be returned to the most abject age."

As for the lām in (li-kay), al-Ḥawfī said: it is the lām of kay, a lām that entered upon (kay) for emphasis, and it is connected to (yuradd). Those who have investigated the grammarians' views regarding such a case as (li-kay) hold that kay is a verbal particle (ḥarf maṣdarī) when the lām enters upon it, and it functions like an, while the lām is a preposition (jārra). So from kay and the present tense verb after it there forms a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the genitive governed by the lām, in its implied sense. Accordingly, the lām here did not enter on (kay) for emphasis, because their meanings and their functions differ: the lām indicates causation, while kay is a verbal particle and the lām is a preposition, and kay is a particle that governs the subjunctive.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It seems that it is the lām of ṣayrūrah (lām of becoming), and the meaning is: so that his state after knowing things becomes one in which he knows nothing. This is an expression of the paucity of his knowledge, not that he knows absolutely nothing."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "So that he comes to a state resembling his state of forgetfulness, and he learns something, then quickly forgets it, so that if he is asked about it he does not know it." It was also said: "So that he does not understand anything after his first understanding." It was said: "So that he does not know any increase in knowledge beyond his knowledge." End of quote.

The word (shayʾan) is in the accusative either by the verbal noun, according to the Basran school's preference for the closer governing element, or by (yaʿlama), according to the Kufan school's preference for the element that precedes.

When He mentioned the decline of strength and power and the absence of knowledge that occur in old age, He mentioned His knowledge and power, which do not change, do not alter, and to which contingent events do not reach. The attribute of knowledge follows what is adjacent to it, namely the absence of knowledge. It was also previously mentioned that there is a reason for concluding with these two attributes.

When He, exalted is He, mentioned our creation, then our causing to die, and the variation in our ages, He mentioned our variation in provision, and that our provision is superior to the provision of the slaves, though they are human beings like us. It may be that the slave is better than the master in intellect, religion and conduct. And the one who is favoured in provision does not share with his slave what he has been given, so that they are equal. It would have been fitting for him to give back the surplus of what he has been given to them and to make them equal in food and clothing. Thus it is related of Abū Dharr that his slave was dressed, and his waist-wrap and his cloak were like his own cloak, without any difference, acting on the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "They are your brothers, so clothe them with what you wear, and feed them with what you eat."

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda that the statement ﴿So those who have been favoured do not give up their provision to them﴾ is by way of parable, meaning: those who are favoured in provision are not right to share with their slaves in what they have been given until their conditions are equal. If this is the case among human beings, how then do you, O disbelievers, attribute to Allah, exalted is He, that He associates with His divinity idols and images, and those among the angels and others who are worshipped, when they are all His slaves and His creation?

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that the verse alludes to ʿĪsā, son of Maryam, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet, the best of blessings and peace.

The exegetes said: "This verse is like His words: ﴿He has struck for you a parable from yourselves﴾ [al-Rūm: 28]" ... (p-515) "the verse."

It was also said: the meaning is that the masters and the slaves, I provide for all of them, so they are equal in My provision. Therefore let the masters not suppose that they give anything of provision to their slaves from themselves; rather that is delivered to them through their hands.

According to this opinion, (fahum fīhi sawāʾ) is a nominal sentence stating that all are equal in that Allah, exalted is He, is their provider. According to the other two opinions, the sentence is in the place of the answer to a negation, as if it were said: "So they would be equal."

It was also said: it is an interrogative sentence from which the hamza has been deleted. The estimate is: "Are they equal in it?" meaning: they are not equal in provision, rather favouring is inevitable. Then He asked about their denial of His blessing, as an interrogative of denial, and He used the word "blessing" which includes provision and other countless blessings. That is: the One who has favoured you with origination first, and then with what sustains your life, is worthy that His blessings be thanked and not denied.

Abū Bakr, from ʿĀṣim, Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and al-Aʿraj, in one of the reports from him, read (tajḥadūna) with the letter tāʾ, addressing the subject of (faḍḍala): as a rebuke for them for denying the blessing of Allah.

When He, exalted is He, mentioned His favour in bringing into being, then in the provision with which some are favoured over others, He mentioned His favour in what establishes human welfare, that with which one is comforted, which one relies on for help, and which serves him. The phrase ﴿from yourselves﴾ may mean from your own kind and species, and it may also mean by way of the creation of Ḥawwāʾ from a rib of the ribs of Ādam, so that this is attributed to the sons of Ādam. Both possibilities are figurative.

The apparent meaning is that the conjunction of (ḥafadatan) with (banīn) indicates that all of them are from the spouses, and that the grandchildren are other than the sons. Al-Ḥasan said: "They are the sons of your son." Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Azharī said: "The ḥafada are the children of children," and Ibn al-ʿArabī preferred this. Ibn ʿAbbās also said: "The banūn are the young children, and the ḥafada are their elders." Muqātil said the opposite. It was also said: "They are the daughters, because they serve in the houses in the most complete service." In this view, (banīn) was restricted to males because it is the masculine plural, as He said: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾ [al-Kahf: 46], while adornment lies in maleness.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās: "They are the children of the wife, from a husband other than the one who has her in his keeping." It was also said: (wa-ḥafadatan) is in the accusative governed by an implied (jaʿala), and they are not included in being among the spouses. Ibn Masʿūd, ʿAlqama, Abū al-Ḍuḥā and Ibrāhīm ibn Jubayr said: "The ṣihr (in-laws) are the relatives of the wife, such as her father and her brother." Mujāhid said: "They are the helpers, the assistants and the servants." A group said: "The ḥafada are the banūn," meaning: they combine sonship with service, so it is a conjunction of attributes for a single described subject.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said, in substance: "These opinions are based on the assumption that each person has been given sons and grandchildren from his spouse, and this is generally true of most people. In my view it is possible that His words ﴿from your spouses﴾ are general and collective: that is, from the spouses of mankind Allah has made sons, and from them He has made service, and in this way the verse arranges the blessing that encompasses the world. The word ḥafada remains correct in its linguistic sense, since no human being in his entirety can dispense with ḥafada." End of quote.

In His words ﴿spouses from yourselves﴾ there is an indication of the falsehood of the Arabs' belief that a human may marry a jinn and have intercourse with her, to the point that they related this about ʿAmr ibn Hind, that he married a siʿlāt (a female ghoul).

(مِن) in (الطَّيِّباتِ) is partitive (lit-tab'id, "some of"), because all the good things belong to Paradise, and what is in this world is only a sample (unmudhaj) of them. The apparent meaning of (الطَّيِّباتِ) here is "the pleasant things" (al-mustaladdhat), not "the lawful" (al-halal), because those addressed are disbelievers who are not bound by the Law (shar').

When the Exalted mentioned His favour in creating spouses and the two ways in which they benefit people, He then mentioned His favour in provision (rizq). "The good things" (al-tayyibat) is general, covering plants, fruits, grains, drinks, and animals. It has also been said: "The good things" are the spoils of war (al-ghana'im). It has also been said: they are what comes without toil (nasab). Muqatil said: "The falsehood" (al-batil) is Satan, and "the blessing of Allah" (ni'mat Allah) is Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Kalbi said: it is obedience to Satan in what is lawful and unlawful. It has also been said: it is the hoped-for intercession (shafa'a) and blessing (barakah) of the idols.
