What he mentioned, that *aw* means *bal* (rather), is the view of al-Farra', and it is not valid, because the transition (*iḍrāb*) is of two kinds, and neither is valid here. The first: that it be a cancellation of the preceding predication, and that it was not what was intended. This is impossible here, because it would result in a predication that does not correspond. The second: that it be a transition from one thing to another without cancelling that preceding thing. This is also impossible here, because of the contradiction between reporting that it is like the blink of an eye in speed and reporting that it is nearer, so both cannot be true together.

The author of *al-Ghaniyyan* said: "Although this is hard to grasp literally, what is intended is exaggeration, according to the way of the Arabs and the masters of composition." How excellent is the saying of the poet al-Ablah on this meaning:

> The lightning said to him, and the wind said to him, both together, and they are what they are:
> "Do you run with us?" He said: "If I become energetic, I will make you both laugh at yourselves."
> "I am the return of the glance, I have outpaced it toward the goal in speed, so who are you two?"

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the matter of the Hour and that it is certainly coming, this indicated the Hereafter's creation. The earlier description of them with the absence of knowledge was mentioned, so He mentioned the first creation, which is bringing them out from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing, as an alert to the occurrence of the later creation. Then He mentioned His favor upon them in giving them the senses, which are the means of perceiving things and attaining knowledge. Since the first creation was mentioned, and He made what they know by as one of the greatest blessings upon them, He said: ﴿so that you may give thanks﴾. The discussion of *ummahat* (mothers) was mentioned in al-Nisa'.

Hamza read with a kasra on the hamza and the mim here, and in al-Nur, al-Zumar and al-Najm, and al-Kisa'i read with a kasra on the hamza in them. Al-A'mash read with deletion of the hamza and a kasra on the mim, and Ibn Abi Layla read with its deletion and a fatha on the mim. Abu Hatim said: "Deleting the hamza is bad, but the reading of Ibn Ubayy is more correct." End of quotation. It was more correct because the kasra on the mim occurs only to assimilate it to the vowel of the hamza; when the hamza is deleted, the assimilation disappears. By contrast, Ibn Abi Layla's reading leaves the mim on its own vowel.

*Lā taʿlamūna* ("you do not know") is a circumstantial clause (*jumla ḥāliyya*), meaning: "while not knowing." It has been said: "You do not know anything of what the covenant taken from you in the loins of your fathers was, or anything of what was decreed for you of happiness or misery, or anything of your benefits." The more appropriate is the general sense of the word "anything," especially in the context of negation. Wahb said: "The child is born wary for seven days; he does not perceive comfort or pain." It is possible that *wajaʿala* (and He made) is conjoined to ﴿He brought you out﴾, so it is one part within the scope of the predicate of the subject; and it is possible that it is a new statement conjoined to the initial sentence, like the beginning of it.

The meaning of the hearing, the sights and the hearts is their sensing and perceiving, so the faculty is expressed by the organ. Abu Abdullah al-Razi (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) said, in substance: "The reason the word *fu'ad* (heart) is given in the paucity plural (*jam' qilla*, the plural form for small numbers) is that it was created only for true, certain knowledge, whereas most people are preoccupied with bestial acts, so their hearts are not really hearts. For this reason the paucity plural is used for it." End of his words, summarized. This is a delirious statement. Were it not for the eminence of the one who said it and his having written it in books, I would not have mentioned it. What should be said about this is what al-Zamakhshari said: that *afida* is among the paucity plurals that have come to function like plurals of abundance and paucity alike, when no other form of it is attested in usage, as with *shusu'* (the plural of *shis'*, "sandal-thong") which has no other plural form. So it follows that pattern. End of his words. However, al-Zamakhshari's claim that no plural of *shis'* other than *shusu'* occurs is not correct. A paucity plural also occurs for it: they say *ash-sa'* (*ashsa'*). So he should have said: "*shusu'* has been given precedence (as the common plural)."

Ibn Amir, Hamza, Talha, al-A'mash and Ibn Hurmuz read *alam tarawa* (ﷺ not applicable) with the second person "you" (*ta'* of address), while the rest of the seven readers read it with *ya'* (third person). Ibn Atiyya said: "There is a difference of report from al-Hasan, Isa al-Thaqafi, Asim and Abu Amr."

When the Exalted mentioned the three means of knowledge, hearing, sight and reason, the first two being the means of perceiving the sensible and the third the means of perceiving the intelligible, He confined the mention of the means of perceiving the sensible to sight, since it is the most striking for what is observed by it of the great creatures at their varied distances, such as observing the luminous bodies in the spheres. He placed the flying animal as the object of consideration and wonder here, for its flight in the air despite the weight of its body is among the things that cause wonder and are taken as a lesson. The verse also includes mention of the means of perceiving by reason, in that the bird does not fall, since there is nothing beneath it to support it and nothing above it to which it is attached. Thus reason knows that there is a holder of it who is able to hold it up, and He is God the Exalted, as the Exalted said: ﴿Have they not considered the birds above them, spreading and folding their wings? None holds them up except the Most Merciful. Indeed, He is Seer of all things.﴾ (67:19). Thus the verse brings together the mention of the means of sense perception and the means of reasoning.

The meaning of *musakhkharat* ("made subservient") is "made pliable," and it is in the passive form to indicate that it has a subjector. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "This is evidence of the perfection of God's power and wisdom, for He the Exalted created the bird with a form by which flight is possible for it. He gave it a wing that it spreads at one time and folds at another, like what the swimmer does in water. He created the air with a form by which flight is possible. He created it in a subtle form by which piercing and passing through it is easy. Were it not for that, flight would not be possible." End of his words. His statement is drawn from the words of al-Qadi, who said: "He attributed the holding to Himself because He is the one who gave the instruments, for the sake of which the bird was able to perform those actions. Since He is the one who causes that, this attribution is valid." End of his words.

What we say is that the bird could have flown even had no wing been created for it, and it could have pierced a dense object by the power of God the Exalted (p-523), and the one who holds it in the atmosphere of the sky is God the Exalted. Proof has been established that all actions are created by God, and proof has been established that He the Exalted is the Doer who chooses. So we do not say: "Were it not for the wing and the subtlety of the air, flight would not be possible, and were it not for the instruments, it would not be possible."

Al-Zamakhshari said, in agreement with their words: "*Musakhkharat*: made pliable for flight by what He created for them of wings and the suitable causes for that." Then he rightly concluded with his statement: "None holds them up in their gripping and spreading and standing except God by His power." End of his words.

*La-ayat* ("indeed signs"): it is in the plural and not the singular, because the signs in it include the lightness of the bird which God placed in it so that it may rise by it, its weight which He placed in it so that it may descend, the space between the sky and the earth, and the holding which belongs to God the Exalted. Or it is plural in consideration of what is in this verse and the one before it. He said: *li-qawmin yu'minun* ("for a people who believe"), for they are those who benefit from consideration. And because the verse includes that the one who subjects them and holds them is God, this is a report from Him the Exalted which only the believer confirms.

﴿ضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا عَبْدًا مَمْلُوكًا لا يَقْدِرُ عَلى شَيْءٍ ومَن رَزَقْناهُ مِنّا رِزْقًا حَسَنًا فَهو يُنْفِقُ مِنهُ سِرًّا وجَهْرًا هَلْ يَسْتَوُونَ الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ بَلْ أكْثَرُهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ﴿وضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا رَجُلَيْنِ أحَدُهُما أبْكَمُ لا يَقْدِرُ عَلى شَيْءٍ وهو كَلٌّ عَلى مَوْلاهُ أيْنَما يُوَجِّهْهُ لا يَأْتِ بِخَيْرٍ هَلْ يَسْتَوِي هو ومَن يَأْمُرُ بِالعَدْلِ وهو عَلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ ﴿ولِلَّهِ غَيْبُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ وما أمْرُ السّاعَةِ إلّا كَلَمْحِ البَصَرِ أوْ هو أقْرَبُ إنَّ اللَّهَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾ ﴿واللَّهُ أخْرَجَكم مِن بُطُونِ أُمَّهاتِكم لا تَعْلَمُونَ شَيْئًا وجَعَلَ لَكُمُ السَّمْعَ والأبْصارَ والأفْئِدَةَ لَعَلَّكم تَشْكُرُونَ﴾ ﴿ألَمْ يَرَوْا إلى الطَّيْرِ مُسَخَّراتٍ في جَوِّ السَّماءِ ما يُمْسِكُهُنَّ إلّا اللَّهُ إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لَآياتٍ لِقَوْمٍ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ﴿واللَّهُ جَعَلَ لَكم مِن بُيُوتِكم سَكَنًا وجَعَلَ لَكم مِن جُلُودِ الأنْعامِ بُيُوتًا تَسْتَخِفُّونَها يَوْمَ ظَعْنِكم ويَوْمَ إقامَتِكم ومِن أصْوافِها وأوْبارِها وأشْعارِها أثاثًا ومَتاعًا إلى حِينٍ﴾ [An-Nahl: 80] ﴿واللَّهُ جَعَلَ لَكم مِمّا خَلَقَ ظِلالًا وجَعَلَ لَكم مِنَ الجِبالِ أكْنانًا وجَعَلَ لَكم سَرابِيلَ تَقِيكُمُ الحَرَّ وسَرابِيلَ تَقِيكم بَأْسَكم كَذَلِكَ يُتِمُّ نِعْمَتَهُ عَلَيْكم لَعَلَّكم تُسْلِمُونَ﴾ [An-Nahl: 81] ﴿فَإنْ تَوَلَّوْا فَإنَّما عَلَيْكَ البَلاغُ المُبِينُ﴾ [An-Nahl: 82] ﴿يَعْرِفُونَ نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ ثُمَّ يُنْكِرُونَها وأكْثَرُهُمُ الكافِرُونَ﴾ [An-Nahl: 83] ﴿ويَوْمَ نَبْعَثُ مِن كُلِّ أُمَّةٍ شَهِيدًا ثُمَّ لا يُؤْذَنُ لِلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا ولا هم يُسْتَعْتَبُونَ﴾ [An-Nahl: 84] (p-518)

Al-Kall (الكَلُّ): the burden, the heavy one. The orphan is sometimes called kall because of his burden on the one who supports him. The poet said:
"A devourer of the orphan's wealth before his youth, when the orphan's bone is not firm."

Al-kall also means one who has neither child nor parent, and kall means dependents (ʿiyāl); its plural is kulūl. Al-lamḥ (اللَّمْحُ) is a quick glance: "lamaḥahu lamḥan wa lamaḥānan." Al-jaww (الجَوُّ) is the space between the sky and the earth. It is said that it is what lies adjacent to the earth in the direction of height, and al-lawḥ and al-sukkāk are farther than it. Al-ẓaʿn (الظَّعْنُ) is the travel of the nomads in search of pasture and moving from one place to another; al-ẓaʿn also means the howdah (the litter on a camel). Ṣūf (wool) is for sheep, waabr (fine hair/fleece) is for camels, and shaʿr (hair) is for goats, as the lexicographers said regarding His words ﴿ومِن أصْوافِها﴾ [An-Nahl: 80] "and of their wool," etc.

Athāth (الأثاثُ): Al-Mufaḍḍal said: it is household goods such as carpets and coverings. Al-Farrāʾ said: it has no singular from its own form, just as matāʿ (مَتاعُ, goods) has no singular from its own form. If you pluralized it you would say ʾaʾthiṯa for the few and ʾuṯuṯ for the many. Abū Zayd said: its singular is uthātha. Al-Khalīl said: its root is from their saying athatha al-nabāt wa al-shaʿr (the plants and the hair became thick), so it is athīth when it becomes dense. Imru' al-Qays said:
"And a tress that adorns the back, jet-black and raven, thick like the cluster of the palm laden with dates."

Al-kinn (الكِنُّ) is what protects and shields from wind, rain and other things; and from the mountains, it is the cave (al-ghār). Istaʿtabtu al-rajula means aʿtabtuhu, i.e., I removed from him what he was reproached and blamed for; the noun is al-ʿutbā. The form istafʿala has come with the meaning of afʿala, like istadaynahu and adaynahu.

﴿ضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا عَبْدًا مَمْلُوكًا لا يَقْدِرُ عَلى شَيْءٍ ومَن رَزَقْناهُ مِنّا رِزْقًا حَسَنًا فَهو يُنْفِقُ مِنهُ سِرًّا وجَهْرًا هَلْ يَسْتَوُونَ الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ بَلْ أكْثَرُهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ﴿وضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا رَجُلَيْنِ أحَدُهُما أبْكَمُ لا يَقْدِرُ عَلى شَيْءٍ وهو كَلٌّ عَلى مَوْلاهُ أيْنَما يُوَجِّهْهُ لا يَأْتِ بِخَيْرٍ هَلْ يَسْتَوِي هو ومَن يَأْمُرُ بِالعَدْلِ وهو عَلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ ﴿ولِلَّهِ غَيْبُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ وما أمْرُ السّاعَةِ إلّا كَلَمْحِ البَصَرِ أوْ هو أقْرَبُ إنَّ اللَّهَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾ ﴿واللَّهُ أخْرَجَكم مِن بُطُونِ أُمَّهاتِكم لا تَعْلَمُونَ شَيْئًا وجَعَلَ لَكُمُ السَّمْعَ والأبْصارَ والأفْئِدَةَ لَعَلَّكم تَشْكُرُونَ﴾ ﴿ألَمْ يَرَوْا إلى الطَّيْرِ مُسَخَّراتٍ في جَوِّ السَّماءِ ما يُمْسِكُهُنَّ إلّا اللَّهُ إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لَآياتٍ لِقَوْمٍ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾: The occasion (munāsabah) for striking this example: when Allah, exalted is He, explained their misguidance in associating others with Him, though that other neither brings benefit nor harm to itself or to its worshipper, He struck for them the example of a slave under another's ownership, incapable of disposing of anything, and a free, wealthy man who disposes of what Allah has given him. If these two are not equal in your sight, though they are of one kind and share humanity, then how do you associate with Allah and equate with Him what is His creation, subdued by His power, whether a human or other, despite the vast difference in attributes? And the Originator of existence cannot be resembled by anything of His creation, and no sane person can liken anything else to Him.

Mujāhid said: this is a parable for Allah and the idols. Qatādah said: it is for the believer and the disbeliever. The disbeliever is the slave who is owned, who gains nothing from his worship in the Hereafter, and "the one whom We have provided for" is the believer. Ibn Jubayr said: it is a parable for the miser and the generous; end.

Since the word ʿabd (عَبْدٌ, slave) may be applied to the free, it was specified by "mamlūk" (owned). Since the owned slave may have some disposal and power, like the one given permission (al-maʾdhūn lahu) and the mukātab (one contracted to buy his freedom), it was specified by His words "incapable of anything." The meaning is: incapable of anything of disposal over property, because he is capable of some movements: standing, sitting, eating, drinking, sleeping, and other things. The apparent reading is that "man" (مَن) is a relative pronoun, meaning "and the one whom We have provided for," and the context of the relative clause and what follows indicates that it refers to the free man. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: it is a qualifying (موصوفة) form. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the apparent reading is that it is a qualifying form, as if He said: "and a free man whom We have provided for," to match "a slave." It does not preclude it being a relative. Al-Ḥawfī said: "man" means "alladhī" (the one who). Striking the parable for two specific persons described by widely differing attributes does not require identifying them. What is reported about identifying them, that they are ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān (may Allah be pleased with him) and a slave of his, or that they are Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him) and Abū Jahl, has no sound chain of transmission.

The pronoun in "yastawūn" (they are equal) is plural, not dual, though two were mentioned earlier, because "man" may be intended as a plural, in which case the plural pronoun is consistent with the inclusion of the owned slave and the wealthy ones in the plural. It is as if it were said: "a slave owned," and the owners (al-mullāk) are those who are provided for and who spend. It may also be that "ʿabdan mamlūkan" is meant as a genus, so a plural pronoun may refer to it and to the genus of the wealthy. It may also refer to slaves and free persons, even though no plural has preceded, because the two classes are indicated by "a slave owned" and "the one whom We have provided for."

﴿قُلِ الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾ [Al-ʿAnkabūt: 63]: The apparent reading is that it is addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ). It was said that it may be addressed to the one whom Allah has provided for, commanding him to praise Allah for distinguishing him with this power over that weak one. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "Al-ḥamdu lillāh" is thanks for the clarity of this parable and for the opponent's submission to it, as when you say to one who has submitted to your argument and accepted it, building upon it your saying: "Allah is greatest, on this such and such follows." So when He said here "Are they equal?", it is as if the opponent said to Him: "No," and He said: "Praise be to Allah, the argument is manifest"; end. It was also said: "Al-ḥamdu lillāh" means He alone deserves praise, not what they worship besides Him, since the idols have no favor upon them to be praised for; rather complete praise is for Allah, because He is the Bestower and the Creator. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Praise be to Allah for what He has done for His friends and for bestowing upon them the blessing of monotheism."

The apparent reading is the negation of knowledge from most of them, because among them are those for whom the truth became clear and who returned to it; or "most" refers to most of creation, because most are polytheists. It was said that the intended meaning is generality, i.e., "rather, they do not know." The object of "yaʿlamūn" (they know) is omitted: either because the meaning is the negation of knowledge from most, without considering its object, or because it is omitted and follows from the statements whose cause is His saying "Praise be to Allah."

﴿وضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا رَجُلَيْنِ﴾, i.e., the account of two men. Al-Zamakhsharī said: this is a second parable, which He struck for Himself and for what He pours out upon His servants and what encompasses them of the traces of His mercy, kindness and blessings, religious and worldly, and for the idols which are dead and neither harm nor benefit. The mute (al-abkam) is the one born deaf-mute, who neither understands nor is understood.

﴿وهُوَ كَلٌّ عَلى مَوْلاهُ﴾, i.e., a burden, and a dependent upon the one who takes charge of his affairs and supports him. ʾAynamā yuwajjihhu: wherever he sends him and directs him in a matter of need or support, an important matter: he brings no benefit and achieves no success. "Are they equal, he and one who has sound senses, beneficial, possessing sufficiency together with right guidance and piety; so he commands people to justice, and he is himself upon a straight path, upon a righteous way and a sound religion"; end. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "one of them is mute" is a parable for the disbeliever, and "the one who commands justice" is the believer. Qatādah said: this is a parable of Allah, exalted is He, and the idols: the idols are like the mute who has no speech and is unable to do anything, and he is a dependent upon whoever is close to him, a relative or friend, just as the idols need to be carried, served, and burdened with, and no good whatsoever comes from them. Also from Qatādah and others: this is a parable which Allah struck for Himself and for the idol. The mute who is unable to do anything is the idol, and the one who commands justice is Allah, exalted is He. This is not so, because He said "two men as a parable," so the counterpart of the mute, described with those attributes, must be a man described with what opposes those attributes of speech, power and sufficiency. But He omitted the counterpart, because its opposite indicates it. Then it was said: "Are they equal?", meaning that mute with those attributes and this speaking one. So the mention of their equality is also evidence of the omitted counterpart. Since muteness is the first of the attributes mentioned, and from it the subsequent attributes are determined by the capacity for equality in speech, and its fruit of commanding justice is other than it, while he is upon a straight way: wherever he turns, good comes from him and benefits; he is not a burden on anyone. It is established in the first principles of reason that the mute, meaning the incapable, is not equal in intellect and nobility to the speaking, able, perfect one, though they are equal in humanity. So it is more fitting and more deserving to judge that an inanimate object is not equal to the Lord of the Worlds in deserving worship. And as we said regarding the previous parable, the parable does not require identifying the two persons struck by it; similarly here. So identifying the mute as Abū Jahl and the one who commands justice as ʿAmmār, or as Ubayy ibn Khalaf and ʿUthmān ibn Maẓʿūn, or as Hāshim ibn ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith, who was hostile to the Messenger (ﷺ), has no sound chain of transmission.

Abdullah, Alqama, Ibn Wabbab, Mujahid and Talha read *yuwajjihu* with a single silent hāʾ, in the active voice (*mabniyyan*). Its subject is a pronoun referring back to *mawlāhu* (his guardian), and the object pronoun is omitted because the meaning indicates it. It is also permissible for the subject pronoun to refer back to the mute man (*al-abkam*), with the verb being intransitive: *wajjaha* meaning *tawajjaha* (to turn toward). The meaning would then be: "Wherever he turns." From Abdullah also: *tuwajjihhu* with two hāʾs and the second person prefix (*tāʾ al-khiṭāb*). The majority read it with the prefix *yāʾ* and two hāʾs. From Alqama, Ibn Wabbab and Talha: *yuwajjah* with a single silent hāʾ, the verb being in the passive voice. From Alqama and Talha: *yuwajjihu*, with a kasra on the jīm and a single hāʾ with a ḍamma.

The author of *al-Lawāmiʿ* said: "If this reading is authentic, then the hāʾ, which is the final radical of the verb, has been deleted to avoid geminating (*tafḍʿīf*), and because pronouncing it with gemination is difficult. Or it was not intended as a conditional, but rather as an imperative: 'Wherever he is, let him turn (it).' The object pronoun has been deleted from it. The deletion of the yāʾ in *lā yaʾti bi-khayr* (﴿he does not bring good﴾) would then be for lightening, like *yawma yaʾti* and *idhā yasri*." End of quotation.

*Ayna* does not leave the conditional or interrogative sense. Abu Hatim said: "This reading is weak, because the jussive (*al-jazm*) is obligatory." End of quotation. The way this reading may be justified, if it is authentic, is that *ayna-ma* is a conditional particle, treated analogously to *idhā* because they share the conditional character. Then the yāʾ of *lā yaʾti* was deleted for lightening, or it was jussified through the assumption that it had been pronounced with the unassimilated *ayna-ma* functioning as in the reading of the one who read ﴿Indeed, whoever fears God and is patient﴾ (Yusuf: 90) in one of the two ways. The meaning of *yuwajjah* would then be *yatawajjah* (he turns), so it is an intransitive verb and not transitive.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned that to Him belongs the unseen (*ghayb*) of the heavens and the earth, which is what is hidden from the servants and whose knowledge is concealed from them. The apparent connection is with His saying: ﴿Indeed, God knows and you do not know﴾ (al-Nahl: 74). He informed that He alone has the knowledge of the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and with perfect power to bring the Hour, which you deny, in the blink of an eye or even quicker. The meaning of this information is that the gods you worship lack these two attributes that belong to the deity: all-encompassing knowledge of the unseen, and absolute, complete power. Whoever says that His saying ﴿and who commands justice﴾ refers to God, exalted is He, mentions the connection of this sentence to what precedes it, namely that whoever commands justice, and who is on a straight path, is the perfect one in knowledge and power. This sentence clarifies that.

It has been said: "The unseen here is what cannot be perceived by the senses and cannot be grasped by the intellect." Al-Mufaḍḍal said: "What is hidden from creation is within His grasp and nothing escapes Him." It has also been said: it refers to what is in His saying: ﴿Indeed, with God is the knowledge of the Hour﴾ (Luqman: 34). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or he meant by the unseen of the heavens and the earth the Day of Resurrection, in that its knowledge is hidden from the people of the heavens and the earth, none of whom has come to know of it."

It has been said: since the Hour is coming without fail, it is brought close, like the blink of an eye. Al-Zajjaj said: "He did not mean that the Hour comes in the blink of an eye. He only described the speed of the power to bring it about, i.e., He says to a thing 'Be,' and it is." It has been said: this is an illustration of nearness, as you say: "A year is nothing but a moment." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is near with God, even if it is delayed, as they say of the thing you consider near: ﴿like the blink of an eye or even nearer﴾ when you exaggerate in considering it near." Similar is His saying: ﴿and they ask you to hasten the punishment﴾ (al-ʿAnkabut: 53), ﴿and God will not break His promise﴾ (al-Hajj: 47), ﴿and indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ (al-Hajj: 47), meaning: it is near to Him, while it is far from you.

It has been said: the meaning is that the establishment of the Hour, the causing of the living to die, and the raising of the dead from the first and the last, will occur in the nearest time He has willed.

﴿Indeed, God is over all things competent﴾ (al-ʿAnkabut: 20), so He is able to establish the Hour and resurrect creation, since that is among the things within His power. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The meaning, according to Qatada and others, is: the Hour and its establishment are within God's power only when He says to it 'Be,' so if a human being happened to witness this, it would be so swift that he would doubt whether it was like the blink of an eye or nearer than that. So *aw*, in this case, is in its original sense of doubt. It has also been said that it is for choice." End of quotation.

Doubt and choice are both far-fetched, because this is an announcement from God, exalted is He, about the matter of the Hour, and doubt is impossible for Him. Also, choice occurs only in prohibited matters, like the saying: "Take from my wealth a dinar or a dirham," or in obligations, like the verse of expiations: ﴿And those who divorce by zihar﴾ (al-Mujadila: 3). *Aw* here is for obscuring the matter from the addressee, like His saying: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾ (al-Saffat: 147), and His saying: ﴿Our command came upon it by night or by day﴾ (Yunus: 24). God knows their number and when His command will come upon them, just as He knows the matter of the Hour, but it was obscured from the addressee. That *aw* here is for obscuring was mentioned by al-Zajjaj here. Al-Qadi said: "This is not valid, because the establishment of the Hour is not a state of obligation such that it could be said that He brings it at a time—meaning the Qadi's time—so that the obscuring would be from the addressee at that time, and it is not a time of obligation." What we say is: the obscuring occurred at the time of the preceding address concerning the matter of the Hour, not at the time of its coming. It is not a condition of obscuring from the addressee in reporting something that the time of the report and the time of that thing's occurrence be the same. Do you not see, in His saying: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾ (al-Saffat: 147), how the time of the report was later than the time of that sending and their existence as a hundred thousand or more?

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "'The blink of the eye' (*lamḥ al-baṣar*) is the movement of the body by the glance from the top of the pupil, and it is composed of parts, and those parts are numerous. The time in which the blink takes place is composed of successive moments, and God is able to establish the Resurrection in one of those moments. Therefore He said: ﴿or it is nearer﴾. Since the swiftest of states and events in our minds is the blink of the eye, He mentioned it, then said: 'or it is nearer,' as an alert to what we have mentioned. The intended meaning is not the manner of doubt; rather, the meaning is: 'Indeed, it is nearer.'" End of quotation, and there is some abridgement in it.

What he mentioned, that *aw* means *bal* (rather), is the view of al-Farra', and it is not valid, because the transition (*iḍrāb*) is of two kinds, and neither is valid here. The first: that it be a cancellation of the preceding predication, and that it was not what was intended. This is impossible here, because it would result in a predication that does not correspond. The second: that it be a transition from one thing to another without cancelling that preceding thing. This is also impossible here, because of the contradiction between reporting that it is like the blink of an eye in speed and reporting that it is nearer, so both cannot be true together.

The author of *al-Ghaniyyan* said: "Although this is hard to grasp literally, what is intended is exaggeration, according to the way of the Arabs and the masters of composition." How excellent is the saying of the poet al-Ablah on this meaning:

> The lightning said to him, and the wind said to him, both together, and they are what they are:
> "Do you run with us?" He said: "If I become energetic, I will make you both laugh at yourselves."
> "I am the return of the glance, I have outpaced it toward the goal in speed, so who are you two?"

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the matter of the Hour and that it is certainly coming, this indicated the Hereafter's creation. The earlier description of them with the absence of knowledge was mentioned, so He mentioned the first creation, which is bringing them out from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing, as an alert to the occurrence of the later creation. Then He mentioned His favor upon them in giving them the senses, which are the means of perceiving things and attaining knowledge. Since the first creation was mentioned, and He made what they know by as one of the greatest blessings upon them, He said: ﴿so that you may give thanks﴾. The discussion of *ummahat* (mothers) was mentioned in al-Nisa'.

Hamza read with a kasra on the hamza and the mim here, and in al-Nur, al-Zumar and al-Najm, and al-Kisa'i read with a kasra on the hamza in them. Al-A'mash read with deletion of the hamza and a kasra on the mim, and Ibn Abi Layla read with its deletion and a fatha on the mim. Abu Hatim said: "Deleting the hamza is bad, but the reading of Ibn Ubayy is more correct." End of quotation. It was more correct because the kasra on the mim occurs only to assimilate it to the vowel of the hamza; when the hamza is deleted, the assimilation disappears. By contrast, Ibn Abi Layla's reading leaves the mim on its own vowel.

*Lā taʿlamūna* ("you do not know") is a circumstantial clause (*jumla ḥāliyya*), meaning: "while not knowing." It has been said: "You do not know anything of what the covenant taken from you in the loins of your fathers was, or anything of what was decreed for you of happiness or misery, or anything of your benefits." The more appropriate is the general sense of the word "anything," especially in the context of negation. Wahb said: "The child is born wary for seven days; he does not perceive comfort or pain." It is possible that *wajaʿala* (and He made) is conjoined to ﴿He brought you out﴾, so it is one part within the scope of the predicate of the subject; and it is possible that it is a new statement conjoined to the initial sentence, like the beginning of it.

The meaning of the hearing, the sights and the hearts is their sensing and perceiving, so the faculty is expressed by the organ. Abu Abdullah al-Razi (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) said, in substance: "The reason the word *fu'ad* (heart) is given in the paucity plural (*jam' qilla*, the plural form for small numbers) is that it was created only for true, certain knowledge, whereas most people are preoccupied with bestial acts, so their hearts are not really hearts. For this reason the paucity plural is used for it." End of his words, summarized. This is a delirious statement. Were it not for the eminence of the one who said it and his having written it in books, I would not have mentioned it. What should be said about this is what al-Zamakhshari said: that *afida* is among the paucity plurals that have come to function like plurals of abundance and paucity alike, when no other form of it is attested in usage, as with *shusu'* (the plural of *shis'*, "sandal-thong") which has no other plural form. So it follows that pattern. End of his words. However, al-Zamakhshari's claim that no plural of *shis'* other than *shusu'* occurs is not correct. A paucity plural also occurs for it: they say *ash-sa'* (*ashsa'*). So he should have said: "*shusu'* has been given precedence (as the common plural)."

Ibn Amir, Hamza, Talha, al-A'mash and Ibn Hurmuz read *alam tarawa* (ﷺ not applicable) with the second person "you" (*ta'* of address), while the rest of the seven readers read it with *ya'* (third person). Ibn Atiyya said: "There is a difference of report from al-Hasan, Isa al-Thaqafi, Asim and Abu Amr."

When the Exalted mentioned the three means of knowledge, hearing, sight and reason, the first two being the means of perceiving the sensible and the third the means of perceiving the intelligible, He confined the mention of the means of perceiving the sensible to sight, since it is the most striking for what is observed by it of the great creatures at their varied distances, such as observing the luminous bodies in the spheres. He placed the flying animal as the object of consideration and wonder here, for its flight in the air despite the weight of its body is among the things that cause wonder and are taken as a lesson. The verse also includes mention of the means of perceiving by reason, in that the bird does not fall, since there is nothing beneath it to support it and nothing above it to which it is attached. Thus reason knows that there is a holder of it who is able to hold it up, and He is God the Exalted, as the Exalted said: ﴿Have they not considered the birds above them, spreading and folding their wings? None holds them up except the Most Merciful. Indeed, He is Seer of all things.﴾ (67:19). Thus the verse brings together the mention of the means of sense perception and the means of reasoning.

The meaning of *musakhkharat* ("made subservient") is "made pliable," and it is in the passive form to indicate that it has a subjector. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "This is evidence of the perfection of God's power and wisdom, for He the Exalted created the bird with a form by which flight is possible for it. He gave it a wing that it spreads at one time and folds at another, like what the swimmer does in water. He created the air with a form by which flight is possible. He created it in a subtle form by which piercing and passing through it is easy. Were it not for that, flight would not be possible." End of his words. His statement is drawn from the words of al-Qadi, who said: "He attributed the holding to Himself because He is the one who gave the instruments, for the sake of which the bird was able to perform those actions. Since He is the one who causes that, this attribution is valid." End of his words.

What we say is that the bird could have flown even had no wing been created for it, and it could have pierced a dense object by the power of God the Exalted (p-523), and the one who holds it in the atmosphere of the sky is God the Exalted. Proof has been established that all actions are created by God, and proof has been established that He the Exalted is the Doer who chooses. So we do not say: "Were it not for the wing and the subtlety of the air, flight would not be possible, and were it not for the instruments, it would not be possible."

Al-Zamakhshari said, in agreement with their words: "*Musakhkharat*: made pliable for flight by what He created for them of wings and the suitable causes for that." Then he rightly concluded with his statement: "None holds them up in their gripping and spreading and standing except God by His power." End of his words.

*La-ayat* ("indeed signs"): it is in the plural and not the singular, because the signs in it include the lightness of the bird which God placed in it so that it may rise by it, its weight which He placed in it so that it may descend, the space between the sky and the earth, and the holding which belongs to God the Exalted. Or it is plural in consideration of what is in this verse and the one before it. He said: *li-qawmin yu'minun* ("for a people who believe"), for they are those who benefit from consideration. And because the verse includes that the one who subjects them and holds them is God, this is a report from Him the Exalted which only the believer confirms.

﴿ضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا عَبْدًا مَمْلُوكًا لا يَقْدِرُ عَلى شَيْءٍ ومَن رَزَقْناهُ مِنّا رِزْقًا حَسَنًا فَهو يُنْفِقُ مِنهُ سِرًّا وجَهْرًا هَلْ يَسْتَوُونَ الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ بَلْ أكْثَرُهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ﴿وضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا رَجُلَيْنِ أحَدُهُما أبْكَمُ لا يَقْدِرُ عَلى شَيْءٍ وهو كَلٌّ عَلى مَوْلاهُ أيْنَما يُوَجِّهْهُ لا يَأْتِ بِخَيْرٍ هَلْ يَسْتَوِي هو ومَن يَأْمُرُ بِالعَدْلِ وهو عَلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ ﴿ولِلَّهِ غَيْبُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ وما أمْرُ السّاعَةِ إلّا كَلَمْحِ البَصَرِ أوْ هو أقْرَبُ إنَّ اللَّهَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾ ﴿واللَّهُ أخْرَجَكم مِن بُطُونِ أُمَّهاتِكم لا تَعْلَمُونَ شَيْئًا وجَعَلَ لَكُمُ السَّمْعَ والأبْصارَ والأفْئِدَةَ لَعَلَّكم تَشْكُرُونَ﴾ ﴿ألَمْ يَرَوْا إلى الطَّيْرِ مُسَخَّراتٍ في جَوِّ السَّماءِ ما يُمْسِكُهُنَّ إلّا اللَّهُ إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لَآياتٍ لِقَوْمٍ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ﴿واللَّهُ جَعَلَ لَكم مِن بُيُوتِكم سَكَنًا وجَعَلَ لَكم مِن جُلُودِ الأنْعامِ بُيُوتًا تَسْتَخِفُّونَها يَوْمَ ظَعْنِكم ويَوْمَ إقامَتِكم ومِن أصْوافِها وأوْبارِها وأشْعارِها أثاثًا ومَتاعًا إلى حِينٍ﴾ [An-Nahl: 80] ﴿واللَّهُ جَعَلَ لَكم مِمّا خَلَقَ ظِلالًا وجَعَلَ لَكم مِنَ الجِبالِ أكْنانًا وجَعَلَ لَكم سَرابِيلَ تَقِيكُمُ الحَرَّ وسَرابِيلَ تَقِيكم بَأْسَكم كَذَلِكَ يُتِمُّ نِعْمَتَهُ عَلَيْكم لَعَلَّكم تُسْلِمُونَ﴾ [An-Nahl: 81] ﴿فَإنْ تَوَلَّوْا فَإنَّما عَلَيْكَ البَلاغُ المُبِينُ﴾ [An-Nahl: 82] ﴿يَعْرِفُونَ نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ ثُمَّ يُنْكِرُونَها وأكْثَرُهُمُ الكافِرُونَ﴾ [An-Nahl: 83] ﴿ويَوْمَ نَبْعَثُ مِن كُلِّ أُمَّةٍ شَهِيدًا ثُمَّ لا يُؤْذَنُ لِلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا ولا هم يُسْتَعْتَبُونَ﴾ [An-Nahl: 84] (p-518)

Al-Kall (الكَلُّ): the burden, the heavy one. The orphan is sometimes called kall because of his burden on the one who supports him. The poet said:
"A devourer of the orphan's wealth before his youth, when the orphan's bone is not firm."

Al-kall also means one who has neither child nor parent, and kall means dependents (ʿiyāl); its plural is kulūl. Al-lamḥ (اللَّمْحُ) is a quick glance: "lamaḥahu lamḥan wa lamaḥānan." Al-jaww (الجَوُّ) is the space between the sky and the earth. It is said that it is what lies adjacent to the earth in the direction of height, and al-lawḥ and al-sukkāk are farther than it. Al-ẓaʿn (الظَّعْنُ) is the travel of the nomads in search of pasture and moving from one place to another; al-ẓaʿn also means the howdah (the litter on a camel). Ṣūf (wool) is for sheep, waabr (fine hair/fleece) is for camels, and shaʿr (hair) is for goats, as the lexicographers said regarding His words ﴿ومِن أصْوافِها﴾ [An-Nahl: 80] "and of their wool," etc.

Athāth (الأثاثُ): Al-Mufaḍḍal said: it is household goods such as carpets and coverings. Al-Farrāʾ said: it has no singular from its own form, just as matāʿ (مَتاعُ, goods) has no singular from its own form. If you pluralized it you would say ʾaʾthiṯa for the few and ʾuṯuṯ for the many. Abū Zayd said: its singular is uthātha. Al-Khalīl said: its root is from their saying athatha al-nabāt wa al-shaʿr (the plants and the hair became thick), so it is athīth when it becomes dense. Imru' al-Qays said:
"And a tress that adorns the back, jet-black and raven, thick like the cluster of the palm laden with dates."

Al-kinn (الكِنُّ) is what protects and shields from wind, rain and other things; and from the mountains, it is the cave (al-ghār). Istaʿtabtu al-rajula means aʿtabtuhu, i.e., I removed from him what he was reproached and blamed for; the noun is al-ʿutbā. The form istafʿala has come with the meaning of afʿala, like istadaynahu and adaynahu.

﴿ضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا عَبْدًا مَمْلُوكًا لا يَقْدِرُ عَلى شَيْءٍ ومَن رَزَقْناهُ مِنّا رِزْقًا حَسَنًا فَهو يُنْفِقُ مِنهُ سِرًّا وجَهْرًا هَلْ يَسْتَوُونَ الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ بَلْ أكْثَرُهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ﴿وضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا رَجُلَيْنِ أحَدُهُما أبْكَمُ لا يَقْدِرُ عَلى شَيْءٍ وهو كَلٌّ عَلى مَوْلاهُ أيْنَما يُوَجِّهْهُ لا يَأْتِ بِخَيْرٍ هَلْ يَسْتَوِي هو ومَن يَأْمُرُ بِالعَدْلِ وهو عَلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ ﴿ولِلَّهِ غَيْبُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ وما أمْرُ السّاعَةِ إلّا كَلَمْحِ البَصَرِ أوْ هو أقْرَبُ إنَّ اللَّهَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾ ﴿واللَّهُ أخْرَجَكم مِن بُطُونِ أُمَّهاتِكم لا تَعْلَمُونَ شَيْئًا وجَعَلَ لَكُمُ السَّمْعَ والأبْصارَ والأفْئِدَةَ لَعَلَّكم تَشْكُرُونَ﴾ ﴿ألَمْ يَرَوْا إلى الطَّيْرِ مُسَخَّراتٍ في جَوِّ السَّماءِ ما يُمْسِكُهُنَّ إلّا اللَّهُ إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لَآياتٍ لِقَوْمٍ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾: The occasion (munāsabah) for striking this example: when Allah, exalted is He, explained their misguidance in associating others with Him, though that other neither brings benefit nor harm to itself or to its worshipper, He struck for them the example of a slave under another's ownership, incapable of disposing of anything, and a free, wealthy man who disposes of what Allah has given him. If these two are not equal in your sight, though they are of one kind and share humanity, then how do you associate with Allah and equate with Him what is His creation, subdued by His power, whether a human or other, despite the vast difference in attributes? And the Originator of existence cannot be resembled by anything of His creation, and no sane person can liken anything else to Him.

Mujāhid said: this is a parable for Allah and the idols. Qatādah said: it is for the believer and the disbeliever. The disbeliever is the slave who is owned, who gains nothing from his worship in the Hereafter, and "the one whom We have provided for" is the believer. Ibn Jubayr said: it is a parable for the miser and the generous; end.

Since the word ʿabd (عَبْدٌ, slave) may be applied to the free, it was specified by "mamlūk" (owned). Since the owned slave may have some disposal and power, like the one given permission (al-maʾdhūn lahu) and the mukātab (one contracted to buy his freedom), it was specified by His words "incapable of anything." The meaning is: incapable of anything of disposal over property, because he is capable of some movements: standing, sitting, eating, drinking, sleeping, and other things. The apparent reading is that "man" (مَن) is a relative pronoun, meaning "and the one whom We have provided for," and the context of the relative clause and what follows indicates that it refers to the free man. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: it is a qualifying (موصوفة) form. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the apparent reading is that it is a qualifying form, as if He said: "and a free man whom We have provided for," to match "a slave." It does not preclude it being a relative. Al-Ḥawfī said: "man" means "alladhī" (the one who). Striking the parable for two specific persons described by widely differing attributes does not require identifying them. What is reported about identifying them, that they are ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān (may Allah be pleased with him) and a slave of his, or that they are Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him) and Abū Jahl, has no sound chain of transmission.

The pronoun in "yastawūn" (they are equal) is plural, not dual, though two were mentioned earlier, because "man" may be intended as a plural, in which case the plural pronoun is consistent with the inclusion of the owned slave and the wealthy ones in the plural. It is as if it were said: "a slave owned," and the owners (al-mullāk) are those who are provided for and who spend. It may also be that "ʿabdan mamlūkan" is meant as a genus, so a plural pronoun may refer to it and to the genus of the wealthy. It may also refer to slaves and free persons, even though no plural has preceded, because the two classes are indicated by "a slave owned" and "the one whom We have provided for."

﴿قُلِ الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾ [Al-ʿAnkabūt: 63]: The apparent reading is that it is addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ). It was said that it may be addressed to the one whom Allah has provided for, commanding him to praise Allah for distinguishing him with this power over that weak one. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "Al-ḥamdu lillāh" is thanks for the clarity of this parable and for the opponent's submission to it, as when you say to one who has submitted to your argument and accepted it, building upon it your saying: "Allah is greatest, on this such and such follows." So when He said here "Are they equal?", it is as if the opponent said to Him: "No," and He said: "Praise be to Allah, the argument is manifest"; end. It was also said: "Al-ḥamdu lillāh" means He alone deserves praise, not what they worship besides Him, since the idols have no favor upon them to be praised for; rather complete praise is for Allah, because He is the Bestower and the Creator. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Praise be to Allah for what He has done for His friends and for bestowing upon them the blessing of monotheism."

The apparent reading is the negation of knowledge from most of them, because among them are those for whom the truth became clear and who returned to it; or "most" refers to most of creation, because most are polytheists. It was said that the intended meaning is generality, i.e., "rather, they do not know." The object of "yaʿlamūn" (they know) is omitted: either because the meaning is the negation of knowledge from most, without considering its object, or because it is omitted and follows from the statements whose cause is His saying "Praise be to Allah."

﴿وضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا رَجُلَيْنِ﴾, i.e., the account of two men. Al-Zamakhsharī said: this is a second parable, which He struck for Himself and for what He pours out upon His servants and what encompasses them of the traces of His mercy, kindness and blessings, religious and worldly, and for the idols which are dead and neither harm nor benefit. The mute (al-abkam) is the one born deaf-mute, who neither understands nor is understood.

﴿وهُوَ كَلٌّ عَلى مَوْلاهُ﴾, i.e., a burden, and a dependent upon the one who takes charge of his affairs and supports him. ʾAynamā yuwajjihhu: wherever he sends him and directs him in a matter of need or support, an important matter: he brings no benefit and achieves no success. "Are they equal, he and one who has sound senses, beneficial, possessing sufficiency together with right guidance and piety; so he commands people to justice, and he is himself upon a straight path, upon a righteous way and a sound religion"; end. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "one of them is mute" is a parable for the disbeliever, and "the one who commands justice" is the believer. Qatādah said: this is a parable of Allah, exalted is He, and the idols: the idols are like the mute who has no speech and is unable to do anything, and he is a dependent upon whoever is close to him, a relative or friend, just as the idols need to be carried, served, and burdened with, and no good whatsoever comes from them. Also from Qatādah and others: this is a parable which Allah struck for Himself and for the idol. The mute who is unable to do anything is the idol, and the one who commands justice is Allah, exalted is He. This is not so, because He said "two men as a parable," so the counterpart of the mute, described with those attributes, must be a man described with what opposes those attributes of speech, power and sufficiency. But He omitted the counterpart, because its opposite indicates it. Then it was said: "Are they equal?", meaning that mute with those attributes and this speaking one. So the mention of their equality is also evidence of the omitted counterpart. Since muteness is the first of the attributes mentioned, and from it the subsequent attributes are determined by the capacity for equality in speech, and its fruit of commanding justice is other than it, while he is upon a straight way: wherever he turns, good comes from him and benefits; he is not a burden on anyone. It is established in the first principles of reason that the mute, meaning the incapable, is not equal in intellect and nobility to the speaking, able, perfect one, though they are equal in humanity. So it is more fitting and more deserving to judge that an inanimate object is not equal to the Lord of the Worlds in deserving worship. And as we said regarding the previous parable, the parable does not require identifying the two persons struck by it; similarly here. So identifying the mute as Abū Jahl and the one who commands justice as ʿAmmār, or as Ubayy ibn Khalaf and ʿUthmān ibn Maẓʿūn, or as Hāshim ibn ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith, who was hostile to the Messenger (ﷺ), has no sound chain of transmission.

Abdullah, Alqama, Ibn Wabbab, Mujahid and Talha read *yuwajjihu* with a single silent hāʾ, in the active voice (*mabniyyan*). Its subject is a pronoun referring back to *mawlāhu* (his guardian), and the object pronoun is omitted because the meaning indicates it. It is also permissible for the subject pronoun to refer back to the mute man (*al-abkam*), with the verb being intransitive: *wajjaha* meaning *tawajjaha* (to turn toward). The meaning would then be: "Wherever he turns." From Abdullah also: *tuwajjihhu* with two hāʾs and the second person prefix (*tāʾ al-khiṭāb*). The majority read it with the prefix *yāʾ* and two hāʾs. From Alqama, Ibn Wabbab and Talha: *yuwajjah* with a single silent hāʾ, the verb being in the passive voice. From Alqama and Talha: *yuwajjihu*, with a kasra on the jīm and a single hāʾ with a ḍamma.

The author of *al-Lawāmiʿ* said: "If this reading is authentic, then the hāʾ, which is the final radical of the verb, has been deleted to avoid geminating (*tafḍʿīf*), and because pronouncing it with gemination is difficult. Or it was not intended as a conditional, but rather as an imperative: 'Wherever he is, let him turn (it).' The object pronoun has been deleted from it. The deletion of the yāʾ in *lā yaʾti bi-khayr* (﴿he does not bring good﴾) would then be for lightening, like *yawma yaʾti* and *idhā yasri*." End of quotation.

*Ayna* does not leave the conditional or interrogative sense. Abu Hatim said: "This reading is weak, because the jussive (*al-jazm*) is obligatory." End of quotation. The way this reading may be justified, if it is authentic, is that *ayna-ma* is a conditional particle, treated analogously to *idhā* because they share the conditional character. Then the yāʾ of *lā yaʾti* was deleted for lightening, or it was jussified through the assumption that it had been pronounced with the unassimilated *ayna-ma* functioning as in the reading of the one who read ﴿Indeed, whoever fears God and is patient﴾ (Yusuf: 90) in one of the two ways. The meaning of *yuwajjah* would then be *yatawajjah* (he turns), so it is an intransitive verb and not transitive.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned that to Him belongs the unseen (*ghayb*) of the heavens and the earth, which is what is hidden from the servants and whose knowledge is concealed from them. The apparent connection is with His saying: ﴿Indeed, God knows and you do not know﴾ (al-Nahl: 74). He informed that He alone has the knowledge of the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and with perfect power to bring the Hour, which you deny, in the blink of an eye or even quicker. The meaning of this information is that the gods you worship lack these two attributes that belong to the deity: all-encompassing knowledge of the unseen, and absolute, complete power. Whoever says that His saying ﴿and who commands justice﴾ refers to God, exalted is He, mentions the connection of this sentence to what precedes it, namely that whoever commands justice, and who is on a straight path, is the perfect one in knowledge and power. This sentence clarifies that.

It has been said: "The unseen here is what cannot be perceived by the senses and cannot be grasped by the intellect." Al-Mufaḍḍal said: "What is hidden from creation is within His grasp and nothing escapes Him." It has also been said: it refers to what is in His saying: ﴿Indeed, with God is the knowledge of the Hour﴾ (Luqman: 34). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or he meant by the unseen of the heavens and the earth the Day of Resurrection, in that its knowledge is hidden from the people of the heavens and the earth, none of whom has come to know of it."

It has been said: since the Hour is coming without fail, it is brought close, like the blink of an eye. Al-Zajjaj said: "He did not mean that the Hour comes in the blink of an eye. He only described the speed of the power to bring it about, i.e., He says to a thing 'Be,' and it is." It has been said: this is an illustration of nearness, as you say: "A year is nothing but a moment." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is near with God, even if it is delayed, as they say of the thing you consider near: ﴿like the blink of an eye or even nearer﴾ when you exaggerate in considering it near." Similar is His saying: ﴿and they ask you to hasten the punishment﴾ (al-ʿAnkabut: 53), ﴿and God will not break His promise﴾ (al-Hajj: 47), ﴿and indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ (al-Hajj: 47), meaning: it is near to Him, while it is far from you.

It has been said: the meaning is that the establishment of the Hour, the causing of the living to die, and the raising of the dead from the first and the last, will occur in the nearest time He has willed.

﴿Indeed, God is over all things competent﴾ (al-ʿAnkabut: 20), so He is able to establish the Hour and resurrect creation, since that is among the things within His power. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The meaning, according to Qatada and others, is: the Hour and its establishment are within God's power only when He says to it 'Be,' so if a human being happened to witness this, it would be so swift that he would doubt whether it was like the blink of an eye or nearer than that. So *aw*, in this case, is in its original sense of doubt. It has also been said that it is for choice." End of quotation.

Doubt and choice are both far-fetched, because this is an announcement from God, exalted is He, about the matter of the Hour, and doubt is impossible for Him. Also, choice occurs only in prohibited matters, like the saying: "Take from my wealth a dinar or a dirham," or in obligations, like the verse of expiations: ﴿And those who divorce by zihar﴾ (al-Mujadila: 3). *Aw* here is for obscuring the matter from the addressee, like His saying: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾ (al-Saffat: 147), and His saying: ﴿Our command came upon it by night or by day﴾ (Yunus: 24). God knows their number and when His command will come upon them, just as He knows the matter of the Hour, but it was obscured from the addressee. That *aw* here is for obscuring was mentioned by al-Zajjaj here. Al-Qadi said: "This is not valid, because the establishment of the Hour is not a state of obligation such that it could be said that He brings it at a time—meaning the Qadi's time—so that the obscuring would be from the addressee at that time, and it is not a time of obligation." What we say is: the obscuring occurred at the time of the preceding address concerning the matter of the Hour, not at the time of its coming. It is not a condition of obscuring from the addressee in reporting something that the time of the report and the time of that thing's occurrence be the same. Do you not see, in His saying: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾ (al-Saffat: 147), how the time of the report was later than the time of that sending and their existence as a hundred thousand or more?

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "'The blink of the eye' (*lamḥ al-baṣar*) is the movement of the body by the glance from the top of the pupil, and it is composed of parts, and those parts are numerous. The time in which the blink takes place is composed of successive moments, and God is able to establish the Resurrection in one of those moments. Therefore He said: ﴿or it is nearer﴾. Since the swiftest of states and events in our minds is the blink of the eye, He mentioned it, then said: 'or it is nearer,' as an alert to what we have mentioned. The intended meaning is not the manner of doubt; rather, the meaning is: 'Indeed, it is nearer.'" End of quotation, and there is some abridgement in it.

What he mentioned, that *aw* means *bal* (rather), is the view of al-Farra', and it is not valid, because the transition (*iḍrāb*) is of two kinds, and neither is valid here. The first: that it be a cancellation of the preceding predication, and that it was not what was intended. This is impossible here, because it would result in a predication that does not correspond. The second: that it be a transition from one thing to another without cancelling that preceding thing. This is also impossible here, because of the contradiction between reporting that it is like the blink of an eye in speed and reporting that it is nearer, so both cannot be true together.

The author of *al-Ghaniyyan* said: "Although this is hard to grasp literally, what is intended is exaggeration, according to the way of the Arabs and the masters of composition." How excellent is the saying of the poet al-Ablah on this meaning:

> The lightning said to him, and the wind said to him, both together, and they are what they are:
> "Do you run with us?" He said: "If I become energetic, I will make you both laugh at yourselves."
> "I am the return of the glance, I have outpaced it toward the goal in speed, so who are you two?"

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the matter of the Hour and that it is certainly coming, this indicated the Hereafter's creation. The earlier description of them with the absence of knowledge was mentioned, so He mentioned the first creation, which is bringing them out from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing, as an alert to the occurrence of the later creation. Then He mentioned His favor upon them in giving them the senses, which are the means of perceiving things and attaining knowledge. Since the first creation was mentioned, and He made what they know by as one of the greatest blessings upon them, He said: ﴿so that you may give thanks﴾. The discussion of *ummahat* (mothers) was mentioned in al-Nisa'.

Hamza read with a kasra on the hamza and the mim here, and in al-Nur, al-Zumar and al-Najm, and al-Kisa'i read with a kasra on the hamza in them. Al-A'mash read with deletion of the hamza and a kasra on the mim, and Ibn Abi Layla read with its deletion and a fatha on the mim. Abu Hatim said: "Deleting the hamza is bad, but the reading of Ibn Ubayy is more correct." End of quotation. It was more correct because the kasra on the mim occurs only to assimilate it to the vowel of the hamza; when the hamza is deleted, the assimilation disappears. By contrast, Ibn Abi Layla's reading leaves the mim on its own vowel.

*Lā taʿlamūna* ("you do not know") is a circumstantial clause (*jumla ḥāliyya*), meaning: "while not knowing." It has been said: "You do not know anything of what the covenant taken from you in the loins of your fathers was, or anything of what was decreed for you of happiness or misery, or anything of your benefits." The more appropriate is the general sense of the word "anything," especially in the context of negation. Wahb said: "The child is born wary for seven days; he does not perceive comfort or pain." It is possible that *wajaʿala* (and He made) is conjoined to ﴿He brought you out﴾, so it is one part within the scope of the predicate of the subject; and it is possible that it is a new statement conjoined to the initial sentence, like the beginning of it.

The meaning of the hearing, the sights and the hearts is their sensing and perceiving, so the faculty is expressed by the organ. Abu Abdullah al-Razi (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) said, in substance: "The reason the word *fu'ad* (heart) is given in the paucity plural (*jam' qilla*, the plural form for small numbers) is that it was created only for true, certain knowledge, whereas most people are preoccupied with bestial acts, so their hearts are not really hearts. For this reason the paucity plural is used for it." End of his words, summarized. This is a delirious statement. Were it not for the eminence of the one who said it and his having written it in books, I would not have mentioned it. What should be said about this is what al-Zamakhshari said: that *afida* is among the paucity plurals that have come to function like plurals of abundance and paucity alike, when no other form of it is attested in usage, as with *shusu'* (the plural of *shis'*, "sandal-thong") which has no other plural form. So it follows that pattern. End of his words. However, al-Zamakhshari's claim that no plural of *shis'* other than *shusu'* occurs is not correct. A paucity plural also occurs for it: they say *ash-sa'* (*ashsa'*). So he should have said: "*shusu'* has been given precedence (as the common plural)."

Ibn Amir, Hamza, Talha, al-A'mash and Ibn Hurmuz read *alam tarawa* (ﷺ not applicable) with the second person "you" (*ta'* of address), while the rest of the seven readers read it with *ya'* (third person). Ibn Atiyya said: "There is a difference of report from al-Hasan, Isa al-Thaqafi, Asim and Abu Amr."

When the Exalted mentioned the three means of knowledge, hearing, sight and reason, the first two being the means of perceiving the sensible and the third the means of perceiving the intelligible, He confined the mention of the means of perceiving the sensible to sight, since it is the most striking for what is observed by it of the great creatures at their varied distances, such as observing the luminous bodies in the spheres. He placed the flying animal as the object of consideration and wonder here, for its flight in the air despite the weight of its body is among the things that cause wonder and are taken as a lesson. The verse also includes mention of the means of perceiving by reason, in that the bird does not fall, since there is nothing beneath it to support it and nothing above it to which it is attached. Thus reason knows that there is a holder of it who is able to hold it up, and He is God the Exalted, as the Exalted said: ﴿Have they not considered the birds above them, spreading and folding their wings? None holds them up except the Most Merciful. Indeed, He is Seer of all things.﴾ (67:19). Thus the verse brings together the mention of the means of sense perception and the means of reasoning.

The meaning of *musakhkharat* ("made subservient") is "made pliable," and it is in the passive form to indicate that it has a subjector. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "This is evidence of the perfection of God's power and wisdom, for He the Exalted created the bird with a form by which flight is possible for it. He gave it a wing that it spreads at one time and folds at another, like what the swimmer does in water. He created the air with a form by which flight is possible. He created it in a subtle form by which piercing and passing through it is easy. Were it not for that, flight would not be possible." End of his words. His statement is drawn from the words of al-Qadi, who said: "He attributed the holding to Himself because He is the one who gave the instruments, for the sake of which the bird was able to perform those actions. Since He is the one who causes that, this attribution is valid." End of his words.

What we say is that the bird could have flown even had no wing been created for it, and it could have pierced a dense object by the power of God the Exalted (p-523), and the one who holds it in the atmosphere of the sky is God the Exalted. Proof has been established that all actions are created by God, and proof has been established that He the Exalted is the Doer who chooses. So we do not say: "Were it not for the wing and the subtlety of the air, flight would not be possible, and were it not for the instruments, it would not be possible."

Al-Zamakhshari said, in agreement with their words: "*Musakhkharat*: made pliable for flight by what He created for them of wings and the suitable causes for that." Then he rightly concluded with his statement: "None holds them up in their gripping and spreading and standing except God by His power." End of his words.

*La-ayat* ("indeed signs"): it is in the plural and not the singular, because the signs in it include the lightness of the bird which God placed in it so that it may rise by it, its weight which He placed in it so that it may descend, the space between the sky and the earth, and the holding which belongs to God the Exalted. Or it is plural in consideration of what is in this verse and the one before it. He said: *li-qawmin yu'minun* ("for a people who believe"), for they are those who benefit from consideration. And because the verse includes that the one who subjects them and holds them is God, this is a report from Him the Exalted which only the believer confirms.

﴿ضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا عَبْدًا مَمْلُوكًا لا يَقْدِرُ عَلى شَيْءٍ ومَن رَزَقْناهُ مِنّا رِزْقًا حَسَنًا فَهو يُنْفِقُ مِنهُ سِرًّا وجَهْرًا هَلْ يَسْتَوُونَ الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ بَلْ أكْثَرُهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ﴿وضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا رَجُلَيْنِ أحَدُهُما أبْكَمُ لا يَقْدِرُ عَلى شَيْءٍ وهو كَلٌّ عَلى مَوْلاهُ أيْنَما يُوَجِّهْهُ لا يَأْتِ بِخَيْرٍ هَلْ يَسْتَوِي هو ومَن يَأْمُرُ بِالعَدْلِ وهو عَلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ ﴿ولِلَّهِ غَيْبُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ وما أمْرُ السّاعَةِ إلّا كَلَمْحِ البَصَرِ أوْ هو أقْرَبُ إنَّ اللَّهَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾ ﴿واللَّهُ أخْرَجَكم مِن بُطُونِ أُمَّهاتِكم لا تَعْلَمُونَ شَيْئًا وجَعَلَ لَكُمُ السَّمْعَ والأبْصارَ والأفْئِدَةَ لَعَلَّكم تَشْكُرُونَ﴾ ﴿ألَمْ يَرَوْا إلى الطَّيْرِ مُسَخَّراتٍ في جَوِّ السَّماءِ ما يُمْسِكُهُنَّ إلّا اللَّهُ إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لَآياتٍ لِقَوْمٍ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ﴿واللَّهُ جَعَلَ لَكم مِن بُيُوتِكم سَكَنًا وجَعَلَ لَكم مِن جُلُودِ الأنْعامِ بُيُوتًا تَسْتَخِفُّونَها يَوْمَ ظَعْنِكم ويَوْمَ إقامَتِكم ومِن أصْوافِها وأوْبارِها وأشْعارِها أثاثًا ومَتاعًا إلى حِينٍ﴾ [An-Nahl: 80] ﴿واللَّهُ جَعَلَ لَكم مِمّا خَلَقَ ظِلالًا وجَعَلَ لَكم مِنَ الجِبالِ أكْنانًا وجَعَلَ لَكم سَرابِيلَ تَقِيكُمُ الحَرَّ وسَرابِيلَ تَقِيكم بَأْسَكم كَذَلِكَ يُتِمُّ نِعْمَتَهُ عَلَيْكم لَعَلَّكم تُسْلِمُونَ﴾ [An-Nahl: 81] ﴿فَإنْ تَوَلَّوْا فَإنَّما عَلَيْكَ البَلاغُ المُبِينُ﴾ [An-Nahl: 82] ﴿يَعْرِفُونَ نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ ثُمَّ يُنْكِرُونَها وأكْثَرُهُمُ الكافِرُونَ﴾ [An-Nahl: 83] ﴿ويَوْمَ نَبْعَثُ مِن كُلِّ أُمَّةٍ شَهِيدًا ثُمَّ لا يُؤْذَنُ لِلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا ولا هم يُسْتَعْتَبُونَ﴾ [An-Nahl: 84] (p-518)

Al-Kall (الكَلُّ): the burden, the heavy one. The orphan is sometimes called kall because of his burden on the one who supports him. The poet said:
"A devourer of the orphan's wealth before his youth, when the orphan's bone is not firm."

Al-kall also means one who has neither child nor parent, and kall means dependents (ʿiyāl); its plural is kulūl. Al-lamḥ (اللَّمْحُ) is a quick glance: "lamaḥahu lamḥan wa lamaḥānan." Al-jaww (الجَوُّ) is the space between the sky and the earth. It is said that it is what lies adjacent to the earth in the direction of height, and al-lawḥ and al-sukkāk are farther than it. Al-ẓaʿn (الظَّعْنُ) is the travel of the nomads in search of pasture and moving from one place to another; al-ẓaʿn also means the howdah (the litter on a camel). Ṣūf (wool) is for sheep, waabr (fine hair/fleece) is for camels, and shaʿr (hair) is for goats, as the lexicographers said regarding His words ﴿ومِن أصْوافِها﴾ [An-Nahl: 80] "and of their wool," etc.

Athāth (الأثاثُ): Al-Mufaḍḍal said: it is household goods such as carpets and coverings. Al-Farrāʾ said: it has no singular from its own form, just as matāʿ (مَتاعُ, goods) has no singular from its own form. If you pluralized it you would say ʾaʾthiṯa for the few and ʾuṯuṯ for the many. Abū Zayd said: its singular is uthātha. Al-Khalīl said: its root is from their saying athatha al-nabāt wa al-shaʿr (the plants and the hair became thick), so it is athīth when it becomes dense. Imru' al-Qays said:
"And a tress that adorns the back, jet-black and raven, thick like the cluster of the palm laden with dates."

Al-kinn (الكِنُّ) is what protects and shields from wind, rain and other things; and from the mountains, it is the cave (al-ghār). Istaʿtabtu al-rajula means aʿtabtuhu, i.e., I removed from him what he was reproached and blamed for; the noun is al-ʿutbā. The form istafʿala has come with the meaning of afʿala, like istadaynahu and adaynahu.

﴿ضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا عَبْدًا مَمْلُوكًا لا يَقْدِرُ عَلى شَيْءٍ ومَن رَزَقْناهُ مِنّا رِزْقًا حَسَنًا فَهو يُنْفِقُ مِنهُ سِرًّا وجَهْرًا هَلْ يَسْتَوُونَ الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ بَلْ أكْثَرُهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ﴿وضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا رَجُلَيْنِ أحَدُهُما أبْكَمُ لا يَقْدِرُ عَلى شَيْءٍ وهو كَلٌّ عَلى مَوْلاهُ أيْنَما يُوَجِّهْهُ لا يَأْتِ بِخَيْرٍ هَلْ يَسْتَوِي هو ومَن يَأْمُرُ بِالعَدْلِ وهو عَلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ ﴿ولِلَّهِ غَيْبُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ وما أمْرُ السّاعَةِ إلّا كَلَمْحِ البَصَرِ أوْ هو أقْرَبُ إنَّ اللَّهَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾ ﴿واللَّهُ أخْرَجَكم مِن بُطُونِ أُمَّهاتِكم لا تَعْلَمُونَ شَيْئًا وجَعَلَ لَكُمُ السَّمْعَ والأبْصارَ والأفْئِدَةَ لَعَلَّكم تَشْكُرُونَ﴾ ﴿ألَمْ يَرَوْا إلى الطَّيْرِ مُسَخَّراتٍ في جَوِّ السَّماءِ ما يُمْسِكُهُنَّ إلّا اللَّهُ إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لَآياتٍ لِقَوْمٍ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾: The occasion (munāsabah) for striking this example: when Allah, exalted is He, explained their misguidance in associating others with Him, though that other neither brings benefit nor harm to itself or to its worshipper, He struck for them the example of a slave under another's ownership, incapable of disposing of anything, and a free, wealthy man who disposes of what Allah has given him. If these two are not equal in your sight, though they are of one kind and share humanity, then how do you associate with Allah and equate with Him what is His creation, subdued by His power, whether a human or other, despite the vast difference in attributes? And the Originator of existence cannot be resembled by anything of His creation, and no sane person can liken anything else to Him.

Mujāhid said: this is a parable for Allah and the idols. Qatādah said: it is for the believer and the disbeliever. The disbeliever is the slave who is owned, who gains nothing from his worship in the Hereafter, and "the one whom We have provided for" is the believer. Ibn Jubayr said: it is a parable for the miser and the generous; end.

Since the word ʿabd (عَبْدٌ, slave) may be applied to the free, it was specified by "mamlūk" (owned). Since the owned slave may have some disposal and power, like the one given permission (al-maʾdhūn lahu) and the mukātab (one contracted to buy his freedom), it was specified by His words "incapable of anything." The meaning is: incapable of anything of disposal over property, because he is capable of some movements: standing, sitting, eating, drinking, sleeping, and other things. The apparent reading is that "man" (مَن) is a relative pronoun, meaning "and the one whom We have provided for," and the context of the relative clause and what follows indicates that it refers to the free man. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: it is a qualifying (موصوفة) form. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the apparent reading is that it is a qualifying form, as if He said: "and a free man whom We have provided for," to match "a slave." It does not preclude it being a relative. Al-Ḥawfī said: "man" means "alladhī" (the one who). Striking the parable for two specific persons described by widely differing attributes does not require identifying them. What is reported about identifying them, that they are ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān (may Allah be pleased with him) and a slave of his, or that they are Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him) and Abū Jahl, has no sound chain of transmission.

The pronoun in "yastawūn" (they are equal) is plural, not dual, though two were mentioned earlier, because "man" may be intended as a plural, in which case the plural pronoun is consistent with the inclusion of the owned slave and the wealthy ones in the plural. It is as if it were said: "a slave owned," and the owners (al-mullāk) are those who are provided for and who spend. It may also be that "ʿabdan mamlūkan" is meant as a genus, so a plural pronoun may refer to it and to the genus of the wealthy. It may also refer to slaves and free persons, even though no plural has preceded, because the two classes are indicated by "a slave owned" and "the one whom We have provided for."

﴿قُلِ الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾ [Al-ʿAnkabūt: 63]: The apparent reading is that it is addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ). It was said that it may be addressed to the one whom Allah has provided for, commanding him to praise Allah for distinguishing him with this power over that weak one. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "Al-ḥamdu lillāh" is thanks for the clarity of this parable and for the opponent's submission to it, as when you say to one who has submitted to your argument and accepted it, building upon it your saying: "Allah is greatest, on this such and such follows." So when He said here "Are they equal?", it is as if the opponent said to Him: "No," and He said: "Praise be to Allah, the argument is manifest"; end. It was also said: "Al-ḥamdu lillāh" means He alone deserves praise, not what they worship besides Him, since the idols have no favor upon them to be praised for; rather complete praise is for Allah, because He is the Bestower and the Creator. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Praise be to Allah for what He has done for His friends and for bestowing upon them the blessing of monotheism."

The apparent reading is the negation of knowledge from most of them, because among them are those for whom the truth became clear and who returned to it; or "most" refers to most of creation, because most are polytheists. It was said that the intended meaning is generality, i.e., "rather, they do not know." The object of "yaʿlamūn" (they know) is omitted: either because the meaning is the negation of knowledge from most, without considering its object, or because it is omitted and follows from the statements whose cause is His saying "Praise be to Allah."

﴿وضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا رَجُلَيْنِ﴾, i.e., the account of two men. Al-Zamakhsharī said: this is a second parable, which He struck for Himself and for what He pours out upon His servants and what encompasses them of the traces of His mercy, kindness and blessings, religious and worldly, and for the idols which are dead and neither harm nor benefit. The mute (al-abkam) is the one born deaf-mute, who neither understands nor is understood.

﴿وهُوَ كَلٌّ عَلى مَوْلاهُ﴾, i.e., a burden, and a dependent upon the one who takes charge of his affairs and supports him. ʾAynamā yuwajjihhu: wherever he sends him and directs him in a matter of need or support, an important matter: he brings no benefit and achieves no success. "Are they equal, he and one who has sound senses, beneficial, possessing sufficiency together with right guidance and piety; so he commands people to justice, and he is himself upon a straight path, upon a righteous way and a sound religion"; end. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "one of them is mute" is a parable for the disbeliever, and "the one who commands justice" is the believer. Qatādah said: this is a parable of Allah, exalted is He, and the idols: the idols are like the mute who has no speech and is unable to do anything, and he is a dependent upon whoever is close to him, a relative or friend, just as the idols need to be carried, served, and burdened with, and no good whatsoever comes from them. Also from Qatādah and others: this is a parable which Allah struck for Himself and for the idol. The mute who is unable to do anything is the idol, and the one who commands justice is Allah, exalted is He. This is not so, because He said "two men as a parable," so the counterpart of the mute, described with those attributes, must be a man described with what opposes those attributes of speech, power and sufficiency. But He omitted the counterpart, because its opposite indicates it. Then it was said: "Are they equal?", meaning that mute with those attributes and this speaking one. So the mention of their equality is also evidence of the omitted counterpart. Since muteness is the first of the attributes mentioned, and from it the subsequent attributes are determined by the capacity for equality in speech, and its fruit of commanding justice is other than it, while he is upon a straight way: wherever he turns, good comes from him and benefits; he is not a burden on anyone. It is established in the first principles of reason that the mute, meaning the incapable, is not equal in intellect and nobility to the speaking, able, perfect one, though they are equal in humanity. So it is more fitting and more deserving to judge that an inanimate object is not equal to the Lord of the Worlds in deserving worship. And as we said regarding the previous parable, the parable does not require identifying the two persons struck by it; similarly here. So identifying the mute as Abū Jahl and the one who commands justice as ʿAmmār, or as Ubayy ibn Khalaf and ʿUthmān ibn Maẓʿūn, or as Hāshim ibn ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith, who was hostile to the Messenger (ﷺ), has no sound chain of transmission.

Abdullah, Alqama, Ibn Wabbab, Mujahid and Talha read *yuwajjihu* with a single silent hāʾ, in the active voice (*mabniyyan*). Its subject is a pronoun referring back to *mawlāhu* (his guardian), and the object pronoun is omitted because the meaning indicates it. It is also permissible for the subject pronoun to refer back to the mute man (*al-abkam*), with the verb being intransitive: *wajjaha* meaning *tawajjaha* (to turn toward). The meaning would then be: "Wherever he turns." From Abdullah also: *tuwajjihhu* with two hāʾs and the second person prefix (*tāʾ al-khiṭāb*). The majority read it with the prefix *yāʾ* and two hāʾs. From Alqama, Ibn Wabbab and Talha: *yuwajjah* with a single silent hāʾ, the verb being in the passive voice. From Alqama and Talha: *yuwajjihu*, with a kasra on the jīm and a single hāʾ with a ḍamma.

The author of *al-Lawāmiʿ* said: "If this reading is authentic, then the hāʾ, which is the final radical of the verb, has been deleted to avoid geminating (*tafḍʿīf*), and because pronouncing it with gemination is difficult. Or it was not intended as a conditional, but rather as an imperative: 'Wherever he is, let him turn (it).' The object pronoun has been deleted from it. The deletion of the yāʾ in *lā yaʾti bi-khayr* (﴿he does not bring good﴾) would then be for lightening, like *yawma yaʾti* and *idhā yasri*." End of quotation.

*Ayna* does not leave the conditional or interrogative sense. Abu Hatim said: "This reading is weak, because the jussive (*al-jazm*) is obligatory." End of quotation. The way this reading may be justified, if it is authentic, is that *ayna-ma* is a conditional particle, treated analogously to *idhā* because they share the conditional character. Then the yāʾ of *lā yaʾti* was deleted for lightening, or it was jussified through the assumption that it had been pronounced with the unassimilated *ayna-ma* functioning as in the reading of the one who read ﴿Indeed, whoever fears God and is patient﴾ (Yusuf: 90) in one of the two ways. The meaning of *yuwajjah* would then be *yatawajjah* (he turns), so it is an intransitive verb and not transitive.
