Al-'adl (justice) is the performance of every obligation concerning beliefs, laws, and conduct with people in the fulfillment of trusts, the abandonment of injustice, fairness, and the giving of rights. Al-ihsan (good conduct) is the performance of every recommended act. This was said by Ibn Atiyyah. al-Zamakhshari said: Al-'adl is the obligatory, because Allah, may He be exalted and glorified, was just in it toward His servants, making what He imposed on them fall within their capacity. Al-ihsan is the recommended, and its command was linked to them all, because an obligation must inevitably involve some shortcoming, which the recommended act compensates for; end of quote. In his statement "within their capacity" there is a trace of i'tizal (the Mu'tazila tendency). From Ibn Abbas: al-'adl is "There is no god but Allah," and al-ihsan is the performance of the obligatory duties. Also from him: al-'adl is the truth. From Sufyan ibn Uyaynah: it is the equality of inner and outer conduct in action. al-Mawardi mentioned that it is judging by the truth, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And when you judge between people, to judge with justice﴾ [An-Nisa: 58]. Abu Sulayman said: al-'adl in the language of the Arabs is fairness. It was also said: it is the removal of rivals. It was said: al-'adl is in actions and al-ihsan is in words.

Giving to close relatives (iytaʾ dhi al-qurba) is maintaining family ties (silat al-rahim). It falls under good conduct, but it was singled out for mention out of concern for it and as an encouragement to do good to them. Al-fahsha' is adultery, or what its ugliness is manifest among sins. Its doer is always concealed in it, or it is the abomination of an act or statement, or stinginess, or what requires the prescribed punishment in this world and punishment in the Hereafter, or transgressing the limits of Allah. These are opinions, the first of which is from Ibn Abbas. Al-munkar is polytheism according to Muqatil, or what has been promised the Fire according to Ibn al-Sa'ib, or the contradiction between inner and outer conduct according to Ibn Uyaynah, or what does not require a prescribed punishment in this world but does bring punishment in the Hereafter, or what the intellects reject. These are opinions. It appears that it is more general than al-fahsha', since it includes sins, vices, and wrongdoing. Al-baghy is arrogance through injustice and seeking to achieve it. It falls under al-munkar, and it was singled out for mention out of concern for avoiding it. In what is commanded and what is forbidden, he combined what is obligatory and recommended, and what is forbidden and disliked, because they share a common element, which is the demand in the command and the abandonment in the prohibition. (p. 530)

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: He commanded three things and forbade three things. Justice ('adl) is the middle path between excess (ifrat) and deficiency (tafrit), and this applies to beliefs ('aqa'id) and to the religious duties of the servants (a'mal al-ru'a).

Ibn 'Abbas said: Justice is "There is no god but God" (la ilaha illa Allah). It affirms one God, so it is neither pure negation of God (ta'til mahd) nor affirmation of more than one god. Affirming that He is All-Knowing and All-Powerful, with necessary attributes (wajib al-sifat), is not a denial of attributes, nor does it affirm an attribute that is newly originated and changing. The fact that a servant's act occurs through God's power and the motive (da'iyah) He placed in him is not pure compulsion (jabr mahd), nor is it the servant's independent possession of the act. That God brings out of the Fire whoever among the people of monotheism (ahl al-tawhid) entered it is not irja' (postponement of judgment regarding sinners), nor is it eternal punishment (takhlid) for sin.

As for the religious duties of the servants: the obligations (taklif) incumbent on them are not a claim that there is no obligation. Nor is it a claim of tormenting oneself and avoiding what the natural disposition inclines toward, such as eating good food, marrying, throwing oneself from a high place, and retaliation (qisas), blood-money (diyah), or pardon ('afw). It is not an excessive strictness in fixing retaliation as in the law of Moses, peace be upon him, nor an absolute, mandatory pardon as in the law of Jesus, peace be upon him. Avoiding a menstruating woman only in the matter of sexual intercourse is not total avoidance as in the law of Moses, peace be upon him, nor is intercourse with her during menstruation permitted as in the law of Jesus, peace be upon him. And circumcision (ikhtitan) is not leaving the foreskin (qulfah) intact, nor cutting off the organ, as the Manichaeans held.

God says: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [2:143]; ﴿And those who, when they spend﴾ [25:67]. Do not make the two verses [identical].

It is well known that they say: "By justice the heavens and the earth stand." Its meaning: if the proportions of the elements were not balanced, and some of them were greater, excess would prevail and the natures would be reversed. If the sun came close to the world, the heat would become enormous and everything in it would burn; and if it were farther away, heat and cold would become equal. Likewise are the measures of the movements of the stars and the degrees of their speed and slowness.

Ihsan (excellence) is exceeding what is obligatory in acts of obedience, in quantity and quality, in motives and in restraints, and in total immersion in witnessing the stations of servanthood ('ubudiyyah) and lordship (rububiyyah). Among ihsan is compassion (shafaqah) toward creation, its root being maintaining ties of kinship (silat al-rahim). The forbidden thing is three.

That is because He placed in the human soul four powers: the appetitive power (shahwaniyyah), which is the pursuit of pleasures; the irascible power (ghadabiyyah), which is inflicting harm; and the imaginative power (wahmiyyah), which is satanic and strives for haughtiness and dominance over people. So indecency (fahsha') is what arises from the appetitive power when it goes beyond the discipline of the Sharia; the reprehensible (munkar) is what arises from the irascible power; and transgression (baghy) is what arises from the imaginative power. End of his words, that which was extracted from his speech; may God pardon him.

When God had commanded those three and forbidden those three, He said: ﴿He admonishes you with it﴾, meaning: with what He mentioned of command and prohibition. The meaning is: He alerts you in the best way, ﴿that you may remember﴾, that is, that you may be alert to what you were commanded and forbidden. The "covenant of God" (ahd Allah) is knowledge of what a person has pledged and bound himself to, from what agrees with the Sharia.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is the pledge of allegiance (bay'ah) to the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, to Islam: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you do but pledge allegiance to God﴾ [48:10]. It seems he had in mind what was said: that it was revealed concerning those who pledged allegiance to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, to Islam; this was narrated from Buraydah.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: It refers to what was among the alliances of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic era) in matters of enjoining good or forbidding evil.

Maymun ibn Mihran said: It is fidelity to whomever you have made a covenant with, whether Muslim or disbeliever, for the covenant is due to God.

Al-Asamm said: It is jihad and what has been obligated concerning wealth as a right.

It was also said: it is the oath by God. ﴿And do not break oaths after their confirmation﴾: He forbade breaking them after they had been confirmed, meaning: after they were affirmed by the name of God, His guarantee, His witnessing, and His oversight, because the guarantor watches over the state of the one he guarantees.

﴿And do not be like a woman who unravels her thread after it has been spun, into pieces﴾, that is: in breaking the covenant after confirming it by God, be not like the foolish (wahra') woman who spins thread and then unravels it into strands (nakthan), which is what is undone of its twisting. The comparison does not require specifying the one compared to.

Al-Suddi and 'Abd Allah ibn Kathir said: she was a foolish woman in Mecca. From al-Kalbi and Muqatil: she was from Quraysh, a clumsy woman named Rayta daughter of Sa'd ibn Taym, nicknamed Jafra'. She used a spindle the length of a forearm, a whorl the size of a finger, and a large spindle-disc in proportion to them. She and her maidservants would spin from morning until noon, then she would order them and they would unravel what they had spun.

From Mujahid: this is the practice of the women of Najd, where one of them unravels her yarn, then fluffs it, mixes it with wool, and spins it again.

Ibn al-Anbari said: Rayta daughter of 'Amr al-Murriyyah, whose nickname was al-Jafra', from the people of Mecca; she was well known to the addressees.

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿after strength﴾ is: after a power (shiddah) that came about from the twisting of the strands of the thread. If we took it as a single strand, it would not unravel into pieces. Nakth in the language is the rope when its strands come apart.

Mujahid said: The meaning is "after a strand has been twisted into strength."

Al-Dakhal means corruption and deceit (al-daghal). They made faith a means to deception and treachery, because the one to whom the oath is sworn feels secure, so the swearer can harm him with what he wants. They said: it was revealed concerning the Arabs who, when they allied with a tribe and another larger group came, they would ally with the larger group and betray the smaller one.

It was also said: "Because one nation is more numerous than another" (an takuna antum azyada khabaran), where the verb is attributed to a nation (ummah), and the intended meaning is the addressees.

Ibn Bahr said: al-dakhal and the one who enters into a thing without being part of it; "dakhalan" is the second object (maf'ul thani).

It was also said: it is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), and "an takuna" means: because of [the fact] that it is. "Hiya arba" is a subject and predicate.

The Kufans permitted that "hiya" be an 'imad (a pronoun of separation, which they call fasl), so that "arba" would be in the accusative position. This is not permitted according to the Basrans because "ummah" is indefinite.

The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the verbal noun formed from "an takuna": that is, because of the fact that one nation is more numerous than another, He tests you by it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: so that He may see whether you hold fast to the rope of fidelity to the covenant of God and to what you have bound upon yourselves and confirmed with the oaths of the allegiance to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, or whether you are deceived by the multitude of Quraysh, their wealth, their strength, and the paucity, poverty, and weakness of the believers. ﴿And He will surely make clear to you﴾: a warning and caution against opposing the religion of Islam. End of his words.

It was also said: it refers to fidelity to the covenant. Ibn Jubayr, Ibn al-Sa'ib, and Muqatil said: it refers to the multitude.

Ibn al-Anbari said: since its feminine form is not a true feminine, it was treated according to the sense of the masculine, just as "al-sayhah" (the cry) is treated according to the sense of "al-siyah" (the shouting).

The Kufans permitted that "hiya" be an 'imad (a pronoun of separation, which they call fasl), so that "arba" would be in the accusative position. This is not permitted according to the Basrans because "ummah" is indefinite.

The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the verbal noun formed from "an takuna": that is, because of the fact that one nation is more numerous than another, He tests you by it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: so that He may see whether you hold fast to the rope of fidelity to the covenant of God and to what you have bound upon yourselves and confirmed with the oaths of the allegiance to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, or whether you are deceived by the multitude of Quraysh, their wealth, their strength, and the paucity, poverty, and weakness of the believers. ﴿And He will surely make clear to you﴾: a warning and caution against opposing the religion of Islam. End of his words.

It was also said: it refers to fidelity to the covenant. Ibn Jubayr, Ibn al-Sa'ib, and Muqatil said: it refers to the multitude.

Ibn al-Anbari said: since its feminine form is not a true feminine, it was treated according to the sense of the masculine, just as "al-sayhah" (the cry) is treated according to the sense of "al-siyah" (the shouting).

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 16, verses 93–97:**

﴿And if God had willed, He would have made you one community. But He leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. And you will surely be questioned about what you used to do.﴾ ﴿And do not take your oaths as means of deceit among yourselves, lest a foot slip after being firm and you taste evil for having averted [others] from the way of God, and you will have a great punishment.﴾ ﴿And do not exchange the covenant of God for a small price. Indeed, what is with God is better for you, if you only knew.﴾ ﴿What you have will end, but what is with God is lasting. And We will surely reward those who were patient with the best of what they used to do.﴾ ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer – We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them with the best of what they used to do.﴾: This will (mashi'ah) is the will of choice according to the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah. He tested people with commands and prohibitions so that each one would go toward what was made easy for him, and this is due to the right of the King, who is not questioned about what He does. Had He willed, they would all have been upon one path, either guidance or misguidance, but He differentiated: some are for happiness and some are for wretchedness. So He created guidance and misguidance, and He threatened them with being questioned about their deeds – and this is a questioning of rebuke, not a questioning of inquiry, and the questioning of inquiry is what is negated in [some] verses. The doctrine of the Mu'tazilah is that this will is a will of compulsion. Al-'Askari said: The meaning is that He is able to gather you upon Islam by compulsion, but He did not do that; and He created you so that He might punish whom He wills for disobedience to Him and reward whom He wills for obedience to Him, and He does not will any of that except that he deserves it. It is also possible that the meaning is: had He willed, He would have created you in Paradise, but He did not do that, so that He might reward the obedient among you and punish the disobedient.

Then He said: "And you will surely be questioned about what you used to do"; that is, the questioning of reckoning and recompense. In this there is evidence that "misguidance" (al-idlal) in the verse means punishment; for if misguidance meant turning away from the religion, questioning them would have no meaning. Al-Zamakhshari said: "One community" means upright, submitting to Islam by way of compulsion and constraint, and He is capable of that; but wisdom required that He leave astray whom He wills – that is, He forsakes whoever He knows chooses disbelief and persists in it – and guide whom He wills – that is, He shows kindness to whoever God knows chooses faith. That is, He built the matter upon choice, and upon what one deserves by it of kindness and forsaking, of reward and punishment, and He did not indicate compulsion, by which nothing of that is deserved. He confirmed this with His saying: "And you will surely be questioned about what you used to do." If this one were compelled to misguidance and guidance, He would not have established for them a deed about which they would be questioned; the end [of the quotation]. They said: He repeated the prohibition against making oaths a means of deceit, out of concern for it and as an emphasis in forbidding it, because of its great importance in the religion. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "and its recurrence in people's dealings." Al-Zamakhshari said: as an emphasis upon them and to make manifest the greatness of what they commit of it; the end [of the quotation]. It was also said: it was repeated because the two meanings differ: the first forbids entering into oaths and breaking the covenant in terms of few or many; here the prohibition is against the deceit that is in oaths by which one intends to seize rights. So it is as if He said: "a deceit among yourselves, so that you may use them to cut off the wealth of the Muslims." I say: the prohibition against making oaths a means of deceit has not been repeated; rather, there preceded a report that they had made their oaths a means of deceit, justified by a specific reason, namely that one community should be more numerous than another. The prohibition came with His saying "and do not take," a resumed, prescriptive statement concerning making oaths a means of deceit in general, so it includes all forms of swearing in sales, appropriating financial rights, and other things. "Lest [a foot] slip" (fa-tazilla) is in the accusative as a response to the prohibition. It is a metaphor for one who was upright, fell into a great matter, and collapsed, because when a foot slips a person turns from a state of good to a state of evil. Kuthayyir said: "When we met, I held firm, and [the other] slipped." Al-Zamakhshari said: "lest your feet slip from the road of Islam after being firm upon it." [He then asks:] "Why did you make the foot singular and indefinite?" [He answers:] "To magnify that a single foot should slip from the path of truth after it had been firm upon it; how much more so many feet?" The end [of the quotation]. We say: the plural is sometimes considered as a whole in terms of its being a whole, and sometimes each individual is considered. When the whole is considered, the predication is taken to indicate collectivity; and when each individual is considered, the predication agrees with the plural form in many cases, so it is plural for what is predicated of it, and agrees with each individual, so it is singular, as in His saying: "And she prepared for them a couch" [Yusuf: 31], where "couch" (mut-taka') is singular because in His saying "for them" (lahunna) a meaning for each one had been considered. Had it been intended as collective, or as many in the second respect, it would have been "couches" (mutta-ka'at). Upon this meaning should be understood the poet's saying:

"For I have found that the lean ones – their provision dies and perishes, so take from my provision."

That is: I saw every lean one. For this reason the pronoun in "dies and perishes" is singular. Since the meaning here is: none of you should take [oaths as deceit], the phrase "lest a foot slip" comes in consideration of this meaning; then He said "and you taste" in consideration of the whole, or of the plural form in its many aspect. If we say that the predication is to each individual, then the verse addresses the prohibition against making oaths a means of deceit both in terms of the whole and in terms of each individual, and this is indicated by the singularity of "foot" and the plurality of the pronoun in "and you taste." The particle "mā" in "for what you averted" is verbal-masdariyyah (i.e., it forms a verbal noun), meaning: for your turning away, or for your turning others away from the way of God, because if they broke the oaths and apostatized, the breaking of them would be taken as a precedent for others, and they would be reviled for it. The tasting of evil is in this world.

"And you will have a great punishment" – that is, in the Hereafter. "Evil" (al-su') is what harms them of killing, plundering, captivity, expulsion, and other things that cause them harm.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: His saying "for having averted [others] from the way of God" indicates that the verse concerns those who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and on this basis al-Zamakhshari interpreted it; he said: because they had broken the oaths of the pledge. But it does not indicate this exclusively; rather, breaking oaths in the pledge falls within the general meaning.

"And do not exchange the covenant of God for a small price": this is a prohibition against breaking what is between God Most High and the servant in order to take a trifling portion of the goods of this world. Al-Zamakhshari said: There was a people among those who had embraced Islam in Mecca whom Satan adorned for them out of their anxiety at what they saw of the dominance of the Quraysh and their oppression of the Muslims and their harming of them. When they had promised them, if they returned, that they would break what they had pledged to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), God made them firm. "And do not exchange": do not substitute for the covenant of God and the pledge of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) a small price, a trifling worldly good, which is what the Quraysh were promising and wishing for them if they returned – that what is with God of your victory and spoils and the reward of the Hereafter is better for you. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is a verse prohibiting bribery and taking wealth in exchange for abandoning what the taker is obligated to do, or doing what he is obligated to refrain from, for this is the covenant that God took from His servants concerning these matters. God Most High made clear the difference between the state of this world and the state of the Hereafter, that this world passes away and ends for the human being, and he passes away from it, while what is in the Hereafter is lasting and permanent. His saying "and what is with God is lasting" indicates that the bliss of Paradise does not end, and in this is an argument against Jahm ibn Safwan, who claimed that the bliss of Paradise is cut off. 'Asim and Ibn Kathir read "wa-la-najziyanna" with a nun, and the rest of the seven read it with a ya'. "Were patient" means: they struggled against themselves in keeping the covenant of Islam, and against the harm of the disbelievers, and in abandoning sins, and in earning wealth in a manner that is not lawful. "With the best of what they used to do": it was said: of voluntary acts of worship, and they were the best because their performance was not made obligatory, so the person would perform supererogatory acts by choice, not being bound by them. It was also said: He mentioned "the best" as an encouragement to doing it, although the recompense is for good and for better. It was also said: "the best" here means "good," so it is not the comparative form (af'al) used for preference. What appears is that the intended meaning of "the best" here is patience, that is: "and We will surely reward those who were patient with their patience," that is, with the recompense of their patience; and He made patience the best of deeds because all the obligations require it, so patience is their head, and therefore it is the best.

"Whoever" (man) is suitable for the singular and the masculine and their derivatives. But the singular and masculine come to the mind readily, so the verse specifies both types so that the promise includes both.

"While being a believer" is a circumstantial clause (jumlah hallliyyah), and faith is a condition for righteous deeds, restricting His saying: "Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it" [al-Zalzalah: 7]; or it is meant that the atom's weight is of faith, as occurs concerning those who come out of the Fire among the disobedient believers.

The apparent meaning of His saying "We will surely cause him to live a good life" [p-534] is that this is in this world, and this is the view of the majority. What indicates it is His saying "and We will surely reward them with their reward," meaning in the Hereafter. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd said: this refers to Paradise. Shurayk said: in the grave. 'Ali, Wahb ibn Munabbih, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan in one narration from them said it is contentment (al-qana'ah); and from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak: lawful provision; and also from him: happiness. 'Ikrimah said: obedience. Qatadah said: provision day by day. Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid said: good provision and righteous deeds. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: the sweetness of obedience. It was said: well-being and sufficiency; it was said: contentment with the decree. Al-Mawardi mentioned both. Al-Zamakhshari said: the believer who does righteous deeds, if he is well-off, then there is no discussion about him; and if he is poor, then with him is what makes his life pleasant, which is contentment and satisfaction with God Most High's distribution. As for the wicked person, if he is poor, there is no problem regarding his affair; and if he is well-off, then greed does not leave him to enjoy his life. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He made life good for the righteous through the expansion of their souls, their attainment, and the strength of their hope; hope for the soul is a pleasurable matter, and because they belittled this world, its worries were removed from them. If to this is added lawful wealth, health, and contentment, that is perfection; otherwise, the good (al-tayyib) in what we have mentioned is constant.

The pronoun in "We will surely cause him to live" returns to the wording of "whoever" (man), in the singular; and in "and We will surely reward them" it returns to its meaning in the plural, so it is plural. It is narrated from Nafi': "wa-la-yajziyannahum," with a ya' instead of a nun, shifting from the first-person pronoun to the third-person pronoun. It should be understood as an implied second oath, not as coordinated with "fa-la-nuhyiyannahu," so it would be the coordination of an oath-clause upon an oath-clause, both of which are elided. It cannot be coordination of an answer upon an answer, because the predications differ, and because the second would lead to the speaker reporting about himself by means of a report about an absent party, and that is not permissible. Accordingly, it is not permissible to say: "Zayd, I said, 'By God, I will surely strike Hind, and let him surely negate her'," meaning "and let Zayd surely negate her." But if you take it as an implied second oath, it is permissible: that is, "and Zayd said, 'He will surely negate her'," because in this construction you may relate its wording and you may relate its meaning. From the first is: "and they will surely swear by God, 'We intended nothing but the best'" [al-Tawbah: 107]; and from the second is: "They swear by God that they did not say" [al-Tawbah: 74]. Had it come according to the wording, it would have been "what we said."

If this one were compelled to misguidance and guidance, He would not have established for them a deed about which they would be questioned; the end [of the quotation]. They said: He repeated the prohibition against making oaths a means of deceit, out of concern for it and as an emphasis in forbidding it, because of its great importance in the religion. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "and its recurrence in people's dealings." Al-Zamakhshari said: as an emphasis upon them and to make manifest the greatness of what they commit of it; the end [of the quotation]. It is a metaphor for one who was upright, fell into a great matter, and collapsed, because when a foot slips a person turns from a state of good to a state of evil. Had it been intended as collective, or as many in the second respect, it would have been "couches" (mutta-ka'at). Upon this meaning should be understood the poet's saying:

The tasting of evil is in this world.

Since the meaning here is: none of you should take [oaths as deceit], the phrase "lest a foot slip" comes in consideration of this meaning; then He said "and you taste" in consideration of the whole, or of the plural form in its many aspect. If we say that the predication is to each individual, then the verse addresses the prohibition against making oaths a means of deceit both in terms of the whole and in terms of each individual, and this is indicated by the singularity of "foot" and the plurality of the pronoun in "and you taste." The particle "mā" in "for what you averted" is verbal-masdariyyah (i.e., it forms a verbal noun), meaning: for your turning away, or for your turning others away from the way of God, because if they broke the oaths and apostatized, the breaking of them would be taken as a precedent for others, and they would be reviled for it. The tasting of evil is in this world.

"And you will have a great punishment" – that is, in the Hereafter. "Evil" (al-su') is what harms them of killing, plundering, captivity, expulsion, and other things that cause them harm.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: His saying "for having averted [others] from the way of God" indicates that the verse concerns those who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and on this basis al-Zamakhshari interpreted it; he said: because they had broken the oaths of the pledge. But it does not indicate this exclusively; rather, breaking oaths in the pledge falls within the general meaning.

"And do not exchange the covenant of God for a small price": this is a prohibition against breaking what is between God Most High and the servant in order to take a trifling portion of the goods of this world. Al-Zamakhshari said: There was a people among those who had embraced Islam in Mecca whom Satan adorned for them out of their anxiety at what they saw of the dominance of the Quraysh and their oppression of the Muslims and their harming of them. When they had promised them, if they returned, that they would break what they had pledged to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), God made them firm. "And do not exchange": do not substitute for the covenant of God and the pledge of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) a small price, a trifling worldly good, which is what the Quraysh were promising and wishing for them if they returned – that what is with God of your victory and spoils and the reward of the Hereafter is better for you. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is a verse prohibiting bribery and taking wealth in exchange for abandoning what the taker is obligated to do, or doing what he is obligated to refrain from, for this is the covenant that God took from His servants concerning these matters. God Most High made clear the difference between the state of this world and the state of the Hereafter, that this world passes away and ends for the human being, and he passes away from it, while what is in the Hereafter is lasting and permanent. His saying "and what is with God is lasting" indicates that the bliss of Paradise does not end, and in this is an argument against Jahm ibn Safwan, who claimed that the bliss of Paradise is cut off. 'Asim and Ibn Kathir read "wa-la-najziyanna" with a nun, and the rest of the seven read it with a ya'. "Were patient" means: they struggled against themselves in keeping the covenant of Islam, and against the harm of the disbelievers, and in abandoning sins, and in earning wealth in a manner that is not lawful. "With the best of what they used to do": it was said: of voluntary acts of worship, and they were the best because their performance was not made obligatory, so the person would perform supererogatory acts by choice, not being bound by them. It was also said: He mentioned "the best" as an encouragement to doing it, although the recompense is for good and for better. It was also said: "the best" here means "good," so it is not the comparative form (af'al) used for preference. What appears is that the intended meaning of "the best" here is patience, that is: "and We will surely reward those who were patient with their patience," that is, with the recompense of their patience; and He made patience the best of deeds because all the obligations require it, so patience is their head, and therefore it is the best.

"Whoever" (man) is suitable for the singular and the masculine and their derivatives. But the singular and masculine come to the mind readily, so the verse specifies both types so that the promise includes both.

"While being a believer" is a circumstantial clause (jumlah hallliyyah), and faith is a condition for righteous deeds, restricting His saying: "Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it" [al-Zalzalah: 7]; or it is meant that the atom's weight is of faith, as occurs concerning those who come out of the Fire among the disobedient believers.

The apparent meaning of His saying "We will surely cause him to live a good life" [p-534] is that this is in this world, and this is the view of the majority. What indicates it is His saying "and We will surely reward them with their reward," meaning in the Hereafter. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd said: this refers to Paradise. Shurayk said: in the grave. 'Ali, Wahb ibn Munabbih, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan in one narration from them said it is contentment (al-qana'ah); and from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak: lawful provision; and also from him: happiness. 'Ikrimah said: obedience. Qatadah said: provision day by day. Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid said: good provision and righteous deeds. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: the sweetness of obedience. It was said: well-being and sufficiency; it was said: contentment with the decree. Al-Mawardi mentioned both. Al-Zamakhshari said: the believer who does righteous deeds, if he is well-off, then there is no discussion about him; and if he is poor, then with him is what makes his life pleasant, which is contentment and satisfaction with God Most High's distribution. As for the wicked person, if he is poor, there is no problem regarding his affair; and if he is well-off, then greed does not leave him to enjoy his life. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He made life good for the righteous through the expansion of their souls, their attainment, and the strength of their hope; hope for the soul is a pleasurable matter, and because they belittled this world, its worries were removed from them. If to this is added lawful wealth, health, and contentment, that is perfection; otherwise, the good (al-tayyib) in what we have mentioned is constant.

The pronoun in "We will surely cause him to live" returns to the wording of "whoever" (man), in the singular; and in "and We will surely reward them" it returns to its meaning in the plural, so it is plural. It is narrated from Nafi': "wa-la-yajziyannahum," with a ya' instead of a nun, shifting from the first-person pronoun to the third-person pronoun. It should be understood as an implied second oath, not as coordinated with "fa-la-nuhyiyannahu," so it would be the coordination of an oath-clause upon an oath-clause, both of which are elided. It cannot be coordination of an answer upon an answer, because the predications differ, and because the second would lead to the speaker reporting about himself by means of a report about an absent party, and that is not permissible. Accordingly, it is not permissible to say: "Zayd, I said, 'By God, I will surely strike Hind, and let him surely negate her'," meaning "and let Zayd surely negate her." But if you take it as an implied second oath, it is permissible: that is, "and Zayd said, 'He will surely negate her'," because in this construction you may relate its wording and you may relate its meaning. From the first is: "and they will surely swear by God, 'We intended nothing but the best'" [al-Tawbah: 107]; and from the second is: "They swear by God that they did not say" [al-Tawbah: 74]. Had it come according to the wording, it would have been "what we said."

(p. 535) Commentary of Abu Hayyan (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on Surah 16, verses 98–103:

﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord.﴾ ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as a guardian and those who associate partners with Him.﴾ ﴿And when We substitute a verse in place of another verse—and God knows best what He sends down—they say, "You are only a fabricator." Rather, most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿Say, "The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth, to strengthen those who believe, and as guidance and good tidings for the Muslims."﴾ ﴿And We certainly know that they say, "He is only being taught by a human." The tongue of the one they point to is foreign, while this is a clear Arabic tongue.﴾

When He, exalted is He, mentioned "And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things" (An-Nahl: 89), and mentioned some of the things that He had clarified in the Book, and then mentioned His saying, "Whoever does righteous deeds" (An-Nahl: 97), He mentioned what protects the reciter in his recitation from the whispering and prompting of Satan. So He addressed the listener, commanding him to seek refuge from Satan when he begins to recite. If the address is verbally directed to the Messenger (ﷺ), then what is meant is his community (*ummah*), since the recitation of the Qur'an is among the most excellent righteous deeds, as is reported in the hadith: "Indeed, the reward for reciting each letter is ten good deeds." The apparent sense is that the seeking of refuge comes immediately before the recitation. Some of the transmitters from Hamzah have reported this, and it is reported from Ibn Sirin that he said: "Whenever you recite the Fatihah, when you say *Amin*, then seek refuge." It is also reported from Abu Hurayrah, Malik, and Dawud.

The recitation follows it, as is reported from Hamzah and the majority, by leaving this apparent sense and interpreting it to mean: "When you intend to recite." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Because the act occurs at the moment of intention and will, without a separation and in accordance with it, so it is connected by a strong cause and an evident association, like His saying: '*When you rise to prayer, wash your faces*' (Al-Ma'idah: 6), and like His saying (ﷺ): '*When you eat, say the name of God.*'" Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "*Fa-idha* (then when) is a connective between the two statements, and the Arabs use it in such cases. The meaning of the verse is: 'When you begin reciting the Qur'an, then seek refuge,' a command to seek refuge." The majority hold it to be recommended (*mandub*), but 'Ata' holds it to be obligatory. The apparent sense is the request to seek refuge at the time of recitation in general. The apparent sense is that the Satan referred to is Iblis and his helpers. It is said that it is general to every rebellious, insolent one among jinn and humans, as He said: "*the devils of humankind and jinn*."

There is disagreement about the manner of seeking refuge. What the majority of reciters and others have adopted and chosen is: "I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan," based on what 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, and Jubayr ibn Mut'im reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "that he sought refuge during recitation with this exact wording."

He, exalted is He, negated Satan's authority over the believers. The word *sultan* (authority) here means domination and control. The meaning is that they do not accept from him, nor obey him in what he wants from them of following his footsteps, as He said: "*Indeed, over My servants you have no authority*" (Al-Hijr: 42). And as He informed about him, when He said in the account of his followers: "*I had no authority over you, except that I called you and you responded to me*" (Ibrahim: 22). It is said that *sultan* here means proof, and the apparent sense of the report is the negation of his domination over the believers absolutely. It is said: he has no authority over them because they seek refuge from him. It is said: he has no ability to compel them to sin. The pronoun in *bihi* (in him) refers to *bihim* (them). It is said it refers to Satan, and this is the apparent sense because the pronouns are consistent. The meaning is: "those who, by their association of Iblis (with God), are associators of God." Or the *ba'* may be causal (*sababiyyah*), and the command to seek refuge implies that it turns away Satan's cunning, as if it included reliance upon God and turning exclusively toward Him.

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the sending down of the Book as an explanation of all things, and commanded seeking refuge at the time of its recitation, He mentioned the result of Satan's guardianship over his polytheist followers and what he casts to them of falsehoods. So he cast to them the denial of abrogation (*naskh*) when they saw the substitution of one verse in place of another. The discussion of abrogation has preceded in Al-Baqarah. The apparent sense is that this substitution removed a verse both in wording and in meaning. It is possible that the substitution concerns the ruling while the wording remains. The unbelievers found in this a criticism of the religion, and they did not know that the benefits differ according to differences in times and persons, and just as the abrogation of one law by another occurs, it also occurs within a single law.

He, exalted is He, informed that He is the knower of what He sends down, not you, and what He sends down is either what He confirms or what He removes. The knowledge of that returns to Him, and it accords with events and benefits. This is the wisdom of sending it down piece by piece. This sentence is a parenthetical insertion between the condition and its answer. It is said: it may be possible that it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*). They exaggerated in attributing fabrication to the Messenger by means of the word *innama* (only), by the direct address, and by the active participle indicating permanence. He said: "Rather, most of them," because some of them know and disbelieve out of obstinacy. The object of "they do not know" is omitted, because the meaning indicates it: that is, they do not know that the laws are wisdoms and benefits.

This verse indicates the occurrence of the abrogation of the Qur'an by the Qur'an. *Ruh al-Qudus* (the Holy Spirit) here is Jibril (peace be upon him), without disagreement, and it has preceded why he was named *Ruh al-Qudus*. He attributed the Lord to the second-person pronoun (*ka*, "your Lord") to honor the Messenger (ﷺ) by the exclusivity of the attribution, and turning away from them (the unbelievers), since He did not attribute it to them. *Bil-haqq* (in truth) is a circumstantial element: that is, accompanied by truth, whether it is abrogating or abrogated. All of it is linked with truth, and nothing of falsehood touches it. Its meaning, "to strengthen," is that they do not waver regarding any part of it because it was abrogated; rather, the abrogation confirms them in their faith, since they know that all of it is from God. Because of the soundness of their faith and the tranquility of their hearts, they know that He is wise, and that all His acts proceed from wisdom, so all of them are correct. The restriction of the purpose clause to the Muslims indicates that the unbelievers are characterized by the opposite: the affliction of agitation, the shaking of their beliefs, and their misguidance.

It was read *liyuthbita* (to strengthen) with a lightened form from *athbata*. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Huda wa bushra*" (guidance and good tidings) are objects of purpose for both, coordinated with the position of *liyuthbita*." It has been explained earlier: this is his view, and the response to it has preceded in similar cases, such as His saying: "*so that you may make clear to them that about which they differ*" (An-Nahl: 64), and "*guidance and mercy*" in this surah. The coordination of it to the verbal noun formed from *an* and the verb is not impossible, because it is in the genitive, so *huda wa bushra* would be in the genitive, as you say: "I came to do good to Zayd and honor Khalid," since the meaning is "for doing good to Zayd." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that *huda wa bushra* be in the nominative by supposing an omitted subject, i.e., "and it is guidance and good tidings."

When they attributed to him (peace be upon him) fabrication, which is lying against God, they were not content with that, until they made that fabrication which they attributed to him to be a human teaching him. So it is not he who invented it; rather, the inventor is someone else, and he is only transmitting from him. The apparent meaning of their saying, "You are only a fabricator," is that its meaning is "one who invents falsehood," and this contradicts being taught by a human. So it is possible that his saying "fabricator" refers to attributing that to God, and it is possible that they were two groups: one group went to the view that he himself was the fabricator, and another group held that he learned it from a human.

*Yu'allimu* (is teaching) is a present-tense form in wording but past in meaning, that is, "And We certainly knew." The attribution of teaching is to an indefinite, unspecified person. It is said: he is a Roman slave named Habr who belonged to 'Amir ibn al-Hadrami. It is said: 'A'ish or Ya'ish, who was the owner of books, a client of Huwaytib ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza, who had embraced Islam and whose Islam was good. This was said by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. It is said: Abu Fukayhah, a foreigner, a client of a woman in Mecca. It is said his name was Yasar and he was a Jew; this was said by Muqatil and Ibn Jubayr, except that he did not say he was a Jew. Ibn Zayd said: he was a Christian blacksmith named 'Anas. Husayn ibn 'Abdullah ibn Muslim said: We had two Christian boys from the people of 'Ayn al-Tamr, Yasar and Habr, who would read their books in their own language, and the Prophet (ﷺ) would pass by them and hear their recitation. It is said: they were both blacksmiths making swords. The polytheists said: "He learns from them." It was said to one of them about that, and he said: "Rather, he teaches me." Ibn 'Abbas said: There was in Mecca a foreign boy belonging to some of the Quraysh called Bal'am, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to teach him Islam. The Quraysh said: "This one teaches Muhammad from the side of the foreigners." Al-Dahhak said: the reference is to Salman al-Farisi. This was weakened on the ground that Salman embraced Islam only after the Hijrah, while this surah is Meccan except for what has been noted as Medinan.

*Al-lisan* (tongue) here means language. Al-Hasan read *al-lisan alladhi* with the definite article on *lisan*, and the relative clause as its qualifier. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *yalhadun* from *lahada* (triliteral), and this is the reading of 'Abdullah ibn Talhah, al-Sulami, al-A'mash, and Mujahid. The rest of the seven and Ibn al-Qa'qa' read *yulhidun* with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *ha'* from *alhada* (quadriliteral), and both have one meaning. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is said *alhada al-qabr* and *lahadahu*, so one is *mulhid* and the other *mulhud* when he inclines its digging away from straightness, so he digs in one side of it. Then it was used figuratively for every deviation from straightness, so they said: "So-and-so *alhada* in his statement," and "*alhada* in his religion," because he inclined his religion away from all religions, not inclining it from one religion to another. The meaning: the tongue of the man to whom they incline their speech away from straightness is a foreign tongue that is not clear; and this Qur'an is a clear Arabic tongue, possessing clarity and eloquence, as a rejection of their statement and a nullification of their criticism. The end of al-Zamakhshari's words. The apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's statement is that *lisan* in both places means language. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This refers to the Qur'an, and the meaning is: 'This is a stream of speech or utterance of speech,' so it is an elision of a genitive construction (*mudaf*), and this is on the basis that *lisan* here is taken to mean the organ (tongue). *Lisan* in the speech of the Arabs means language, and it is possible that it is meant in this verse." Al-Kirmani said: The meaning is: "You are the most eloquent, the most articulate, and the most capable of speech, in verse and in prose, and you have been unable, and all the Arabs have been unable. So how do you attribute it to a foreigner who is incoherent?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: What is the sentence that is His saying '*the tongue of the one they incline to is foreign*'? What is its place in the grammar? I say: It has no place, because it is a resumptive answer to their statement." Its like is His saying: "*God knows best where to place His message*" (Al-An'am: 124), after His saying: "*When a sign comes to them, they say: We will not believe until we are given what the messengers of God were given*" (Al-An'am: 124). The end of his words. In my view it is possible that it is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*), so its position is in the accusative, and that is more forceful in rebuking them, meaning: they say this while in this state, that is, their knowledge of the foreignness of this human and the clarity of the Arabic of this Qur'an would prevent them from that statement. Just as you say: "You insult so-and-so while he has done good to you," meaning: your knowledge of his good to you should require you to refrain from insulting him. Al-Zamakhshari went to the resumptive reading and did not go to the circumstantial reading, because in his view the coming of a nominal circumstantial clause without *wa* (and) is rare, and that view is very weak, and the coming of that without *wa* is hardly limited in frequency in the speech of the Arabs. This is a view which he followed from al-Farra'. As for "*and God knows best*," the apparent meaning of his statement about it is that it is a clause free of a pronoun referring to the one in the circumstantial state, because the one in the circumstantial state is the pronoun of *qalu* (they said). In this verse, the one in the state is the pronoun of *yaqulun* (they say), and the pronoun in the circumstantial clause is the subject pronoun of *yulhidun*. So the clause, although it lacks the *wa*, contains the pronoun of the one in the state.

Rather, most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿Say, "The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth, to strengthen those who believe, and as guidance and good tidings for the Muslims."﴾ ﴿And We certainly know that they say, "He is only being taught by a human." The tongue of the one they point to is foreign, while this is a clear Arabic tongue.﴾

If the address is verbally directed to the Messenger (ﷺ), then what is meant is his community (*ummah*), since the recitation of the Qur'an is among the most excellent righteous deeds, as is reported in the hadith: "Indeed, the reward for reciting each letter is ten good deeds." The apparent sense is that the seeking of refuge comes immediately before the recitation. Some of the transmitters from Hamzah have reported this, and it is reported from Ibn Sirin that he said: "Whenever you recite the Fatihah, when you say *Amin*, then seek refuge." It is also reported from Abu Hurayrah, Malik, and Dawud.

The recitation follows it, as is reported from Hamzah and the majority, by leaving this apparent sense and interpreting it to mean: "When you intend to recite." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Because the act occurs at the moment of intention and will, without a separation and in accordance with it, so it is connected by a strong cause and an evident association, like His saying: '*When you rise to prayer, wash your faces*' (Al-Ma'idah: 6), and like His saying (ﷺ): '*When you eat, say the name of God.*'" Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "*Fa-idha* (then when) is a connective between the two statements, and the Arabs use it in such cases. The apparent sense is the request to seek refuge at the time of recitation in general. The apparent sense is that the Satan referred to is Iblis and his helpers. It is said that it is general to every rebellious, insolent one among jinn and humans, as He said: "*the devils of humankind and jinn*."

There is disagreement about the manner of seeking refuge. What the majority of reciters and others have adopted and chosen is: "I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan," based on what 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, and Jubayr ibn Mut'im reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "that he sought refuge during recitation with this exact wording."

He, exalted is He, negated Satan's authority over the believers. The word *sultan* (authority) here means domination and control. The meaning is that they do not accept from him, nor obey him in what he wants from them of following his footsteps, as He said: "*Indeed, over My servants you have no authority*" (Al-Hijr: 42). It is said it refers to Satan, and this is the apparent sense because the pronouns are consistent. The meaning is: "those who, by their association of Iblis (with God), are associators of God." The rest of the seven and Ibn al-Qa'qa' read *yulhidun* with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *ha'* from *alhada* (quadriliteral), and both have one meaning. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is said *alhada al-qabr* and *lahadahu*, so one is *mulhid* and the other *mulhud* when he inclines its digging away from straightness, so he digs in one side of it. Then it was used figuratively for every deviation from straightness, so they said: "So-and-so *alhada* in his statement," and "*alhada* in his religion," because he inclined his religion away from all religions, not inclining it from one religion to another. The meaning: the tongue of the man to whom they incline their speech away from straightness is a foreign tongue that is not clear; and this Qur'an is a clear Arabic tongue, possessing clarity and eloquence, as a rejection of their statement and a nullification of their criticism. The end of al-Zamakhshari's words. The apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's statement is that *lisan* in both places means language. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This refers to the Qur'an, and the meaning is: 'This is a stream of speech or utterance of speech,' so it is an elision of a genitive construction (*mudaf*), and this is on the basis that *lisan* here is taken to mean the organ (tongue). *Lisan* in the speech of the Arabs means language, and it is possible that it is meant in this verse." Al-Kirmani said: The meaning is: "You are the most eloquent, the most articulate, and the most capable of speech, in verse and in prose, and you have been unable, and all the Arabs have been unable. So how do you attribute it to a foreigner who is incoherent?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: What is the sentence that is His saying '*the tongue of the one they incline to is foreign*'? What is its place in the grammar? I say: It has no place, because it is a resumptive answer to their statement." Its like is His saying: "*God knows best where to place His message*" (Al-An'am: 124), after His saying: "*When a sign comes to them, they say: We will not believe until we are given what the messengers of God were given*" (Al-An'am: 124). The end of his words. In my view it is possible that it is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*), so its position is in the accusative, and that is more forceful in rebuking them, meaning: they say this while in this state, that is, their knowledge of the foreignness of this human and the clarity of the Arabic of this Qur'an would prevent them from that statement. Just as you say: "You insult so-and-so while he has done good to you," meaning: your knowledge of his good to you should require you to refrain from insulting him. Al-Zamakhshari went to the resumptive reading and did not go to the circumstantial reading, because in his view the coming of a nominal circumstantial clause without *wa* (and) is rare, and that view is very weak, and the coming of that without *wa* is hardly limited in frequency in the speech of the Arabs. This is a view which he followed from al-Farra'. As for "*and God knows best*," the apparent meaning of his statement about it is that it is a clause free of a pronoun referring to the one in the circumstantial state, because the one in the circumstantial state is the pronoun of *qalu* (they said). In this verse, the one in the state is the pronoun of *yaqulun* (they say), and the pronoun in the circumstantial clause is the subject pronoun of *yulhidun*. So the clause, although it lacks the *wa*, contains the pronoun of the one in the state.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 16, verses 104–110 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah, Allah will not guide them, and they will have a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿It is only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah who invent falsehood, and it is they who are the liars.﴾ ﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief, except one who is compelled while his heart is secure in faith, but whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath from Allah, and for them is a great punishment.﴾ ﴿That is because they preferred the worldly life over the Hereafter, and because Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts, hearing, and sight Allah has sealed, and it is they who are the heedless.﴾ ﴿Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter, they are the losers.﴾ ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they were tried, then struggled and were patient, indeed your Lord after that is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾: When the Exalted mentioned their attribution of fabrication to the Messenger (ﷺ), and that what he brought was from Allah, and that it is only taught to him by a human, (p-538) that was a recording against them of the absence of faith. So the Exalted informed about them that Allah will never guide them, since they were deniers of the signs of Allah, which is what the Messenger brought of miracles, especially the Qur'an. Whoever exaggerates in denying the signs of Allah, Allah closes off the door of guidance to him. The Exalted also mentioned His threat of a painful punishment for them. The meaning of "He will not guide them" is: He will not create faith in their hearts. This is a general statement with a specific exception, for a people who disbelieved in the signs of Allah the Exalted did become guided. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Allah will not guide them" means He will not show them kindness (lutf), because they are among the people of abandonment (khidhlan) in this world and of punishment in the Hereafter, not among the people of kindness and reward; end of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (rationalist school). Ibn Atiyya said: What is understood from the existence [of the verse] is that those whom Allah does not guide do not believe in His signs, but in this arrangement He placed first and informed of both, to denounce their act and to censure their error, and this is like His saying: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff: 5]. The intended meaning is what we have mentioned, as if He said: Indeed those who did not believe, Allah did not guide them; end of quote. Al-Qadi said: The strongest of what has been said about this is that "He will not guide them" means He will not guide them to the path of Paradise, and for this reason He said after it: "and for them is a painful punishment." The meaning is that, since they abandoned faith in Allah, Allah will not guide them to Paradise, but will drive them to the Fire. Al-Askari said: It is possible that the meaning is that if they do not believe in these signs, they will not be guided, and by His saying "Allah will not guide them" is meant: they will not be guided. It is only said "Allah guided so-and-so" in an unrestricted sense when he himself became guided. As for one who does not accept guidance, it is said: "Allah guided him, but he did not become guided," as He said: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat: 17]. Then the Exalted rejected their saying: ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ [al-Nahl: 101] with His saying: ﴿It is only those who invent falsehood﴾, meaning: the inventing of falsehood is only fitting for one who does not believe, because he awaits a punishment for it. Since their speech contained "innama" (only), which implies restriction according to some, the response to them also came with "innama," and it came with the word "yaftari" (invents), which implies renewal and recurrence. Then He attached the ruling to the attribute that necessitates fabrication, namely: the absence of faith, and He concluded with His saying: "and it is they who are the liars." This entails emphasis to the utmost degree and restriction by the demonstrative word, the emphasis by the word "hum" (they), the prefixing of "al-" to "al-kadhibun" (the liars), and the fact that it is an active participle, which implies firmness and permanence. So "yaftari" implies renewal, and "al-kadhibun" implies firmness and permanence. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Those" (ula'ika) refers to the Quraysh: "they are the liars," they are those who do not believe, so they are the liars. Or it refers to those who do not believe, meaning: "and it is they who are the liars" in truth, the most complete in lying, because denying the signs of Allah is the greatest lie. Or: "it is they who are the liars": lying is their habit, they do not care about it in anything, and neither honor nor religion restrains them from it. Or: "it is they who are the liars" in their saying: ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ [al-Nahl: 101]; end of quote. The direction with which he began is far-fetched, namely that "those" refers to the Quraysh. The apparent reading is that "man" (whoever) is conditional, in a place of nominative case as the subject, and it is a resumptive statement of information with no connection to what precedes it in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis). Since disbelief occurs by utterance and by belief, he excepted from the disbelievers the one who disbelieves by utterance while his heart is secure in faith, and he permitted him to utter the word of disbelief, since his heart was believing, and that is under compulsion. The meaning is: except one who is compelled to disbelief, who utters the word of disbelief while his heart is secure in faith. The answer to the condition is omitted, because what follows it indicates it; its estimate is: "The disbelievers after faith, other than the compelled, upon them is wrath." It is valid that the exception be from what the omitted answer of the condition contains, meaning: "upon them is wrath, except one who is compelled, so there is no wrath upon him nor punishment, but whoever opens his breast..." Al-Zamakhshari also estimated the answer before the exception, in the view of the one who made "man" conditional. Ibn Atiyya said: A group said that "man" in His saying "whoever disbelieves" is a beginning (subject), and His saying "whoever opens" is a specification from it, and the exception entered to exclude Ammar and his like. The corrective "lakin" (but) is close to the first exception, and His saying "upon them" is the predicate for the first and second "man," since they are one in meaning, because the information in His saying "whoever disbelieves" was only intended for the category that opens its breast to disbelief; end of quote. Although this is as he mentioned, these are two conditional sentences, separated by the particle of correction, so each one must have its own answer separately, and they do not share it. Therefore, estimating an omission is more appropriate according to the discipline of i'rab. They have criticized the view of Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash) in his claim that His saying: ﴿Then peace upon you from the companions of the right﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 91] and His saying: ﴿Then rest and bounty﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 89] are the answer to "amma" (as for), and because this and that are two conditional particles, one of which follows the other. On the basis that "man" is in a nominative place as the subject, it is permissible for it to be conditional as we have mentioned, and it is permissible for it to be relative, with what follows it as its relative clause, and the predicate omitted because what follows indicates it, as we mentioned concerning the omission of the answer of the condition. However, the second "man" cannot be conditional unless a subject is estimated before it, because "man" follows "lakin" (but), so it becomes necessary at that point that "man" be relative. If a subject is estimated after "lakin," it is permissible for it to be conditional in the position of the predicate of that estimated subject, as in the poet's saying:

"But whenever the people seek help, I help"

meaning: "But I, whenever the people seek help, I help." Likewise it is estimated here: "But they are those who opened their breast to disbelief," meaning: among them. Al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for "those who do not believe" and for "the liars." Al-Zajjaj did not permit it except as a substitute for "the liars," because he saw the speech up to the end of the exception as incomplete, so he linked it to what preceded it. Al-Zamakhshari permitted it to be a substitute for "those," so when it is a substitute for "those who do not believe," His saying "and it is they who are the liars" becomes a parenthetical sentence between the substitute and what it substitutes, and the meaning is: "Only the one who invents falsehood is whoever disbelieves in Allah after his faith," and He excepted from them the compelled, who does not fall under the ruling of fabrication. And when (p-540) it is a substitute for "the liars," the estimate is: "and those are whoever disbelieved in Allah after his faith," and when it is a substitute for "those," the estimate is: "and whoever disbelieved in Allah after his faith, they are the liars."

These three possibilities are, in my view, weak. The first implies that no one invents falsehood except one who disbelieves in Allah after his faith, while the reality implies that the one who invents falsehood is the one who does not believe, and whether he was one who disbelieved after faith or one who never believed at all, those who never believed are the majority and the ones who invent falsehood. As for the second, its meaning comes back to that, since the estimate is: "and those, that is, those who do not believe, are whoever disbelieved in Allah after his faith," and those who do not believe are the fabricators. As for the third, it is the same, since the estimate is: "that those pointed to are whoever disbelieved in Allah after his faith, informing about them that they are the liars." Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible for it to be in the accusative case as a dispraise; end of quote. This also is far-fetched. What the eloquence of the speech requires is that all the sentences be independent, not linked to what precedes them in terms of i'rab, but rather in terms of meaning and relevance. In His saying "except one who is compelled" there is evidence that the one compelled is not held accountable for anything, and if the utterance of disbelief or doing what leads to it was excused, then excusing other sins is more fitting. They have discussed the manner of compulsion that permits this, and the details of the matters in which compulsion occurs, and all of that is mentioned in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh). Those who were tortured for Islam while compelled to disbelief were: Khabbab, Suhayb, Bilal, Ammar, his two parents Yasir and Sumayya, Salim, and Habr. They were tortured, and Ammar and Habr responded with the words, so their way was released, while the rest persisted in Islam. Yasir and Sumayya were killed, and they were the first martyrs in Islam. Bilal was tortured while saying: "One, One" (ahad ahad). Khabbab was tortured with fire, and it was not put out except by the fat of his back.

The pronoun in "upon them" (fa-alayhim) is plural according to the meaning of "man," and it is singular in "opens" (sharaha) according to its wording. The apparent reading is that this refers to what they deserved of wrath and punishment, meaning: it is due to them because of their preferring the worldly life over the Hereafter. Al-Zamakhshari said: Their deserving of Allah's abandonment is because of their disbelief; end of quote. This is a Mu'tazilite inclination. The pronoun in "bi-annahum" (because they) refers back to "man" in "whoever opens": since they did the act of one who preferred, they were held to that, even though they were not affirming its ending. But insofar as they turned away from considering it, they were like one who preferred other than it. His saying "they preferred" is an acquisition (taka subb) on their part, to which punishment is attached. "And that Allah does not guide" is an indication of Allah's creation (ikhtira') of disbelief in their hearts. The verse thus combines acquisition and creation, and this is the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna). It was said: "That" refers to apostasy and rushing into disbelief, because they preferred the world over the Hereafter, and because He, the Exalted, did not guide them to faith. The discussion of the sealing over the hearts, hearing, and sights, and the seal upon them, has already preceded.

Then as for those, they are the heedless.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "They are heedless of what is intended for them in the Hereafter." Al-Zamakhshari said: "They are the complete ones in heedlessness, of whom none is more heedless, because heedlessness of considering the outcomes is the utmost and final degree of heedlessness. Since the purpose of the address was that one might gain the happiness of the Hereafter through acts of obedience, and whoever acts contrary to that through acts of disobedience, such as disbelief and other things, his loss is great, so it is said of them: They are the losers, and no others." And who is a greater loser than one who is characterized by those previously mentioned attributes: the state of the wrath of Allah being upon them, the painful punishment, preferring the worldly life, the denial of their guidance, and the report that Allah has sealed their hearts and that they are heedless.

When the Exalted mentioned the condition of one who disbelieves after faith, and the condition of one who is compelled, He mentioned the condition of one who emigrated after being tried. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "This verse is Medinan, and I know of no disagreement on this." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It was revealed, and the Muslims wrote with it to those who had embraced Islam in Mecca that Allah has made for you a way out. So they set out, and the polytheists overtook them and fought them until whoever was saved was saved and whoever was killed was killed. Based on this occasion, their jihad with the Messenger is for Islam." It is also narrated that they set out, followed them, and struggled against their pursuers, so some were killed and some were saved, and then it was revealed; so by jihad is meant their jihad against their pursuers.

Ibn Ishaq said: "It was revealed concerning ʿAmmar, ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿa, and al-Walid ibn al-Walid." Ibn ʿAtiyya said: (p-541) "The mention of ʿAmmar in this context is not sound, for he is of a higher rank than these, and these are rather of the category of: 'except one who is compelled while his heart is at rest in faith' (16:106) — but whoever has expanded in disbelief in breast, upon them is wrath from Allah." (Ibn ʿAtiyya's remark continues as it stands in the text.)

ʿIkrima and al-Hasan said: "It was revealed concerning ʿAbdullah ibn Abi Sarh and those like him," so it is as if He says: "after the Satan had tried them."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Then indeed your Lord is a sign of the distance between the condition of these and the condition of those, namely ʿAmmar and his companions." In al-Zamakhshari's view, "li-lladhina" is in the position of the predicate of "inna." He said: The meaning of "inna rabbaka lahum" is: He is for them, not against them, in the sense that He is their protector and helper, not their enemy and forsaker, just as a king is for a man and not against him, so that he is protected and benefited, not harmed; end of quote. His saying "manfuʿan" is the passive participle of "nafaʿa," and this is its analogical form, since it is a transitive triliteral verb. But al-Ahwazi the grammarian claimed that the passive participle is not used from "nafaʿa," so one does not say "manfuʿ"; I checked this with him in his commentary on the Mujaz of al-Rummani.

Abu al-Baqa said: "The predicate of the first "inna" is his saying: 'inna rabbaka la-ghafurun,' and the second "inna" with its subject is a repetition for emphasis"; end of quote. When the second "inna" with its subject is a repetition for emphasis as mentioned, then what the discipline of Arabic grammar requires is that the predicate of the first "inna" be his saying: "la-ghafurun," and "li-lladhina" be connected to his saying "la-ghafurun" or "rahim," by the rule of operation (i'mal), because the second "inna rabbaka" cannot have a demand on what follows it in terms of i'rab. Just as when you say "qama qama Zayd," Zayd is in the nominative case only by the first "qama," since the second was mentioned for emphasis of the first. It was said: there is no predicate for the first "inna" in wording, because the predicate of the second has made it unnecessary; end of quote. This is not sound, for it cancels the ruling of the first and assigns the ruling to the second, which is the reverse of what preceded, and it is not permissible.

It was also said: "li-lladhina" is connected to a implied element by way of explanation, as if it were said: "I mean for those," that is, "the forgiveness is for those."

The majority read "futinu" in the passive voice, meaning: by torment and compulsion toward the word of disbelief. Ibn ʿAmir read "fatanu" in the active voice. The apparent view is that the pronoun refers to those who emigrated, so the meaning is: they tried themselves by giving the polytheists what they said, as ʿAmmar did. Or, since they were patient upon Islam and were tormented because of that, they became as if they themselves were the ones tormenting themselves. It is also permissible that it refers to the polytheists, meaning: after they tormented the believers, like al-Hadrami and those like him. The pronoun in "min baʿdiha" refers to the verbal nouns understood from the preceding verbs, that is: after the trial, the emigration, the striving, and the patience. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: The pronoun in "baʿdiha" refers to the trial, or the emigration, or the repentance, and the context implies it even though no explicit mention of it has preceded.

Then the Exalted rejected their saying: ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ [al-Nahl: 101] with His saying: ﴿It is only those who invent falsehood﴾, meaning: the inventing of falsehood is only fitting for one who does not believe, because he awaits a punishment for it. Since their speech contained "innama" (only), which implies restriction according to some, the response to them also came with "innama," and it came with the word "yaftari" (invents), which implies renewal and recurrence. Then He attached the ruling to the attribute that necessitates fabrication, namely: the absence of faith, and He concluded with His saying: "and it is they who are the liars." This entails emphasis to the utmost degree and restriction by the demonstrative word, the emphasis by the word "hum" (they), the prefixing of "al-" to "al-kadhibun" (the liars), and the fact that it is an active participle, which implies firmness and permanence. So "yaftari" implies renewal, and "al-kadhibun" implies firmness and permanence. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Those" (ula'ika) refers to the Quraysh: "they are the liars," they are those who do not believe, so they are the liars. Or it refers to those who do not believe, meaning: "and it is they who are the liars" in truth, the most complete in lying, because denying the signs of Allah is the greatest lie. Or: "it is they who are the liars": lying is their habit, they do not care about it in anything, and neither honor nor religion restrains them from it. Or: "it is they who are the liars" in their saying: ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ [al-Nahl: 101]; end of quote. Since disbelief occurs by utterance and by belief, he excepted from the disbelievers the one who disbelieves by utterance while his heart is secure in faith, and he permitted him to utter the word of disbelief, since his heart was believing, and that is under compulsion. The meaning is: except one who is compelled to disbelief, who utters the word of disbelief while his heart is secure in faith. The answer to the condition is omitted, because what follows it indicates it; its estimate is: "The disbelievers after faith, other than the compelled, upon them is wrath." It is valid that the exception be from what the omitted answer of the condition contains, meaning: "upon them is wrath, except one who is compelled, so there is no wrath upon him nor punishment, but whoever opens his breast..." Al-Zamakhshari also estimated the answer before the exception, in the view of the one who made "man" conditional. "But whenever the people seek help, I help"

meaning: "But I, whenever the people seek help, I help." Likewise it is estimated here: "But they are those who opened their breast to disbelief," meaning: among them. Those who were tortured for Islam while compelled to disbelief were: Khabbab, Suhayb, Bilal, Ammar, his two parents Yasir and Sumayya, Salim, and Habr. The pronoun in "upon them" (fa-alayhim) is plural according to the meaning of "man," and it is singular in "opens" (sharaha) according to its wording. The apparent reading is that this refers to what they deserved of wrath and punishment, meaning: it is due to them because of their preferring the worldly life over the Hereafter. Al-Zamakhshari said: Their deserving of Allah's abandonment is because of their disbelief; end of quote. This is a Mu'tazilite inclination. The verse thus combines acquisition and creation, and this is the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna). It was said: "That" refers to apostasy and rushing into disbelief, because they preferred the world over the Hereafter, and because He, the Exalted, did not guide them to faith. The discussion of the sealing over the hearts, hearing, and sights, and the seal upon them, has already preceded.

Then as for those, they are the heedless.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "They are heedless of what is intended for them in the Hereafter." And who is a greater loser than one who is characterized by those previously mentioned attributes: the state of the wrath of Allah being upon them, the painful punishment, preferring the worldly life, the denial of their guidance, and the report that Allah has sealed their hearts and that they are heedless.

When the Exalted mentioned the condition of one who disbelieves after faith, and the condition of one who is compelled, He mentioned the condition of one who emigrated after being tried. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "This verse is Medinan, and I know of no disagreement on this." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It was revealed, and the Muslims wrote with it to those who had embraced Islam in Mecca that Allah has made for you a way out. So they set out, and the polytheists overtook them and fought them until whoever was saved was saved and whoever was killed was killed. Based on this occasion, their jihad with the Messenger is for Islam." It is also narrated that they set out, followed them, and struggled against their pursuers, so some were killed and some were saved, and then it was revealed; so by jihad is meant their jihad against their pursuers.
