Ibn ʿAtiyya said: (p-541) "The mention of ʿAmmar in this context is not sound, for he is of a higher rank than these, and these are rather of the category of: 'except one who is compelled while his heart is at rest in faith' (16:106) — but whoever has expanded in disbelief in breast, upon them is wrath from Allah." ʿIkrima and al-Hasan said: "It was revealed concerning ʿAbdullah ibn Abi Sarh and those like him," so it is as if He says: "after the Satan had tried them."

He said: The meaning of "inna rabbaka lahum" is: He is for them, not against them, in the sense that He is their protector and helper, not their enemy and forsaker, just as a king is for a man and not against him, so that he is protected and benefited, not harmed; end of quote. It was also said: "li-lladhina" is connected to a implied element by way of explanation, as if it were said: "I mean for those," that is, "the forgiveness is for those."

The majority read "futinu" in the passive voice, meaning: by torment and compulsion toward the word of disbelief. Ibn ʿAmir read "fatanu" in the active voice. The apparent view is that the pronoun refers to those who emigrated, so the meaning is: they tried themselves by giving the polytheists what they said, as ʿAmmar did. Or, since they were patient upon Islam and were tormented because of that, they became as if they themselves were the ones tormenting themselves. It is also permissible that it refers to the polytheists, meaning: after they tormented the believers, like al-Hadrami and those like him. The pronoun in "min baʿdiha" refers to the verbal nouns understood from the preceding verbs, that is: after the trial, the emigration, the striving, and the patience. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: The pronoun in "baʿdiha" refers to the trial, or the emigration, or the repentance, and the context implies it even though no explicit mention of it has preceded.

Whoever exaggerates in denying the signs of Allah, Allah closes off the door of guidance to him. The Exalted also mentioned His threat of a painful punishment for them. The meaning of "He will not guide them" is: He will not create faith in their hearts. This is a general statement with a specific exception, for a people who disbelieved in the signs of Allah the Exalted did become guided. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Allah will not guide them" means He will not show them kindness (lutf), because they are among the people of abandonment (khidhlan) in this world and of punishment in the Hereafter, not among the people of kindness and reward; end of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (rationalist school). Ibn Atiyya said: What is understood from the existence [of the verse] is that those whom Allah does not guide do not believe in His signs, but in this arrangement He placed first and informed of both, to denounce their act and to censure their error, and this is like His saying: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff: 5]. The intended meaning is what we have mentioned, as if He said: Indeed those who did not believe, Allah did not guide them; end of quote. The meaning is that, since they abandoned faith in Allah, Allah will not guide them to Paradise, but will drive them to the Fire. Al-Askari said: It is possible that the meaning is that if they do not believe in these signs, they will not be guided, and by His saying "Allah will not guide them" is meant: they will not be guided. It is only said "Allah guided so-and-so" in an unrestricted sense when he himself became guided. As for one who does not accept guidance, it is said: "Allah guided him, but he did not become guided," as He said: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat: 17]. Then the Exalted rejected their saying: ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ [al-Nahl: 101] with His saying: ﴿It is only those who invent falsehood﴾, meaning: the inventing of falsehood is only fitting for one who does not believe, because he awaits a punishment for it. Since their speech contained "innama" (only), which implies restriction according to some, the response to them also came with "innama," and it came with the word "yaftari" (invents), which implies renewal and recurrence. Then He attached the ruling to the attribute that necessitates fabrication, namely: the absence of faith, and He concluded with His saying: "and it is they who are the liars." This entails emphasis to the utmost degree and restriction by the demonstrative word, the emphasis by the word "hum" (they), the prefixing of "al-" to "al-kadhibun" (the liars), and the fact that it is an active participle, which implies firmness and permanence. So "yaftari" implies renewal, and "al-kadhibun" implies firmness and permanence. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Those" (ula'ika) refers to the Quraysh: "they are the liars," they are those who do not believe, so they are the liars. Or it refers to those who do not believe, meaning: "and it is they who are the liars" in truth, the most complete in lying, because denying the signs of Allah is the greatest lie. Or: "it is they who are the liars": lying is their habit, they do not care about it in anything, and neither honor nor religion restrains them from it. Or: "it is they who are the liars" in their saying: ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ [al-Nahl: 101]; end of quote. The direction with which he began is far-fetched, namely that "those" refers to the Quraysh. The apparent reading is that "man" (whoever) is conditional, in a place of nominative case as the subject, and it is a resumptive statement of information with no connection to what precedes it in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis). Since disbelief occurs by utterance and by belief, he excepted from the disbelievers the one who disbelieves by utterance while his heart is secure in faith, and he permitted him to utter the word of disbelief, since his heart was believing, and that is under compulsion. The meaning is: except one who is compelled to disbelief, who utters the word of disbelief while his heart is secure in faith. The answer to the condition is omitted, because what follows it indicates it; its estimate is: "The disbelievers after faith, other than the compelled, upon them is wrath." It is valid that the exception be from what the omitted answer of the condition contains, meaning: "upon them is wrath, except one who is compelled, so there is no wrath upon him nor punishment, but whoever opens his breast..." Al-Zamakhshari also estimated the answer before the exception, in the view of the one who made "man" conditional. Ibn Atiyya said: A group said that "man" in His saying "whoever disbelieves" is a beginning (subject), and His saying "whoever opens" is a specification from it, and the exception entered to exclude Ammar and his like. The corrective "lakin" (but) is close to the first exception, and His saying "upon them" is the predicate for the first and second "man," since they are one in meaning, because the information in His saying "whoever disbelieves" was only intended for the category that opens its breast to disbelief; end of quote. They have criticized the view of Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash) in his claim that His saying: ﴿Then peace upon you from the companions of the right﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 91] and His saying: ﴿Then rest and bounty﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 89] are the answer to "amma" (as for), and because this and that are two conditional particles, one of which follows the other. meaning: "But I, whenever the people seek help, I help." Likewise it is estimated here: "But they are those who opened their breast to disbelief," meaning: among them. They have discussed the manner of compulsion that permits this, and the details of the matters in which compulsion occurs, and all of that is mentioned in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh). Those who were tortured for Islam while compelled to disbelief were: Khabbab, Suhayb, Bilal, Ammar, his two parents Yasir and Sumayya, Salim, and Habr. They were tortured, and Ammar and Habr responded with the words, so their way was released, while the rest persisted in Islam. Yasir and Sumayya were killed, and they were the first martyrs in Islam. Bilal was tortured while saying: "One, One" (ahad ahad). Khabbab was tortured with fire, and it was not put out except by the fat of his back.

The pronoun in "upon them" (fa-alayhim) is plural according to the meaning of "man," and it is singular in "opens" (sharaha) according to its wording. The apparent reading is that this refers to what they deserved of wrath and punishment, meaning: it is due to them because of their preferring the worldly life over the Hereafter. Al-Zamakhshari said: Their deserving of Allah's abandonment is because of their disbelief; end of quote. This is a Mu'tazilite inclination. The pronoun in "bi-annahum" (because they) refers back to "man" in "whoever opens": since they did the act of one who preferred, they were held to that, even though they were not affirming its ending. But insofar as they turned away from considering it, they were like one who preferred other than it. His saying "they preferred" is an acquisition (taka subb) on their part, to which punishment is attached. "And that Allah does not guide" is an indication of Allah's creation (ikhtira') of disbelief in their hearts. The verse thus combines acquisition and creation, and this is the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna). It was said: "That" refers to apostasy and rushing into disbelief, because they preferred the world over the Hereafter, and because He, the Exalted, did not guide them to faith. The discussion of the sealing over the hearts, hearing, and sights, and the seal upon them, has already preceded.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "This verse is Medinan, and I know of no disagreement on this." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It was revealed, and the Muslims wrote with it to those who had embraced Islam in Mecca that Allah has made for you a way out. So they set out, and the polytheists overtook them and fought them until whoever was saved was saved and whoever was killed was killed. Based on this occasion, their jihad with the Messenger is for Islam." It is also narrated that they set out, followed them, and struggled against their pursuers, so some were killed and some were saved, and then it was revealed; so by jihad is meant their jihad against their pursuers.

(Ibn ʿAtiyya's remark continues as it stands in the text.)

They were tortured, and Ammar and Habr responded with the words, so their way was released, while the rest persisted in Islam. Yasir and Sumayya were killed, and they were the first martyrs in Islam. Bilal was tortured while saying: "One, One" (ahad ahad). Khabbab was tortured with fire, and it was not put out except by the fat of his back.

The pronoun in "upon them" (fa-alayhim) is plural according to the meaning of "man," and it is singular in "opens" (sharaha) according to its wording. The apparent reading is that this refers to what they deserved of wrath and punishment, meaning: it is due to them because of their preferring the worldly life over the Hereafter. Al-Zamakhshari said: Their deserving of Allah's abandonment is because of their disbelief; end of quote. This is a Mu'tazilite inclination. The pronoun in "bi-annahum" (because they) refers back to "man" in "whoever opens": since they did the act of one who preferred, they were held to that, even though they were not affirming its ending. But insofar as they turned away from considering it, they were like one who preferred other than it. His saying "they preferred" is an acquisition (taka subb) on their part, to which punishment is attached. "And that Allah does not guide" is an indication of Allah's creation (ikhtira') of disbelief in their hearts. The verse thus combines acquisition and creation, and this is the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna). It was said: "That" refers to apostasy and rushing into disbelief, because they preferred the world over the Hereafter, and because He, the Exalted, did not guide them to faith. The discussion of the sealing over the hearts, hearing, and sights, and the seal upon them, has already preceded.

Then as for those, they are the heedless.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "They are heedless of what is intended for them in the Hereafter." Al-Zamakhshari said: "They are the complete ones in heedlessness, of whom none is more heedless, because heedlessness of considering the outcomes is the utmost and final degree of heedlessness. Since the purpose of the address was that one might gain the happiness of the Hereafter through acts of obedience, and whoever acts contrary to that through acts of disobedience, such as disbelief and other things, his loss is great, so it is said of them: They are the losers, and no others." And who is a greater loser than one who is characterized by those previously mentioned attributes: the state of the wrath of Allah being upon them, the painful punishment, preferring the worldly life, the denial of their guidance, and the report that Allah has sealed their hearts and that they are heedless.

When the Exalted mentioned the condition of one who disbelieves after faith, and the condition of one who is compelled, He mentioned the condition of one who emigrated after being tried. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "This verse is Medinan, and I know of no disagreement on this." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It was revealed, and the Muslims wrote with it to those who had embraced Islam in Mecca that Allah has made for you a way out. So they set out, and the polytheists overtook them and fought them until whoever was saved was saved and whoever was killed was killed. Based on this occasion, their jihad with the Messenger is for Islam." It is also narrated that they set out, followed them, and struggled against their pursuers, so some were killed and some were saved, and then it was revealed; so by jihad is meant their jihad against their pursuers.

Ibn Ishaq said: "It was revealed concerning ʿAmmar, ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿa, and al-Walid ibn al-Walid." Ibn ʿAtiyya said: (p-541) "The mention of ʿAmmar in this context is not sound, for he is of a higher rank than these, and these are rather of the category of: 'except one who is compelled while his heart is at rest in faith' (16:106) — but whoever has expanded in disbelief in breast, upon them is wrath from Allah." (Ibn ʿAtiyya's remark continues as it stands in the text.)

ʿIkrima and al-Hasan said: "It was revealed concerning ʿAbdullah ibn Abi Sarh and those like him," so it is as if He says: "after the Satan had tried them."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Then indeed your Lord is a sign of the distance between the condition of these and the condition of those, namely ʿAmmar and his companions." In al-Zamakhshari's view, "li-lladhina" is in the position of the predicate of "inna." He said: The meaning of "inna rabbaka lahum" is: He is for them, not against them, in the sense that He is their protector and helper, not their enemy and forsaker, just as a king is for a man and not against him, so that he is protected and benefited, not harmed; end of quote. His saying "manfuʿan" is the passive participle of "nafaʿa," and this is its analogical form, since it is a transitive triliteral verb. But al-Ahwazi the grammarian claimed that the passive participle is not used from "nafaʿa," so one does not say "manfuʿ"; I checked this with him in his commentary on the Mujaz of al-Rummani.

Abu al-Baqa said: "The predicate of the first "inna" is his saying: 'inna rabbaka la-ghafurun,' and the second "inna" with its subject is a repetition for emphasis"; end of quote. When the second "inna" with its subject is a repetition for emphasis as mentioned, then what the discipline of Arabic grammar requires is that the predicate of the first "inna" be his saying: "la-ghafurun," and "li-lladhina" be connected to his saying "la-ghafurun" or "rahim," by the rule of operation (i'mal), because the second "inna rabbaka" cannot have a demand on what follows it in terms of i'rab. Just as when you say "qama qama Zayd," Zayd is in the nominative case only by the first "qama," since the second was mentioned for emphasis of the first. It was said: there is no predicate for the first "inna" in wording, because the predicate of the second has made it unnecessary; end of quote. This is not sound, for it cancels the ruling of the first and assigns the ruling to the second, which is the reverse of what preceded, and it is not permissible.

It was also said: "li-lladhina" is connected to a implied element by way of explanation, as if it were said: "I mean for those," that is, "the forgiveness is for those."

The majority read "futinu" in the passive voice, meaning: by torment and compulsion toward the word of disbelief. Ibn ʿAmir read "fatanu" in the active voice. The apparent view is that the pronoun refers to those who emigrated, so the meaning is: they tried themselves by giving the polytheists what they said, as ʿAmmar did. Or, since they were patient upon Islam and were tormented because of that, they became as if they themselves were the ones tormenting themselves. It is also permissible that it refers to the polytheists, meaning: after they tormented the believers, like al-Hadrami and those like him. The pronoun in "min baʿdiha" refers to the verbal nouns understood from the preceding verbs, that is: after the trial, the emigration, the striving, and the patience. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: The pronoun in "baʿdiha" refers to the trial, or the emigration, or the repentance, and the context implies it even though no explicit mention of it has preceded.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 16, verses 111–115:**

﴿On the Day when every soul comes pleading for itself, and every soul is paid in full for what it did, and they will not be wronged.﴾ ﴿And Allah sets forth a parable: a town that was secure and at peace, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place. Yet it denied the favours of Allah, so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they used to do.﴾ ﴿A Messenger had certainly come to them from among themselves, but they denied him, so the punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good, and give thanks for the favour of Allah, if it is Him that you worship.﴾ ﴿He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked. But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor exceeding the limit, then Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

(p. 542) **"Yawma"** (on the Day) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf). Its governing word is **"raḥīm"** (Merciful), or it is in the accusative as an object, its governing verb being "udhkur" (remember). The apparent meaning is that **"kull nafs"** (every soul) is general, so the believer and the disbeliever both plead, and their pleading is with falsehood and denial. Then the messengers and the limbs will bear witness against them, and at that time they will not speak.

A group said: the "pleading" is the saying of every individual among the prophets and others: "Myself, myself!" Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is not pleading or argument; it is merely a desire (for self-preservation). Al-Zamakhshari chose this opinion and joined it to what precedes it, saying: It is as if it were said, "On the Day when every person comes pleading for his own self, not concerned with the affair of others; each one says, 'Myself, myself!'" The meaning of **"mujādala"** (pleading) is making excuses for oneself, like their saying: ﴿These are the ones who led us astray﴾ [al-A'raf: 38] and ﴿We were not associators﴾ [al-An'am: 23], and similar. He also said: The word "nafs" is used for the very essence and self of a thing, and its opposite is "ghayr" (other). "Nafs" also means the whole entity as it is. So the first "nafs" is the whole entity, and the second is its very essence and self.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: That is, "every possessor of a self," then the verb was made to agree with the mentioned annexed noun (muḍāf ilayhi), so it took the feminine marker. The first "nafs" is the known "nafs," and the second means the body, as you say, "the self of a thing" and "its very self," meaning its essence.

Al-'Askari said: A human being is called a "nafs." The Arabs say: "No one came to me except one nafs," meaning one person. In reality the "nafs" does not come, because it is the thing by which a human being lives; (the end of his words).

(If you say): Why did the verb not transitively reach the pronoun, rather than the word "nafs"? (I say): What prevents that is that when the verb is not of the category of "ẓanna" (verbs of thinking, which take two objects) and "faqada" (to lack), its transitive action does not reach its apparent subject nor its pronoun back to its connected pronoun. Therefore the construction did not come as "tujādilu 'anhā" (she pleads for her). For the same reason it is not permitted to say: "Hind struck her," or "Hind, she struck her." Rather you say: "Hind struck herself," and "Hind struck herself." **"Mā 'amilat"** (what it did) means: the recompense for what it did of good or evil.

The verb in **"ta'ti"** (comes), and the pronoun in **"tujādilu"** (pleads), in **"'an nafsihā"** (for itself), in **"tuwaffā"** (is paid in full), and in **"'amilat"** (did), are feminine, taking account of the meaning of **"kull"** (every). If the wording had been followed, it would have been masculine. The poet said:

*Every thick-flowing eye poured over it, so they left every garden like a dirham.*

He used the feminine according to the meaning. As for what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, that the "pleading" here is the pleading of the body against the soul and of the soul against the body, it does not appear to be (correct). He said: The body says, "My Lord, the soul came with Your command; my tongue spoke by it, my eye saw, my foot walked." The soul says, "You earned and disobeyed, not I; you were the bearer and I was the borne." Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: "I shall strike for you both a parable: a blind man who carried a lame man to an orchard, and they both ate of its fruits. So the punishment is upon you both."

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Qatadah that the town whose parable is struck is Makkah, which was not raided and was not attacked, and provisions were brought to it, and Allah favoured it with the Messenger (ﷺ), but it disbelieved, so drought and fear befell it. The expeditions and battles of the Messenger (ﷺ) were struck as a parable for other places that come after them. This (interpretation) is if the verse is Madani. If the verse is Makki, then the hunger of the years and the fear of punishment were due to denial. What supports its being Makki is His saying: ﴿A Messenger had certainly come to them from among themselves, but they denied him﴾. It is also possible that **"qaryatan"** (a town) refers to one of the towns of the earlier peoples.

It is reported from Hafsah that it is Madinah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: In my view it appears that by it is intended an unspecified town, made a parable for Makkah, in the sense of a warning to its people and to others among the towns until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that what is meant is a hypothetical town with this description, or that among the towns of the earlier peoples there was a town of this condition, which Allah struck as a parable for Makkah, as a warning of the like of its outcome; (the end of his words). But it is not permissible that what is meant is a hypothetical town with this description, rather it must have existed, because of His saying: ﴿A Messenger had certainly come to them from among themselves, but they denied him, so the punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers﴾.

**"Kānat āminatan"** (it was secure): He began with the attribute of security, because one cannot establish (a livelihood) for one who is fearful. **"Al-iṭmi'nān"** (being at peace) is an increase in security, so that no fear disturbs it. **"Yaʼtīhā rizquhā"** (its provision comes to it): its sustenance is wide, from all its directions; no direction is hard to reach from it.

**"Anʻum"** (favours) is the plural of **"niʻmah"** (favour), like **"shiddah"** and **"ashudd."** Qutrub said: It is the plural of **"niʻam"** in the sense of "comfort," as one says, "these are days of food and comfort"; (the end of his words). So it would be like **"bu's"** and **"ab'us."** Al-Zamakhshari said: He pluralized **"niʻmah"** by dropping the **tā'** and treating the **tā'** as counted, like **"dir'"** and **"adrur."**

The wise say: There are three things that have no limit: security, health, and sufficiency. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: **"Āminatan"** points to security, **"muṭma'innah"** points to health, because the air of that place, being constantly present in their temperaments, made them at peace with it and settled. **"Yaʼtīhā rizquhā"**: the cause of that is the supplication of Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿So make hearts from among the people incline towards them, and provide them with fruits﴾ [Ibrahim: 37]. He also said: **"Al-anʻum"** is the plural of **"niʻmah"** and a plural of paucity; and it did not come as **"niʻam Allah"** (the favours of Allah in the plural of abundance). This is because he intended to alert by the lesser to the greater, meaning that denying a few favours brought punishment, so denying the many is more deserving of bringing it.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: When that (hunger and fear) touched them, it became like a garment. This is like the saying of al-A'sha:

*When the bedfellow turns her neck, she turns and becomes a garment for him.*

And like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]. And from it is the saying of the poet:

*And after al-Zubayr, Mujashi' wore the garments of she who menstruated and did not wash off the blood.*

As if the shame, when it touched them and clung to them, made them wear it. As for His saying: **"Fa-adhāqahā Allāh"** (so Allah made it taste): it is like His saying: ﴿Taste! Indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49], and like the saying of the poet:

*Take what you have earned, so taste it.*

Al-Zamakhshari said: The "tasting" and the "garment" are two metaphors (isti'arah, metaphorical usage). What is the basis of their soundness? And the metaphorical "tasting" is applied to the "garment." What is the basis of the soundness of applying it? (I say): As for "tasting," it has become in their usage like literal speech, because it is common in calamities and hardships and what touches people from them, so they say, "So-and-so tasted misery and harm." And the "tasting of punishment": he likened what is perceived of the effect of harm and pain to what is perceived of the taste of bitterness and foulness. As for the "garment," it was likened to it because of its enveloping the wearer, what covers a person and clings to him from certain calamities. As for the application of "tasting" to the "garment of hunger and fear," it is because the expression "what covers them from these two and clothes them" has occurred, so it is as if it were said: "He made them taste what covered them of hunger and fear." For them in such cases there are two ways: One is to look at the thing to which the metaphor is applied (al-musta'ār lahu), as is done here. Similar to it is the saying of Kuthayyir:

*Abundant of cloak, when he smiles laughing, the necks of wealth are shut at his laughter.*

He used "cloak" for generosity, because it protects the honour of its owner as a cloak protects what is put upon it. He described it with "abundant," which is a description of generosity and bounty, not a description of a cloak, looking at the thing to which the metaphor is applied. The second is to look at the metaphor itself (al-musta'ār), as in his saying:

*My cloak is disputed by the slave of 'Amr: "Gently, O brother of 'Amr ibn Bakr!"*

*The half that my right hand possesses is mine, and for you, wrap yourself with a half of it.*

He meant by his "cloak" his sword, then he said: "wrap yourself with a half of it," so he looked at the metaphor in the word "i'tijār" (wrapping). If it had been looked at in the case we are discussing, it would have said: "He clothed them with the garment of hunger and fear," and Kuthayyir would have said: "Wide of cloak when he smiles laughing." (the end of his words). This is a good statement.

When the mention of security and the coming of provision had preceded, he set against them hunger, which arises from the cutting off of provision, and fear. He placed hunger first in order to make the latter (the coming of provision) adjacent to the later part, which is the coming of provision, like His saying: ﴿On the Day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black; as for those whose faces turned black﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106]. As for His saying: ﴿Among them are the wretched and the happy﴾ [Hud: 105], then "as for those who are wretched, they are in the Fire," He put first what was begun with. These are two methods.

The majority (of reciters) read **"wa-l-khawf"** (and fear) in the genitive, as a conjunction with **"al-jū'"** (hunger). Abu 'Amr, as reported by al-'Abbas, read **"wa-l-khawfa"** (and fear) in the accusative, as a conjunction with **"libās"** (garment). The author of al-Lawami' said: It is permissible that it be in the accusative by supposing a verb (implied). Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that it be by the omission of the annexed word (muḍāf) and the placing of the annexed-to word (muḍāf ilayhi) in its place; its original form is "wa-libās al-khawf" (and the garment of fear). 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read: **"Fa-adhāqahā Allāh al-khawfa wal-jū'a,"** without mentioning "libās." What I say is that this is an explanation of meaning, not a recitation, because what is transmitted from him is widely known as it is in the consonantal text of the Mushaf. In the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is **"libās al-khawf wal-jū'"** (the garment of fear and hunger), beginning with the counterpart of what he began with in His saying: "was secure." In my view this was in his Mushaf before they gathered what is in the consonantal text of the Mushaf that is now present, in East and West. Therefore, the widely transmitted reading from Ubayy is only like the reading of the community. **"Bi-mā kānū yaṣna'ūn"** (for what they used to do): (this refers to) their ingratitude for the favours of Allah, and among them the denial of the Messenger (ﷺ) who came to them.

The pronoun in **"bi-mā kānū yaṣna'ūn"** refers to what is omitted in His saying: **"Wa-ḍaraba Allāh mathalan qaryatan"** (And Allah struck a parable, a town), that is, the story of the people of a town. He returned the pronoun first to the word "qaryah," then to the omitted annexed noun, like His saying: ﴿Then Our punishment came upon them by night, or while they were resting at midday﴾ [al-A'raf: 4].

The apparent view is that the pronoun in **"wa-laqad jā'ahum"** (And a Messenger had certainly come to them) refers to what it referred to in His saying: "bi-mā kānū yaṣna'ūn." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is possible that the pronoun in "jā'ahum" refers to the people of that town, and this would be about what happened in it, like the town of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, and others. And it is possible that it refers to the people of Makkah. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: When He mentioned the parable, He said: "And a Messenger had certainly come to them" — meaning the people of Makkah — "from among themselves" — meaning from their own selves — "whom they know by his lineage and descent." When the Exalted admonished by striking that parable, this matter was connected to the believers with the "fa" (so), so He commanded the believers to eat what He had provided them and to give thanks for His favour, so that they would be distinct from that town which disbelieved in the favours of Allah.

Since ﴿So it disbelieved in the favours of Allah﴾ had come before, here comes: ﴿and give thanks for the favour of Allah﴾. In al-Baqarah it came: ﴿O you who believe, spend of what We have provided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 254], not mentioning those who disbelieved His favour, and then He said: ﴿and give thanks to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172]. And when He commanded them to eat of what He had provided them, He enumerated for them His prohibited things, and forbade them from forbidding and permitting by their own desires, without following what Allah prescribed through His prophets. Likewise in al-Baqarah the mention of what He forbade came right after His saying: "Eat of what We have provided you," and His saying: **"Innamā ḥarrama"** (He has only forbidden), the verse. The explanation of its like has preceded in al-Baqarah.

Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that *al-kadhiba* be in the accusative as an apposition to the omitted pronoun returning to *ma*, as one says: "The one whom you struck your brother came to me," meaning "whom you struck him, your brother." Abu al-Baqa' also permitted it to be accusative by an implied verb *a'ni* ("I mean"). Al-Kisa'i and al-Zajjaj said: *ma* is a verbal-masdar particle (*ma masdariyyah*), and *al-kadhiba* is in the accusative as a direct object, meaning: "for the description of your tongues of the lie." The object of *la taqulu* ("do not say") is the clause "This is lawful and this is unlawful." The meaning is: "Do not make lawful or unlawful on account of a statement your tongues utter falsely, not with proof or clear evidence." This is a wondrous meaning: it makes their statement as if it were the very essence and pure form of lying. When their tongues utter it, they have, as it were, clothed the lie in its own ornament and form, as in the saying: "His face describes beauty," and "Her eye describes magic."

Al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mur, Talhah, al-A'raj, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn 'Ubayd and Nu'aym ibn Maysarah read *al-kadhibi* (الكَذِبِ) with a kasra on the *ba'*, which is explained as an apposition to *ma*, meaning: "that which your tongues describe, the lie." Al-Zamakhshari and others permitted that *al-kadhibi* in the genitive be an attributive adjective of the verbal-masdar *ma*. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is as if it were said: 'for their describing the lie,' meaning 'the lying,' like His saying: ﴿بِدَمٍ كَذِبٍ﴾ ('with false blood') [Yusuf: 18]. In my view this is not permissible, because they have stated that the verbal-masdar particle *an* (أنْ) does not take an adjective for the masdar formed from it and the verb. Nothing in their speech is found like: "It pleases me that you stood the quick," meaning "your quick standing," nor "I did not marvel that you left the quick," meaning "from your quick departure." The ruling for the remaining verbal-masdar particles is the ruling for *an*, so nothing is found in their speech of an adjective for a masdar formed from *an*, nor from *ma*, nor from *kay*. This is in contrast to a explicit (pronounced) masdar, which may take an adjective. And an implied element does not have the ruling of the expressed one; rather, in this matter one follows only what the Arabs have spoken.

Mu'adh, Ibn Abi 'Ablah and some of the people of Syria read *al-kudhubu* (الكُذُبُ), with a damma on all three letters, as an attributive adjective of *al-alsinah* ("the tongues"), the plural of *kadhub* (كَذُوبٍ, one who lies often). The author of al-Lawami' said: "Or it is the plural of *kadhib* (كاذِبٍ, liar) or *kaddhab* (كَذّابٍ, great liar)." End of quote. So it would be like *sharif* and *shurufun*, or like *kitab* and *kutub*. The author of al-Lawami' attributed this reading to Maslamah ibn Muharib. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Maslamah ibn Muharib read *al-kudhaba* (الكُذَبَ) with a fatha on the *ba'*, as the plural of *kaddhab*, like *kutub* as the plural of *kitab*." The author of al-Lawami' said: "There is also reported from Ya'qub (*al-kudhuba*) with two dammas and the accusative. As for the two dammas, it is the plural of *kaddhab*, which is a masdar, and like *kitab* and *kutub*." Al-Zamakhshari said: "With the accusative, as an expression of reproach, or meaning 'the false words,' or it is the plural of *al-kidhab* from your saying *kadhaba kidhaban*, as Ibn Jinni mentioned." End of quote.

According to the majority's view, the address in "do not say" is to the disbelievers concerning what they made lawful and unlawful of the affairs of the Jahiliyyah. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah held this. Al-'Askari said: "The address is to all the responsible people, meaning: do not name what has not come to you as prohibited or permitted from Allah and His Messenger as lawful or unlawful, so that you would be liars against Allah in your report that He made it lawful and unlawful." End of quote. This is the apparent meaning, since it is an address conjoined to another address, namely: ﴿فَكُلُوا إنَّما حَرَّمَ عَلَيْكم﴾ ("So eat... He has only forbidden to you..."), so it includes all the responsible people.

The *lam* in ﴿لِتَفْتَرُوا﴾ ("so that you fabricate") is the *lam* of cause that does not imply purpose, as al-Zamakhshari said. It is what is called the *lam al-'aqibah* (the *lam* of consequence or outcome), meaning that the fabrication was not their aim. It was said: "Fabrication was not their aim." The apparent meaning is that it is the *lam* of cause, and that they intended the fabrication, as they said: ﴿وجَدْنا عَلَيْها آباءَنا﴾ ("We found our fathers upon it") [al-A'raf: 28], "and Allah commanded us to it." This is not a stress upon what preceded, because it contains lying; for this causal clause contains a warning about the One against Whom they fabricated, who is Allah, exalted is He. Al-Wahidi said: "*Li-tafturu 'ala Allahi al-kadhiba* ('so that you fabricate the lie against Allah') is a substitute for His saying: *li-ma tasifu alsinatukum al-kadhiba* ('for what your tongues describe, the lie'), because their describing the lie is a fabrication against Allah. So he explained their describing by the fabrication against Allah." End of quote. This is on the assumption that *ma* is a masdar particle. But if *ma* means *alladhi*, then the *lam* in *li-ma* is not the *lam* of cause, and what indicates cause cannot be substituted for it. Rather, the *lam* is connected to *la taqulu* ("do not say"), in the manner of its connection in your saying: "Do not say, 'for what Allah made lawful, this is unlawful,'" meaning: do not name the lawful as unlawful; and as you say to Zayd, "'Amr," meaning: do not apply this name to Zayd.

The apparent meaning is that they truly fabricated against Allah, which is the apparent meaning of "fabrication" in the verses of the Qur'an. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is possible that it means that their legislation for their followers was practices that Allah does not approve, a fabrication against Him, because whoever legislates a matter, it is as if he said to his follower: 'This is the truth, and this is what Allah intends.'" Then Allah, exalted is He, informed about those who fabricate lies against Allah, that they will not succeed. *Al-falah* (الفلاح, success) is attaining what is hoped for. Sometimes it is in survival, as the poet said:

*"And the evening and the morning, with which there is no success"*

and sometimes it is in the success of endeavours, as 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras said:

*"Succeed with whatever you wish, for he who is weak is overcome, and the astute is sometimes deceived."*

The nominative of *mata'un* (مَتاعٌ, "enjoyment") is as the predicate of an omitted subject. Al-Zamakhshari estimated: "Their benefit in what they are upon of the deeds of the Jahiliyyah is a little benefit, and its punishment is great." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Their life in this world." Al-'Askari said: "*Mata'* here may be what they made lawful for themselves of what Allah forbade." Abu al-Baqa' said: "Their survival is a little enjoyment." Al-Hawfi said: "*Mata'un qalil* is a subject and predicate." End of quote. It is not valid except with an estimated genitive construction, meaning: "their enjoyment is little."

When He, exalted is He, explained what is lawful and unlawful for the people of Islam, He followed it with what He had specified for the Jews, referring to what was mentioned in Surat al-An'am. This shows that Surat al-An'am was revealed before this surah, since the referral is not valid except by that. *Min qabl* (مِن قَبْلُ, "before") is connected to *qasasna* ("We related"), which is the apparent meaning. It was said it is connected to *harramna* ("We prohibited"), and the omitted element in *min qabl* is estimated as: "before Our prohibition upon the people of your religion." The *su'* (السُّوءُ, "evil") here: Ibn 'Abbas said: "Polytheism before knowledge of Allah." End of quote. It is what harms its doer, such as disbelief and the disobedience of others.

The discussion of *li-alladhina 'amilu* ("for those who did") and what is connected to it has been mentioned in the similar verse: ﴿ثُمَّ إنَّ رَبَّكَ لِلَّذِينَ هاجَرُوا﴾ ("Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated") [al-Nahl: 110], so it is sufficient to not repeat it. Some people said: *bi-jahalatin* (بِجَهالَةٍ, "in ignorance") means: deliberately. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is not here the opposite of knowledge; rather it means transgressing the bounds and recklessness, from the saying: 'Or act foolishly, or be treated foolishly against me,' and the poet's saying:

*"Let no one act foolishly against us, lest we act more foolishly than the foolish."*

The word *jahl* in the sense of the opposite of knowledge often accompanies this, but there is excluded from it the one who acts deliberately, and that is the most common. Rarely is there found among sinners anyone who had no prior knowledge of the gravity of the sin he commits." End of summary. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Bi-jahalatin* is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: they did evil while ignorant, not knowing Allah and His punishment, or not reflecting on the outcome, due to the domination of desire over them." Sufyan said: "Its ignorance is that he delights in his desire and does not care about disobeying his Master." Al-Dahhak said: "By the deception of the present over the outcome." Al-'Askari said: "The meaning is not that He forgives those who do evil in ignorance and does not forgive those who do it without ignorance. Rather, what is meant is that everyone who repents, this is his way. He specified those who do evil in ignorance because most who commit sins commit them with little thought about the outcome, or when desire overcomes them, or in the ignorance of youth. So He mentioned the more common case, in accordance with the custom of the Arabs in such matters."

The demonstrative *dhalika* (ذلك, "that") refers to the doing of evil. *Aslahu* ("they reformed") means: they persisted in giving up that disobedience. It was said: *aslahu* means they believed and obeyed. The pronoun in *min ba'dihа* ("after it") returns to the verbal-masdars understood from the preceding verbs, meaning: after the doing of evil, the repentance, and the reform. It was said it returns to *al-jahalah* (ignorance). It was said it returns to *al-su'* (the evil), in the sense of disobedience.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "With the accusative, as an expression of reproach, or meaning 'the false words,' or it is the plural of *al-kidhab* from your saying *kadhaba kidhaban*, as Ibn Jinni mentioned." End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah held this. It is what is called the *lam al-'aqibah* (the *lam* of consequence or outcome), meaning that the fabrication was not their aim. It was said: "Fabrication was not their aim." The apparent meaning is that it is the *lam* of cause, and that they intended the fabrication, as they said: ﴿وجَدْنا عَلَيْها آباءَنا﴾ ("We found our fathers upon it") [al-A'raf: 28], "and Allah commanded us to it." This is not a stress upon what preceded, because it contains lying; for this causal clause contains a warning about the One against Whom they fabricated, who is Allah, exalted is He. Al-Wahidi said: "*Li-tafturu 'ala Allahi al-kadhiba* ('so that you fabricate the lie against Allah') is a substitute for His saying: *li-ma tasifu alsinatukum al-kadhiba* ('for what your tongues describe, the lie'), because their describing the lie is a fabrication against Allah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is possible that it means that their legislation for their followers was practices that Allah does not approve, a fabrication against Him, because whoever legislates a matter, it is as if he said to his follower: 'This is the truth, and this is what Allah intends.'" *"And the evening and the morning, with which there is no success"*

and sometimes it is in the success of endeavours, as 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras said:

*"Succeed with whatever you wish, for he who is weak is overcome, and the astute is sometimes deceived."*

Al-Zamakhshari estimated: "Their benefit in what they are upon of the deeds of the Jahiliyyah is a little benefit, and its punishment is great." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Their life in this world." Al-'Askari said: "*Mata'* here may be what they made lawful for themselves of what Allah forbade." Abu al-Baqa' said: "Their survival is a little enjoyment." Al-Hawfi said: "*Mata'un qalil* is a subject and predicate." End of quote. It is not valid except with an estimated genitive construction, meaning: "their enjoyment is little."

It was said it is connected to *harramna* ("We prohibited"), and the omitted element in *min qabl* is estimated as: "before Our prohibition upon the people of your religion." *"Let no one act foolishly against us, lest we act more foolishly than the foolish."*

The word *jahl* in the sense of the opposite of knowledge often accompanies this, but there is excluded from it the one who acts deliberately, and that is the most common. **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 16, verses 120–124:**

﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation, devoutly obedient to God, a hanif (one who turns away from all false religions to pure monotheism), and he was not among the polytheists.﴾ ﴿Grateful for His blessings. He chose him and guided him to a straight path.﴾ ﴿And We gave him good in this world, and indeed, in the Hereafter he is among the righteous.﴾ ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Abraham, a hanif, and he was not among the polytheists.﴾ ﴿The Sabbath was only prescribed for those who differed concerning it. Indeed, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which they used to differ.﴾

When God refuted the doctrines of the polytheists in this surah, including their claims of partners with God, their slander against the Prophet ﷺ's prophethood, their declaring lawful what He had made unlawful, and their declaring unlawful what He had made lawful, and since they took pride in their forefather Abraham (peace be upon him) while acknowledging the excellence of his way and the obligation to follow him, He mentioned him at the end of the surah and clarified his method and what he held to of the oneness of God, and his rejection of idols, so that this would move them to follow him. Also, since the mention of the Jews had preceded, this was to show the difference between Abraham's condition and theirs, and the condition of Quraysh.

Mujahid said: he was called "a nation" because he stood alone in faith during his time for a certain period. In al-Bukhari it is related that he said to Sarah: "There is no believer on the earth today except me and you."

The word ummah (nation, community) is a homonym covering several meanings, among them: a large group of people. It is also applied metaphorically to a man who is a model, or a king, or one who stands alone in his way apart from people, and so he was called "a nation." This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah. Ibn Abbas said: he possessed the good that a whole nation possessed. From this, al-Hasan ibn Hani' took his saying:

"It is not difficult for God
To gather the whole world into one person."

It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that he was "a teacher of good." He and Umar applied this term to Mu'adh, saying: "He was a nation, devoutly obedient."

Ibn al-Anbari said: this is like the saying of the Arabs: "So-and-so is a mercy," "a great scholar," and "a great genealogist," intending by the feminine form the extreme degree of the quality attributed to him.

It was also said: ummah means the imam (leader) who is followed, from the root amma–ya'ummu. The form is that of a passive noun, and the form fu'alah may be used for the plural. The explanation of qanit (devoutly obedient) and hanif has already been given.

﴿Grateful for His blessings﴾: It is related that he would not eat his midday meal except with a guest. One day he found no guest, so he delayed his meal. Then he saw a group of angels in human form, so he invited them to eat. They appeared to him as though they had leprosy, so he said: "Now your eating with me is obligatory," in gratitude to God for having granted him health and tested them.

﴿And We gave him good in this world﴾: Qatadah said: God made him beloved to all creation, so all the people of religions befriend him: the Jews, the Christians and the Muslims, and especially the unbelievers of Quraysh, for their pride is only in him. Then he saw a group of angels in human form, so he invited them to eat. They appeared to him as though they had leprosy, so he said: "Now your eating with me is obligatory," in gratitude to God for having granted him health and tested them.

It was also said: the good is the saying of one of us who prays: "as You blessed Abraham." Ibn Abbas said: it is the good remembrance. Al-Hasan said: prophethood. Mujahid said: a tongue of truth. Qatadah said: acceptance, and from him: God's exalting of him by mentioning him. It was also said: righteous offspring in old age. And it was said: wealth that he spends in good and righteousness.

Ibn Fawrak said: He commanded the superior to follow the inferior, since Abraham had been first to the correct saying and acting upon it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The "then" (thumma) in this verse ("Then We revealed to you") carries the meaning of exalting the status of the Messenger of God ﷺ and honoring his position, and indicating that the most noble of what the Friend of God, Abraham (peace be upon him), was given of honor, and the greatest of the blessings he received, was that the Messenger of God ﷺ would follow his religion, despite the great distance of this attribute in rank among the other attributes by which God praised him. ﴿Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom and fair admonition, and argue with them in the best manner. Indeed your Lord knows best who has strayed from His way, and He knows best those who are guided.﴾ ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of what you were punished with. But if you are patient, it is indeed better for the patient.﴾ ﴿And be patient, and your patience is not except through Allah. And do not grieve over them, and do not be in distress because of what they plot.﴾ ﴿Indeed Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good.﴾

Allah the Exalted commanded His Messenger ﷺ to call to the religion of Allah and His law gently, meaning that the one being called should hear his ruling in the form of speech that is correct, close to the self, and most beautifully placed.

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that "wisdom" (al-hikmah) is the Qur'an, and also from him that it is understanding (al-fiqh). It is said that it is prophethood. It is said that it is what prevents corruption from the signs of your Lord, those that encourage and those that warn. "Fair admonition" (al-mawʿizah al-hasanah) is the admonitions of the Qur'an, according to Ibn ʿAbbas, and also from him: the good manners that they recognize. Ibn Jarir said: they are the counted lessons in this surah. Ibn ʿIsa said: "wisdom" is what is known through the ranks of actions, and "fair admonition" is that desire be mixed with fear, and warning with glad tidings. Al-Zamakhshari said: "to the way of your Lord" means Islam; "with wisdom" means with a firm, correct statement, which is the clear proof that makes the truth evident and removes doubt; "and fair admonition" is that which is not hidden from them, that you advise them with it and intend what benefits them in it. It is permissible that it means the Qur'an, i.e., call them with the Book which is wisdom and fair admonition, and argue with them in the best way of argument, with gentleness and softness, without harshness or rebuke. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "fair admonition" is warning, promise of reward, and gentle treatment of the person by honoring and encouraging him, and placing him in the condition of one who accepts virtues, and the like.
